08_learning/00_start_here.title: Start Here: Learning Jainism from the Agamas
08_learning/00_start_here.content:
Start Here: Learning Jainism from the Agamas
This is a short learning path through the Jain Agamas, the canonical scriptures preserved from Bhagwan Mahavira’s teaching. Every verse here was read from the page scans of the jainaagam.org Gujarati editions in this vault. You get the original verse (Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, as printed), then its English translation, then a one-line note where it helps. Each verse links to the scan it came from, so you can always check the source.
The path (read in order)

Foundations: What Jainism Is: the Jinas, what dharma is, the goal (liberation) and the fourfold path to it, and why a human life is rare.
Reality: Soul, Matter and Karma: what exists, what the soul is, how karma binds and how it is shed.
Way of Life: Non-violence, Awareness, Simplicity: how this view of reality turns into daily living.
Conduct: Vows, Speech and Inner Discipline: the householder’s vows, right speech, and winning over anger, pride, deceit and greed.
Relationships: Forgiveness, Friendship, Respect: how to treat others: forgiveness, friendship toward all, respect for elders, and worth judged by conduct.

Next: the whole Uttaradhyayan
After the path, read the Uttaradhyayan chapter by chapter: 36 short modules, one per chapter. Then the Dashvaikalik, the Acharang and the Avashyak.
How to use it

Read one file at a time. Each one takes about 15 minutes and builds on the one before.
Read the verse aloud once, even if you don’t know Prakrit. Then read the English.
When a verse stays with you, open its scan and read the Gujarati commentary (vivechan) around it. That is where the depth is.
Each file ends with Go deeper, which names the chapters to read next.

08_learning/01_foundations.title: 1 · Foundations: What Jainism Is
08_learning/01_foundations.content:
1 · Foundations: What Jainism Is
A “Jain” is a follower of the Jinas, the “conquerors”: souls who defeated attachment and aversion inside themselves and then taught the way they had found. Jainism is that way, which is dharma. Its goal is liberation (moksha), freedom from the cycle of birth and death, and its path is right knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity. These first verses are the ones a Jain says every day, and they set out who we honour, what dharma is, why this human life matters, and where the path leads.
1. Whom a Jain bows to: the five supreme beings

णमो अरिहंताणं
णमो सिद्धाणं
णमो आयरियाणं
णमो उवज्झायाणं
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं

Homage to the Arihantas (the living Jinas, who have destroyed the inner enemies).
Homage to the Siddhas (the liberated souls).
Homage to the Acharyas (the leaders of the order).
Homage to the Upadhyayas (the teachers).
Homage to all the Sadhus (monks and nuns) in the world.
In short: The Navkar (Namaskar) mantra names no person or god. It bows to qualities: the soul that has conquered itself, the soul that is free, and those who walk and teach that path.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 1st Avashyak (Samayik), sutra 1 · scan (printed page 8)
2. The four auspicious, the four highest, the four refuges

चत्तारि मंगलं-अरिहंता मंगलं, सिद्धा मंगलं, साहू मंगलं, केवलि-पण्णतो
धम्मो मंगलं ।


चत्तारि लोगुत्तमा-अरिहंता लोगुत्तमा, सिद्धा लोगुत्तमा, साहू लोगुत्तमा,
केवलि-पण्णतो धम्मो लोगुत्तमो ।


चत्तारि सरणं पवज्जामि- अरिहंते सरणं पवज्जामि, सिद्धे सरणं पवज्जामि,
साहू सरणं पवज्जामि, केवलि पण्णत्तं धम्मं सरणं पवज्जामि ।

Four things are auspicious (mangal): the Arihantas, the Siddhas, the Sadhus, and the dharma taught by the all-knowing ones (kevalis).
Four things are the highest in the world (lokottama): the Arihantas, the Siddhas, the Sadhus, and the dharma taught by the kevalis.
I take refuge (sharan) in four: I take refuge in the Arihantas, in the Siddhas, in the Sadhus, and in the dharma taught by the kevalis.
In short: The commentary says coconuts, kumkum and rice cannot truly remove obstacles; only these four can. When life feels unsafe, this is where a Jain turns.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 4th Avashyak (Pratikraman), Path 2 “Mangalik”, sutras 1–3 · scan 1 (printed page 45) · scan 2 (p. 47) · scan 3 (p. 48)
3. What dharma is: non-violence, restraint, austerity

धम्मो मंगलमुक्किट्ठं, अहिंसा संजमो तवो, ।
देवा वि तं णमंसंति, जस्स धम्मे सया मणो ॥

Dharma is the highest good (mangal). It is non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapa). Even the gods bow to the one whose mind is always set on dharma.
In short: This is the first verse of the Dashvaikalik and the shortest definition of Jain dharma: not rituals, but not harming, holding yourself back, and disciplining yourself.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra 1.1 (Drumapushpika) · scan (printed page 3)
4. The four rare things

चत्तारि परमंगाणि, दुल्लहाणीह जंतुणो ।
माणुसत्तं सुई सद्धा, संजमम्मि य वीरियं ॥१॥

In this world, four supreme things are hard for a living being to obtain: human birth, hearing the dharma (shruti), faith in it (shraddha), and energy (virya) to practise restraint (samyama).
In short: Each step is rarer than the one before. Being born human is not enough; you also have to hear the truth, believe it, and then actually put effort into living it.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 3.1 (Chaturangiya) · scan (printed page 66)
5. Human birth is truly rare

दुल्लहे खलु माणुसे भवे, चिरकालेण वि सव्वपाणिणं ।
गाढा य विवाग कम्मुणो, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥४॥

A human birth is truly hard to obtain, even over a very long time, for all living beings, because the results (vipaka) of karma are dense and heavy. So, Gautama, do not be careless (pramada) even for a moment (samaya).
In short: Mahavira says this to his chief disciple, Gautama. If the one closest to him needed reminding, so do we: this life is the chance, and it should not be wasted.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 10.4 (Drumapatraka) · scan (printed page 183)
6. Life falls like a yellow leaf

दुमपत्तए पंडुयए जहा, णिवडइ राइगणाण अच्चए ।
एवं मणुयाण जीवियं, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥१॥

As a leaf of a tree turns yellow and falls when its nights and days are over, so is the life of human beings. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
In short: The rare human life is also short and uncertain. The right response is not fear but wakefulness: do what matters now.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 10.1 (Drumapatraka) · scan (printed page 182)
7. The path: knowledge, faith, conduct, austerity

णाणं च दंसणं चेव, चरित्तं च तवो तहा ।
एस मग्गो त्ति पण्णत्तो, जिणेहिं वरदंसीहिं ॥


णाणं च दंसणं चेव, चरित्तं च तवो तहा ।
एयं मग्गमणुपत्ता, जीवा गच्छंति सुग्गइं ॥

Knowledge (jnana), faith or right seeing (darshana), conduct (charitra) and austerity (tapa): this is the path, as taught by the Jinas, who see all things perfectly.
Knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity: souls who follow this path reach the good destination (sugati), liberation.
In short: Jainism is not only belief and not only rules. It is four things practised together, each one “right” (samyak).
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 28.2–3 (Mokshamarga-gati) · scan (printed page 135)
8. Why the order matters: faith → knowledge → conduct → liberation

णादंसणिस्स णाणं, णाणेण विणा ण हुंति चरणगुणा ।
अगुणिस्स णत्थि मोक्खो, णत्थि अमोक्खस्स णिव्वाणं ॥

Without right faith (samyag darshana) there is no right knowledge. Without right knowledge, the virtues of conduct do not arise. Without those virtues there is no freedom from karma (moksha). And without freedom from karma there is no final release (nirvana).
In short: The path is a chain. It starts with seeing things rightly: what the soul is, what karma is. Good behaviour that grows out of that understanding is what leads to freedom.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 28.30 (Mokshamarga-gati) · scan (printed page 150)
9. What each of the four does

णाणेण जाणइ भावे, दंसणेण य सद्दहे ।
चरित्तेण णिगिण्हाइ, तवेण परिसुज्झइ ॥

Through knowledge one knows the realities (bhava); through faith one believes in them; through conduct one stops (new karma from flowing in); through austerity one becomes purified (of karma already bound).
In short: Knowledge shows, faith accepts, conduct closes the door to new karma, and austerity clears out the old. You need all four.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 28.35 (Mokshamarga-gati) · scan (printed page 156)
10. The goal: the end of all suffering

खवित्ता पुव्वकम्माइं, संजमेण तवेण य ।
सव्वदुक्खपहीणट्ठा, पक्कमंति महेसिणो ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Having destroyed their past karmas through restraint and austerity, the great sages, seeking freedom from all suffering, go forth (to liberation). So I say.
In short: This is where the path ends: not in a heaven, but in the complete end of suffering, which the soul reaches by its own effort.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 28.36 (Mokshamarga-gati) · scan (printed page 157)
Go deeper

Uttaradhyayan ch. 28 (Mokshamarga-gati): the whole chapter (36 verses). It covers the six substances, the nine realities (tattvas), the ten kinds of interest in dharma (ruchi), the eight limbs of right faith, the five kinds of conduct and the twelve austerities.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 3 (Chaturangiya): the rest of the four rare things, including how souls wander through births (3.2–3.7) and why hearing dharma and faith are rarer still (3.8–3.10).
Uttaradhyayan ch. 10 (Drumapatraka): Mahavira’s 36 “do not be careless, Gautama” verses on how short life is and how hard each stage of birth is to gain.
Dashvaikalik ch. 1–4: from the definition of dharma (ch. 1) to the six kinds of living beings and the great vows (ch. 4). It is the first text traditionally taught to new monks.
Avashyak Sutra: the six daily duties (samayik, praise of the 24 Jinas, homage to the guru, pratikraman, kayotsarga, renunciation), the real source of a Jain’s daily prayers.

08_learning/02_reality.title: 2 · Reality: Soul, Matter and Karma
08_learning/02_reality.content:
2 · Reality: Soul, Matter and Karma
This part is about what Jainism says is real. There are souls (jiva), which know and feel, and non-soul things (ajiva) such as matter, space and time. Karma is fine matter that sticks to the soul when it acts with attachment and aversion, and it can be stopped and worn away. If you see things this way, your happiness and suffering are no longer someone else’s doing. They come from your own soul, and that makes you responsible for them and also able to change them.
1. The first question: who am I, where did I come from?

सुयं मे आउसं ! तेणं भगवया एवमक्खायं– इहमेगेसिं णो सण्णा भवइ । तं जहा– पुरत्थिमाओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि, दाहिणाओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि, पच्चत्थिमाओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि, उत्तराओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि, उड्ढाओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि, अहे दिसाओ वा आगओ अहमंसि, अण्णयरीओ दिसाओ वा अणुदिसाओ वा आगओ अहमंसि।
एवमेगेसिं णो णायं भवइ– अत्थि मे आया उववाइए, णत्थि मे आया उववाइए, के अहं आसी, के वा इओ चुओ इह पेच्चा भविस्सामि । ॥ १ ॥

O long-lived one, I have heard that the Blessed One (Bhagavan Mahavira) said this. Here, some beings have no awareness (sanna) of where they came from. They do not know whether they came from the east, the south, the west, the north, from above, from below, or from some other direction or in-between direction. So some do not know: “Does my soul (aya, atma) take birth again (uvavaie), or does it not? Who was I before? And when I leave this life, what will I become in the next?”
In short: The Agamas begin with you, not with God or the world. The first thing to ask is whether you are a soul that carries on from one life to the next.
Source: Acharang 1.1.1.1 (Shastra-parijna, first uddeshak) · scan (printed page 2)
2. Whoever knows the soul also accepts the world, karma and action

से जं पुण जाणेज्जा सहसम्मइयाए परवागरणेणं अण्णेसिं वा अंतिए सोच्चा, तं जहा– पुरत्थिमाओ वा दिसाओ आगओ अहमंसि जाव अण्णयरीओ दिसाओ वा अणुदिसाओ वा आगओ अहमंसि ।
एवमेगेसिं जं णायं भवइ अत्थि मे आया उववाइए, जो इमाओ दिसाओ वा अणुदिसाओ वा अणुसंचरइ, सव्वाओ दिसाओ सव्वाओ अणुदिसाओ जो आगओ अणुसंचरइ, सोऽहं । से आयावाई लोयावाई कम्मावाई किरियावाई । ॥ २ ॥

Some people do come to know it. One may know it by his own understanding (such as memory of a past life), from the explanation of the Tirthankara, or by hearing it from others: “I came from the east … or from some other direction or in-between direction.” So some know: “My soul takes birth again. The one who wanders through these directions and in-between directions, who has come from every direction and moves on through them, that one am I (so’ham).” Such a person believes in the soul (aya-vai), believes in the world (loya-vai), believes in karma (kamma-vai) and believes in action (kiriya-vai).
In short: These four go together. Once you accept a lasting soul, you also accept a real world it moves through, karma that carries it, and actions that create that karma.
Source: Acharang 1.1.1.2 · scan (printed page 4)
3. The world is living and non-living things

जीवा चेव अजीवा य, एस लोए वियाहिए ।
अजीव देसमागासे, अलोए से वियाहिए ॥ २ ॥

Living beings (jiva) and non-living things (ajiva): this is called the world (loka). The part of the non-living that is space (agasa) alone is called the non-world (aloka).
In short: Everything that exists is either soul or not soul. Past the edge of the inhabited world there is only empty space.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 36.2 (Jivajiva-vibhakti) · scan (printed page 366)
4. The six substances that make up the world

धम्मो अहम्मो आगासं, कालो पुग्गल जंतवो ।
एस लोगो त्ति पण्णत्तो, जिणेहिं वरदंसीहिं ॥ ७ ॥
धम्मो अहम्मो आगासं, दव्वं इक्किक्कमाहियं ।
अणंताणि य दव्वाणि, कालो पुग्गल जंतवो ॥ ८ ॥
गइ लक्खणो उ धम्मो, अहम्मो ठाण लक्खणो ।
भायणं सव्वदव्वाणं, णहं ओगाह लक्खणं ॥ ९ ॥

The medium of motion (dhamma), the medium of rest (adhamma), space (agasa), time (kala), matter (puggala, pudgala) and souls (jantu, jiva): the Jinas, who see everything, have taught that these make up the world.
Dhamma, adhamma and space are each said to be a single substance (davva, dravya). Time, matter and souls are infinite in number.
Dhamma’s mark is helping things move (gai). Adhamma’s mark is helping things stay still (thana). Space (naha) holds all substances, and its mark is giving them room (ogaha).
In short: Your soul is one of countless souls. It lives among matter in a shared space and time, and nothing in this list is a creator.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 28.7–9 (Mokshamarga-gati) · scan (printed page 138)
5. What marks the soul: knowing and experiencing

वत्तणा लक्खणो कालो, जीवो उवओग लक्खणो ।
णाणेणं दंसणेणं च, सुहेण य दुहेण य ॥ १० ॥
णाणं च दंसणं चेव, चरित्तं च तवो तहा ।
वीरियं उवओगो य, एयं जीवस्स लक्खणं ॥ ११ ॥

Time’s mark is change, the passing of things (vattana). The soul’s mark is awareness (uvaoga, upayoga). The soul is known through knowledge (nana), perception (damsana), happiness and suffering.
Knowledge, perception, conduct (caritta), austerity (tava), energy (viriya) and awareness: these are the marks of the soul.
In short: Only the soul knows and feels. Matter does neither. The book notes that no other substance has these qualities.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 28.10–11 · scan (printed page 139)
6. The nine realities (tattva)

जीवाजीवा य बंधो य, पुण्णं पावासवो तहा ।
संवरो णिज्जरा मोक्खो, संतेए तहिया णव ॥ १४ ॥

Soul (jiva), non-soul (ajiva), bondage (bandha), merit (punna, punya), demerit (pava, papa), inflow of karma (asava, ashrava), stopping the inflow (samvara), shedding karma (nijjara, nirjara) and liberation (mokkha, moksha): these nine are the true realities.
In short: This is the whole story in one verse. Soul meets matter, karma flows in and binds, then the inflow is stopped and old karma is shed until the soul is free. The next verse (28.15) says that believing in these nine is right faith (samyaktva).
Source: Uttaradhyayan 28.14 · scan (printed page 142)
7. The eight kinds of karma that keep the soul wandering

अट्ठ कम्माइं वोच्छामि, आणुपुव्विं जहक्कमं ।
जेहिं बद्धो अयं जीवो, संसारे परिवट्टइ ॥ १ ॥
णाणस्सावरणिज्जं, दंसणावरणं तहा ।
वेयणिज्जं तहा मोहं, आउकम्मं तहेव य ॥ २ ॥
णामकम्मं च गोयं च, अंतरायं तहेव य ।
एवमेयाइं कम्माइं, अट्ठेव उ समासओ ॥ ३ ॥

I will describe, one after another in their order, the eight karmas. Bound by them, this soul goes round and round in the cycle of birth and death (samsara).
They are: the karma that covers knowledge (nanavaraniya), the karma that covers perception (damsanavarana), the karma that brings pleasant and painful feeling (veyaniya), the karma that deludes (moha), the karma that fixes the lifespan (au-kamma), the karma that shapes the body and its features (nama), the karma that sets status by birth (goya, gotra), and the karma that blocks one’s powers (antaraya). In brief, these are the eight karmas.
In short: Karma covers and limits what the soul already has. It covers knowledge, perception, happiness and energy. It does not add anything new.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 33.1–3 (Karma-prakriti) · scan v.1 (printed page 313), scan v.2–3 (printed page 314)
8. Your own soul is your hell and your heaven

अप्पा णई वेयरणी, अप्पा मे कूडसामली ।
अप्पा कामदुहा धेणू, अप्पा मे णंदणं वणं ॥ ३६ ॥
अप्पा कत्ता विकत्ता य, दुहाण य सुहाण य ।
अप्पा मित्तममित्तं च, दुप्पट्ठिय-सुपट्ठिओ ॥ ३७ ॥

My own soul (appa) is the Vaitarani river and the Kutashalmali tree of hell. My own soul is the wish-fulfilling cow (kamadhenu) and the Nandana garden of heaven.
The soul is the maker and the unmaker of its own sufferings and joys. Set on a good path, the soul is its own friend. Set on a bad path, it is its own enemy.
In short: No god, fate or other person is finally to blame for your suffering or praised for your happiness. The monk Anathi says this to King Shrenik to explain what it really means to have no protector.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 20.36–37 (Mahanirgranthiya) · scan (printed page 425)
9. How karma is stopped and shed: the lake that dries up

जहा महातलायस्स, सण्णिरुद्धे जलागमे ।
उस्सिंचणाए तवणाए, कमेणं सोसणा भवे ॥ ५ ॥
एवं तु संजयस्सावि, पावकम्म णिरासवे ।
भवकोडी संचियं कम्मं, तवसा णिज्जरिज्जइ ॥ ६ ॥

A big lake dries up little by little once its inflowing channels are blocked, the water is drawn out and the sun heats it.
In the same way, once a restrained person (samjaya) has stopped the inflow of bad karma, the karma gathered over millions of births is shed (nijjarijjai) through austerity (tava).
In short: First close the channels (samvara), then dry out what is already there (nirjara). Austerity does little good while new karma keeps flowing in.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 30.5–6 (Tapomarga-gati) · scan (printed page 226)
10. Putting it together: the four tools that free the soul
You met Uttaradhyayan 28.35–36 in Foundations §9–10. Read it again now. Knowledge and faith show you the nine realities above, while conduct closes the inflow (samvara) and austerity burns off what is stored (nirjara).
Go deeper

Uttaradhyayan ch. 28 (Mokshamarga-gati), read in full. It covers the five kinds of knowledge, substance, quality and mode (dravya, guna, paryaya), the marks of matter (28.12–13), the kinds of right faith and conduct, and the twelve austerities.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 33 (Karma-prakriti). It lists the sub-types of each of the eight karmas and explains how long karma stays bound and how strongly it acts.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 36 (Jivajiva-vibhakti). This is the full map of non-soul (the kinds of matter, atoms and clusters) and of souls (liberated souls, siddha-shila, and the living beings of earth, water, fire, air and plants, mobile beings, hell-beings, animals, humans and gods).
Acharang Book 1, ch. 1 (Shastra-parijna). After the opening on the soul it goes through the six classes of living beings one by one, and it is the root of ahimsa.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 30 (Tapomarga-gati) and ch. 34 (Leshya). Chapter 30 describes the external and internal austerities that shed karma, and chapter 34 describes the soul’s “colourings” (leshya) that go with its thoughts.

08_learning/03_way_of_life.title: 3 · Way of Life: Non-violence, Awareness, Simplicity
08_learning/03_way_of_life.content:
3 · Way of Life: Non-violence, Awareness, Simplicity
Jainism is lived in small acts: how you walk, eat, speak, what you own and how you react when things go well or badly. The texts build this on one plain fact, that every living being wants to live and does not want pain, so harming none (ahimsa) is the centre of the path. Around it sit care and awareness in every act, not wasting a moment, holding things without clinging, staying even in gain and loss, and not insisting that only your view is right.
1. Every being loves its life

णत्थि कालस्स णागमो । सव्वे पाणा पियाउया सुहसाया दुक्खपडिकूला अप्पियवहा पियजीविणो जीविउकामा । सव्वेसिं जीवियं पियं ।

There is nothing death does not come to. All living beings (prana) love their life-span, want happiness and are averse to suffering; being killed is unwelcome to them; they hold life dear and wish to live. To all, life is dear.

सव्वे जीवा वि इच्छंति, जीविउं ण मरिज्जिउं ।
तम्हा पाणिवहं घोरं, णिग्गंथा वज्जयंति णं ॥

All beings wish to live, not to die. Therefore the unattached ones (nirgranthas) give up the terrible act of killing living beings.
In short: The ant, the cow and you want the same thing: to go on living without pain. That shared wish is the whole reason for non-violence.
Source: Acharang 1.2.3, sutra 4 · scan (printed page 66); Dashvaikalik 6.11 (numbered 6.10 in some editions) · scan (printed page 249)
2. Non-violence is the pure, eternal dharma

से बेमि– जे य अईया जे य पडुप्पण्णा जे य आगमिस्सा अरहंता भगवंतो ते सव्वे एवमाइक्खंति, एवं भासंति, एवं पण्णवेंति, एवं परूवेंति– सव्वे पाणा सव्वे भूया सव्वे जीवा सव्वे सत्ता ण हंतव्वा, ण अज्जावेयव्वा, ण परिघेयव्वा, ण परियावेयव्वा, ण उद्दवेयव्वा ।
एस धम्मे सुद्धे णिइए सासए समिच्च लोयं खेयण्णेहिं पवेइए । तं जहा– उट्ठिएसु वा अणुट्ठिएसु वा, उवट्ठिएसु वा, अणुवट्ठिएसु वा, उवरयदंडेसु वा अणुवरयदंडेसु वा सोवहिएसु वा अणुवहिएसु वा, संजोगरएसु वा असंजोगरएसु वा ।

I say: all the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the present and the future, say this, speak this, teach this and explain this: no living thing of any kind (prana, bhuta, jiva, sattva) should be killed, ordered about by force, enslaved, tormented or harassed. This is the dharma that is pure, permanent and eternal, made known by those who know, after seeing the world as it is. It was taught to all alike: to those ready to practise and those not, to those who have come forward and those who have not, to those who have laid down violence and those who have not, to those with possessions and those without, to those attached to relations and those free of them.
In short: This rule does not change with time or with who is listening. It covers not only killing, but also bullying, owning and tormenting others.
Source: Acharang 1.4.1, sutra 1 · scan (printed page 140)
3. The one you would harm is yourself

तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं हंतव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं अज्जावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परियावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परिघेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं उद्दवेयव्वं ति मण्णसि ।

The one you think should be killed is in truth you. The one you think should be ordered about is you. The one you think should be tormented is you. The one you think should be held captive is you. The one you think should be harassed is you.
In short: Before you hurt anyone, put yourself in their place; the pain is the same. Harm done to another also harms your own soul.
Source: Acharang 1.5.5, sutra 6 · scan (printed page 207)
4. The essence of all knowledge

एवं खु णाणिणो सारं, जं ण हिंसइ किंचणं ।
अहिंसा समयं चेव, एतावंतं वियाणिया ॥

This, truly, is the essence of the wise person’s knowledge: that he harms no one at all. Know just this much: non-violence, and the equality (samata) of all beings that follows from it.
In short: However much you learn, if it does not make you stop harming, it has missed the point.
Source: Sutrakritang 1.1.4.10 · scan (printed page 66)
5. First knowledge, then compassion

पढमं णाणं तओ दया, एवं चिट्ठइ सव्वसंजए ।
अण्णाणी किं काही, किं वा णाहीइ सेयपावगं ॥

First knowledge (jnana), then compassion (daya); this is how every self-restrained person stands firm. What can the ignorant do? How will he know what is good and what is harmful?
In short: Kindness needs understanding. You cannot protect life you do not know is there, so learn what is living and what harms it.
Source: Dashvaikalik 4.10 · scan (printed page 114)
6. Do everything with care

जयं चरे जयं चिट्ठे, जयमासे जयं सए ।
जयं भुंजंतो भासंतो पावकम्मं ण बंधइ ॥

Walk with care (yatana), stand with care, sit with care, lie down with care. One who eats with care and speaks with care does not bind harmful karma (papa karma).
In short: Life cannot stop moving, eating and talking, but each of these can be done awake and watchful. Care, not inactivity, is what keeps you from harm.
Source: Dashvaikalik 4.8 · scan (printed page 109)
7. Do not waste even a moment
This is the refrain of Uttaradhyayan ch.10, samayam goyama ma pamayae (“Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment”). The verse and its translation are in Foundations §6. In daily life it means bringing awareness to each act, as in §6 above.
8. Possessiveness is attachment, not things

ण सो परिग्गहो वुत्तो, णायपुत्तेण ताइणा ।
मुच्छा परिग्गहो वुत्तो, इइ वुत्तं महेसिणा ॥

The Protector, Jnataputra (Mahavira), did not call these things (the monk’s clothes, bowl and the like) possession (parigraha). Clinging (murchha) is possession: so said the great sage.
In short: What binds you is not the object but the grip you hold it with. Use what you need, and watch the clinging.
Source: Dashvaikalik 6.21 · scan (printed page 256)
9. Even in gain and loss, praise and blame

णिम्ममो णिरहंकारो, णिस्संगो चत्तगारवो ।
समो य सव्वभूएसु, तसेसु थावरेसु य ॥९०॥
लाभालाभे सुहे दुक्खे, जीविए मरणे तहा ।
समो णिंदा पसंसासु, तहा माणावमाणओ ॥९१॥

Free of “mine”, free of ego, unattached, having dropped pride, he was even-minded towards all beings, moving (trasa) and fixed (sthavara). In gain and loss, in pleasure and pain, in life and death, in blame and praise, in honour and insult, he stayed the same (sama).
In short: This describes the monk Mrigaputra, but it is a goal for anyone: let good and bad news reach you without throwing you off balance.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 19.90–91 · scan 90 (printed page 404) · scan 91 (printed page 405)
10. Do not praise only your own view

सयं सयं पसंसंता, गरहंता परं वइं ।
जे उ तत्थ विउस्संति, संसारं ते विउस्सिया ॥

Praising each their own view and condemning the words of others, those who show off their cleverness in this stay tightly bound to the cycle of birth and death (samsara).
In short: Arguing to win, and running down others’ views, is itself a bond. Jain many-sidedness (anekantavada) begins with this humility: your view may be only part of the truth.
Source: Sutrakritang 1.1.2.23 · scan (printed page 35)
Go deeper

Dashvaikalik ch. 4 (Shadjivanika): the six kinds of living beings, the five great vows and the rules of care in daily acts; the full set of verses 4.1–4.11 on careless and careful living.
Dashvaikalik ch. 6 (Mahachar Katha): the eighteen points of conduct, including non-violence, truth, not stealing, celibacy, non-possession and not eating at night.
Acharang book 1, ch. 1 (Shastra Parijna) and ch. 4 (Samyaktva): why earth, water, fire, air and plants are living, and how non-violence follows from right faith.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 10 (Drumapatrak): the whole “do not be careless, Gautama” chapter, on the rarity of human birth.
Uttaradhyayan ch. 19 (Mrigaputriya): a prince who gives up everything; ends with the portrait of an even-minded monk.

08_learning/04_conduct.title: 4 · Conduct: Vows, Speech and Inner Discipline
08_learning/04_conduct.content:
4 · Conduct: Vows, Speech and Inner Discipline
Right conduct (samyak charitra) is the third jewel: knowing and believing are not enough until they change how you act, speak and react. The Agamas give a householder (shravak) a practical, graded path of twelve vows, the same path the monk walks in full through the five great vows. Underneath every vow sits the real work: careful speech and the conquest of anger, pride, deceit and greed, which the texts call conquering yourself.
1. A householder can take vows without leaving home

१५ … णो खलु अहं तहा संचाएमि मुंडे भवित्ता अगाराओ अणगारियं पव्वइत्तए । अहं णं देवाणुप्पियाणं अंतिए पंचाणुव्वइयं सत्त-सिक्खावइयं दुवालसविहं गिहिधम्मं पडिवज्जिस्सामि । अहासुहं देवाणुप्पिया! मा पडिबंधं करेह।

(Ananda, a rich householder of Vanijyagram, says to Mahavira:) ”…I am not able, as those kings and others are, to shave my head and go forth from home into homelessness. In your presence, beloved of the gods, I will take up the twelve-fold householder’s dharma: five small vows (anuvrata) and seven training vows (shikshavrata).” Mahavira replies: “Do as brings you happiness, beloved of the gods. Do not delay.”
In short: Mahavira did not demand that everyone become a monk. A layperson who keeps limited vows is a real follower of the path.
Source: Upasakdashang 1, sutra 15 · scan (printed page 15)
2. The first three small vows: no gross violence, lying or stealing

१६ तए णं से आणंदे गाहावई समणस्स भगवओ महावीरस्स अंतिए तप्पढमयाए थूलगं पाणाइवायं पच्चक्खाइ, जावज्जीवाए दुविहं तिविहेणं, ण करेमि, ण कारवेमि, मणसा वयसा कायसा ।
१७ तयाणंतरं च णं थूलगं मुसावायं पच्चक्खाइ, जावज्जीवाए दुविहं तिविहेणं ण करेमि ण कारवेमि, मणसा वयसा कायसा।
१८ तयाणंतरं च णं थूलगं अदिण्णादाणं पच्चक्खाइ, जावज्जीवाए दुविहं तिविहेणं, ण करेमि, ण कारवेमि, मणसा वयसा कायसा ।


Then Ananda the householder, in the presence of Shramana Bhagavan Mahavira, first renounced gross harming of living beings (sthula pranatipata): for life, in two ways and three modes — “I will not do it and I will not have it done, by mind, by speech, by body.”
After that he renounced gross false speech (sthula mrishavada), for life, in the same two ways and three modes.
After that he renounced gross taking of what is not given (sthula adattadana), for life, in the same two ways and three modes.

In short: “Gross” (thulaga) means the deliberate, avoidable harm, lie or theft; the unavoidable harm of running a home and business is not yet covered. The householder gives up doing and causing; approving is left open, which the monk later closes.
Source: Upasakdashang 1, sutras 16-18 · scan (printed page 16)
3. The fourth and fifth small vows: limits on sex and on wealth

१९ तयाणंतरं च णं सदारसंतोसिए परिमाणं करेइ, णण्णत्थ एक्काए सिवाणंदाए भारियाए, अवसेसं सव्वं मेहुणविहिं पच्चक्खामि ।
२० तयाणंतरं च णं इच्छा परिमाणं करेमाणे हिरण्ण-सुवण्णविहि-परिमाणं करेइ, णण्णत्थ चउहिं हिरण्णकोडीहिं णिहाणपउत्ताहिं, चउहिं वुड्ढिपउत्ताहिं, चउहिं पवित्थर-पउत्ताहिं, अवसेसं सव्वं हिरण्णसुवण्णविहिं पच्चक्खामि ।


After that he set a limit of contentment with his own wife (svadara-santosha): “Apart from my one wife Sivananda, I renounce all other sexual activity.”
After that, limiting his desires (iccha-parimana), he set a limit on gold and silver: “Apart from four crore of gold coins kept as treasure, four crore put out in business, and four crore in household goods, I renounce all other gold and silver.”

In short: The fifth vow is not poverty but a ceiling you choose and then do not cross. Ananda goes on (sutras 21-24) to cap his cattle at four herds of ten thousand, his land at 500 ploughs, and his carts and vehicles at fixed numbers.
Source: Upasakdashang 1, sutras 19-20 · scan (printed page 17) · scan (printed page 19)
4. The supporting vows: limit what you consume, cut harm with no purpose

२५ तयाणंतरं च णं उवभोग-परिभोगविहिं पच्चक्खाएमाणे, उल्लणियाविहि परिमाणं करेइ । णण्णत्थ एगाए गंधकासाईए, अवसेसं सव्वं उल्लणियाविहिं पच्चक्खामि ।
४६ तयाणंतरं च णं चउव्विहं अणट्ठादंडं पच्चक्खाइ, तं जहा- अवज्झाणायरियं पमायायरियं, हिंसप्पयाणं, पावकम्मोवएसे ।


After that, renouncing (beyond a limit) things of single and repeated use (upabhoga-paribhoga), he set a limit on towels: “Apart from one fragrant, reddish towel, I renounce all other towels.”
After that he renounced the four kinds of purposeless harm (anartha-danda): brooding on ill (apadhyana), careless conduct (pramada), handing out the means of violence (himsa-pradana), and advising others to do harmful deeds (papa-karmopadesha).

In short: Sutra 25 opens a list of 26 daily items (tooth-sticks, fruit, oil, food, clothes, ornaments…) each given a limit. Anartha-danda is harm you get nothing from: idle worry and spite, waste, lending weapons, egging others on.
Source: Upasakdashang 1, sutras 25, 46 · scan (printed page 21) · scan (printed page 26)
5. Samayika: forty-eight minutes of equanimity, and how it goes wrong

५६ तयाणंतरं च णं सामाइयस्स समणोवासएणं पंच अइयारा [पेयाला] जाणियव्वा, ण समायरियव्वा, तं जहा- मणदुप्पणिहाणे, वयदुप्पणिहाणे, कायदुप्पणिहाणे, सामाइयस्स सइअकरणया, सामाइयस्स अणवट्ठियस्स करणया ।

After that, the lay follower (shramanopasaka) should know, and not commit, the five main faults (atichara) of the samayika vow: misdirecting the mind, misdirecting speech, misdirecting the body, forgetting to do samayika (or forgetting one is in it), and doing samayika irregularly or carelessly.
In short: Samayika is a set period of sitting in equanimity, giving up all harmful activity. The faults show what it really asks: not just sitting still, but keeping mind and tongue still too.
Source: Upasakdashang 1, sutra 56 · scan (printed page 39)
The twelve vows of a householder, in short (Ananda’s text counts them as 5 small vows + 7 training vows; later tradition splits the 7 into 3 gunavratas and 4 shikshavratas):

Ahimsa anuvrata - no deliberate harm to moving beings.
Satya anuvrata - no gross lies.
Achaurya anuvrata - no gross theft.
Svadara-santosha - sexual relations only with one’s own spouse.
Iccha-parimana - a fixed limit on wealth and possessions.
Dig-vrata - a limit on the distance one travels or does business in each direction.
Upabhoga-paribhoga-parimana - a limit on daily consumables and durables (Ananda’s 26 items).
Anartha-danda-viramana - giving up the four kinds of purposeless harm.
Samayika - regular periods of equanimity.
Deshavakashika - a further, short-term narrowing of area and activity (for a day or night).
Paushadhopavasa - a full day of fasting and living like a monk.
Atithi-samvibhaga - sharing food and necessities with monks and nuns.

6. The monk’s first great vow: the same vow, with no exceptions

७ पढमे भंते ! महव्वए पाणाइवायाओ वेरमणं; सव्वं भंते ! पाणाइवायं पच्चक्खामि। से सुहुमं वा बायरं वा तसं वा थावरं वा, णेव सयं पाणे अइवाएज्जा, णेवण्णेहिं पाणे अइवायावेज्जा, पाणे अइवायंते वि अण्णे ण समणुजाणेज्जा जावज्जीवाए, तिविहं तिविहेणं मणेणं वायाए काएणं ण करेमि ण कारवेमि करंतं पि अण्णं ण समणुजाणामि, तस्स भंते । पडिक्कमामि णिंदामि गरिहामि अप्पाणं वोसिरामि । पढमे भंते ! महव्वए उवट्ठिओमि सव्वाओ पाणाइवायाओ वेरमणं ।

“The first great vow (mahavrata), Bhante, is abstaining from harming living beings. Bhante, I renounce all harming of life. Whether a being is subtle or gross, moving or stationary, I will not harm it myself, I will not have others harm it, and I will not approve of others who harm it — for life, in three ways and three modes: by mind, speech and body I will not do it, not cause it, and not approve another doing it. Of that, Bhante, I step back (pratikramana), I censure it, I condemn it, and I give up that self. Bhante, I stand in the first great vow: abstaining from all harming of life.”
In short: Compare with section 2: the householder renounces gross harm in two ways; the monk renounces all harm, including to the smallest and to plants and earth-beings, in three ways. The same formula then repeats for the second to fifth great vows (all lying, all taking what is not given, all sexual activity, all possessiveness), and a sixth, not eating at night. The small vows are the great vows scaled to a life in the world.
Source: Dashvaikalik 4, sutra 7 · scan (printed page 77)
7. What makes speech right

३ असच्चमोसं सच्चं च, अणवज्जमकक्कसं ।
समुप्पेहमसंदिद्धं, गिरं भासिज्ज पण्णवं ॥

A wise person should speak what is true, or what is neither true nor false (plain practical speech), and that speech should be free of harm (anavadya), not harsh, thought over beforehand, and free of doubt or ambiguity.
In short: Four tests before speaking: does it harm, is it harsh, have I thought it through, is it clear?
Source: Dashvaikalik 7.3 · scan (printed page 292)
8. True but hurtful words are also wrong

११ तहेव फरुसा भासा, गुरुभूओवघाइणी ।
सच्चा वि सा ण वत्तव्वा, जओ पावस्स आगमो ॥
१२ तहेव काणं काणे त्ति, पंडगं पंडगे त्ति वा ।
वाहियं वावि रोगि त्ति, तेणं चोरे त्ति णो वए ॥


Likewise, harsh speech that deeply wounds living beings should not be spoken even if it is true, because it brings in sin (papa).
Likewise, do not call a one-eyed man “one-eyed”, a eunuch “eunuch”, a sick man “diseased”, or a thief “thief”.

In short: Truth is necessary but not sufficient. Labels that wound, even accurate ones, are a form of violence.
Source: Dashvaikalik 7.11-12 · scan (printed page 298)
9. The four passions (kashaya) and what they destroy

३७ कोहं माणं च मायं च, लोभं च पाववड्ढणं ।
वमे चत्तारि दोसे उ, इच्छंतो हियमप्पणो ॥
३८ कोहो पीइं पणासेइ, माणो विणय णासणो ।
माया मित्ताणि णासेइ, लोहो सव्व विणासणो ॥


Anger (krodha), pride (mana), deceit (maya) and greed (lobha) increase sin. One who wants his own good should vomit out these four faults.
Anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility (vinaya), deceit destroys friendships, greed destroys everything.

In short: Each passion has a specific casualty in daily life. Notice which relationship or quality is being eaten away and you know which passion is at work.
Source: Dashvaikalik 8.37-38 · scan (printed page 354)
10. The antidote to each passion

३९ उवसमेण हणे कोहं, माणं मद्दवया जिणे ।
मायं च अज्जवभावेण, लोभं संतोसओ जिणे ॥
४० कोहो य माणो य अणिग्गहीया, माया य लोभो य पवड्ढमाणा ।
चत्तारि एए कसिणा कसाया, सिंचंति मूलाइं पुणब्भवस्स ॥


Destroy anger by calm (upashama), conquer pride by gentleness (mardava), deceit by straightforwardness (arjava), and greed by contentment (santosha).
Anger and pride left unchecked, deceit and greed left growing — these four black passions water the roots of rebirth.

In short: The vows control behaviour; this verse works on the source. Practise the opposite quality, not just suppression.
Source: Dashvaikalik 8.39-40 · scan (printed page 355)
11. Master yourself first

१५ अप्पा चेव दमेयव्वो, अप्पा हु खलु दुद्दमो ।
अप्पा दंतो सुही होइ, अस्सिं लोए परत्थ य ॥१५॥

It is the self (mind and senses) that must be tamed, for the self is truly hard to tame. One whose self is tamed is happy in this world and in the next.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 1.15 · scan (printed page 11)
12. The greatest victory

३४ जो सहस्सं सहस्साणं, संगामे दुज्जए जिणे ।
एगं जिणेज्ज अप्पाणं, एस से परमो जओ ॥३४॥
३५ अप्पाणमेव जुज्झाहि, किं ते जुज्झेण बज्झओ ।
अप्पाणमेवमप्पाणं, जिणित्ता सुहमेहए ॥३५॥
३६ पंचिंदियाणि कोहं, माणं मायं तहेव लोहं च ।
दुज्जयं चेव अप्पाणं, सव्वं अप्पे जिए जियं ॥३६॥

(Nami, a king who has renounced his kingdom, answers Indra, who urges him to first conquer the kings who have not bowed to him:)
34. One may conquer a thousand thousand (ten lakh) warriors in a hard battle; but if he conquers one, his own self, that is his supreme victory.
35. Fight with yourself; what use is fighting outside? By conquering the self through the self one gains happiness.
36. The five senses, anger, pride, deceit and greed — and the self, so hard to conquer: when the self is conquered, all of these are conquered.
In short: This is where the whole chapter points. The vows, the careful speech and the four antidotes are all ways of fighting this one battle.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 9.34-36 · scan (printed page 168) · scan (printed page 169)
Go deeper

Upasakdashang ch.1 (whole chapter): Ananda’s full list of 26 consumption limits, the five faults (atichara) of each of the twelve vows, the fifteen forbidden trades (karmadana), and the eleven lay stages (pratima).
Upasakdashang ch.2-10: nine more householders who kept the same vows under trial; Kamadeva (ch.2) is the best known.
Dashvaikalik ch.4: all six great vows of a monk and the care for six classes of living beings (chha jivanikaya).
Dashvaikalik ch.7 (Suvakya-shuddhi): the full guide to speech, including what not to say about people, nature and the future.
Uttaradhyayan ch.9 (Nami-pravrajya) and ch.1 (Vinaya-shruta): the dialogue on inner versus outer conquest, and humility and self-control in a student.

08_learning/05_relationships.title: 5 · Relationships: Forgiveness, Friendship, Respect
08_learning/05_relationships.content:
5 · Relationships: Forgiveness, Friendship, Respect
The Agamas say a great deal about how to live with others, not only how to live with yourself. Their teaching runs in one line: hold friendship toward every living being, ask and give forgiveness without holding anything back, be humble (vinaya) toward those who teach you, speak with care, and judge people by what they do rather than the family they were born into. Alongside this they say plainly that family and wealth, however dear, cannot carry your karma for you. This is the side of Jainism you use every day, at home, at work and on Samvatsari.
1. Hold friendship toward all beings

समिक्ख पंडिए तम्हा, पास जाइपहे बहू ।
अप्पणा सच्चमेसिज्जा, मेत्तिं भूएहिं कप्पए ॥२॥

Therefore the wise person, having looked at the many paths of birth (the countless forms in which beings are born and die) and thought about them, should seek the truth by his own self, and should hold friendship (maitri) toward all beings.
In short: Every creature is on the same round of birth and death as you are. Seeing that clearly leads to friendship with all of them, not just the people you like.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 6.2 · scan (printed page 114)
2. Ask forgiveness even for harm you did without noticing

इच्छामि पडिक्कमिउं इरियावहियाए विराहणाए गमणागमणे पाणक्कमणे बीयक्कमणे हरियक्कमणे ओसा उत्तिंग पणग दग मट्टी मक्कडा संताणा संकमणे जे मे जीवा विराहिया एगिंदिया बेइंदिया तेइंदिया चउरिंदिया पंचिंदिया अभिहया वत्तिया लेसिया संघाइया संघट्टिया परियाविया किलामिया उद्दविया ठाणाओठाणं संक्कामिया जीवियाओ ववरोविया तस्स मिच्छामि दुक्कडम् ।

I wish to turn back (pratikraman) from the harm done while walking, in going and coming: in treading on living creatures, on seeds, on green plants, on dew, ant-holes, fungus, living water and living earth, and spiders’ webs. Whatever beings I have harmed, with one sense, two, three, four or five senses: if I have struck them, covered them with dust, crushed them against the ground, heaped them together, touched them painfully, distressed them, wearied them, frightened them, moved them from one place to another, or taken their life, may that wrong of mine be fruitless (micchami dukkadam).
In short: “Micchami dukkadam” is not a greeting; it is a real apology, and it is owed even to an ant you stepped on without seeing. If you apologise for that much, apologising to people is easy.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, Avashyak 4, Path 4 (Iriyavahiya / Gamanagaman Pratikraman Sutra) · scan (printed page 54)
3. Forgive everyone, and ask everyone to forgive you

खामेमि सव्वे जीवा, सव्वे जीवा वि खमंतु मे ।
मित्तीमे सव्व भूएसू, वेरं मज्झं ण केणइ ॥१॥

I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship toward all beings; I have enmity toward none.
In short: Forgiveness goes both ways: you give it and you ask for it, at the same time and to everyone. The commentary says that only when enmity is gone from the heart can a person move toward freedom from attachment.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, Avashyak 4, Path 10 (Kshamapana Sutra) v.1 · scan (printed page 126)
4. What asking forgiveness does to you

खमावणयाए णं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ?
खमावणयाए णं पल्हायणभावं जणयइ । पल्हायण भावमुवगए य सव्वपाण-भूय-जीव- सत्तेसु मित्तीभावमुप्पाएइ । मित्तीभावमुवगए यावि जीवे भावविसोहिं काऊण णिब्भए भवइ ।

“Lord, what does the soul gain by asking forgiveness (kshamapana)?” “By asking forgiveness the soul gains gladness of mind. With a glad mind it develops friendship toward all living things, beings, souls and creatures. Having reached friendship, it purifies its feelings and becomes free of fear.”
In short: The commentary explains the last step: once you have asked forgiveness and given it, nobody is your enemy, so there is no one left to fear. Saying sorry is good for the person who says it.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 29.19 · scan (printed page 179)
5. Humility is the root of dharma

मूलाउ खंधप्पभवो दुमस्स, खंधाउ पच्छा समुवेंति साहा ।
साहप्पसाहा विरुहंति पत्ता, तओ सि पुप्फं च फलं रसो य ॥
एवं धम्मस्स विणओ, मूलं परमो से मोक्खो ।
जेण कित्तिं सुयं सिग्घं, णीसेसं चाभिगच्छइ ॥

From the root of a tree grows the trunk; from the trunk come the branches; from the branches the smaller branches, and then the leaves; after that come its flowers, its fruit and its juice. In the same way, humility (vinaya) is the root of dharma, and its highest fruit is liberation (moksha). Through vinaya a person gains good name, learning (shruta), praise, and everything else in full.
In short: Vinaya means humility, respect and readiness to be taught. Everything else in religious life grows out of it; without it nothing takes root.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra 9.2.1–2 · scan (printed page 399)
6. What a humble student looks like

आणाणिद्देसकरे, गुरुणमुववायकारए ।
इंगियागारसंपण्णे, से विणीए त्ति वुच्चइ ॥२॥

One who carries out the instructions and directions of his teachers (guru), stays close to them, and understands their signs and moods, is called humble (vinita).
In short: Respect is shown by listening, staying near and paying attention, not just by bowing. The same applies to parents and elders.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 1.2 · scan (printed page 3)
7. When an elder is upset with you

आयरियं कुवियं णच्चा, पत्तिएण पसायए ।
विज्झवेज्ज पंजलिउडो, वएज्ज ण पुणो त्ति य ॥४१॥

Knowing that the teacher (acharya) is angry, the student should win back his good will with loving words, calm him with folded hands, and say: “I will not do it again.”
In short: Do not argue back or sulk. Own your part, apologise in gentle words, and promise to do better; that is forgiveness put into practice.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 1.41 · scan (printed page 24)
8. Speak only when needed, never falsely, and take hard words well

णापुट्ठो वागरे किंचि, पुट्ठो वा णालियं वए ।
कोहं असच्चं कुव्विज्जा, धारिज्जा पियमप्पियं ॥१४॥

Do not say anything unless asked; when asked, do not tell a lie. If anger arises, make it fruitless (let it go before it acts). Take both pleasant and unpleasant words (from the teacher) as if they were pleasant.
In short: The commentary tells of a mother whose son had been killed; when the killer begged for refuge, she told her other son to let him go, because anger does not have to be acted on. Hard words from people who mean you well are a gift, not an insult.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 1.14 · scan (printed page 10)
9. Even the truth must not be used to wound
Dashvaikalik 7.11–12 teaches that true words spoken to hurt (calling someone “one-eyed”, “diseased” or “thief”) are still wrong speech. The verses are in Conduct §8.
10. People are worth what they do, not what they are born as

समयाए समणो होइ, बंभचेरेण बंभणो ।
णाणेण य मुणी होइ, तवेण होइ तावसो ॥
कम्मुणा बंभणो होइ, कम्मुणा होइ खत्तिओ ।
वइस्सो कम्मुणा होइ, सुद्दो हवइ कम्मुणा ॥

One becomes a shramana by equanimity (samata), a brahmin by celibacy (brahmacharya), a muni by knowledge, and an ascetic (tapasa) by austerity (tapa). One becomes a brahmin by one’s actions, a kshatriya by one’s actions, a vaishya by one’s actions, and a shudra by one’s actions.
In short: The verse just before says a shaven head, chanting “Om”, living in a forest or wearing bark does not make anyone holy. Judge people, including yourself, by conduct, never by caste, family or outward signs. The commentary adds that all humans are equal and form one kind.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 25.32–33 · scan 25.32 (printed page 91) · scan 25.33 (printed page 92)
11. Love your family, but know they cannot carry your karma

माया पिया ण्हुसा भाया, भज्जा पुत्ता य ओरसा ।
णालं ते तव ताणाय, लुप्पंतस्स सकम्मुणा ॥३॥
ण तस्स दुक्खं विभयंति णाइओ, ण मित्तवग्गा ण सुया ण बंधवा।
इक्को सयं पच्चणुहोइ दुक्खं, कत्तारमेव अणुजाइ कम्मं ॥२३॥

Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and your own sons: none of them can protect you when you suffer from your own karma. Kinsmen cannot share his suffering, nor can friends, sons or relatives. He alone experiences his suffering himself; karma follows only the one who did it.
In short: This is not a call to love family less. It warns against doing wrong “for the family” or for wealth, because the results of that wrong will be yours alone.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra 6.3 · scan (printed page 114); Uttaradhyayan Sutra 13.23 · scan (printed page 251)
Go deeper

Avashyak Sutra, Avashyak 4 (Pratikraman): the full daily confession, from Iriyavahiya to the Kshamapana Sutra. This is the text behind Samvatsari and “micchami dukkadam”.
Uttaradhyayan ch.1 (Vinaya-shruta): verses on the humble and the arrogant student, how to sit, speak, ask questions and take correction.
Dashvaikalik ch.9 (Vinaya-samadhi, 4 sections) for the fruits of humility, and ch.7 (Suvakya-shuddhi) for a full guide to truthful, gentle speech.
Uttaradhyayan ch.25 (Yajniya) and ch.12 (Harikeshiya): two stories of a monk who meets brahmins proud of their birth, and what makes a person truly worthy.
Uttaradhyayan ch.13 (Chitta-Sambhutiya) and ch.14 (Ishukariya): two brothers, and a priest’s family, deciding what family, pleasure and wealth are really worth.
