09_modules/00_acharang_index.title: Acharang Sutra: All Chapters
09_modules/00_acharang_index.content:
Acharang Sutra: All Chapters
The Acharang is the first of the Angas (the book says both Shvetambara and Digambara traditions put it first, since a code of conduct is the first need of the Sangha): the conduct (achara) of the monk, taught mostly in short prose sutras. Book 1 (nine chapters, the seventh lost) is about non-violence toward all six kinds of life and waking up inside; Book 2 gives the practical rules for food, lodging, walking, speech, clothes and bowls, and ends with Mahavira’s life, the five great vows and their bhavanas. Each module gives the chapter’s point in one line, what it teaches in the chapter’s own order, and key passages in Prakrit with plain English, checked against the scans. References read chapter.section.sutra.
New here? Start with Book 1 chapters 1 (knowing the weapon), 2 (conquest of the world), 4 (right faith) and 9 (Mahavira’s own practice), then Book 2 chapter 15 (the five great vows).
Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha)























































#ChapterIn one line1.1Knowing the Weapon Shastra Parijna (શસ્ત્ર પરિજ્ઞા)first know that you are a soul that has come from somewhere and goes on, then see that earth, water, fire, plants, moving creatures and air are all alive and feel pain as you do, and give up every “weapon” against them, by your own hand, through others, and by approval.1.2Conquest of the World Lok Vijay (લોક વિજય)the “world” to conquer is inside you, the sense of “mine” over family, wealth and pleasures; none of it can protect you from old age, illness or death, so use this short human life now, while the senses still work, to live without possessiveness.1.3Cold and Heat Shitoshniya (શીતોષ્ણીય)stay awake: bear the “cold” of pleasant things and the “heat” of painful things with the same even mind, cast out anger, pride, deceit and greed, and be your own friend, because only a self that restrains itself is freed from suffering.1.4Right Faith Samyaktva (સમ્યક્ત્વ)all the Tirthankaras of past, present and future teach one pure, eternal dharma, that no living being is to be harmed; hold to it with true understanding, never give it up, and burn away karma with detachment from the body.1.5Essence of the World Lokasara (લોકસાર)what is truly worth having in this world is not pleasure or possessions but dharma, knowledge, restraint and finally liberation, so fight the enemy within, live close to the guru, trust the Jina’s word, and see every other being as yourself.1.6Shaking Off Dhuta (ધૂત)as dust is shaken off a cloth, the monk shakes off karma by leaving home and family, owning almost nothing, bearing every hardship calmly, holding to the Jina’s command, and at the end letting go of the body itself.1.7Great Comprehension Mahaparijna (મહાપરિજ્ઞા)this seventh chapter is lost; the book gives only its name, what it is believed to have taught (seeing clearly the faults born of delusion and giving them up), and why it was left out when the scriptures were written down.1.8Liberation Vimoksha (વિમોક્ષ)a monk frees himself step by step, from loose company, from food and lodging made for him, from clothes, from the help of others and from the taste of food, until, when the body can no longer carry restraint, he gives it up calmly in one of three ways of dying in equanimity, wanting neither life nor death.1.9Mahavira's Practice Upadhana-shruta (ઉપધાનશ્રુત)the chapter shows that everything the earlier chapters ask of a monk, Lord Mahavira himself lived out, wandering without clothes or shelter, silent, beaten and set upon by dogs, fasting and meditating for some twelve and a half years without a single lapse into negligence.
Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha)
Book 2’s sixteen chapters are grouped into nine modules: 5 and 6 together, and the seven short septets (8–14) together.























































#ChapterIn one line2.1Seeking Alms Pindaishana (પિંડૈષણા)a monk or nun accepts only food and water that is free of life and free of faults, taken without greed, deceit or harm to anyone, and eats it with equanimity, because how the food is sought decides whether the restraint it feeds stays pure.2.2Seeking Lodging Shayyaishana (શય્યૈષણા)just as a monk seeks faultless food, he seeks a faultless place to stay, one not built or repaired for him, free of living creatures and of householders’ life, asked for with permission and returned with care, and he stays in it with equanimity whether it is good or bad.2.3Careful Walking Irya (ઈર્યા)a monk or nun walks only to serve restraint, stays in one place through the rains and wanders the rest of the year, watches the ground so that no living being is hurt, and meets rivers, boatmen, soldiers, hunters, wild animals and robbers with silence, care and an unshaken calm.2.4Kinds of Speech Bhashajata (ભાષાજાત)a monk or nun speaks only after thinking, free of anger, pride, deceit and greed, using only true or ordinary speech that is gentle and harms no being: no rash predictions, no insults, no praise that encourages violence, and no words that point a hunter or a woodcutter to his prey.2.5Clothes and Bowls Vastraishana and Patraishana (વસ્ત્રૈષણા, પાત્રૈષણા)a monk or nun keeps only a few plain clothes and simple bowls of gourd, wood or clay, begs them free of every fault, inspects them before taking them, wears them as received without washing or dyeing for looks, and stays unattached to them even when robbers take them.2.6Permission to Stay Avagraha-pratima (અવગ્રહ પડિમા)a monk or nun, vowed never to take what is not given, uses no place and no thing, not even a fellow monk’s, without the owner’s permission, sets clear limits of space and time when asking, shares what he has with fellow monks, and behaves with courtesy toward everyone he lodges among.2.7The Seven Septets Sapta-saptika (સપ્ત સપ્તિકા)seven short chapters guard a monk’s everyday life from every side: where he may stand still, sit to study and relieve himself, how he must not go out of his way for sounds and sights, and why he must not let a householder, or even a fellow monk, wash, rub, adorn or treat his body.2.8Bhavana, the Five Vows Bhavana (ભાવના)the chapter first tells Lord Mahavira’s life from his descent into the womb to omniscience, to strengthen faith, and then gives the five great vows he taught the monks, each with five supporting practices (bhavana), to strengthen conduct.2.9Vimukti, Release Vimukti (વિમુક્તિ)in twelve verses the last chapter of the Acharang shows the way out: see that every dwelling is temporary, leave home and possessions, bear abuse like a mountain bears wind, keep the great vows, and the monk sheds his bonds as a snake sheds its old skin.

09_modules/00_avashyak_index.title: Avashyak Sutra: All Chapters
09_modules/00_avashyak_index.content:
Avashyak Sutra: All Chapters
The Avashyak gives the six essential duties (avashyak) done every day: equanimity (samayik), praise of the 24 Tirthankaras, bowing to the Guru (vandana), turning back from faults (pratikraman), standing still beyond the body (kayotsarga) and vows of renunciation (pratyakhyan). The last module is the book’s section on the householder’s twelve vows, which the book says comes from Haribhadra’s commentary. Each module has the sutras in Prakrit with plain English, checked against the scans.
New here? Read them in order; they are the order of the daily rite. A householder can start with 1 (samayik), 4 (pratikraman, ending in khamemi savve jiva) and 7 (the householder’s vows).













































#ChapterIn one line1Equanimity Samayik (પ્રથમ આવશ્યક : સામાયિક)the first daily duty is equanimity: bow to the five supreme beings, then give up all sinful activity in mind, speech and body, turn back from past wrongs, and drop the self that did them.2Praise of the 24 Chaturvimshatistava (બીજો આવશ્યક : ચતુર્વિંશતિસ્તવ)the seeker keeps the 24 Tirthankaras, who reached perfect equanimity, before his eyes by praising their names, and asks of them only health of the soul, right understanding and the highest calm.3Bowing to the Guru Vandana (ત્રીજો આવશ્યક : વંદના)the disciple asks leave to come near the Guru, touches his feet, asks after his day and his practice, and begs forgiveness for every disrespect, because humility toward the Guru is the root of every good that follows.4Turning Back Pratikraman (ચોથો આવશ્યક : પ્રતિક્રમણ)each day the monk looks back over everything he did, waking and sleeping, walking, begging and studying, turns back from every lapse with “may that wrong of mine be undone”, renews his faith and vows, and ends by forgiving and asking forgiveness of every living being.5Letting Go of the Body Kayotsarga (કાયોત્સર્ગ)after confessing his faults, the practitioner stands still, silent and absorbed in good meditation, giving up attachment to the body, to heal what confession has not yet healed and to destroy sinful karma.6Vows of Renunciation Pratyakhyan (પ્રત્યાખ્યાન)having cleaned out past faults, the practitioner closes the door on future karma by taking a time-bound vow to give up food (from one muhurta after sunrise up to a full fast), keeps it pure, closes it properly, and ends the whole Avashyak with the Namotthunam in praise of the Arihantas and Siddhas.7The Householder's Vows Shravak Vrat (શ્રાવક વ્રત)a lay follower first turns from wrong belief to right faith, then takes twelve vows sized to household life (five small vows, three supporting vows, four training vows), learns the faults that weaken each one, and at life’s end may let go of the body in sallekhana.

09_modules/00_dashvaikalik_index.title: Dashvaikalik Sutra: All Chapters
09_modules/00_dashvaikalik_index.content:
Dashvaikalik Sutra: All Chapters
The Dashvaikalik is a compact guide to the conduct of a monk: ten chapters and two closing chulikas on what dharma is, how to live carefully among living beings, how to seek food, speak and act without harm, and how humility leads to composure. Each module gives the chapter’s point in one line, what it teaches in the chapter’s own order, and its key verses in Prakrit with plain English, checked against the scans.
New here? Start with 1 (dharma and the bee), 4 (the six kinds of living beings), 7 (pure speech), 8 (anger, pride, deceit, greed) and 9 (humility).






































































#ChapterIn one line1The Monk and the Bee Drumapushpika (दुमपुप्फिया)dharma, made of non-violence, restraint and austerity, is the highest good, and a monk keeps his body alive the way a bee feeds on flowers: a little from many, taking only what is freely given, and hurting no one.2The Groundwork of Monkhood Shramanyapurvaka (सामण्णपुव्वयं)no one can live as a monk without first giving up desire for sense pleasures, and when the mind slips, as Rathanemi’s did, it must be brought back at once, as Rajimati brought him back with a few hard words.3Minor Rules of Conduct Kshullakachara Katha (क्षुल्लकाचार कथा)a monk who wants to be free keeps away from a long list of small-looking comforts and habits (the tradition counts fifty-two), because each one brings harm to living beings, attachment to the body or dependence on householders; by keeping clear of them he burns off his karma.4The Six Kinds of Living Beings Chhajjivaniya (छज्जीवणिया, Gujarati छ जीवनिकाय)earth, water, fire, air, plants and moving creatures are all alive, so the monk takes the five great vows and the vow against night eating, does everything with care, and grows from knowing the living and non-living all the way to liberation.5Seeking Alms Pindaishana (पिंडैषणा)a monk lives only on food he begs, so he must seek it, take it and eat it in a way that hurts no living being, burdens no giver and feeds no craving, and the giver who gives expecting nothing and the monk who takes expecting nothing both reach a good state.6The Great Conduct Mahachara Katha (महाचार कथा)when kings and others ask a teacher how Jain monks live, he answers with eighteen rules of conduct (the six vows, care for the six classes of living beings, and six more rules), and says that a monk who keeps them all wipes out old karma and reaches liberation.7Pure Speech Suvakya Shuddhi (सुवाक्य शुद्धि)a monk speaks only what is true or plainly practical, and even then only after thinking, so that his words never hurt anyone, never push anyone towards harm, and never claim more than he knows.8The Treasure of Conduct Achara Pranidhi (आचार प्रणिधि)taking initiation is only entering school; this chapter is a store of practical guidance on how a monk then lives day by day, guarding living beings, his taste, his speech, his passions and his celibacy, until karma clears from him like clouds from the moon.9Composure Through Humility Vinay Samadhi (विनय समाधि)humility towards the guru (vinaya) is the root of the tree of dharma and liberation is its fruit; disrespect burns up a disciple’s own virtues, while the humble disciple grows, becomes worthy of honour, and finds composure (samadhi) in humility, learning, austerity and conduct.10The True Monk Sa Bhikkhu (स भिक्खू, Gujarati સ ભિક્ષુ)living on alms does not make a true monk; he is the one who protects all six kinds of living beings, keeps the great vows, bears every hardship like the earth, gives up pride and craving, and so reaches the state from which there is no return.Chulika 1Delight in Restraint Rativakya (रतिवाक्या)for a monk whose mind has turned against restraint and who is thinking of going home, the chulika gives eighteen points to reflect on and a set of pictures of the fallen monk’s regret, so that he finds delight in restraint again and resolves to give up the body rather than the teaching.Chulika 2The Solitary Way Vivikta Charya (विविक्त चर्या)the world swims with the current of the senses and stays in the round of birth and death; the monk swims against it, wandering without attachment, living simply, examining his own faults every night, and always guarding the soul.

Built from the machine translation of the Gujarati edition (jainaagam.org). Key verses checked by hand against the scans; other details may carry small slips. · Uttaradhyayan chapters · Learning path

09_modules/00_uttaradhyayan_index.title: Uttaradhyayan Sutra: All 36 Chapters
09_modules/00_uttaradhyayan_index.content:
Uttaradhyayan Sutra: All 36 Chapters
The Uttaradhyayan holds Bhagwan Mahavira’s last teachings: 36 chapters on how to live, what is real, and how the soul gets free. Each module below gives the chapter’s point in one line, what it teaches in the chapter’s own order, and its key verses in Prakrit with plain English, checked against the scans.
New here? Start with 3 (the four rare things), 10 (the falling leaf), 9 (Nami), 25 (the true brahmin), 28 (the path) and 32 (sources of negligence).






























































































































































































#ChapterIn one line1Humility Vinayashrutahumility (vinaya) towards the teacher is the root of dharma: the humble disciple who obeys, restrains himself and welcomes correction gains knowledge, honour, and in the end liberation or a high heaven.2Enduring Hardships Parishahaa monk will meet twenty-two kinds of hardship, from hunger and insults to doubt about the faith, and he bears each one calmly, inside his vows, as a way of shedding karma.3The Four Rare Things Chaturangiyafour things are hard to get, each harder than the one before: a human life, hearing the dharma, believing it, and actually living it. The one who gets all four ends suffering for good.4Life Cannot Be Mended Asamskritaa broken life cannot be joined again, and neither wealth nor family can save you from your own karma, so do not put dharma off: live awake, without negligence (pramada), until the body ends.5Two Kinds of Death Akamamaraniyaeveryone dies, but the fool dies unwillingly, in fear, again and again, while the one who lives with restraint meets death calmly, by choice, and so cuts the round of births short.6The Monk Free of Knots Kshullaka-Nirgranthiyaignorance ties us in knots, and neither family, wealth nor clever words can untie them; only a monk who drops every possession and attachment, and stays watchful, becomes truly free of knots (nirgrantha).7The Fattened Ram Urabhriyathe one who fattens on pleasure is like a ram fed well only for the guest’s table: he trades a long, bright future for a few short years of enjoyment, so keep your human birth as capital and grow it.8Kapila and Greed Kapiliyato escape a bad rebirth, let go of attachments, harm no living being, eat only to keep up restraint, and see through greed, which grows with every gain, as Kapila found when two grams of gold turned into a wish for millions.9Nami's Renunciation Namipravrajya (नमिप्रव्रज्या)when King Nami leaves his kingdom, Indra comes disguised as a Brahmin and tests him with ten worldly duties, and Nami answers each one by turning it inward: the real city, fort, war and wealth are inside the soul.10The Falling Leaf Drumapatrakalife falls like a yellow leaf from a tree, and a human birth with everything needed for dharma is very hard to get, so do not be careless (pramada) even for a moment.11The Glory of the Learned Bahushrut Puja (બહુશ્રુત પૂજા)a monk becomes deeply learned (bahushrut) only through humility, self-control and staying with his teacher; such a learned monk shines above all others, and his learning carries him and others to liberation.12The True Sacrifice Harikeshiya (હરિકેશીય)a monk born among outcastes shows the proud Brahmins at a sacrifice that a person is made high by conduct, not by birth, and that the true sacrifice and the true bath happen inside the soul, through austerity, restraint and dharma.13Two Brothers, Two Paths Chitta-Sambhutiyatwo brothers who were together for five lives meet again in the sixth, one a monk and one an emperor; the monk urges the emperor to let go of pleasures, the emperor cannot, and so one reaches liberation and the other the lowest hell.14King Ishukara Ishukariyatwo boys wake to their past life and leave home, and their reasons, that the soul is real, life is short and only dharma protects, win over their father, their mother, the queen and at last the king, until all six reach liberation.15The True Monk Sabhikshukabegging does not make a monk. A true monk (bhikshu) lives for liberation alone: he wants no honour, bears every hardship calmly, earns nothing by magic or medicine, flatters no one, fears nothing, and wanders free and alone. Each verse ends with the same words, “he is a monk”.16The Supports of Celibacy Brahmacharya Samadhisthancelibacy is the heart of a monk’s practice, and ten simple guards (where he lives, what he says, sees, hears, remembers, eats and wears, and how he treats the senses) keep it safe; the one who keeps it is honoured even by the gods and reaches liberation.17The Bad Monk Papashramaniyaa monk who takes his vows “like a lion” but then lives “like a jackal”, for comfort, sleep, tasty food and his own way, is called a bad monk (papa-shramana); the one who drops all these faults is honoured like nectar.18King Sanjaya Sanjayiya (Samyatiya)a hunting king meets a silent monk, learns that he too must give others the fearlessness he begged for, and renounces; a fellow monk then shows him that the great kings of old all won liberation by leaving one-sided views behind and walking the Jina’s path of knowledge and conduct.19Mrigaputra Mrigaputriyaa pampered prince sees a monk, remembers that he was once a monk himself, and answers every warning his parents give about the hard monk’s life with the far worse pains he has already suffered in hell, until they let him go to live “like a deer” and he reaches liberation.20The Great Nirgrantha Mahanirgranthiyano wealth, family or doctor can protect us from suffering; only the soul that takes up restraint and keeps it truly has a protector, and a monk who lets his restraint slip becomes unprotected again.21Samudrapala Samudrapaliyaa rich young merchant sees a condemned man led to execution, understands that every bad deed bears its fruit, becomes a monk, bears every hardship with an even mind, and crosses the ocean of birth and death.22Rathanemi RathanemiyaPrince Arishtanemi turns back from his own wedding out of compassion for the animals penned up for the feast; Rajemati follows him into renunciation, and later, alone in a cave, her firm words bring the wavering monk Rathanemi back to restraint.23Keshi and Gautama Keshi-Gautamiyatwo great monks, one from Parshvanatha’s line and one from Mahavira’s, meet to settle why their rules differ; through twelve questions they show that the goal is one, the outer rules suit different people, and the real path is inner: conquering the mind, cutting craving, cooling the passions.24Mothers of the Teaching Pravachanamatathe whole of a monk’s life rests on eight “mothers”: five kinds of careful action (samiti) in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling things and disposing of waste, and three restraints (gupti) of mind, speech and body; whoever keeps them well is soon free.25The True Brahmin Yajniyaa monk turned away from his brother’s sacrificial hall answers with a teaching, not anger: a true brahmin is made by inner qualities and deeds, not by birth or ritual, and the real sacrifice is restraint; the brother is won over and both reach liberation.26Proper Conduct Samacharia monk’s whole day and night, from the ten courtesies he shows his teacher and fellow monks to the hours of study, meditation, alms, sleep and confession, is laid out as one careful routine, and living it frees him from all suffering.27The Unruly Bullocks Khalunkiyaa good disciple carries the cart of dharma like a willing ox, but bad disciples behave like unruly bullocks, and the elder Garga, unable to set his own disciples right, left them and went on alone, calm and steady.28The Path to Liberation Mokshamarga Gatithe path to liberation has four parts: knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity. Knowledge shows what is true, faith holds to it, conduct stops new karma coming in, and austerity burns up the old.29Right Effort Samyak Parakram (Sammatta-parakkame)for each of 73 practices, from longing for liberation to the final stillness, the disciple asks “Lord, what does the soul gain by this?”, and each answer shows how that one practice, done rightly, carries the soul all the way to freedom.30The Path of Austerity Tapomarga Gatifirst close the channels through which karma flows in. Then dry up what has gathered over countless lives with twelve kinds of austerity: six outer, which work through the body, and six inner, which work through the mind and heart.31Rules of Conduct Charan Vidhiconduct comes down to one rule: turn away from lack of restraint and turn toward restraint. The chapter then counts up from one to thirty-three, naming what a monk must give up, take up or simply know. Each verse ends with the same promise: “that monk does not stay in the round of rebirth.”32Sources of Negligence Pramadasthanasuffering does not come from the objects of the senses but from our attachment and aversion toward them; the one who stays even-minded among them, like a lotus leaf in water, is freed from all suffering.33The Nature of Karma Karma Prakritithe soul wanders because it is bound by eight kinds of karma; know their kinds, their length and their strength, and then stop new karma coming in and destroy the old.34The Colours of the Soul Leshyathe soul’s states, coloured by the passions, come in six shades from black to white; the dark three lead to a bad birth and the bright three to a good one, so a monk should leave the dark and hold to the bright.35The Homeless Monk's Path Anagara Marga Gatia monk who has left home must not let home’s bonds creep back; he lives in a simple place, does not build, cook, buy or sell, eats only to keep going, wants no honour, and so ends all suffering.36The Living and the Non-living Jivajiva-Vibhaktithe whole world is made of the living and the non-living; the chapter maps every kind of each, from atoms to the siddhas, so that a monk who knows and trusts this map delights in restraint, dies well, and reaches liberation.

Built from the machine translation of the Gujarati edition (jainaagam.org). Key verses checked by hand against the scans; other details may carry small slips. · Learning path · Dashvaikalik chapters

09_modules/acharang_1_01_knowing_the_wea.title: Module · Acharang 1: Knowing the Weapon
09_modules/acharang_1_01_knowing_the_wea.content:
Acharang 1 · Shastra Parijna (શસ્ત્ર પરિજ્ઞા): Knowing the Weapon
In one line: first know that you are a soul that has come from somewhere and goes on, then see that earth, water, fire, plants, moving creatures and air are all alive and feel pain as you do, and give up every “weapon” against them, by your own hand, through others, and by approval.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 1 (39 sutras, 7 sections), translated pages 63–107 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (1.2.4 = section 2, sutra 4). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The name means “knowing the weapon, and giving it up”. A weapon is whatever destroys a being: knives and swords outwardly, attachment and aversion inwardly, because they damage the soul’s own qualities. “Knowing” (parijna) has two sides: to understand (jna-parijna) and to renounce (pratyakhyan-parijna). Non-violence rests on knowing the soul (introduction, p. 63).
Many do not know where they came from or where they will go. Sudharma tells Jambu what he heard from Mahavira: some beings do not know from which direction they came, whether their soul is reborn, who they were, or what they will become after this body (1.1.1).
Knowing “that am I” makes a believer in the soul. By one’s own memory of past lives, by a Tirthankara’s teaching, or by hearing a learned teacher, a person knows: “the one who wanders through all the directions is I.” Such a person affirms the soul, the world, karma and action, and only he can practise non-violence well (1.1.2; commentary).
Action has 27 forms, and people act for four reasons. “I did, I had it done, I approved”, in past, present and future, by mind, speech and body, makes 27 ways of binding karma. People harm beings for this life, for praise, honour and worship, for release from birth and death (that is, for religion), and to ward off pain. One who understands and drops these is a sage “who has understood action” (parinnayakamme) (1.1.3–6).
Earth is alive and feels pain like a person who cannot speak. Some who call themselves homeless monks still dig and work the earth and so kill it and the beings in it. Such harm is “a knot, delusion, death and hell”. Earth beings feel pain as a man blind and dumb from birth feels a blade he cannot cry out against, as a healthy man feels cuts from foot to head, and as one struck dead or knocked unconscious feels the blow (1.2.1–6).
Water is alive, and using it is also taking what is not given. A true homeless monk is upright, on the path, without deceit, and keeps the faith with which he left home. Deny that water lives and you deny your own self. Water is itself living and many beings live in it; and since the water beings never gave anyone their lives, a pond-owner’s permission does not make using it innocent. Other ascetics who say “drinking and bathing is allowed for us” are still not freed from the sin (1.3.1–7).
Fire is the sharpest weapon. Whoever knows the weapon knows the non-weapon, restraint (samyama), and the reverse. The negligent person is “the rod” of violence; the wise resolve, “what I did before through carelessness, I will not do now.” Fire also burns the creatures living in earth, grass, leaves, wood, cow dung and rubbish, and the moths that fall into it (1.4.1–5).
Plants live as we live. Attachment to sights and sounds is itself the world, a whirlpool; a monk who keeps indulging them is a householder in a monk’s robe. A plant, like the human body, is born, grows, is conscious, withers when cut, takes food, is impermanent, grows and wanes, and changes (1.5.1–5).
Moving creatures fear pain, and are killed for every reason. There are eight kinds by birth, from egg-born to the gods and hell beings. Every being wants its own peace; for all of them pain is a great fear. Yet people kill for sacrifice, skin, flesh, blood, horns, teeth, bones, for a purpose or for none, and out of revenge or fear: “he hurt mine, he is hurting mine, he will hurt mine” (1.6.1–4).
Air last, and then all six. Air is taught last because its beings cannot be seen. One who knows his own inner life knows others’: weigh others against yourself. Those whose passions are calmed do not wish to live by harming. Some take vows yet do not delight in the discipline; the sage does not even wish for wrong action. The chapter ends: neither harm the six kinds of beings, nor have them harmed, nor approve of it (1.7.1–6).

Key passages
1.1.2 · “That am I”: the believer in the soul

एवमेगेसिं जं णायं भवइ– अत्थि मे आया उववाइए, जो इमाओ दिसाओ वा अणुदिसाओ वा अणुसंचरइ, सव्वाओ दिसाओ सव्वाओ अणुदिसाओ जो आगओ अणुसंचरइ, सोऽहं । से आयावाई लोयावाई कम्मावाई किरियावाई ।

So some come to know: “My soul exists and is reborn. The one who moves through these directions and in-between directions, who has come from all the directions and wanders on, that am I.” Such a person affirms the soul, the world, karma and action.
1.2.4 · Harm is a knot, delusion, death and hell

से तं संबुज्झमाणे आयाणीयं समुट्ठाए । सोच्चा भगवओ अणगाराणं वा अंतिए इहमेगेसिं णायं भवइ– एस खलु गंथे, एस खलु मोहे, एस खलु मारे, एस खलु णरए ।

Understanding this, the seeker takes up what is worth taking up, restraint. Having heard it from the Lord or from the homeless monks, some here come to know: “This, indeed, is the knot (of bondage); this, indeed, is delusion; this, indeed, is death; this, indeed, is hell.”
1.3.3 · Deny the world and you deny yourself

लोगं च आणाए अभिसमेच्चा अकुतोभयं ।
से बेमि– णेव सयं लोगं अब्भाइक्खेज्जा, णेव अत्ताणं अब्भाइक्खेज्जा । जे लोगं अब्भाइक्खइ, से अत्ताणं अब्भाइक्खइ; जे अत्ताणं अब्भाइक्खइ, से लोगं अब्भाइक्खइ ।

Knowing the world (here, the water beings) by the Lord’s teaching, practise the restraint in which no one has any fear. I say: one should not deny the world, nor deny one’s own self. Whoever denies the world denies himself; whoever denies himself denies the world.
1.5.4 · A plant is like a human body

से बेमि इमं पि जाइधम्मयं, एयं पि जाइधम्मयं । इमं पि वुड्ढिधम्मयं, एयं पि वुड्ढिधम्मयं । इमं पि चित्तमंतयं, एयं पि चित्तमंतयं । इमं पि छिण्णं मिलाइ, एयं पि छिण्णं मिलाइ । इमं पि आहारगं, एयं पि आहारगं ।

I say: this (human body) is born, and this (plant) is born. This grows, and this grows. This is conscious, and this is conscious. This withers when cut, and this withers when cut. This takes food, and this takes food. (The sutra goes on: both are impermanent, not lasting, grow and waste, and change.)
1.6.1 · For every being, pain is a great fear

णिज्झाइत्ता पडिलेहित्ता पत्तेयं परिणिव्वाणं । सव्वेसिं पाणाणं सव्वेसिं भूयाणं सव्वेसिं जीवाणं सव्वेसिं सत्ताणं अस्सायं अपरिणिव्वाणं महब्भयं दुक्खं ति बेमि ।

Having reflected and looked carefully: each one wants its own peace. For all creatures, all beings, all living things and all sentient beings, discomfort and unrest are a great fear and suffering. Thus I say.
1.7.1 · Weigh others against yourself

पहू एजस्स दुगुंछणाए । आयंकदंसी अहियं ति णच्चा । जे अज्झत्थं जाणइ से बहिया जाणइ, जे बहिया जाणइ से अज्झत्थं जाणइ । एयं तुलमण्णेसिं । इह संतिगया दविया णावकंखंति जीविउं ।

One who sees the suffering harm brings, and knows it as harmful, is able to give up harming the air beings. Whoever knows what is within knows what is outside; whoever knows what is outside knows what is within. Weigh others against yourself in this way. Here, those whose passions are calmed and whose hearts are soft with compassion do not wish to live by harming.
Checked against the scans: 1.1.2 · 1.2.4 · 1.3.3 · 1.5.4 · 1.6.1 · 1.7.1

09_modules/acharang_1_02_conquest_of_the.title: Module · Acharang 2: Conquest of the World
09_modules/acharang_1_02_conquest_of_the.content:
Acharang 2 · Lok Vijay (લોક વિજય): Conquest of the World
In one line: the “world” to conquer is inside you, the sense of “mine” over family, wealth and pleasures; none of it can protect you from old age, illness or death, so use this short human life now, while the senses still work, to live without possessiveness.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 2 (39 sutras, 6 sections), translated pages 109–162 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (2.3.4 = section 3, sutra 4). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The world to be conquered is the world inside. The introduction explains that “world” here means the inner world of attachment, aversion, anger, pride, deceit and greed; conquer that and the outer cycle of birth and death is conquered too. Some read the old name as Lokavichaya, “examining the world”; the book says both readings fit (introduction, pp. 109–110).
Sense objects are the root, and “mine” is the chain. What the senses enjoy is the root of worldly life. The person who wants them says: “my mother, my father, my brother, my sister, my wife, my sons, my daughters, my friends, my goods, my food and clothes”, and so burns day and night, works at all hours, grabs, steals and harms living beings again and again (2.1.1).
Your own people cannot save you. As hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch weaken with age, a man grows confused; his family may scorn him, or he them. When illness comes, those he lives with may leave him. “They cannot protect you or shelter you, and you cannot protect or shelter them.” So do not be careless even for a moment: age and youth are passing (2.1.2–4).
Know your moment. Each being has its own pleasure and pain. While the five senses are still whole, work properly for the good of the soul (2.1.5).
Discontent with restraint, and its cure. The wise one who drives out discontent (arati) is freed in a moment. Some take vows saying “we will own nothing”, then accept pleasures when they come, and end up “neither on this shore nor the other”, neither householder nor monk. The true homeless one meets greed with non-greed and does not take the pleasures that come to him (2.2.1–3).
People harm for strength, fear and hope. People hurt beings to build their own strength, or that of family, friends, the dead, gods, kings, thieves, guests, the poor and ascetics; out of fear; in the hope of reward; even thinking “this will free me from sin”. The wise do none of it, nor cause it, nor approve it (2.2.4–5).
No one is high and no one is low. The soul has been born in a high family many times and in a low family many times, so it is neither less nor more. Who then would boast of family or pride? Blindness, deafness, lameness and the like come from one’s own carelessness. All beings love life, like pleasure, hate pain; and wealth piled up is split by heirs, stolen by thieves, seized by kings, lost, or burnt in a house fire (2.3.1–7).
Desire is a thorn you put in yourself. Even when ill, some grieve only for lost pleasures. “Give up hope and craving, O steady one; you yourself have taken in that thorn.” The book calls the pull to women a great delusion that leads to suffering, death and hell. Monks’ rule: if a householder gives nothing, do not be angry; if he gives little, do not scold him; if refused, go away calmly (2.4.1–5).
How a monk lives from others’ kitchens. Householders cook for their own families and guests; the homeless monk takes only faultless food, never buys or has anything bought, and knows the right time, his strength, the measure and the moment. He is not proud when he gets, does not grieve when he does not, and does not store even plenty. The body is as unclean inside as outside; pleasures once given up are like spittle not to be licked up again. The greedy man, busy with “I did this, I will do that”, lives as if he were immortal. A monk may not take or give treatment that kills or harms beings (2.5.1–9).
Drop “mine” and you have dropped possessions. The steady one bears neither discontent with restraint nor delight in pleasures; he eats plain, dry food and shakes off the body of karma. He who sees the self delights in the self. He teaches the rich and the poor alike, but with skill, first knowing who the listener is. This teaching is not needed by one who sees; it is for the ignorant, who keep circling in their sorrow (2.6.1–8).

Key passages
2.1.2 · They cannot protect you

जेहिं वा सद्धिं संवसइ ते वा णं एगया णियगा तं पुव्विं परिवयंति, सो वा ते णियगे पच्छा परिवएज्जा । णालं ते तव ताणाए वा सरणाए वा, तुमं पि तेसिं णालं ताणाए वा सरणाए वा । से ण हासाए, ण किड्डाए, ण रईए, ण विभूसाए ।

The very relatives he lives with may one day speak against him first, or he may later speak against them. They are not able to protect you or give you shelter, and you are not able to protect them or give them shelter. (In old age) he is no longer fit for laughter, play, love or adornment.
2.1.5 · Know the moment, while the senses last

जाणित्तु दुक्खं पत्तेयं सायं । अणभिक्कंतं च खलु वयं संपेहाए खणं जाणाहि पंडिए ।
जाव सोयपण्णाणा अपरिहीणा, जाव णेत्तपण्णाणा अपरिहीणा, जाव घाणपण्णाणा अपरिहीणा जाव जीहपण्णाणा अपरिहीणा जाव फासपण्णाणा अपरिहीणा, इच्चेतेहिं विरूवरूवेहिं पण्णाणेहिं अपरिहीणेहिं आयट्ठं सम्मं समणुवासेज्जासि ॥ त्ति बेमि ।

Knowing that pain and pleasure are each one’s own, and seeing that your life has not yet run out, know the moment, O wise one. While hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch have not declined, while all these powers are still whole, work properly for the good of the soul. Thus I say.
2.3.4 · Death will come; all love life

णत्थि कालस्स णागमो । सव्वे पाणा पियाउया सुहसाया दुक्खपडिकूला अप्पियवहा पियजीविणो जीविउकामा । सव्वेसिं जीवियं पियं ।

There is no such thing as death not coming. All living beings hold their life dear; they like pleasure and dislike pain; they shrink from being killed and love to live; they want to live. To all, life is dear.
2.6.2 · Give up “mine”

जे ममाइयमइं जहाइ से जहाइ ममाइयं । से हु दिट्ठपहे मुणी जस्स णत्थि ममाइयं । तं परिण्णाय मेहावी विदित्ता लोगं, वंता लोगसण्णं, से मइमं परक्कमेज्जासि । त्ति बेमि ।

Whoever gives up the sense of “mine” gives up what he called his. The sage who has nothing he calls “mine” is the one who has seen the path. Knowing this, and knowing the world, the wise one should throw off the world’s ways of thinking and strive in restraint. Thus I say.
2.6.3 · The steady one (verses 1–2)

णारइं सहइ वीरे, वीरे णो सहइ रइं ।
जम्हा अविमणे वीरे, तम्हा वीरे ण रज्जइ ॥१॥
सद्दे फासे अहियासमाणे, णिविंद णंदिं इह जीवियस्स ।
मुणी मोणं समादाय, धुणे कम्मसरीरगं ॥२॥

The steady one does not put up with discontent in restraint, and does not put up with delight in pleasures. Because his mind is not disturbed, the steady one is not attached. Bearing sounds, touches and the rest, turn away from delight in this unrestrained life. Taking up the sage’s way, the sage shakes off the body of karma.
2.6.5 · Seeing the self, delighting in the self

जे अणण्णदंसी से अणण्णारामे, जे अणण्णारामे से अणण्णदंसी ।

One who sees nothing other (than the self) delights in nothing other; one who delights in nothing other sees nothing other. The commentary also reads it as: one who does not look at others’ faults delights in the self.
Checked against the scans: 2.1.2 · 2.1.5, end · 2.3.4 · 2.6.2 · 2.6.3 · 2.6.5

09_modules/acharang_1_03_cold_and_heat.title: Module · Acharang 3: Cold and Heat
09_modules/acharang_1_03_cold_and_heat.content:
Acharang 3 · Shitoshniya (શીતોષ્ણીય): Cold and Heat
In one line: stay awake: bear the “cold” of pleasant things and the “heat” of painful things with the same even mind, cast out anger, pride, deceit and greed, and be your own friend, because only a self that restrains itself is freed from suffering.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 3 (27 sutras, 4 sections), translated pages 163–200 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (3.4.3 = section 4, sutra 3). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

“Cold” is what pleases, “heat” is what hurts. The introduction explains the name: of a monk’s twenty-two hardships, two are “cold” (women and being honoured) and twenty are “hot”; pleasant sights, sounds and respect are cold, pain, illness and trouble are heat. A seeker passes through both with equanimity (introduction, p. 163).
The ignorant sleep; the sage is always awake. The commentary explains that this is sleep of the soul: wrong belief, carelessness and passion. A monk may sleep at night and still be awake to his own self. Knowing that pain is unwelcome to every being in the world, he puts down every weapon (3.1.1–2).
Who is a sage. One who has fully understood sounds, forms, smells, tastes and touches, without attachment or aversion, has the self, knowledge, scripture, dharma and pure conduct; he knows the world by wisdom and is rightly called a sage (muni) (3.1.3).
Bear both, and stay alert. The free one (nirgrantha) has let go of craving for cold and heat; he bears dislike and delight and does not feel hardship as pain. Seeing beings tormented by old age and death, live carefully: the deceitful and careless return to the womb again and again, while the straight one, who is indifferent to sounds and sights and keeps death in view, is freed from death (3.1.4–5).
Karma is the root of every label. Whoever knows the weapon knows the non-weapon (restraint), and the reverse. For one without karma there are no worldly labels at all; every condition comes from karma, and violence is its root. Seen by neither extreme, attachment nor aversion, the wise one strives (3.1.6–8).
Cut the tip and the root. In verse: see birth and growth here today, and that every being wants comfort; one who sees evenly does no wrong. Those greedy for pleasure pile up karma and are born again. Laughing at harm only grows one’s own enmity. Cut off the tip (karma) and the root (lack of restraint). Much wrong has been done before; be steady in truth (3.2.1).
Craving is a sieve. A man of many minds tries to fill a sieve, and so he kills, torments and seizes others, even whole lands. Seeing that pleasures are hollow, the wise do not go back to them; even the gods are born and die. Kill anger and pride; see greed as a great hell; human birth is the chance to rise, so harm no living being (3.2.2–4).
Restraint must come from within. See others as yourself. If one avoids wrong only out of fear or shame before others, monkhood is not the reason. Be detached from all forms, great or small. Discontent and joy do not touch the one who lives without grasping. “You are your own friend; why look for a friend outside?” Hold to truth, and the wise one crosses death (3.3.1–5).
Vomit out the passions. Anger, pride, deceit and greed are to be cast out like vomit. Whoever knows the one (the self) knows all. The careless have fear on every side; the careful have none. Subdue the one and you subdue many; overcome one passion and you overcome the others. Weapons are sharper and sharper; the non-weapon, restraint, has no degrees (3.4.1–8).
The chain from anger to suffering. Whoever sees anger sees pride, and so on through deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, delusion, the womb, birth, death, hell and animal birth, to suffering; the wise one turns away from all of them. For the one who truly sees, no affliction remains (3.4.9–10).

Key passages
3.1.1 · Asleep and awake

सुत्ता अमुणी, मुणिणो सया जागरंति ।

The ignorant are asleep; sages are always awake.
3.1.4 · Beyond cold and heat

सीओसिणच्चाई से णिग्गंथे, अरइ-रइ सहे फरुसियं णो वेदेइ । जागर वेरोवरए वीरे । एवं दुक्खा पमोक्खसि ।

The free one (nirgrantha) has given up craving for cold and heat; he bears dislike and delight and does not feel hardship as pain. Be awake, O hero, and turn away from enmity. In this way you will be freed from suffering.
3.2.2 · Filling a sieve

अणेगचित्ते खलु अयं पुरिसे, से केयणं अरिहइ पूरइत्तए । से अण्णवहाए अण्णपरियावाए अण्णपरिग्गहाए जणवयवहाए जणवय परियावाए जणवय-परिग्गहाए ।

This man of many minds is trying to fill a sieve. For that he kills others, torments others and seizes others; he kills, torments and seizes whole peoples.
3.3.4 · You are your own friend

पुरिसा! तुममेव तुमं मित्तं, किं बहिया मित्तमिच्छसि ? जं जाणेज्जा उच्चालइयं तं जाणेज्जा दुरालइयं, जं जाणेज्जा दुरालइयं तं जाणेज्जा उच्चालइयं । पुरिसा ! अत्ताणमेव अभिणिगिज्झ, एवं दुक्खा पमोक्खसि ।

O man, you yourself are your friend; why do you want a friend outside? Know that the one who throws off karma is the one bound for liberation, and the one bound for liberation is the one who throws off karma. O man, restrain your own self; in this way you will be freed from suffering.
3.4.2 · Know one, know all

जे एगं जाणइ से सव्वं जाणइ, जे सव्वं जाणइ से एगं जाणइ ।

Whoever knows the one knows all; whoever knows all knows the one. (The commentary: one who truly knows the self also knows and takes up full restraint; and only one who knows a thing with all its aspects knows even one thing.)
3.4.3 · The careless are afraid everywhere

सव्वओ पमत्तस्स भयं, सव्वओ अप्पमत्तस्स णत्थि भयं ।

The careless person has fear from every side; the careful person has no fear from any side.
Checked against the scans: 3.1.1 · 3.1.4 · 3.2.2 · 3.3.4 · 3.4.2 · 3.4.3

09_modules/acharang_1_04_right_faith.title: Module · Acharang 1.4: Right Faith
09_modules/acharang_1_04_right_faith.content:
Acharang 1.4 · Samyaktva (સમ્યક્ત્વ): Right Faith
In one line: all the Tirthankaras of past, present and future teach one pure, eternal dharma, that no living being is to be harmed; hold to it with true understanding, never give it up, and burn away karma with detachment from the body.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 4 (21 sutras, 4 sections), translated pages 201–226 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (4.2.8 = section 2, sutra 8). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Right faith (samyaktva) is the foundation of liberation. The introduction calls knowing and trusting the real nature of things samyaktva, and says the four sections take up in turn right knowledge, right faith, right conduct and right austerity (introduction, p.201).
Every Tirthankara teaches the same thing: do not harm any living being. Past, present and future Arihants all say that no living being may be struck, ruled by force, enslaved, tormented or harmed. This dharma is pure, eternal and everlasting, and it was taught for everyone: those already practising and those not, those listening and those absent, the violent and the non-violent, those with possessions and those without (4.1.1).
Having found it, keep it and live it. This teaching is true; having taken it up, one should not hide one’s strength or drop one’s faith. Turn away from what the senses meet, do not chase worldly regard, and strive day and night without negligence; the negligent are outside dharma (4.1.2–4).
Bondage or freedom depends on the inner state, not the outer setting. What is a door of inflow of karma (asrava) can become a door of shedding, and the reverse. The commentary gives Sthulibhadra, who stayed pure in a courtesan’s house, and Nagashri, who bound karma while giving alms with a spiteful mind (4.2.1).
Death cannot be escaped, and cruel deeds lead to long suffering. Driven by desire and seized by time, beings are born again and again; those who do cruel deeds stay long in places of suffering such as hell, and those who do not, do not. The wise teach even the afflicted and the careless, for anyone can wake up (4.2.2–3).
The noble answer to those who say violence is no fault. Some ascetics and Brahmins claim that killing and enslaving beings is faultless. The noble call this an ignoble statement and ask each of them: is suffering pleasant to you or unpleasant? Honestly answered, suffering is unpleasant, fearful and painful to every living being (4.2.4–8).
Detach from the body and burn karma as fire burns old wood. Ignore those turned away from dharma. Those who lay down violence shed karma. Seeing the soul as alone, thin the body and the passions by austerity, while keeping the mind calm; the commentary warns that austerity must not bring dejection (4.3.1–3).
Give up anger. Life is short; know the suffering anger brings now and later. Those who have withdrawn from sinful deeds are free of karma’s cause, so never set the soul ablaze with passion (4.3.4–5).
Practise to the end, as the heroes did. Leaving old ties, the monk wears down the body by austerity in three growing stages, living in celibacy. One who keeps the Jina’s command neither at the start nor at the end cannot keep it in the middle. Seeing that karma bears fruit, the wise cut off the outer stream and walk the path of the heroes, who carry no further burden of karma (4.4.1–4).

Key passages
4.1.1 · The eternal dharma of non-violence

से बेमि- जे य अईया जे य पडुप्पण्णा जे य आगमिस्सा अरहंता भगवंतो ते सव्वे एवमाइक्खंति, एवं भासंति, एवं पण्णवेंति, एवं परूवेंति- सव्वे पाणा सव्वे भूया सव्वे जीवा सव्वे सत्ता ण हंतव्वा, ण अज्जावेयव्वा, ण परिघेयव्वा, ण परियावेयव्वा, ण उद्दवेयव्वा ।
एस धम्मे सुद्धे णिइए सासए समिच्च लोयं खेयण्णेहिं पवेइए ।

I say: all the Arihant Lords of the past, the present and the future say this, speak this, proclaim this and set this forth: no living being, no creature, no soul, no sentient being is to be struck, ruled by force, enslaved, tormented or harmed. This dharma is pure, eternal and everlasting; the Knowers declared it after seeing the world as it is.
4.2.1 · Inflow and shedding depend on the mind

जे आसवा ते परिस्सवा, जे परिस्सवा ते आसवा । जे अणासवा ते अपरिस्सवा, जे अपरिस्सवा ते अणासवा ।
एते य पए संबुज्झमाणे लोगं च आणाए अभिसमेच्चा पुढो पवेइयं ।

What are doors of karmic inflow (asrava) can become doors of shedding; what are doors of shedding can become doors of inflow. What is not inflow may fail to become shedding; what is not shedding may also not become inflow. Understanding these words, and seeing the world by the Lord’s command, one should not take up the causes of inflow.
4.2.8 · Ask them: is suffering pleasant to you?

पुव्वं णिकाय समयं पत्तेयं पत्तेयं पुच्छिस्सामो- हं भो पावादुया ! किं भे सायं दुक्खं उदाहु असायं ? समिया पडिवण्णे या वि एवं बूया- सव्वेसिं पाणाणं सव्वेसिं भूयाणं सव्वेसिं जीवाणं सव्वेसिं सत्ताणं असायं अपरिणिव्वाणं महब्भयं दुक्खं । त्ति बेमि ।

Having first set out our own teaching, we will ask each teacher of another view: “Philosophers, is suffering pleasant to you, or unpleasant?” Answering truly, they must say: “For all living beings, all creatures, all souls, all sentient beings, suffering is unpleasant, unwelcome, greatly fearful and painful.” Thus I say.
4.3.3 · As fire burns old wood

इह आणाकंखी पंडिए अणिहे एगमप्पाणं संपेहाए धुणे सरीरं, कसेहि अप्पाणं, जरेहि अप्पाणं । जहा जुण्णाइं कट्ठाइं हव्ववाहो पमत्थइ एवं अत्तसमाहिए अणिहे।

Here the wise one who seeks to follow the command, unattached, seeing the soul as alone, shakes off the karmic body. Make yourself lean, wear yourself down. As fire quickly burns old dry wood, so the monk, settled in the self and unattached to the body, burns away karma.
4.4.2 · No beginning and no end, then no middle

णेत्तेहिं पलिछिण्णेहिं आयाणसोयगढिए बाले अव्वोच्छिण्णबंधणे अणभिक्कंत संजोए । तमंसि अविजाणओ आणाए लंभो णत्थि त्ति बेमि । जस्स णत्थि पुरा पच्छा, मज्झे तस्स कुओ सिया ?

Even while holding back the eyes and other senses, the foolish one stays caught in the stream of sins and sense objects; he does not cut his bonds or go beyond his attachments. Lost in darkness and not understanding, he gains nothing from the Jina’s command. Thus I say. For one who has it neither at the beginning nor at the end, how can there be any in the middle?
Checked against the scans: 4.1.1 · 4.2.1 · 4.2.8 · 4.3.3 · 4.4.2

09_modules/acharang_1_05_essence_of_the_.title: Module · Acharang 1.5: Essence of the World
09_modules/acharang_1_05_essence_of_the_.content:
Acharang 1.5 · Lokasara (લોકસાર): Essence of the World
In one line: what is truly worth having in this world is not pleasure or possessions but dharma, knowledge, restraint and finally liberation, so fight the enemy within, live close to the guru, trust the Jina’s word, and see every other being as yourself.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 5 (41 sutras, 6 sections), translated pages 227–281 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (5.3.4 = section 3, sutra 4). The chapter is also called “Avanti”, from the first word of sections 1–3. 16 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The essence of the world is dharma, and the essence of restraint is liberation. The introduction quotes the Niryukti: dharma is the essence of the world, knowledge the essence of dharma, restraint the essence of knowledge, and nirvana the essence of restraint. Pleasures, wealth and the body are without essence (introduction, pp.227–228).
Pleasures are hard to drop, and life is a dewdrop on a blade of grass. Whoever harms beings, with a purpose or without one, is born among those same beings. Because pleasures are heavy to give up, one stays inside death’s reach and far from liberation. The fool’s life is as unsteady as a drop of water on a blade of kusa grass shaken by the wind (5.1.1–3).
Guard celibacy, and do not hide a fault. One who understands what unsettles celibacy can get free of worldly life. A monk who breaks it and then hides it from the guru commits a second folly. The section also warns against the false lone monk who is full of anger, pride, deceit and greed and says “let no one see me”, and against those who teach that ignorance frees (5.1.4–7).
This human body is the moment; do not waste it. One who lives without harming sees “this is the opportunity” and “this is the moment for this body”. When illness comes, bear it calmly: the body breaks, does not last and changes all the time. Possessions, small or large, living or not, become a great fear. Bondage and liberation lie in one’s own inner state (5.2.1–5).
Fight yourself, not others. The one free of possessions should not hide his strength. Some rise and never fall, some rise and fall, some never rise. Fight the passions within, for a chance to fight that battle is rare. The one who falls is caught by forms and by violence. What is right is monkhood, and monkhood is what is right; the lax, the crooked and the home-minded cannot keep it (5.3.1–7).
A young monk should not wander alone; he should live near the guru. An immature monk alone is easily angered, proud and overcome by hardship. Instead he should see with the guru’s eyes, rest his mind in the guru, put the guru first and live near him. Walking with care, a monk who harms a creature by accident binds only light karma and cleans it by atonement (5.4.1–4).
When desire troubles a monk, the book gives remedies. In order: eat plain food, eat less, stand in meditation, travel from village to village, and give up food. Turn the mind away from women; do not talk of them, stare at them or seek closeness. The commentary says the same teaching applies to nuns with respect to men (5.4.5–7).
The great teacher is like a full lake, and the Jina’s word is beyond doubt. A mind full of doubt finds no peace. That alone is true and beyond doubt which the Jinas taught; differences among monks come from their own karma, not from the teaching. Right thinking makes even hard things right; wrong thinking spoils even right ones (5.5.1–5).
The one you would harm is yourself. The one you think fit to kill, rule, torment, enslave or trouble is you. So the straightforward, awakened one neither kills nor makes others kill. The self is the knower, and the knower is the self (5.5.6–8).
Test every teaching by the Agama, and know the liberated soul. Some act against the command, some fail to act on it; stay near the guru. A tested monk may live without support. Streams of karmic inflow run above, below and across; close them and cross the round of birth and death. The liberated soul has no shape, colour, smell, taste, touch, body or sex; words turn back and reason cannot reach it (5.6.1–7).

Key passages
5.2.4 · Bondage and freedom lie within

से सुयं च मे अज्झत्थयं च मे, बंधपमोक्खो अज्झत्थेव ।

I have heard it, and I have reflected on it and experienced it myself: bondage and release come from within, from the soul’s own inner states.
5.3.4 · Fight the battle within

इमेण चेव जुज्झाहि, किं ते जुज्झेण बज्झओ ? जुद्धारिहं खलु दुल्लहं । जहेत्थ कुसलेहिं परिण्णाविवेगे भासिए ।

Fight with this very self. What good to you is fighting outside enemies? What is fit for this battle is truly hard to find. For it the wise ones have taught knowing and letting go: understanding the enemy, and separating yourself from it.
5.5.2 · That alone is true

वितिगिच्छासमावण्णेणं अप्पाणेणं णो लहइ समाहिं । सिया वेगे अणुगच्छंति, असिया वेगे अणुगच्छंति । अणुगच्छमाणेहिं अणणुगच्छमाणे कहं ण णिव्विज्जे ? तमेव सच्चं णीसंकं जं जिणेहिं पवेइयं ।

A soul caught in doubt does not find inner peace (samadhi). Some follow the command, some do not. How could one who does not follow it not be disheartened by those who do? That alone is true and beyond doubt which the Jinas have taught.
5.5.6 · You are the one

तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं हंतव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं अज्जावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परियावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परिघेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं उद्दवेयव्वं ति मण्णसि ।

The one you think fit to kill is you yourself. The one you think fit to rule over is you. The one you think fit to torment is you. The one you think fit to seize and enslave is you. The one you think fit to trouble to death is you.
5.5.8 · The self is the knower

जे आया से विण्णाया, जे विण्णाया से आया । जेण वियाणइ से आया । तं पडुच्च पडिसंखाए । एस आयावाई समियाए परियाए वियाहिए । त्ति बेमि ।

The self is the knower, and the knower is the self. That by which one knows is the self. One should reflect on the self in this light. Such a one is called a true believer in the self, and his restraint is right. Thus I say.
5.6.7 · Where words turn back (opening lines)

सव्वे सरा णियट्टंति, तक्का जत्थ ण विज्जइ, मई तत्थ ण गाहिया । ओए अप्पइट्ठाणस्स खेयण्णे ।
से ण दीहे, ण हस्से, ण वट्टे, ण तंसे, ण चउरंसे, ण परिमंडले, ण किण्हे, ण णीले, ण लोहिए, ण हालिद्दे, ण सुक्किले, ण सुब्भिगंधे, ण दुब्भिगंधे, ण तित्ते, ण कडुए, ण कसाए, ण अंबिले, ण महुरे, ण कक्खडे, ण मउए, ण गरुए, ण लहुए ण सीए, ण उण्हे, ण णिद्धे, ण लुक्खे, ण काऊ ण रुहे, ण संगे, ण इत्थी, ण पुरिसे, ण अण्णहा ।

All words turn back from it; reason does not reach it; the mind cannot grasp it. Alone and free of the stain of karma, it knows the state beyond the world. It is not long or short, round, triangular, square or ring-shaped; not black, green, red, yellow or white; not sweet-smelling or foul-smelling; not pungent, bitter, astringent, sour or sweet; not hard or soft, heavy or light, cold or hot, smooth or rough. It has no body, is not born again, has no tie to karma, and is neither female, male nor other. (The print has no “not salty” in the sutra, though the word meanings list ण लवणे; the print is kept as it stands.)
Checked against the scans: 5.2.4 · 5.3.4 · 5.5.2 · 5.5.6 · 5.5.8 · 5.6.7

09_modules/acharang_1_06_shaking_off.title: Module · Acharang 1.6: Shaking Off
09_modules/acharang_1_06_shaking_off.content:
Acharang 1.6 · Dhuta (ધૂત): Shaking Off
In one line: as dust is shaken off a cloth, the monk shakes off karma by leaving home and family, owning almost nothing, bearing every hardship calmly, holding to the Jina’s command, and at the end letting go of the body itself.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 6 (32 sutras, 5 sections), translated pages 282–328 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (6.2.5 = section 2, sutra 5). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

“Dhuta” means shaking off. Shaking dust off clothes is outward shaking off; making the eight kinds of karma fall away is the inner kind. Renunciation and restraint are called dhuta because karma falls away through them (introduction, p.282).
The one who knows teaches those ready to hear. One who understands the kinds of beings in every way teaches incomparable knowledge to listeners who are eager, have laid down violence, are calm and can tell good from harm. Some then strive like heroes; others, lacking understanding, lose heart (6.1.1–2).
Most people stay stuck, like a tortoise under weeds or a tree in its place. A tortoise in a lake covered with weeds and lotus leaves cannot find the way up; a tree, however battered, never leaves its spot. So people born into families, attached to forms, weep in their suffering and do not get free. The commentary tells of the tortoise that once saw the stars through a gap and lost it while fetching its family (6.1.3).
See the suffering, and do not kill to cure the body. The text names sixteen diseases that come to people as the fruit of their own deeds, and shows beings tormenting one another everywhere. Killing creatures to heal this fragile body cannot cure karma; one should not kill any being, even for treatment (6.1.4–6).
From the womb to the great sage, and the family’s tears. The teacher announces the way of shaking off karma and traces how a being is conceived, grows, wakes up, goes forth and step by step becomes a great sage. When he sets out, his parents weep, “Do not leave us”; he does not take refuge in them (6.1.7–8).
Some fall away; the true monk stands alone. Some take vows and then, unable to bear hardship and drawn by pleasures, throw away robe, bowl and blanket, and die unsatisfied. The steadfast monk reflects “nothing is mine, I am alone”, bears abuse and blows as the fruit of past deeds, and never returns to household life. “Obeying the command is my dharma” (6.2.1–6).
Few clothes, no worries, and the dharma like an island. The monk who has few or no clothes does not think “my cloth is worn, I must beg thread and needle”. He bears grass, cold, heat and insects, and grows light. Monks with three robes, two, one or none must not look down on one another (commentary). The dharma taught by the noble ones is an island that never goes under, and the teacher raises disciples as a bird raises its young (6.3.1–5).
The proud disciple and the fallen monk. Some disciples, once learned, grow harsh, say “this is not the Jina’s command”, call good monks bad, and take the easy exceptions as their rule. Some who leave still describe right conduct honestly; others, fallen from knowledge and faith, ruin their restraint while keeping its form. People say of them, “he has fallen from monkhood”. So follow the Agama always (6.4.1–7).
Teach everyone, harm no one, and be a refuge. Out of compassion for the world the monk should teach in every direction, to those who practise and those who do not, about peace, restraint, calm, liberation, purity, straightforwardness, gentleness, lightness and non-violence. Teaching without harming himself, his listeners or any being, he becomes a refuge like an island that does not sink (6.5.1–4).
Giving up the body is the front line of the battle. One who is not shaken by hardship has dropped anger, pride, deceit and greed. At life’s end, laying down the body is the front of the war against karma; struck or not, the monk stays steady as a plank of wood and awaits death until body and soul part (6.5.5–6).

Key passages
6.1.3 · The tortoise and the tree

से बेमि–से जहा वि कुम्मे हरए विणिविट्ठचित्ते पच्छण्णपलासे, उम्मग्गं से णो लहइ । भंजगा इव सण्णिवेसं णो चयंति । एवं एगे अणेगरूवेहिं कुलेहिं जाया । रूवेहिं सत्ता कलुणं थणंति, णियाणओ ते ण लहंति मोक्खं ।

I say: as a tortoise in a lake covered with lotus leaves, its mind set on getting out, cannot find the way up; and as trees do not leave their place; so some beings, born in many kinds of families and attached to forms, weep piteously, yet because of their own karma they do not find release.
6.2.2 · “Nothing is mine; I am alone”

अहेगे धम्ममायाय आयाणप्पभिइसु पणिहिए चरे अप्पलीयमाणे दढे । सव्वं गिद्धिं परिण्णाय । एस पणए महामुणी ।
अइयच्च सव्वओ संगं ण महं अत्थि त्ति, इति एगो अहमंसि, जयमाणे, एत्थ विरए अणगारे सव्वओ मुंडे रीयंते जे अचेले परिवुसिए संचिक्खइ ओमोयरियाए ।

Some take up the dharma and live it with care, bearing hardship, clinging to nothing, firm. Having seen through all craving and let it go, such a one, bent on ending karma, is a great sage. Going beyond every attachment, thinking “nothing is mine; I am alone”, striving, the homeless monk who has turned away here, shaven in every sense, with few or no clothes, stays steady in restraint and eats less than his fill.
6.2.5 · The command is my dharma

आणाए मामगं धम्मं, एस उत्तरवादे इह माणवाणं वियाहिए ।
एत्थोवरए तं झोसमाणे आयाणिज्जं परिण्णाय परियाएण विगिंचइ ।

“To live by the command is my dharma”: this is the highest teaching given to human beings here. Settled in it, wearing karma away, understanding what binds, he removes it through the life of a monk.
6.5.2 · What to teach, and to whom

दयं लोगस्स जाणित्ता पाईणं पडीणं दाहिणं उदीणं आइक्खे विभए किट्टए वेयवी ।
से उट्ठिएसु वा अणुट्ठिएसु वा सुस्सूसमाणेसु पवेयए- संतिं विरइं उवसमं णिव्वाणं सोयं अज्जवियं मद्दवियं लाघवियं अणइवत्तियं सव्वेसिं पाणाणं सव्वेसिं भूयाणं सव्वेसिं जीवाणं सव्वेसिं सत्ताणं, अणुवीइ भिक्खू धम्ममाइक्खेज्जा ।

Out of compassion for the world, the one who knows should teach in the east, west, south and north, explain in detail and praise the dharma. To all who wish to hear, whether they already practise or not, he should teach peace, restraint, calm, liberation, purity, straightforwardness, gentleness, lightness and not overstepping (non-violence). Thinking of the good of all living beings, all creatures, all souls and all sentient beings, the monk should teach the dharma.
6.5.6 · The front line of the battle

कायस्स वियाघाए एस संगामसीसे वियाहिए । से हु पारंगमे मुणी । अवि हम्ममाणे फलगावतट्ठी कालोवणीए कंखेज्ज कालं जाव सरीरभेउ । त्ति बेमि ।

Letting the body go is called the front line of the battle. That sage truly reaches the far shore. Even if he is struck, he stays steady like a plank of wood; when death draws near he waits for it calmly until the body falls away. Thus I say.
Checked against the scans: 6.1.3 and continued · 6.2.2 · 6.2.5 · 6.5.2 and continued · 6.5.6

09_modules/acharang_1_07_great_comprehen.title: Module · Acharang 1.7: Great Comprehension
09_modules/acharang_1_07_great_comprehen.content:
Acharang 1.7 · Mahaparijna (મહાપરિજ્ઞા): Great Comprehension
In one line: this seventh chapter is lost; the book gives only its name, what it is believed to have taught (seeing clearly the faults born of delusion and giving them up), and why it was left out when the scriptures were written down.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 7 (no sutras survive; the book says it had 7 sections), translated pages 329–330 (data/translations/acharang-1/). 4 minutes.
What the chapter teaches
The book prints no text for this chapter. Everything below is what its two-page introduction says about it.

The name means knowing deeply and letting go. “Mahaparijna” means knowing the faults that arise from delusion through great, special knowledge, and giving them up through the understanding that renounces. In practice it means taking up the great vows, the careful practices (samiti) and restraints (gupti), bearing hardships, conquering the senses and passions, austerity, study and self-examination, so as to destroy deluding karma (p.329).
The Niryukti explains the word and its last verse gives the theme. The Acharanga Niryukti, as it survives, explains “maha” and “parijna” and the kinds of parijna. Its last verse says the monk should bear the trials of attraction to heavenly and human women and give them up in mind, speech and body; that giving-up is called Mahaparijna (p.329).
The chapter had seven sections and is now lost. Its name is mentioned in the Samavayanga Sutra. From old commentaries it seems to have dealt mostly with trials caused by heavenly and human women and other situations that stir up delusion, teaching the monk to stay completely unmoved (p.329).
It may also have held special powers. By one old account it also contained formulas for powers such as moving through the sky, kept to protect monks in times of unbearable trouble. The Avashyaka Niryukti verse below and the Prabhavakacharita both say that Arya Vajraswami drew the sky-travel power from it (p.329).
Why it was left out. Judging it unfit to write down, because it described what stirs up delusion and contained special powers, Devarddhigani Kshamashramana, with the agreement of other learned monks, let it drop when the scriptures were put in writing. The book argues that the acharyas kept the right to edit the texts at that time, since written texts spread without limit while oral learning stays contained (pp.329–330).
The evidence for when it was dropped. The Niryukti author, Bhadrabahu II, lived only 40–50 years after Devarddhigani; he names the chapter and its seven sections but quotes no sutra, meaning or commentary from it. So the book concludes it had already been dropped when the scriptures were written. The Churni author followed the Niryukti, and the commentator Shilankacharya says only that it was discontinued (p.330).
A parallel case, and the book’s regret. The book compares the Prashnavyakarana Sutra, whose present contents do not match the descriptions of it in the Nandi, Thananga and Samavayanga, because such editorial changes were not recorded. It ends with sorrow that so fine a chapter has passed entirely out of sight (p.330).

Key passages
No sutra of this chapter survives. The one Prakrit line the book quotes is a verse from the Avashyaka Niryukti, cited as evidence of what the chapter held.
Avashyaka Niryukti v.769 · Arya Vajra and the Mahaparijna

जेणुद्धरिया विज्जा आगाससमा महापरिण्णाओ ।
वंदामि अज्जवइरं अपच्छिमो जो सुयधराणं ॥ ७६९ ॥

I bow to Arya Vajra, who drew out from the Mahaparijna the power of moving through the sky. The book does not explain the last phrase, about his place among the holders of scripture (unclear in the source). It takes the verse only as showing that Vajraswami drew certain powers from this chapter.
Checked against the scans: v.769 · p.330

09_modules/acharang_1_08_liberation.title: Module · Acharang 1.8: Liberation
09_modules/acharang_1_08_liberation.content:
Acharang 1.8 · Vimoksha (વિમોક્ષ): Liberation
In one line: a monk frees himself step by step, from loose company, from food and lodging made for him, from clothes, from the help of others and from the taste of food, until, when the body can no longer carry restraint, he gives it up calmly in one of three ways of dying in equanimity, wanting neither life nor death.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 8 (30 sutras in sections 1–7 and 25 verses in section 8, 8 sections), translated pages 331–397 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (8.2.3 = section 2, sutra 3). 16 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Liberation (vimoksha) means release from delusion and karma. The introduction explains that release from a shackle is material release; release from the passions and from karma is spiritual release. It grows by degrees, from the person with right faith to the monk, and is complete in the perfected ones. The three ways of dying in equanimity (bhakta-pratyakhyana, ingita-marana, padapopagamana) are also called liberation because they lead to it (introduction, pp.331–332).
Keep dealings over food and requisites few. A monk should not, without a purpose and with great show of regard, give food, clothes, bowls or service to other monks outside his own eating circle. The commentary says this is to cut down outward business, not to breed dislike; for a sick, weak or helpless monk, giving and serving are allowed (8.1.1, 8.2.4). To a well-conducted monk of the same observance he gives and serves with respect (8.2.5).
Do not accept invitations from ascetics of other faiths, and do not be caught in one-sided views. Some ascetics harm beings, take what is not given, and argue that the world is eternal or not, has an end or not, that there is hell or no hell, each claiming his own way frees from karma. Their teaching is not well stated as the Lord’s is. With a quarrelsome opponent the monk guards his speech or keeps silent (8.1.2–4).
Dharma is giving up sin, in any place and at any age. All views accept some sin; going beyond it is the great discernment. Dharma is “neither in the village nor in the forest” but in the soul, and people have woken up in all three stages of life. So the wise one neither harms the six kinds of living beings, nor has them harmed, nor approves of it (8.1.5–6).
Refuse food or lodging made for you, even if it costs you a beating. If a householder cooks, buys, borrows or seizes food, or builds a dwelling, for the monk, the monk politely refuses: “I have renounced such activity.” If the giver, angered, strikes him or orders him beaten, the steadfast monk endures it, and then either explains monks’ conduct to someone ready to listen or stays silent (8.2.1–3).
Take only what the body needs for restraint, and do not warm yourself at a fire. Some take up the monk’s life in middle age, the age the commentary calls generally the best for it. The body grows by food and is broken by hardship, so the monk knows the right time, his strength and the right measure (8.3.1–2). A monk shivering with cold tells the kind householder that the senses do not trouble him, he simply cannot bear the cold, yet he may not light a fire or have one lit for him (8.3.3).
Fewer clothes, more lightness. Sections 4 to 7 describe monks who vow to keep three garments, two, one, or none but a waist-cloth. Such a monk does not ask for one more, does not wash or dye his cloth, and as summer comes he lets worn-out cloth go. “Attaining lightness, he becomes endowed with austerity” is the refrain of every vow (8.4.1–2, 8.5.1–2, 8.6.1, 8.7.1–2).
A hard exception, stated for the sake of celibacy. Section 4 says that if a monk is trapped by a woman’s advances and cannot otherwise keep his vow, it is better for him to give up his life than to break celibacy, and calls that death timely and freeing. The commentary explains it as an emergency exception, not the rule; the rule is the slow, prepared death of the wise (8.4.3, commentary pp.361–362).
Stand on your own: refuse food brought to you, choose how you will give and take service, know you are alone, and do not chase taste. A weak monk still refuses food a householder brings to his lodging (8.5.3). Monks may vow, in four set ways, whether they will fetch food for fellow monks and whether they will accept it; illness and spare food allow set exceptions (8.5.4, 8.7.3). A monk who thinks “I am alone; no one is mine and I am no one’s” knows himself as alone (8.6.2). He does not move a morsel from cheek to cheek to savour it (8.6.3).
When the body fails, three ways of dying in equanimity. First the monk reduces food and thins the passions (sallekhana), then he lies on a grass bed in a clean, lifeless place. In bhakta-pratyakhyana he gives up food (8.5.5); in ingita-marana he also refuses all help and moves only inside a fixed area (8.6.4, 8.8.12–18); in padapopagamana, the highest, he lies still like a tree, renouncing body, activity and movement (8.7.4, 8.8.19–25). Section 8 puts it in verse: do not long to live or to die, let creatures feed on the body without driving them off, see that “the hardships are in the body, not in me”, and refuse even the pleasures a god may offer (8.8.1–25).

Key passages
8.1.5 · Dharma is neither in the village nor in the forest

सव्वत्थ सम्मयं पावं । तमेव उवाइकम्म, एस महं विवेगे वियाहिए । गामे अदुवा रण्णे, णेव गामे णेव रण्णे, धम्ममायाणह पवेइयं माहणेण मइमया । जामा तिण्णि उदाहिया जेसु इमे आयरिया संबुज्झमाणा समुट्ठिया, जे णिव्वुडा पावेहिं कम्मेहिं अणियाणा ते वियाहिया ।

Sin is accepted in some form by every view; going beyond it is the great discernment that has been declared. Dharma can be practised in a village or in a forest, yet it is neither in the village nor in the forest: know the dharma taught by the all-knowing Lord. Three stages of life are named, in each of which noble ones have woken up and taken up restraint. Those who have turned away from sinful deeds are called free of karma.
8.4.2 · Letting the worn-out cloth go

अह पुण एवं जाणेज्जा–उवाइक्कंते खलु हेमंते, गिम्हे पडिवण्णे, से अहापरिजुण्णाइं वत्थाइं परिट्ठवेज्जा, अदुवा संतरुत्तरे, अदुवा ओमचेलिए, अदुवा एगसाडे, अदुवा अचेले । लाघवियं आगममाणे । तवे से अभिसमण्णागए भवइ। जहेयं भगवया पवेइयं तमेव अभिसमेच्चा सव्वओ सव्वत्ताए सम्मत्तमेव समभिजाणिज्जा ।

When he knows that winter has passed and summer has come, he should lay aside the garments that have worn out: keeping three, or fewer, or a single cloth, or none. Attaining lightness, he gains austerity as well. Understanding this just as the Lord taught it, he should know it rightly, fully and in every way.
8.6.2 · I am alone

जस्स णं भिक्खुस्स एवं भवइ– एगो अहमंसि, ण मे अत्थि कोइ, ण याहमवि कस्सइ । एवं से एगागिणमेव अप्पाणं समभिजाणेज्जा । लाघवियं आगममाणे तवे से अभिसमण्णागए भवइ । जहेयं भगवया पवेइयं तमेव अभिसमेच्चा सव्वओ सव्वत्ताए सम्मत्तमेव समभिजाणिज्जा ।

A monk to whom this thought comes, “I am alone; no one is mine, and I am no one’s”, should know himself as truly alone. Attaining lightness, he gains austerity. Understanding this just as the Lord taught it, he should know it rightly, fully and in every way.
8.8.4 · Want neither life nor death

जीवियं णाभिकंखेज्जा, मरणं णो वि पत्थए ।
दुहओ वि ण सज्जेज्जा, जीविए मरणे तहा ॥

He should not long to live, nor wish to die. He should cling to neither, life or death.
8.8.5 · Seek the purity within

मज्झत्थो णिज्जरापेही, समाहिमणुपालए ।
अंतो बहिं विउसिज्ज, अज्झत्थं सुद्धमेसए ॥

Even-minded and intent on shedding karma, he should keep his inner composure (samadhi). Letting go of what is inside (the passions) and what is outside (the body and its things), he should seek the purity of the inner self.
8.8.21 · The hardships are in the body, not in me

अचित्तं तु समासज्ज, ठावए तत्थ अप्पगं ।
वोसिरे सव्वसो कायं, ण मे देहे परीसहा ॥

Having reached a place free of living beings, he should settle himself there and give up the body completely, thinking: “These hardships are in the body; they are not mine.”
Checked against the scans: 8.1.5 · 8.4.2 · 8.6.2 · 8.8.4–5 · 8.8.21
