09_modules/acharang_1_09_mahaviras_pract.title: Module · Acharang 1.9: Mahavira's Practice
09_modules/acharang_1_09_mahaviras_pract.content:
Acharang 1.9 · Upadhana-shruta (ઉપધાનશ્રુત): Mahavira’s Practice
In one line: the chapter shows that everything the earlier chapters ask of a monk, Lord Mahavira himself lived out, wandering without clothes or shelter, silent, beaten and set upon by dogs, fasting and meditating for some twelve and a half years without a single lapse into negligence.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 1 (First Shrutaskandha), chapter 9 (70 verses, 4 sections), translated pages 398–436 (data/translations/acharang-1/). The book numbers the verses afresh in each section, so references below read section.verse (9.3.8 = section 3, verse 8). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

“Upadhana” is the support of austerity, and this is the account heard of the Lord’s own practice. The introduction says spiritual upadhana is knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity, and that upadhana also means shaking off karma, as water washes a cloth. The chapter was written so that a practitioner is sure the earlier rules are not imagination but were lived by Mahavira (introduction, pp.398–399).
He went forth in winter and soon gave up even his one cloth. “As I have heard it, I shall tell”: the Lord took initiation in the cold season and left at once. He resolved not to wrap himself in the divine garment placed on his shoulder; he kept it, as earlier Tirthankaras had, for thirteen months and then let it go and lived unclothed. For over four months bees and other creatures, drawn by the fragrance on his body, crawled on him and stung him (9.1.1–4, 9.1.22).
He walked with eyes on the path and said nothing. He watched the ground a man’s length ahead, and children, frightened of his fixed gaze, gathered and shouted “Strike him!” He did not look sideways or behind and did not answer when spoken to. He did not engage with women who came to him, did not mix with householders, did not reply even to greetings, and so was sometimes struck with sticks by people who took offence (9.1.5–10, 9.1.21).
Even before initiation he lived as a renouncer. For a little more than two years he stayed at home without drinking cold, unboiled water, living alone in thought, giving up care of the body, calm. The commentary says he stayed those two years at his elder brother Nandivardhana’s request after their parents’ death (9.1.11).
He knew all six kinds of beings to be living and harmed none. Earth, water, fire, air, plants and moving beings all have life; stationary beings can be born as moving ones and moving ones as stationary, each by its own karma. Seeing this, he gave up all violence, done, caused or approved, and saw that possessions bring suffering (9.1.12–17).
He ate only pure food and wanted nothing for the body. He did not eat food made for him, did not use a householder’s cloth or bowl, knew the measure of food, was not greedy for taste, did not even wipe his eye or scratch his body (9.1.18–20). “This is the way the wise, desireless Lord followed” closes each section (9.1.23).
He stayed wherever he could, and slept little. Empty houses, assembly halls, water-sheds, shops, workshops, rest-houses, garden houses, cremation grounds and the foot of trees served him for nearly thirteen years, striving day and night. He did not sleep much; he woke himself, sometimes walking outside at night to throw off drowsiness (9.2.1–6).
Snakes, birds, thieves, guards and angry people afflicted him; he stayed silent and calm. Asked “Who is in here?”, he would answer “I am a monk”, or keep silent, taking this as the highest dharma, and bore their anger without any thought of revenge. In bitter winter, when other ascetics wrapped themselves up or lit fires, he stood in an open shelter, sometimes going out at night to stand in meditation (9.2.7–16).
In the Ladha country he was beaten and set upon by dogs. In that hard, remote land the people struck him with sticks, fists, spears, clods and potsherds, tore his flesh, threw dust on him, lifted him and dashed him down; few held back the dogs and many urged them on. Other ascetics there carried sticks against dogs; he laid aside all violence and gave up care of the body, and went through it all like an elephant at the front of battle (9.3.1–14).
His austerity, alms-round and meditation. Healthy, he still ate less than his fill and took no medicine; he gave up purges, oiling, bathing, massage and cleaning his teeth. For eight months he lived on rice, ground meal and pulses; he fasted for half a month, a month, over two months, up to six months without water (9.4.1–7). He sought alms so as not to disturb hungry crows or other beggars, took whatever came, and meditated in steady postures, free of passion; in all that time “he did not commit negligence even once” (9.4.8–17).

Key passages
9.1.12–13 · All six kinds of beings are alive

पुढविं च आउकायं च, तेउकायं च वायुकायं च ।
पणगाइं बीयहरियाइं, तसकायं च सव्वसो णच्चा ॥
एयाइं संति पडिलेहे, चितमंताइ से अभिण्णाय ।
परिवज्जियाण विहरित्था, इति संखाय से महावीरे ॥

Knowing fully the earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied and air-bodied beings, moulds and fungus, seeds and green plants, and moving beings; seeing that all these exist and knowing them to be living, Mahavira understood this and wandered having given up harming them.
9.1.21 · Eyes on the path

अप्पं तिरियं पेहाए, अप्पं पिट्ठओ उ पेहाए ।
अप्पं बुइए अपडिभाणी, पंथपेही चरे जयमाणे ॥

He did not look to the side, nor look behind. Silent, not answering even when spoken to, he walked with care, watching the path.
9.2.4 · Nearly thirteen years, day and night

एतेहिं मुणी सयणेहिं, समणे आसि पतेरस वासे ।
राइंदिवं पि जयमाणे, अप्पमत्ते समाहिए झाइ ॥

In these resting places the sage, the Shramana, lived for nearly thirteen years. Striving day and night, free of negligence and composed, he meditated.
9.3.7–8 · Like an elephant at the front of battle

णिहाय दंडं पाणेहिं, तं वोसिज्ज कायमणगारे ।
अह गामकंटए भगवं, ते अहियासए अभिसमेच्चा ॥
णागो संगामसीसे वा, पारए तत्थ से महावीरे ।
एवं पि तत्थ लाढेहिं, अलद्धपुव्वो वि एगया गामो ॥

Laying aside all violence toward living beings and giving up care for his own body, the homeless Lord bore the villagers’ thorn-sharp words and blows, knowing them to shed karma. Like an elephant at the front of a battle, Mahavira went through to the far side. Even so, in Ladha, at times he did not reach even a village.
9.4.15 · Not negligent even once

अकसायी विगयगेही य सद्द-रूवेसु अमुच्छिए झाइ ।
छउमत्थे विप्परक्कममाणे, ण पमायं सइं पि कुव्वित्था ॥

Free of passions, free of craving, not infatuated by sounds, forms and the like, he meditated. Striving hard while still not omniscient (chhadmastha), he did not fall into negligence (pramada) even once.
Checked against the scans: 9.1.12–13 · 9.1.21 · 9.2.4 · 9.3.7–8 · 9.4.15

09_modules/acharang_2_01_seeking_alms.title: Module · Acharang 2.1: Seeking Alms
09_modules/acharang_2_01_seeking_alms.content:
Acharang 2.1 · Pindaishana (પિંડૈષણા): Seeking Alms
In one line: a monk or nun accepts only food and water that is free of life and free of faults, taken without greed, deceit or harm to anyone, and eats it with equanimity, because how the food is sought decides whether the restraint it feeds stays pure.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 1 (105 sutras, 11 sections), translated pages 71–163 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (1.3.5 = section 3, sutra 5). Every section closes with the same refrain: “this is the whole of the monk’s or nun’s conduct; endowed with the careful practices (samiti), let them always strive.” 25 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Food must be both lifeless and faultless. The commentary names two tests: the food must be free of life (prasuka) and free of the faults of seeking (eshaniya). Food touched by insects, moss, seeds, green plants, raw water or living dust is refused; if taken by mistake, the living things are picked out in a secluded place, and what cannot be cleaned is laid down on lifeless ground. Whole or under-roasted grain that can still sprout is refused; split or well-roasted grain is accepted (1.1.1–3).
No food made or bought for monks. Food cooked, bought, borrowed, snatched, taken without the owner’s leave or carried in for one monk or nun, or for many, is never accepted, even after others have eaten from it. Food made for “shramanas, brahmins, guests, the poor and beggars” in general may be taken only once it has passed to someone else, been taken out or been eaten from. The monk does not go for alms with followers of other faiths, householders or lax monks, avoids families famous for giving daily charity, and goes to ordinary, blameless families. If he hears devout people say “let us give them our own food and cook again for ourselves”, or sees a relative start cooking for him, he refuses, and he says so at once instead of keeping quiet and refusing later; nor does he visit his relatives’ homes before alms time (1.1.4–11, 1.2.2, 1.9.1–3).
Stay away from festivals and feasts. At festival meals served to crowds of beggars the monk waits until the giving is done, then asks a family member. He does not even plan to go to a feast (sankhadi) more than half a yojana away; he turns the other way. The commentary lists the harms: craving for taste, food made specially for him, sickness from rich food, jostling crowds, drink and sexual danger, and the deceit of loitering near a feast house. Only an uncrowded feast, on a clear path, may be visited, as an exception (1.2.1–5, 1.3.1–4, 1.4.1).
Doubt means no. If the monk is unsure whether food is acceptable, he does not take it. He carries his needed requisites, does not go out in rain, fog, dust storms or swarms of insects, and does not take food from the houses of crowned kings (1.3.5–8).
Do not make the householder’s work harder. He does not enter while cows are being milked or food is still cooking; he waits out of sight. He does not hurry for the first portion set aside for charity, does not take a straight path that is broken, blocked by fierce animals or full of feeding birds, does not open a closed gate without permission, and does not stand where other beggars can see him and be crowded out (1.4.2, 1.5.1–6, 1.6.1).
Dignity at the door. He does not lean on the doorframe, stand near the washing or bathing place, peer into the house, point with his finger, flatter the giver, or speak harshly when refused. If the giver washes a hand or ladle with raw water to serve him, or fans hot food, he asks them not to, and refuses if they do (1.6.2–7, 1.7.6).
Food resting on living things is refused. Food fetched down by ladder from a height, dug out of a deep jar, taken from a clay-sealed pot, or placed on earth, water, fire, plants or creatures is refused, because the householder may fall or harm the six kinds of living beings. Raw, uncut vegetables, fruit, sprouts, garlic and seeds “untouched by a weapon” are refused; wash-water is accepted only when its taste and colour have changed (1.7.1–10, 1.8.1–16).
No deceit about food. Sending visiting monks to other villages so as to eat first at one’s own relatives’ homes, eating the good portions and throwing away the plain, keeping a shared gift for oneself, giving choice pieces to favourites, hiding tasty food under plain food, or eating on the way back are all called “a station of deceit” (maya-sthana). Extra food is offered first to nearby fellow monks. Not relishing smells is also taught here (1.4.3, 1.5.7, 1.8.2, 1.9.4–7, 1.10.1–3).
Honesty when things go wrong. If something unwanted, such as salt given in place of sugar, is accepted by mistake, the monk goes back and asks the giver whether it was given knowingly. Food meant for another person is taken only with that person’s leave. Food with much waste (bony fruit, cane pieces, shells) is refused (1.9.8, 1.10.4–7).
Serve the sick truthfully, and take vows without pride. A monk carrying good food for a sick monk must not run it down as bitter or sour to keep it for himself. The chapter ends with the seven ways of seeking food and seven of seeking water, from “clean hand, clean vessel” to “food others throw away”, taken as personal vows; whoever takes one must not say “they are wrong, I alone am right” (1.11.1–11).

Key passages
1.1.1 · Food touched by living things

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गाहावइकुलं पिंडवायपडियाए अणुपविट्ठे समाणे से जं पुण जाणेज्जा– असणं वा पाणं वा खाइमं वा साइमं वा; पाणेहिं वा पणएहिं वा बीएहिं वा हरिएहिं वा; संसत्तं, उम्मिस्सं, सीओदएण वा ओसित्तं, रयसा वा परिघासियं; तहप्पगारं असणं वा पाणं वा खाइमं वा साइमं वा; परहत्थंसि वा परपायंसि वा अफासुयं अणेसणिज्जं ति मण्णमाणे लाभे वि संते णो पडिगाहेज्जा ।

When a monk or nun has entered a householder’s home for alms and sees that the food, drink, snacks or relishes are touched or mixed with small creatures, moss, seeds or green plants, sprinkled with raw water or covered with living dust, then, whether it is in the giver’s hand or vessel, knowing it to be living and unacceptable, they should not accept it even when it is offered.
1.3.5 · When in doubt, do not take

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गाहावइकुलं पिंडवायपडियाए अणुपविट्ठे समाणे से जं पुण जाणेज्जा– असणं वा पाणं वा खाइमं वा साइमं वा एसणिज्जे सिया, अणेसणिज्जे सिया ? वितिगिंछासमावण्णेण अप्पाणेणं असमाहडाए लेस्साए तहप्पगारं असणं वा पाणं वा खाइमं वा साइमं वा लाभे संते णो पडिगाहेज्जा।

If a monk or nun, in a householder’s home, wonders, “Is this food acceptable, or is it not?”, then with the mind in doubt and unsettled they should not accept that food, even when it is offered.
1.9.5 · Eat the good with the plain

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गाहावईकुलं पिंडवाय पडियाए पविट्ठे समाणे अण्णयरं भोयणजायं पडिगाहेत्ता सुब्भिं-सुब्भि भोच्चा दुब्भिं-दुब्भि परिट्ठवेइ। माइट्ठाणं संफासे । णो एवं करेज्जा । सुब्भि वा दुब्भि वा सव्वं भुंजे ण छड्डए ।

If a monk or nun accepts some food, eats the tasty parts and throws away the poor parts, that is deceit. They should not do this. Good or poor, they should eat all of it and throw nothing away.
1.10.2 · Hide nothing in the bowl

से एगइओ मणुण्णं भोयणजायं पडिगाहेत्ता पंतेण भोयणेण पलिच्छाएइ मामेयं दाइयं संतं; दट्टूणं सयमाइए; तं जहा– आयरिए वा जाव गणावच्छेइए वा । णो खलु मे कस्सइ किंचि वि दायव्वं सिया । माइट्ठाणं संफासे । णो एवं करेज्जा ।
से तमायाए तत्थ गच्छेज्जा, गच्छेत्ता पुव्वामेव उत्ताणए हत्थे पडिग्गहं कट्टु इमं खलु इमं खलु त्ति आलोएज्जा । णो किंचि वि णिगूहेज्जा ।

A monk receives fine food and covers it with plain food, thinking, “If the acharya or the other elders see it, they will take it for themselves; I should not have to give any of it to anyone.” That is deceit; he should not do it. He should take the food to them, hold the bowl up on his open hand and show it: “This is here, and this is here.” He should hide nothing at all.
1.11.11 · No pride in one’s vow

इच्चेयासिं सत्तण्हं पिंडेसणाणं सत्तण्हं पाणेसणाणं अण्णयरं पडिमं पडिवज्जमाणे णो एवं वएज्जा– मिच्छा पडिवण्णा खलु एए भयंतारो, अहमेगे सम्मं पडिवण्णे ।
जे एए भयंतारो एयाओ पडिमाओ पडिवज्जित्ताणं विहरंति, जो य अहमंसि एयं पडिमं पडिवज्जित्ताणं विहरामि; सव्वे ते उ जिणाणाए उवट्ठिया अण्णोण्णसमाहीए; एवं च णं विहरंति ।

Whoever takes up any one of these seven ways of seeking food or seven ways of seeking water should not say, “These revered monks have taken it up wrongly; I alone have taken it up rightly.” Rather: “Those revered monks who live by these vows, and I who live by this one, are all standing in the Jina’s command, each according to his own peace of mind.” This is how they live.
Checked against the scans: 1.1.1 · 1.3.5 · 1.9.5 · 1.10.2 · 1.11.11

09_modules/acharang_2_02_seeking_lodging.title: Module · Acharang 2.2: Seeking Lodging
09_modules/acharang_2_02_seeking_lodging.content:
Acharang 2.2 · Shayyaishana (શય્યૈષણા): Seeking Lodging
In one line: just as a monk seeks faultless food, he seeks a faultless place to stay, one not built or repaired for him, free of living creatures and of householders’ life, asked for with permission and returned with care, and he stays in it with equanimity whether it is good or bad.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 2 (63 sutras, 3 sections), translated pages 164–207 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read section.sutra (2.3.30 = section 3, sutra 30). “Lodging” (shayya) here means the whole dwelling where monks stand, sleep, sit and study, and also the plank or grass bed they use (introduction, p. 164). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

First, a place free of creatures. A lodging full of eggs, insects or cobwebs is not used for standing, sleeping or sitting. A clear one is used only after inspecting (pratilekhana) and sweeping (pramarjana) it. A hut of grass or straw is judged the same way (2.1.1, 2.2.5).
Not built for monks. A lodging built, bought, borrowed, seized or set up for one or many Jain monks or nuns, or for a counted list of shramanas and beggars that includes them, is never used. One built for wanderers in general may be used once others have lived in it (2.1.2–4).
Not repaired for monks, until others have used it. If the householder has walled, thatched, plastered, polished or perfumed the place for the monk, widened its doors, or moved out plants, stools and tools, the monk may not stay until someone else has lived there. The commentary explains why lodging differs from food: a building is used again and again, so once others use it, the chain of fault ends (2.1.5–8).
Not high up and open on all sides. A loft, platform or roof is used only in serious need, and there the monk does not wash or relieve himself, because he could slip and hurt himself and other living beings (2.1.9).
Not shared with a householder’s family. A lodging with women, children, animals and food in it is avoided. Living there, a sick monk may be oiled, bathed and warmed by a fire lit for him; quarrels, fires, jewellery and adorned young women stir his mind; women wanting a strong son may tempt him; householders’ habits of washing clash with his; they cook and fetch firewood for him; and if a thief slips in when he opens the door at night, he is suspected either way (2.1.10–15, 2.2.1–4).
Not where wanderers keep coming and going, and not beyond the time allowed. Staying on after a month’s stay or the monsoon stay, or coming back before twice and three times that period has passed, are faults (2.2.6–8).
Nine kinds of lodging “action” (kriya). Of the buildings faithful people put up, two are faultless: one already used by other wanderers (abhikranta) and one the householder built for himself (alpa-savadya, “one-sided”: the monk is a monk both outwardly and inwardly). A building made for monks with great harm to the six kinds of beings makes the monk “two-sided”, a monk in dress and a householder within (2.2.7–15).
Ask properly, and take nothing from the host. A faultless lodging is hard to find. The monk asks the owner or caretaker for the time and the space he allows, learns the owner’s name and family, and never accepts food from that house. He avoids houses where people quarrel, oil and bathe each other, go naked, or where the walls are painted with figures. In a small, dark lodging he feels his way, “first with the hand, then with the foot” (2.3.1–12).
The plank or grass bed. It must be free of creatures, light, returnable and sturdy. Four vows govern it: ask for a named kind, ask only for what is seen, use only what is already in the lodging, or use only what is already spread; if none is found, the vowed monk sits through the night. Borrowed bedding is cleaned, sunned and shaken before it is returned (2.3.13–24).
Care in sleep, and equanimity. The monk inspects the ground for excreta first; lays his bed only after the acharya, elders, the young, old, sick and guest monks have taken their places; does not let his hand, foot or body touch another monk’s; and covers his mouth when he coughs, sneezes or yawns. Even or uneven, windy or still, dusty or clean, full of mosquitoes or not, he lives there without the least dejection (2.3.25–31).

Key passages
2.1.1 · A place free of living beings

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा अभिकंखेज्जा उवस्सयं एसित्तए, से अणुपविसित्ता गामं वा णगरं वा जाव रायहाणिं वा; से जं पुण उवस्सयं जाणेज्जा– सअंडं सपाणं जाव संताणयं, तहप्पगारे उवस्सए णो ठाणं वा सेज्जं वा णिसीहियं वा चेएज्जा ।
से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा से जं उवस्सयं जाणेज्जा– अप्पंडं जाव संताणयं, तहप्पगारे उवस्सए पडिलेहित्ता पमज्जित्ता तओ संजयामेव ठाणं वा सेज्जं वा, णिसीहियं वा चेएज्जा ।

A monk or nun who wishes to seek a lodging enters a village, town or capital. If they find a lodging full of eggs, creatures and cobwebs, they should not stand, sleep or sit in it. If they find one free of eggs and cobwebs, they should inspect it and sweep it, and only then, with care, stand, sleep or sit there.
2.1.10 · Not among householders

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा से जं पुण उवस्सयं जाणेज्जा– सइत्थियं सखुड्डं सपसुभत्तपाणं; तहप्पगारे सागारिए उवस्सए णो ठाणं वा सेज्जं वा णिसीहियं वा चेएज्जा ।

If a monk or nun finds that a lodging has women, children and small creatures, animals, and food and drink in it, they should not stand, sleep or sit in such a lodging shared with householders.
2.2.7 · Staying too long

से आगंतारेसु वा जाव परियावसहेसु वा जे भयंतारो उडुबद्धियं वा वासावासियं वा कप्पं उवाइणावित्ता तत्थेव भुज्जो-भुज्जो संवसंति, अयमाउसो कालाइक्कंतकिरिया यावि भवइ ।

Revered monks who, in rest-houses or wanderers’ hermitages, complete the month’s stay or the monsoon stay and then go on living there again and again: this, O long-lived one, is the fault of overstaying the time (kalatikranta kriya).
2.3.3 · Asking for a lodging

से आगंतारेसु वा आरामागारेसु वा, गाहावइकुलेसु वा, परियावसहेसु वा अणुवीई उवस्सयं जाएज्जा । जे तत्थ ईसरे, जे तत्थ समहिट्ठाए; ते उवस्सयं अणुण्णवेज्जा– कामं खलु आउसो ! अहालंदं अहापरिण्णायं वसिस्सामो जाव आउसंतो जाव आउसंतस्स उवस्सए जाव साहम्मिया, एतावताव उवस्सयं गिण्हिस्सामो, तेण परं विहरिस्सामो ।

Having thought it over, the monk asks for a lodging in a rest-house, garden house, family home or hermitage. He asks permission of the owner or the one in charge: “O long-lived one, as you wish: for as long as you allow and in as much space as you give, we shall stay, as many fellow monks as we are. Only that much of the lodging shall we take; after that we shall move on.”
2.3.28 · Not touching one another in sleep

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा बहुफासुए सेज्जासंथारए सयमाणे णो अण्णमण्णस्स हत्थेण हत्थं, पाएण पायं, काएण कायं आसाएज्जा । से अणासायमाणे तओ संजयामेव बहुफासुए सेज्जासंथारए सएज्जा ।

A monk or nun sleeping on a clean bed should not touch another’s hand with a hand, foot with a foot, or body with a body, which would be disrespect. Without giving offence, they should sleep with care on the clean bed.
2.3.30 · Equanimity in any lodging

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा समा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, विसमा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, पवाया वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, णिवाया वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, ससरक्खा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, अप्पससरक्खा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, सदंस-मसगा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, अप्पदंस-मसगा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, सपरिसाडा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, अपरिसाडा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, सउवसग्गा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, णिरुवसग्गा वेगया सेज्जा भवेज्जा, तहप्पगाराहिं सेज्जाहिं संविज्जमाणाहिं पग्गहियतरागं विहारं विहरेज्जा । णो किंचि वि गिलाएज्जा ।

Sometimes a monk or nun gets an even lodging, sometimes an uneven one; sometimes windy, sometimes still; sometimes dusty, sometimes nearly free of dust; sometimes full of gnats and mosquitoes, sometimes nearly free of them; sometimes crumbling, sometimes sound; sometimes troubled, sometimes untroubled. Whatever lodging they get, they should live there with firm resolve and not feel the slightest dejection. The commentary adds the monk’s thought: “What can one night do?”
(The print reads अप्पससरक्खा, kept as printed; the sense, “with little dust”, fits अप्पसरक्खा, and the extra स may be a misprint.)
Checked against the scans: 2.1.1 · 2.1.10 · 2.2.7 · 2.3.3 · 2.3.28 · 2.3.30

09_modules/acharang_2_03_careful_walking.title: Module · Acharang 2.3: Careful Walking
09_modules/acharang_2_03_careful_walking.content:
Acharang 2.3 · Irya (ઈર્યા): Careful Walking
In one line: a monk or nun walks only to serve restraint, stays in one place through the rains and wanders the rest of the year, watches the ground so that no living being is hurt, and meets rivers, boatmen, soldiers, hunters, wild animals and robbers with silence, care and an unshaken calm.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 3 (56 sutras, 3 sections), translated pages 208–238 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (3.2.3 = section 2, sutra 3). 14 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Walking with care (irya samiti) has four parts. The introduction says a monk walks only for a proper purpose (serving the order, knowledge, faith and conduct), only in daylight, only on a fit path, and only with care for the six kinds of living beings. Like food and lodging, walking is needed to keep the body that carries restraint (introduction, p.208).
In the rains, stay in one place; after the rains, move on. When the rains come, the paths fill with small creatures, new sprouts and webs, so the monk stops wandering and settles for the four months. He picks a place with room for study and for relieving himself, where boards and bedding and pure alms are easy to get and the place is not crowded with other beggars. When the four months and a few days more have passed and the paths are clear, he wanders again; if the paths are still full of life, he waits (3.1.1–5).
Look a yoke’s length ahead and step around life. On the road the monk looks ahead about three and a half cubits. Seeing small creatures, he lengthens, shortens or turns his step, and takes another path if there is one, rather than going straight through seeds, greens, water or living earth (3.1.6–7).
Avoid dangerous regions and long wildernesses. If another road is open, he does not go through border lands of robbers and people who will not listen, through kingless or warring kingdoms, or through a forest that takes many days to cross. The Kevali calls this a cause of karmic bondage: he may be taken for a spy or thief and beaten or robbed, and rain on a long road breeds life he would harm (3.1.8–10).
How to cross by boat. He does not board a boat bought, borrowed, launched or bailed out for his sake. He boards a boat that crosses the river, after binding his things together, wiping his body and taking a conditional fast to death (sagari santhara). In the boat he does no work for the boatman, stays silent when told to row, bail or plug a hole, and if the boat leaks he does not raise an alarm but gives up attachment to body and goods and stays in calm absorption (samadhi) (3.1.11–19).
Thrown into the river, he stays calm. If people call him dead weight and plan to throw him over, he first says he will step into the water himself. If they throw him anyway, he feels neither pleased nor upset and does not rise to hurt them. In the water he does not thrash his limbs or dive and surface; he floats, drops his things if he tires, and on the bank waits until his body dries by itself (3.2.1–8).
No talk on the road; wading and rough ground. He does not walk while chatting. He wades only shallow water, below the knee, without touching limb to limb or bathing for comfort. He does not wipe muddy feet on green plants, avoids ditches, walls and pits where he might fall and clutch at plants, and goes round army camps, where a soldier may drag him as a spy, which he bears calmly (3.2.9–18).
Do not stare, and walk humbly with seniors. He does not point, bend and gaze at forts, palaces, shrines, lakes or forests, for animals and birds take fright. Walking with the Acharya, Upadhyaya or a senior monk, he does not jostle them and does not speak while they answer travellers’ questions (3.3.1–6).
Do not tell where the animals went. Asked by travellers about animals, plants, water, fire, grain or an army, or how big and how far a village is, he does not answer. The commentary explains that the questioner may be a hunter, and the monk would share in the killing; he stays silent, or says “I do not know” (3.2.19, 3.3.7–11).
Fearless before beasts and robbers. Seeing a fierce bull or a leopard, he does not leave the road, climb a tree or plunge into water, and seeks no shelter, army or weapon. If robbers demand his cloth or bowl, he lays it on the ground, does not beg pitifully for it back, and afterwards complains to no villager or king. The commentary says the monk is himself fearless and gives fearlessness to all beings (3.3.12–16).

Key passages
3.1.1 · Stay put when the rains come

से भिक्खु वा भिक्खुणी वा से जं पुण जाणेज्जा- अब्भुवगए खलु वासावासे अभिपवुट्ठे, बहवे पाणा अभिसंभूया, बहवे बीया अहुणुब्भिण्णा, अंतरा से मग्गा बहुपाणा बहुबीया जाव संताणगा, अणभिकंता पंथा, णो विण्णाया मग्गा, सेवं णच्चा णो गामाणुगामं दूइज्जेज्जा, तओ संजयामेव वासावासं उवल्लिएज्जा ।

When a monk or nun sees that the rainy season has come and rain has fallen, that many creatures have been born and many seeds have just sprouted, that the roads are full of living beings, seeds and webs, untrodden and hard to make out, then he or she should not wander from village to village, but should settle carefully for the rainy-season stay.
3.1.6 · Look a yoke’s length ahead

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गामाणुगामं दुइज्जमाणे पुरओ जुगमायं पेहमाणे, दट्ठूण तसे पाणे, उद्धट्टु पायं रीएज्जा, साहट्टु पायं रीएज्जा, उक्खिप्प पायं रीएज्जा, तिरिच्छं वा कट्टु पायं रीएज्जा, सइ परक्कमे संजयामेव परक्कमेज्जा, णो उज्जुयं गच्छेज्जा, तओ संजयामेव गामाणुगामं दुइज्जेज्जा ।

Wandering from village to village, the monk or nun looks ahead a yoke’s length. Seeing small moving creatures, he walks with a long step, a short step, a raised foot or a sideways foot. If there is another way, he takes it with care and does not go straight on; and so, with care, he wanders from village to village.
3.2.3 · Thrown into the water

से णेवं वयंतं परो सहसा बलसा बाहाहिं गहाय णावाओ उदगंसि पक्खिवेज्जा, तं णो सुमणे सिया, णो दुम्मणे सिया, णो उच्चावयं मणं णियच्छेज्जा, णो तेसिं बालाणं घायाए वहाए समुट्ठेज्जा । अप्पुस्सुए जाव समाहीए । तओ संजयामेव उदगंसि पवेज्जा ।

If, even while he says this, someone suddenly and by force seizes him by the arms and throws him from the boat into the water, he should be neither pleased nor displeased, should not let his mind swing high and low, and should not rise up to hurt or kill those ignorant people. Free of agitation, steady in calm absorption, he should float carefully in the water.
3.3.7 · Silence before the hunter

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गामाणुगामं दूइज्जमाणे अंतरा से पाडिपहिया आगच्छेज्जा, ते णं पाडिपहिया एवं वएज्जा- आउसंतो समणा ! अवियाइं एत्तो पडिपहे पासह, तं जहा- मणुस्सं वा गोणं वा महिसं वा पसुं वा पक्खिं वा सरीसवं वा जलयरं वा, से तं मे आइक्खह, दंसेह । तं णो आइक्खेज्जा, णो दंसेज्जा, णो तस्स तं परिण्णं परिजाणेज्जा, तुसिणीओ उवेहेज्जा, जाणं वा णो जाणं ति वएज्जा । तओ संजयामेव गामाणुगामं दूइजेज्जा ।

If travellers on the road ask, “Long-lived monk, did you see along this way a man, an ox, a buffalo, an animal, a bird, a reptile or a water creature? Tell us, show us,” he should not tell, should not show, should not take up the request, but stay silent; or, though he knows, he may say “I do not know.” Then he should wander on with care. The commentary gives two readings of the last phrase: in hard moments, to protect the animals, he says he does not know; normally, he simply does not say that he knows, and stays silent.
Note: the print ends this sutra with दूइजेज्जा, where every other sutra has दूइज्जेज्जा; it looks like a misprint, kept as printed.
3.3.15 · Robbed, he complains to no one

ते णं आमोसगा सयं करणिज्जं ति कट्टु अक्कोसंति वा जाव उद्दवेंति वा, वत्थं वा पायं वा कंबलं वा पायपुंछणं वा आच्छिंदेज्ज वा अवहरेज्ज वा, परिट्ठवेज्ज वा, तं णो गामसंसारियं कुज्जा, णो रायसंसारियं कुज्जा, णो परं उवसंकमित्तु बूया- आउसंतो गाहावई ! एए खलु आमोसगा उवगरणपडियाए सयं करणिज्जं ति कट्टु अक्कोसंति वा जाव परिट्ठवेंति वा । एयप्पगारं मणं वा वइं वा णो पुरओ कट्टु विहरेज्जा । अप्पुस्सुए जाव समाहीए तओ संजयामेव गामाणुगामं दूइज्जेज्जा ।

If the robbers, doing what robbers do, abuse him, beat him or try to kill him, and snatch, carry off or throw away his cloth, bowl, blanket or foot-wiper, he should not report it to the village or to the king, nor go to a householder and say, “Long-lived householder, these robbers abused me and threw away my things.” He should not even give such a thought room in mind or speech, but, free of agitation and steady in calm, wander on with care.
Checked against the scans: 3.1.1 · 3.1.6 · 3.2.3 · 3.3.7 · 3.3.15

09_modules/acharang_2_04_kinds_of_speech.title: Module · Acharang 2.4: Kinds of Speech
09_modules/acharang_2_04_kinds_of_speech.content:
Acharang 2.4 · Bhashajata (ભાષાજાત): Kinds of Speech
In one line: a monk or nun speaks only after thinking, free of anger, pride, deceit and greed, using only true or ordinary speech that is gentle and harms no being: no rash predictions, no insults, no praise that encourages violence, and no words that point a hunter or a woodcutter to his prey.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 4 (33 sutras, 2 sections), translated pages 239–259 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (4.2.19 = section 2, sutra 19). 11 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Speech is matter, and a monk mostly keeps silent. The introduction explains that speech is made of particles of speech-matter which the soul takes in and sends out as words. A monk usually keeps silence (vachana gupti); when he must speak, he speaks with care in speech (bhasha samiti), so that his words bind no karma and hurt no one. The commentary notes the chapter is very close to Dashvaikalik chapter 7 (introduction, p.239).
Do not speak from anger, pride, deceit or greed, and do not predict. Speech moved by the passions, or harsh speech, knowing or unknowing, is sinful and is to be dropped. A monk also does not speak with certainty about what will or will not happen: whether another monk will come back with food, whether someone came or will come. If he turns out wrong, people lose faith and his vow of truth is broken (4.1.1).
Know the sixteen forms of speech and use them exactly. Singular, dual and plural; feminine, masculine and neuter; inner, praising, blaming and their mixtures; past, present and future; present and absent. The monk speaks after reflection, with clear meaning, using the form the thing needs (4.1.2).
Of four kinds of speech, a monk uses two. All Tirthankaras teach four kinds: true, false, mixed, and neither true nor false (ordinary, everyday speech). Speech exists as speech only while it is being spoken. Even true speech is not to be spoken if it is sinful, harsh, bitter, cruel, cutting, divisive, tormenting or harmful to beings; a monk speaks only subtle, well-weighed truth and ordinary speech that are free of these faults (4.1.3–6).
Address people with respect, never with abuse. He does not call a man or woman “fool”, “slave’s son”, “dog”, “thief” or “liar”, or add “and your parents are the same”. He calls them by name, or “long-lived one”, “sister”, “lay follower”, “lover of dharma” (4.1.7–10).
Nature is not a god, and a monk takes no side in rain or war. He does not call the sky, cloud or lightning a god, and does not say “may it rain”, “may the crop grow”, “may the sun rise”, “may the king win”. He says plainly, “the cloud has gathered”, “the cloud has rained”. Wishing for rain approves harm to living beings, and wishing a king victory approves war (4.1.11–12).
Do not wound with true words. He does not call anyone “leper”, “diabetic”, “one-handed” or “noseless”, for such words hurt and anger. He may call people “vigorous”, “radiant”, “renowned”, “handsome”. The commentary: truth that causes pain is itself a kind of violence (4.2.1–2).
Do not praise what was made by harm. Seeing buildings or prepared food, he does not say “well made”, “beautifully done”, “worth making”, for praise invites the householder to make more. If he must speak, he says it was made with effort and activity (arambha), or that it is pleasing to see or tasty (4.2.3–6).
Do not point people to animals, trees, fruit or grain. He does not say an animal is “fat, fit to kill or cook”, a cow “fit to milk or yoke”, a tree “fit for a door, a boat or a plough”, fruit “ripe, ready to pick”, grain “ready to cut or roast”. He describes them only as they are: “well grown”, “full-bodied”, “a fine tall tree”, “heavy with fruit”, “the ears have come” (4.2.7–16).
Describe the senses’ objects neutrally, and speak slowly. He calls a sound pleasant or unpleasant, a colour black or white, a taste bitter or sweet, just as it is, with no liking or dislike. The section closes with the whole chapter in one sutra: drop the four passions and speak after reflection, with certainty, after hearing fully, without haste, with discernment (4.2.17–20).

Key passages
4.1.1 · Speech moved by the passions

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा इमाइं वइ-आयाराइं सोच्चा णिसम्म इमाइं अणायाराइं अणायरियपुव्वाइं जाणेज्जा- जे कोहा वा वायं विउंजंति, जे माणा वा वायं विउंजंति, जे मायाए वा वायं विउंजंति, जे लोभा वा वायं विउंजंति, जाणओ वा फरुसं वयंति, अजाणओ वा फरुसं वयंति । सव्वमेयं सावज्जं वज्जेज्जा विवेगमायाए ।

Having heard and taken to heart these rules of speech, a monk or nun should know the misconduct in speech that earlier sages never practised: speaking from anger, from pride, from deceit or from greed, and speaking harshly, knowingly or unknowingly. With discernment, one should give up all of this as sinful.
4.1.3 · The four kinds of speech

अह भिक्खू जाणेज्जा चत्तारि भासज्जायाइं, तं जहा- सच्चमेगं पढमं भासजायं, बीयं मोसं, तइयं सच्चामोसं, जं णेव सच्चं णेव मोसं णेव सच्चामोसं -असच्चामोसं णाम तं चउत्थं भासज्जायं ।

A monk should know the four kinds of speech: the first is true; the second false; the third true-and-false; and the fourth, which is neither true, nor false, nor true-and-false, is called “neither true nor false” (ordinary, everyday speech).
4.1.5–6 · Even true speech can be sinful

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा से जं पुण जाणेज्जा जा य भासा सच्चा, जा य भासा मोसा, जा य भासा सच्चामोसा जा य भासा असच्चामोसा तहप्पगारं भासं सावज्जं सकिरियं कक्कसं कडुयं णिट्ठुरं फरुसं अण्हयकरिं छेयणकरिं भेयणकरिं परितावणकरिं उद्दवणकरिं भूओवघाइयं अभिकंख णो भासेज्जा ।
से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा से जं पुण जाणेज्जा- जा य भासा सच्चा सुहुमा, जा य भासा असच्चामोसा; तहप्पगारं भासं असावज्जं अकिरियं जाव अभूओवघाइयं अभिकंख भासेज्जा ।

Whether speech is true, false, mixed or ordinary, if it is sinful, karma-binding, harsh, bitter, cruel, rough, opening the inflow of karma, cutting, dividing, tormenting, terrifying or harmful to beings, the monk or nun, having thought it over, should not speak it. But subtle, carefully weighed true speech, and ordinary speech, when they are free of sin and karma-binding activity and harm no being, he or she may speak after thinking it over.
4.2.1 · Do not name a person by his affliction

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा जहा वेगइयाइं रूवाइं पासेज्जा तहावि ताइं णो एवं वएज्जा, तं जहा- गंडी गंडी इ वा कुट्ठी कुट्ठी इ वा जाव महुमेहणी इ वा हत्थच्छिण्णं हत्थच्छिण्णे इ वा पायच्छिण्णे पायछिण्णे इ वा कण्णछिण्णे कण्णछिण्णे इ वा णक्कछिण्णे णक्कछिण्णे इ वा ओट्ठछिण्णे ओट्ठछिण्णे इ वा ।
जे यावण्णे तहप्पगारा, तहप्पगाराहिं भासाहिं बुइया-बुइया कुप्पंति माणवा, ते यावि तहप्पगाराहिं भासाहिं अभिकंख णो भासेज्जा ।

Though a monk or nun sees people with various afflictions, he or she should not address them so: one with a goitre as “goitre!”, a leper as “leper!”, a diabetic as “diabetic!”, or one whose hand, foot, ear, nose or lip has been cut off by that loss. People addressed again and again with such words grow angry, so, having thought it over, one should not speak to them that way.
4.2.19 · The whole chapter in one sutra

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा वंता कोहं च माणं च मायं च लोभं च अणुवीइ णिट्ठाभासी णिसम्मभासी अतुरियभासी विवेगभासी समियाए संजए भासं भासेज्जा ।

The monk or nun, having cast out anger, pride, deceit and greed, should speak as one restrained and careful in speech: after reflecting, with certainty, after hearing and understanding, without haste, and with discernment.
Checked against the scans: 4.1.1 · 4.1.3 · 4.1.5–6 · 4.2.1 · 4.2.19

09_modules/acharang_2_05_clothes_and_bow.title: Module · Acharang 2.5–6: Clothes and Bowls
09_modules/acharang_2_05_clothes_and_bow.content:
Acharang 2.5–6 · Vastraishana and Patraishana (વસ્ત્રૈષણા, પાત્રૈષણા): Clothes and Bowls
In one line: a monk or nun keeps only a few plain clothes and simple bowls of gourd, wood or clay, begs them free of every fault, inspects them before taking them, wears them as received without washing or dyeing for looks, and stays unattached to them even when robbers take them.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapters 5 and 6 (58 sutras: 37 on clothes in 2 sections, 21 on bowls in 2 sections), translated pages 260–297 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (5.1.18 = chapter 5, section 1, sutra 18). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Clothes are kept only for restraint and modesty. Until a monk can live without clothes, he wears them to protect restraint and to cover the body against cold and heat. Clothes are sought, received and used with the same three kinds of care as food (introduction, p.260).
Six plain kinds of cloth, and few of them. Wool, silk-like fibre, hemp, leaf-fibre, cotton and plant-down are allowed. A young, strong, healthy monk wears one kind only. A nun keeps four wraps, one two cubits wide, two three cubits, one four cubits, and may sew pieces together to reach the width. One may not go more than half a yojana to seek cloth (5.1.1–2).
No cloth made, bought or treated for the monk. Cloth made for monks, or bought, washed, dyed, smoothed or perfumed for them, is refused until it has passed into another person’s use. Costly cloth (fine silks, gold-worked cloth, precious blankets) and garments of skins and furs are refused even when offered: they invite attachment, theft and great violence (5.1.3–6).
Four vows (pratima) for seeking cloth. Ask for a named kind; ask for one seen in front of you; ask for a used under- or upper-garment; or ask only for cloth others have thrown away. Whoever keeps one of these must not look down on those who keep another (5.1.7–10).
No promises, no special preparation. If a householder says “come back in a month” or “in a little while”, or offers to buy himself new cloth afterwards, or to perfume, wash or clean the cloth first, the monk declines and asks it be given as it is, now; if it is treated anyway, he refuses it (5.1.11–17).
Inspect before taking. He unfolds the cloth inside and out while it is still the householder’s: an earring, gold, a gem, a creature or a seed might be tied in its hem. He refuses cloth with eggs or webs in it, or that is too small, worn out, only lent, unfit to wear, or not willingly given (5.1.18–21).
No washing for beauty; drying with care. He does not scrub or wash cloth because it is not new or smells. To dry it in the sun he does not lay it on living or damp earth, or on wobbly posts, walls, rocks or rooftops, but on lifeless ground that he has inspected and swept (5.1.22–30).
Wear what you receive, and do not cling. He wears clothes as received, neither washed nor dyed, and does not hide his few clothes from others. He takes his clothes along when he goes out, except in rain, fog, dust-storm or swarms of insects. He does not keep a borrowed cloth by trickery, spoil a good cloth or brighten a poor one, swap cloth to get better, or leave the road for fear of thieves; if robbed, he acts as in chapter 3 (5.2.1–7).
Bowls: gourd, wood or clay, and only one kind. The same rules carry over to bowls: no costly bowls of metal, glass, ivory, horn or leather, nor ones with costly fittings; four vows for seeking; no promises; no oiling, washing or filling the bowl with food specially cooked for the monk; inspect inside before taking (6.1.1–16).
Check the bowl before every alms round, and handle living water with care. Before setting out for alms he looks into the bowl, removes any creature and wipes off dust. If unboiled (living) water has been put in his bowl by mistake, he returns it to the householder, or leaves bowl and water in a lonely spot, or pours the water on damp ground by a reservoir, and lets the bowl dry by itself (6.2.1–5).

Key passages
5.1.1 · One kind of cloth; a nun’s four wraps

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा अभिकंखेज्जा वत्थं एसित्तए । से जं पुण वत्थं जाणेज्जा, तं जहा- जंगिय वा भंगिय वा साणयं वा पोत्तगं वा खोमियं वा तूलकडं वा, तहप्पगारं वत्थं जे णिग्गंथे तरुणे जुगवं बलवं अप्पायंके थिरसंघयणे से एगं वत्थं धारेज्जा, णो बिइयं ।
जा णिग्गंथी सा चत्तारि संघाडीओ धारेज्जा- एगं दुहत्थवित्थारं, दो तिहत्थ वित्थाराओ, एगं चउहत्थवित्थारं ।

A monk or nun who wishes to seek cloth should know its kinds: woollen, silken, hempen, leaf-fibre, cotton, or made of plant-down. Of these, a monk who is young, of a good era, strong, free of illness and firm of body should wear one kind of cloth, not a second. A nun should keep four wraps: one two cubits wide, two three cubits wide, and one four cubits wide.
Note: the print reads जंगिय and भंगिय without the final nasal that the commentary has (जंगियं); kept as printed.
5.1.18 · Unfold it before you take it

सिया से परो णेत्ता वत्थं णिसिरेज्जा, से पुव्वामेव आलोएज्जा- आउसो ! ति वा भइणी ! ति वा तुमं चेव णं संतियं वत्थं अंतोअंतेण पडिलेहिस्सामि । केवली बूया- आयाणमेयं । वत्थंतेण उ बद्धे सिया कुंडले वा गुणे वा हिरण्णे वा सुवण्णे वा मणी वा जाव रयणावली वा पाणे वा बीए वा हरिए वा ।

If the householder brings out a cloth to give, the monk should first say: “Long-lived one, or sister, I will examine this cloth of yours inside and out, end to end, while it is still yours.” The Kevali says taking it unexamined is a cause of bondage: tied in its hem there may be an earring, a thread, silver, gold, a jewel or a string of gems, or a living creature, a seed or a green sprout.
5.2.1 · Wear it as you received it

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा अहेसणिज्जाइं वत्थाइं जाएज्जा, अहापरिग्गहियाइं वत्थाइं धारेज्जा, णो धोएज्जा, णो रएज्जा, णो धोयरत्ताइं वत्थाइं धारेज्जा, अपलिउंचमाणे गामंतरेसु, ओमचेलिए । एयं खलु वत्थधारिस्स सामग्गियं ।

A monk or nun should beg acceptable clothes and wear them just as they were received: not washing them, not dyeing them, not wearing washed and dyed clothes, and not hiding his few, plain clothes as he goes from village to village. This is the whole conduct of a cloth-wearing monk.
6.1.1 · Gourd, wood or clay

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा अभिकंखेज्जा पायं एसित्तए, से जं पुण पायं जाणेज्जा, तं जहा- अलाउपायं वा दारुपायं वा मट्टियापायं वा, तहप्पगारं पायं, जे णिग्गंथे तरुणे जुगवं बलवं अप्पायंके थिरसंघयणे, से एगं पायं धारेज्जा, णो बिइयं ।

A monk or nun who wishes to seek a bowl should know its kinds: a gourd bowl, a wooden bowl, or a clay bowl. Of these, a monk who is young, of a good era, strong, free of illness and firm of body should keep one kind of bowl, not a second.
6.2.1 · Look into the bowl before the alms round

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा गाहावइकुलं पिंडवायपडियाए पविसमाणे पुव्वामेव पेहाए पडिग्गहगं, अवहट्टु पाणे, पमज्जिय रयं, तओ संजयामेव गाहावइकुलं पिंडवायपडियाए णिक्खमेज्ज वा पविसेज्ज वा । केवली बूया आयाणमेयं । अंतो पडिग्गहगंसि पाणे वा बीए वा रए वा परियावज्जेज्जा ।

Before entering a householder’s home for alms, the monk or nun should first look into the bowl, remove any creatures and wipe away dust, and only then go out or enter with care. The Kevali says not doing so is a cause of bondage, for creatures, seeds or dust may have got into the bowl.
Checked against the scans: 5.1.1 · 5.1.18 · 5.2.1 · 6.1.1 · 6.2.1

09_modules/acharang_2_06_permission_to_s.title: Module · Acharang 2.7: Permission to Stay
09_modules/acharang_2_06_permission_to_s.content:
Acharang 2.7 · Avagraha-pratima (અવગ્રહ પડિમા): Permission to Stay
In one line: a monk or nun, vowed never to take what is not given, uses no place and no thing, not even a fellow monk’s, without the owner’s permission, sets clear limits of space and time when asking, shares what he has with fellow monks, and behaves with courtesy toward everyone he lodges among.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 7 (30 sutras, 2 sections), translated pages 298–316 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each section, so references below read chapter.section.sutra (7.2.15 = section 2, sutra 15). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Avagraha means taking with permission. The introduction explains that the word has many meanings; here it chiefly means taking a thing or a place with its owner’s leave, and the limited space so granted. A monk has given up taking what is not given in thought, word and deed, so asking leave runs through his whole life. The chapter is named for the kinds of permission and the seven vows (pratima) about it (introduction, p.298).
The vow behind it all. At initiation the monk resolves to be a homeless, possessionless shramana who eats what others give and does no sinful deed, and renounces all taking of what is not given. He does not take, make others take, or approve of taking anything not given, and he does not even pick up a fellow monk’s umbrella, bowl or staff without asking and without inspecting and wiping it (7.1.1).
Ask with clear limits. In a rest-house, garden house, householder’s home or ascetics’ hermitage, he asks the owner or the one in charge: “We will stay here as long and in as much space as you allow; fellow monks who come will stay within the same limit, and then we will move on.” The commentary: settle exactly which floors and rooms, the ground for waste, and the time (7.1.2).
Share with fellow monks. When monks of his own circle (sambhogika) arrive, he invites them to the food he himself has begged, rather than fetching fresh food for them; to worthy monks of another group he offers the stools and bedding he has begged. The commentary recalls Keshi offering Gautama a seat of straw (7.1.3–4).
Return borrowed things yourself. A needle, knife, ear-pick or nail-cutter borrowed for himself he does not pass to others; he takes it back himself and returns it laid on his open palm or on the ground, not placed hand to hand (7.1.5).
Places he does not ask for. Not on living or damp earth, not on wobbly posts, walls or upper floors; not a place where householders live with fire, water, women, children and animals, whose path runs through a family’s home, where the family quarrel, oil and bathe each other or go naked, or that is covered with pictures. All these disturb study and restraint (7.1.6–13).
Courtesy toward ascetics of other faiths. Lodging where other ascetics or Brahmins stay, he does not move their things in or out, does not wake them, and does nothing that displeases them. The commentary adds: keep the place clean, make no noise, and do not quarrel (7.2.1–2).
In a mango, sugarcane or garlic grove. With the owner’s leave he may stay there. He may accept fruit, cane or garlic only if it has no eggs or webs and has been cut up and made lifeless; whole, uncut pieces he refuses. The commentary says garlic is taken only as medicine (7.2.3–13).
Seven vows for asking lodging. (1) Ask in the usual way. (2) Ask for others and stay where others asked. (3) Ask for others but not stay where others asked. (4) Not ask for others but stay where others asked. (5) Ask only for oneself. (6) Use only the grass or straw already there, else sit or squat all night. (7) Use only a stone or wooden slab already laid, else sit or squat. Whoever keeps one vow does not look down on others (7.2.14).
Five owners whose leave is needed. The elders have taught five kinds of permission: of the lord of the gods (Devendra), of the king, of the householder, of the host whose house one stays in, and of fellow monks (7.2.15–16).

Key passages
7.1.1 · I renounce taking what is not given

समणे भविस्सामि अणगारे अकिंचणे अपुत्ते अपसू परदत्तभोई पावं कम्मं णो करिस्सामि त्ति समुट्ठाए; सव्वं भंते ! अदिण्णादाणं पच्चक्खामि ।
से अणुपविसित्ता गामं वा जाव रायहाणिं वा णेव सयं अदिण्णं, गिण्हेज्जा, णेवण्णेणं अदिण्णं गिण्हावेज्जा, णेवण्णं अदिण्णं गिण्हंतं पि समणुजाणेज्जा।

Having risen up with the resolve, “I will become a shramana: homeless, owning nothing, without son, without cattle, eating what others give; I will do no sinful deed,” he says: “Venerable sir, I renounce all taking of what is not given.” Entering a village or a capital, he should not himself take what is not given, nor make another take it, nor approve of another taking it.
7.1.2 · How to ask for a place

से आगंतारेसु वा, आरामगारेसु वा, गाहावइकुलेसु वा, परियावसहेसु वा अणुवीइ ओग्गहं जाएज्जा, जे तत्थ ईसरे, जे तत्थ समहिट्ठाए ते उग्गहं अणुण्णवेज्जा- कामं खलु आउसो ! अहालंदं अहापरिण्णायं वसामो, जाव आउसो; जाव आउसंतस्स ओग्गहे जाव साहम्मिया एतावताव ओग्गहं ओगिण्हिस्सामो, तेण परं विहरिस्सामो ।

In a rest-house, a garden house, a householder’s home or an ascetics’ hermitage, he should ask for a place after thinking it over, seeking leave from whoever owns it or is in charge: “Long-lived one, we will stay for as long and in as much space as you allow. For as long as your permission runs, fellow monks who come will take only that much space; beyond that we will move on.”
7.2.2 · Do not disturb other ascetics

से किं पुण तत्थ ओग्गहंसि एवोग्गहियंसि ? जे तत्थ समणाण वा माहणाण छत्तए वा जाव चम्मछेयणए वा तं णो अंतोहिंतो बाहिं णीणेज्जा, बहियाओ वा णो अंतो पवेसेज्जा, णो सुत्तं वा णं पडिबोहेज्जा, णो तेसिं किंचि अप्पत्तियं पडिणीयं करेज्जा ।

Having got leave for the place, how should he live there? If other shramanas or Brahmins keep their umbrella or other things, up to a leather-knife, there, he should not carry them from inside to outside or from outside to inside, should not wake one who sleeps, and should do nothing at all to displease or oppose them.
7.2.14 · The sixth vow: only what is already there

अहावरा छट्ठा पडिमा- से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा जस्सेव ओग्गहे उवल्लिएज्जा, जे तत्थ अहासमण्णागए तं जहा- इक्कडे वा जाव पलाले वा, तस्स लाभे संवसेज्जा, तस्स अलाभे उक्कुडुए वा णेसज्जिए वा विहरेज्जा । छट्ठा पडिमा ।

The sixth vow: in whatever place the monk or nun stays with leave, if there is grass or straw already there, he or she may use it; if there is none, he or she passes the time squatting or sitting. This is the sixth vow.
7.2.15 · The five kinds of permission

सुयं मे आउसं तेणं भगवया एवमक्खायं- इह खलु थेरेहिं भगवंतेहिं पंचविहे ओग्गहे पण्णत्ते, तं जहा- देविंदोग्गहे, रायोग्गहे, गाहावइओग्गहे, सागारियओग्गहे, साहम्मियओग्गहे ।

Long-lived one, I have heard the Lord say this: the venerable elders have taught five kinds of permission: that of the lord of the gods, of the king, of the householder, of the host, and of fellow monks.
Note: the translated page numbers this sutra 14; the print numbers it 15 (the seven vows are sutra 14), so 15 is used here.
Checked against the scans: 7.1.1 · 7.1.2 · 7.2.2 · 7.2.14 (sixth vow on p.313) · 7.2.15

09_modules/acharang_2_07_the_seven_septe.title: Module · Acharang 2.8–14: The Seven Septets
09_modules/acharang_2_07_the_seven_septe.content:
Acharang 2.8–14 · Sapta-saptika (સપ્ત સપ્તિકા): The Seven Septets
In one line: seven short chapters guard a monk’s everyday life from every side: where he may stand still, sit to study and relieve himself, how he must not go out of his way for sounds and sights, and why he must not let a householder, or even a fellow monk, wash, rub, adorn or treat his body.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapters 8–14, together called the “seven septets” (101 sutras in 7 chapters: ch.8 has 6, ch.9 has 4, ch.10 has 24, ch.11 has 20, ch.12 has 1, ch.13 has 43, ch.14 has 3), translated pages 317–361 (data/translations/acharang-2/). The book numbers the sutras afresh in each chapter, so references read chapter.sutra (10.23 = chapter 10, sutra 23). 15 minutes.
What the chapters teach

A place for standing (ch.8, Sthana-saptika). A monk who takes a vow only to stand, never to sit or lie down, first finds a place free of eggs, living beings and cobwebs and not built or altered for monks, as the lodging chapter already laid down (8.1). He then takes one of four standing resolves (pratima), each stricter than the last: lean on a lifeless wall, stretch the limbs and step about a little; lean and stretch but not step about; only lean; and finally lean on nothing, move nothing, and stand with all care for the body and its hair and nails given up (8.2–5). Whichever he takes, he must not run down monks who have taken none (8.5).
A place for sitting and study (ch.9, Nishidhika). The study ground (nishidhika, ground for self-study) must likewise be free of living beings and faultless (9.1–2). When two to five monks go there together they must not embrace, kiss, or scratch one another with teeth or nails; the commentary says a lonely place can feed curiosity as well as meditation, so the monk keeps his purpose before his eyes (9.3).
Where a monk may relieve himself (ch.10, Uchchara-prasravana). If he has no wiping cloth he may ask a fellow monk for one (10.1). He must not use ground that has living beings on it, that was prepared or cleaned for monks, where householders move roots and greens, or that is raised, unsteady or on living earth (10.2–9). The commentary: he could fall, and he would harm living beings.
Not in places people use or hold sacred (ch.10). The list is long: where grain or seeds are spread out, rubbish heaps, cracked or muddy ground, cooking places and animal sheds, places where people kill themselves, gardens and temples, city gates and crossroads, cremation grounds, river ghats, new mines and ploughed fields, vegetable plots and groves (10.10–22). The commentary gives the reasons: harm to water, plant and fire beings, people’s anger and disgust, and dishonour to the teaching.
The right way (ch.10). He goes with a pot to a lonely spot where no one comes or watches and nothing lives, relieves himself into the pot, then carries it to lifeless, burnt or similar ground and empties it there with care (10.23). The commentary quotes the Uttaradhyayan’s ten marks of proper ground, and says that where the ground has no owner the monk takes the permission of Shakra (Indra) (pp. 334–335).
Do not go after sounds (ch.11, Shabda-saptika). A monk hears drums, strings, cymbals and wind instruments, the sounds of lakes, forests, towns, gardens, gates and crossroads, animal sheds, animal fights, wedding songs, story-telling and dance halls, quarrels and wars, processions, crowded places and great festivals. He must not set out to go and hear any of them (11.1–18). The commentary: sense objects do not bind karma; attachment and aversion to them do (p. 339). The chapter closes by forbidding attachment to any sound at all, of this world or the next, heard or unheard (11.19).
Do not go after sights (ch.12, Rupa-saptika). The same rule for the eye: garlands, dolls, figures, woodwork, paintings, jewel and ivory work, and everything listed for sounds except the musical instruments (12.1). The commentary compares the monk drawn by beauty to the moth drawn into the flame (p. 347).
Do not accept a householder’s bodily service (ch.13, Parakriya-saptika). Knowing that service done to him by another binds karma, a monk should not want it in his mind, nor ask for it or get it done by speech or body (13.1). The chapter goes through the feet, the whole body, wounds, and boils, piles and fistulas: wiping, pressing, oiling, rubbing with paste, washing, smearing, perfuming, cutting open and draining (13.2–34). Then sweat and dirt, ear and eye wax, trimming hair, picking out lice (13.35–38); being laid in a lap or on a cot, adorned with necklaces and a crown, taken to a garden to be served (13.39–41).
Bear illness rather than harm beings (ch.13). If a householder offers to treat a sick monk with mantra power, pure or impure, or by digging up living roots and greens, the monk does not accept. Pain is sharp, the sutra says, but all living beings feel pain (13.42). The commentary adds that not seeking treatment is the ideal, but an ordinary monk living in a group may, when it cannot be avoided, accept blameless treatment; monks under special vows do not, even then (pp. 357–358).
Nor from one another (ch.14, Anyonya-kriya-saptika). All of chapter 13 applies again between monk and monk, nun and nun: they must not wipe, press or tend each other’s bodies without cause (14.1–2). The commentary makes clear this forbids service done for comfort, pride, habit or fondness; serving a sick, old, fasting or newly ordained monk with a detached mind is still the duty of group-living monks (p. 361).

Key passages
8.5 · The fourth standing resolve

अहावरा चउत्था पडिमा– अचित्तं खलु उवसज्जेज्जा, णो अवलंबेज्जा, णो काएण विप्परिकम्मादी, णो सवियारं ठाणं ठाइस्सामि । वोसट्ठकाए वोसट्ठकेस-मंसु-लोम-णहे संणिरुद्धं वा ठाणं ठाइस्सामि त्ति चउत्था पडिमा ।
इच्चेयासिं चउण्हं पडिमाणं जाव पग्गहियतरागं विहारं विहरेज्जा, णेव किंचि वि वएज्जा ।

The fourth resolve: “I will take a lifeless place; I will not lean on anything, I will not stretch or bend my limbs, I will not step about. Having given up the body, and care of my hair, beard, body-hair and nails, I will stand there, fully restrained.” Having taken any one of these four resolves, the monk lives by it, and says nothing against others.
10.23 · How to relieve oneself

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा सपाययं वा परपाययं वा गहाय से तमायाए एगंतमवक्कमेज्जा, अणावायंसि असंलोयंसि अप्पपाणंसि जाव मक्कडासंताणयंसि अहारामंसि वा उवस्सयंसि वा तओ संजयामेव उच्चारपासवणं वोसिरेज्जा, उच्चारपासवणं वोसिरित्ता से तमायाए एगंतमवक्कमेज्जा, अणावायंसि जाव मक्कडासंताणयंसि अहारामंसि वा झामथंडिलंसि वा अण्णयरंसि वा तहप्पगारंसि थंडिलंसि अचित्तंसि तओ संजयामेव उच्चार-पासवणं परिट्ठवेज्जा ।

A monk or nun takes his own pot or another’s and goes to a lonely spot in a garden or the lodging, where no one comes, no one sees, and there are no living beings or cobwebs, and there carefully relieves himself. Then he takes the pot to a lonely, lifeless place, such as ground outside a garden or burnt ground, and empties it there with care.
11.19 · No attachment to any sound

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा इहलोइएहिं सद्देहिं, परलोइएहिं सद्देहिं, सुएहिं सद्देहिं, असुएहिं सद्देहिं, दिट्ठेहिं सद्देहिं, अदिट्ठेहिं सद्देहिं, इट्ठेहिं सद्देहिं, कंतेहिं सद्देहिं णो सज्जेज्जा, णो रज्जेज्जा, णो गिज्झेज्जा, णो मुज्जेज्जा, णो अज्झोववज्जेज्जा ।

A monk or nun should not cling to, delight in, crave, be infatuated by, or be lost in any sound: sounds of this world or of the other world, sounds heard or unheard, seen or unseen, wished-for or lovely.
13.1 · Service from another binds

परकिरियं अज्झत्थियं संसेइयं णो तं साइए, णो तं णियमे ।

Bodily service done to him by another binds karma. He should not want it in his mind, and should not ask for it or have it done by speech or body.
13.42 · No cure that harms beings

सिया से परो सुद्धेणं वा वइबलेणं तेइच्छं आउट्टे, सिया से परो असुद्धेणं वइबलेणं तेइच्छं आउट्टे, सिया से परो गिलाणस्स सचित्ताणि कंदाणि वा मूलाणि वा तयाणि वा हरियाणि वा खणित्तु वा कड्ढेत्तु कड्ढावेत्तु वा तेइच्छं आउट्टेज्जा, णो तं साइए णो तं णियमे ।
कडुवेयणा कट्टु वेयणा पाण-भूय-जीव-सत्ता वेयणं वेदेंति ।

If a householder wants to treat him with the power of a mantra, pure or impure, or to treat the sick monk by digging up or pulling out living roots, bulbs, bark or greens, he should not want it or have it done. Bitter is the pain, sharp is the pain; yet all breathing, living, sentient beings feel pain.
14.1 · Nor service between monks

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा अण्णमण्णकिरियं अज्झत्थियं संसेइयं णो तं साइए णो तं णियमे ।

Mutual service between monks, or between nuns, also binds karma. A monk or nun should not want it in the mind, and should not ask for it or have it done by speech or body.
Note on 11.19: the print reads मुज्जेज्जा; the translation and the word-meanings read it as मुज्झेज्जा (“be infatuated”). The print is kept as printed.
Checked against the scans: 8.5 · 10.23 · 11.19 · 13.1 · 13.42 · 14.1

09_modules/acharang_2_08_bhavana_the_fiv.title: Module · Acharang 2.15: Bhavana, the Five Vows
09_modules/acharang_2_08_bhavana_the_fiv.content:
Acharang 2.15 · Bhavana (ભાવના): Bhavana, the Five Vows
In one line: the chapter first tells Lord Mahavira’s life from his descent into the womb to omniscience, to strengthen faith, and then gives the five great vows he taught the monks, each with five supporting practices (bhavana), to strengthen conduct.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 15 (61 numbered sutras, some of them in verse), translated pages 362–412 (data/translations/acharang-2/). 18 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Why “bhavana”. The introduction calls bhavana, steady noble reflection, a boat for the monk’s life: a mind not filled with it falls away when hardships come. The first half of the chapter (Mahavira’s life) feeds the reflection on faith; the second half (the vows) feeds the reflection on conduct (pp. 362–363).
Five events under one star. Mahavira’s descent from heaven, transfer from womb to womb, birth, going forth and omniscience all fell under the Uttara-phalguni constellation; his final liberation fell under Svati (s.1).
Descent and the transfer of the embryo. When 75 years and 8½ months of the fourth era were left, on the sixth of the bright half of Ashadha, he came down from the Pushpottara heaven, after a life of twenty sagaropama, into the womb of the Brahmin woman Devananda, wife of Rishabhadatta, in Brahmanakundapura. He had three kinds of knowledge: he knew he would descend and that he had descended, but not the moment itself, which is too subtle (s.2). After 82 days a god, holding it to be the gods’ custom, moved the embryo into the womb of Trishala, wife of Siddhartha, in Kshatriyakundapura; this he knew before, during and after (s.3). The commentary counts the transfer among the ten wonders of this era (p. 368).
Birth, name and family. He was born healthy on the thirteenth of the bright half of Chaitra; gods lit up the night, rained down jewels and flowers and performed the Tirthankara’s consecration (s.4–7). Because the family’s wealth grew from the day he was conceived, his parents named him Vardhamana (s.8). He grew up among five nurses and lived as a young man enjoying the senses without eagerness (s.9–10). He had three names: Vardhamana from his parents, Shramana (ascetic), and Mahavira, given by the gods because he bore fearful hardships (s.11). The sutras name his father, mother, uncle, brother, sister, wife Yashoda, daughter and granddaughter (s.12).
Parents’ end. His parents were lay followers in the line of Parshva. At the end they confessed, repented, lay on a bed of grass, gave up food, and died by the final fast (sallekhana); they were reborn in the Achyuta heaven and will be liberated from Mahavideha (s.13).
Thirty years, a year of giving, and going forth. After thirty years at home, with his parents gone and his vow fulfilled, he gave away everything (s.14). Before going forth a Tirthankara gives a crore and eight lakh gold coins every morning for a year, 388 crore 80 lakh in all, and the Lokantika gods ask him to found the order (s.15–20). Gods led by Shakra bathed and adorned him and carried him in the palanquin Chandraprabha to the Jnatakhanda garden. There, on the tenth of the dark half of Margashirsha, fasting two days without water, he took off his ornaments, pulled out his hair in five handfuls, bowed to the Siddhas and took the vow of equanimity (samayika), and mind-reading knowledge arose in him (s.21–37).
Twelve years of enduring. Sending his relatives away, he resolved that for twelve years he would give up care of the body and bear every hardship from gods, men or animals with patience, forgiveness and calm (s.38). He reached Kummaragama with an hour of daylight left and lived by the highest restraint, austerity, celibacy and patience, bearing all hardships undisturbed (s.39–40).
Omniscience. In the thirteenth year, on the tenth of the bright half of Vaishakha, outside Jrumbhikagrama on the north bank of the Rjuvalika river, in the field of the householder Shyamaka, near a sala tree, squatting in the cow-milking posture in the sun on a two-day waterless fast, deep in meditation, he gained complete, unobstructed, infinite knowledge and vision (kevala), and knew all the states of all beings (s.41–43).
First teaching. He taught first to the gods, then to men; to Gautama and the other monks he taught the five great vows with their bhavanas and the six kinds of living beings (s.44–45). The commentary notes that the first assembly, of gods only, took no vows (pp. 393–394).
The five great vows and twenty-five bhavanas. (1) No harm to any being, with care in walking, a pure mind, pure speech, care in picking up and putting down things, and eating only food looked at in the light (s.46–48). (2) No falsehood, by speaking only after thought and giving up anger, greed, fear and joking (s.49–51). (3) Not taking what is not given, by asking for limited space with thought, eating only with the guru’s permission, keeping to the space granted, asking again and again, and asking fellow monks with thought (s.52–54). (4) Celibacy, by not talking about women, not gazing at them, not recalling past pleasures, not eating too much or rich food, and not using places shared with women, animals or eunuchs (s.55–57). (5) Non-possession, by not clinging to or recoiling from any sound, sight, smell, taste or touch (s.58–60). The monk who keeps these five vows and twenty-five bhavanas as scripture, rule and path direct follows the Lord’s command (s.61).

Key passages
1 · Five events under Uttara-phalguni

तेणं कालेणं तेणं समएणं समणे भगवं महावीरे पंचहत्थुत्तरे यावि होत्था– हत्थुत्तराहिं चुए चइत्ता गब्भं वक्कंते । हत्थुत्तराहिं गब्भाओ गब्भं साहरिए । हत्थुत्तराहिं जाए । हत्थुत्तराहिं सव्वाओ सव्वत्ताए मुंडे भवित्ता अगाराओ अणगारियं पव्वइए । हत्थुत्तराहिं कसिणे पडिपुण्णे अव्वाघाए णिरावरणे अणंते अणुत्तरे केवलवरणाणदंसणे समुप्पण्णे । साइणा भगवं परिणिव्वुए ।

At that time the ascetic Lord Mahavira had five events under Uttara-phalguni: under it he came down from heaven into the womb; under it he was moved from womb to womb; under it he was born; under it he shaved his head, left home completely and became a homeless monk; under it complete, full, unobstructed, unveiled, infinite, supreme knowledge and vision arose in him. Under Svati the Lord attained final liberation.
11 · His three names

समणे भगवं महावीरे कासवगोत्ते, तस्स णं इमे तिण्णि णामधेज्जा एवमाहिज्जंति, तं जहा– अम्मापिउसंतिए वद्धमाणे, सहसम्मुइए समणे, भीमं भयभेरवं उरालं अचेलयं परीसहं सहइ त्ति कट्टु देवेहिं से णामं कयं समणे भगवं महावीरे ।

The ascetic Lord Mahavira was of the Kashyapa clan, and three names of his are told: Vardhamana, given by his parents; Shramana, which arose of itself; and, because he bore terrible, frightful, severe hardships, unclothed, the gods named him “the ascetic Lord Mahavira”.
34 · Going forth

तओ णं समणे भगवं महावीरे दाहिणेणं दाहिणं वामेणं वामं पंचमुट्ठियं लोयं करेत्ता सिद्धाणं णमोक्कारं करेइ, करेत्ता सव्वं मे अकरणिज्जं पावकम्मं ति कट्टु सामाइयं चरित्तं पडिवज्जइ, सामाइयं चरित्तं पडिवज्जेत्ता देवपरिसं च मणुयपरिसं च आलिक्खचित्तभूयमिव ठवेइ ।

Then the ascetic Lord Mahavira, having pulled out his hair in five handfuls, right hand on the right and left hand on the left, bowed to the Siddhas. Saying “All sinful action is not to be done by me”, he took up the conduct of equanimity (samayika); and the assembly of gods and the assembly of men stood still, like a painted picture.
38 · The twelve-year resolve

तओ णं समणे भगवं महावीरे पव्वइए समाणे मित्त-णाइ-सयण-संबंधिवग्गं पडिविसज्जेइ । पडिविसज्जित्ता इमं एयारूवं अभिग्गहं अभिगिण्हइ– बारस वासाइं वोसट्ठकाए चत्तदेहे जे केइ उवसग्गा समुप्पज्जंति, तं जहा– दिव्वा वा माणुसा वा तेरिच्छिया वा, ते सव्वे उवसग्गे समुप्पण्णे समाणे सम्मं सहिस्सामि, खमिस्सामि, तितिक्खिस्सामि अहियासिस्सामि ।

Having gone forth, the Lord sent away his friends, kin and relatives, and took this resolve: “For twelve years, giving up care of the body and attachment to it, whatever hardships come, from gods, men or animals, I will bear them rightly, forgive them, endure them calmly, and endure them gladly.”
46 · The first great vow

पढमं भंते ! महव्वयं पच्चक्खामि सव्वं पाणाइवायं । से सुहुमं वा बायरं वा तसं वा थावरं वा णेव सयं पाणाइवायं करेज्जा णेवण्णेहिं पाणाइवायं कारवेज्जा, णेवण्णं पाणाइवायं करंतं समणुजाणेज्जा जावज्जीवाए तिविहं तिविहेणं मणसा वयसा कायसा तस्स भंते ! पडिक्कमामि णिंदामि गरिहामि अप्पाणं वोसिरामि ।

Venerable one, in the first great vow I give up all harm to life. Whether to subtle or gross, moving or still beings, I will not harm life myself, will not have others harm it, and will not approve of another harming it, for as long as I live, in the three ways, by mind, speech and body. Of that, venerable one, I repent, I condemn it, I censure it before the guru, and I let go of that self.
59 · Senses meet their objects; drop the liking and disliking

तत्थिमा पढमा भावणा– सोयओ णं जीवे मणुण्णामणुण्णाइं सद्दाइं सुणेइ, मणुण्णामणुण्णेहिं सद्देहिं णो सज्जेज्जा णो रज्जेज्जा णो गिज्झेज्जा णो मुज्झेज्जा णो अज्झोववज्जेज्जा णो विणिग्घायमावज्जेज्जा ।
ण सक्का ण सोउं सद्दा, सोयविसयमागया ।
राग दोसा उ जे तत्थ, ते भिक्खू परिवज्जए ॥

The first bhavana of the fifth vow: through the ear a living being hears pleasant and unpleasant sounds; he should not cling to them, delight in them, crave them, be infatuated or lost in them, or be shaken by them. Sounds that reach the ear cannot go unheard; but the liking and disliking that arise there, the monk gives up. (The same is then said of sight, smell, taste and touch.)
Checked against the scans: s.1 · s.11 · s.34 · s.38 · s.46 · s.59

09_modules/acharang_2_09_vimukti.title: Module · Acharang 2.16: Vimukti
09_modules/acharang_2_09_vimukti.content:
Acharang 2.16 · Vimukti (વિમુક્તિ): Vimukti, Release
In one line: in twelve verses the last chapter of the Acharang shows the way out: see that every dwelling is temporary, leave home and possessions, bear abuse like a mountain bears wind, keep the great vows, and the monk sheds his bonds as a snake sheds its old skin.
Source: Acharang Sutra, Book 2 (Second Shrutaskandha), chapter 16 (12 verses, one section), translated pages 413–422 (data/translations/acharang-2/); the appendix on the Tripadi that follows is not part of the chapter. 8 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

What “vimukti” means. The introduction: release from iron chains is outward release; release from attachment, aversion and karma is inner release. Ordinary monks and even the omniscient are partly released; only the Siddha, free of all eight karmas, is wholly released. The chapter sets out the means of inner release (p. 413).
Every dwelling is temporary. Living beings only ever reach a dwelling that does not last. Hearing this teaching and thinking it over, the wise and fearless one should give up the bond of home and renounce violent activity and possessions (v.1). The commentary: the body, family and wealth all pass; the soul alone remains, so it should not cling to any of them (p. 414).
Abuse will come. Men pierce such a monk, restrained toward endless beings and living on pure alms, with harsh words and stones, as arrows pierce an elephant in battle (v.2).
Stand like a mountain. Reviled by such people and struck by harsh words and hard touches, the wise monk endures with an unspoiled mind and does not shake, as a mountain does not shake in the wind (v.3).
Harm no one, bear everything. Calm and looking on evenly, he lives with skilled monks; knowing that suffering is unwelcome to every moving and still being, he hurts none of them and bears all things. Such a great sage is called a true ascetic (v.4).
His virtue grows like a flame. In a monk who knows the supreme path of dharma, is humble, free of craving, meditating and settled, austerity, wisdom and good name grow like the brightness of a flame (v.5).
The vows are light. The Jina, protector of beings, taught the great vows as a safe place for all beings in every direction; great guides that break karma’s bonds, they dispel darkness the way light lights up the three directions (v.6).
Unattached among the attached. The monk moves free among householders who are bound, does not cling to women, gives up wanting honour, depends on neither this world nor the next, and is not caught by sense pleasures (v.7). For such a monk, free of ties, acting with understanding, steady and patient in suffering, the dirt of past karma is burnt off as fire fanned by wind cleans the dross from silver (v.8).
Like a snake’s old skin. Living by understanding, without longing, free of sexual desire, the monk is released from the bed of suffering as a snake leaves its old skin (v.9). The commentary lists the Sthananga’s four “beds of suffering” for a monk: doubting the teaching, wanting gain from others, craving pleasures, and wanting the body cared for (p. 421).
Crossing the ocean. Worldly existence is like a boundless flood, a great ocean no one can swim across with his arms; the wise one who knows it and gives it up is called the one who makes an end (v.10). So too is the one who knows exactly how people are bound and how they are freed (v.11). The one who has no bond at all, in this world or the next, without support and without ties, is freed from the round of birth and death (v.12).

Key passages
1 · Every dwelling is temporary

अणिच्चमावासमुवेंति जंतुणो, पलोयए सोच्चमिदं अणुत्तरं ।
विउसिरे विण्णु अगारबंधणं, अभीरु आरंभपरिग्गहं चए ॥

Living beings come only to a dwelling that does not last. Having heard this supreme teaching and looked into it, the wise one should cast off the bond of home and, fearless, give up violent activity and possessions.
3 · Like a mountain in the wind

तहप्पगारेहिं जणेहिं हीलिए, ससद्दफासा फरुसा उदीरिया ।
तितिक्खए णाणि अदुट्ठचेयसा, गिरिव्व वाएण ण संपवेवए ॥

Reviled by such people, assailed by harsh words and harsh touches, the wise monk endures them with an unspoiled mind, and does not tremble, as a mountain does not tremble in the wind.
4 · The true ascetic

उवेहमाणे कुसलेहिं संवसे, अकंतदुक्खी तस थावरा दुही ।
अलूसए सव्वसहे महामुणी, तहाहि से सुस्समणे समाहिए ॥

Looking on evenly, he lives with skilled monks. Suffering is unwelcome to all beings, moving and still, and they suffer; harming none of them and bearing all things, that great sage is therefore called a true ascetic.
8 · Fire cleans the silver

तहा विप्पमुक्कस्स परिण्णचारिणो, धिईमओ दुक्खखमस्स भिक्खुणो ।
विसुज्झइ जंसि मलं पुरेकडं, समीरियं रुप्पमलं व जोइणा ॥

For the monk who is free of ties, who acts with understanding, who is steady and bears suffering, the dirt of karma done before is cleansed away, as fire fanned by the wind cleans the dross from silver.
9 · The snake’s old skin

से हु परिण्णासमयम्मि वट्टइ, णिराससे उवरय मेहुणे चरे ।
भुजंगमे जुण्णतयं जहा चए, विमुच्चइ से दुहसेज्ज माहणे ॥

He lives by the teaching of understanding; without longing, having stopped all sexual activity, he goes about in restraint. As a snake leaves its old skin, so that monk is freed from the bed of suffering.
12 · No bond anywhere

इमम्मि लोए परए य दोसु वि, ण विज्जइ बंधणं जस्स किंचि वि ।
से हु णिरालंबणमप्पइट्ठिओ, कलंकलीभावपवंच विमुच्चइ ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

The one who has no bond at all, in this world, in the next, or in both, who leans on nothing and is tied to nothing, is freed from the endless round of birth and death. So I say.
Checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3 · v.4 · v.8 · v.9 · v.12
