09_modules/avashyak_01_samayik.title: Module · Avashyak 1: Samayik
09_modules/avashyak_01_samayik.content:
Avashyak 1 · Samayik (પ્રથમ આવશ્યક : સામાયિક): Equanimity
In one line: the first daily duty is equanimity: bow to the five supreme beings, then give up all sinful activity in mind, speech and body, turn back from past wrongs, and drop the self that did them.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 1st Avashyak (2 lessons, 1 sutra each: the Namaskar Mantra and the Samayik pledge Karemi Bhante), translated pages 65–85 (data/translations/avashyak/). Pages 65–71 are the book’s introduction to all six Avashyaks; the chapter text proper starts on page 72. References read L(esson).sutra, with page numbers for the introduction and commentary. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

An Avashyak is a duty that must be done every day and night. There are six: equanimity (Samayik), praise of the 24 Tirthankaras, bowing to the Guru, turning back from faults (Pratikraman), standing still and letting go of the body (Kayotsarga), and renouncing (Pratyakhyan). They are binding on monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen alike, because their work is the soul’s own cleansing, not the body’s needs (pp. 67–68).
Done without attention, it does not count. Reciting the texts by rote and going through the standing and sitting with the mind elsewhere is only the outer form (dravya avashyak). The real thing (bhava avashyak) is done with full attention, seeking no fame or reward, the mind on the meaning, morning and evening (p. 69).
Each duty has its own purpose, and the order is natural. Samayik is giving up sinful activity; the praise of the 24 holds up those who perfected it; bowing honours the virtuous; Pratikraman censures lapses; Kayotsarga heals the wounds of faults; Pratyakhyan holds the virtues gained. The order follows the seeker’s growth: he settles into equanimity, admires those who perfected it, bows to the Guru, repents, purifies himself in meditation, and only then is fit to renounce further (pp. 69–71).
The chapter opens with the Namaskar Mantra, which bows to virtues, not to persons. No individual is named. Arihant, Siddha, Acharya, Upadhyaya and Sadhu are titles a soul earns; the path itself runs upward from Sadhu to Siddha. The word namo means bowing the five limbs outwardly and giving up pride inwardly (L1.1; pp. 72–75).
Arihants come before Siddhas because they teach. Siddhas are higher, but we know of them only through the Arihants’ teaching, and the Arihant, still embodied, shows the path. Arihant and Siddha stand for God, the other three for the Guru (pp. 75–76).
The closing four lines state the fruit. “This fivefold bow destroys all sin and is the first of all auspicious things.” The book notes that the old commentaries explain only the first five lines; some Acharyas treat these four as an appendix (chulika). The commentary lists eight fruits, from health and wealth in this life to heaven, a good birth and finally liberation (pp. 76–77).
Real auspiciousness is inner. Curd, rice and the swastika are outward luck charms that can turn unlucky; bowing, praise and the three jewels never turn bad. The practitioner begins by bowing to the five as someone separate, and ends by becoming what he bows to (pp. 77–78).
The 108 virtues are a tradition, not an Agama count. Arihant 12 + Siddha 8 + Acharya 36 + Upadhyaya 25 + Sadhu 27 = 108. The book says plainly that the Agamas give no count for Arihant, Acharya or Upadhyaya; only the Siddha’s 31 virtues and the Sadhu’s 27 appear in the Agamas (pp. 78–81).
The Samayik pledge is taken freely, before a witness. Karemi, “I undertake”, shows it is the disciple’s own choice. Bhante is the Guru, or God when no Guru is present, or one’s own soul, whose witness matters most. Every explanation of samayik comes to one word: equanimity (L2.1; pp. 81–84).
A monk takes it for life, a householder for a set time. The monk renounces sin in nine ways (doing, causing, approving × mind, speech, body). A householder says jav niyamam, “for as long as the rule lasts”, fixed by tradition at 48 minutes per Samayik, and cannot renounce approval because his business and kitchen run on in his name; so he vows in six ways (some Acharyas say eight) (pp. 84–85).
Turn back, censure, confess, let go. Nindami is censuring one’s own fault inwardly; garihami is confessing it before the Guru, a harder practice because it breaks one’s pride; appanam vosirami gives up not the soul but the self of passions and wrong activity (p. 85).

Key passages
L1.1 · The Namaskar Mantra

णमो अरिहंताणं
णमो सिद्धाणं
णमो आयरियाणं
णमो उवज्झायाणं
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं

I bow to the Arihants. I bow to the Siddhas. I bow to the Acharyas. I bow to the Upadhyayas. I bow to all the Sadhus in the world.
Chulika (p. 76) · The first of all auspicious things

एसो पंच णमोक्कारो सव्व पावप्पणासणो ।
मंगलाणं च सव्वेसिं पढमं हवइ मंगलं ॥

This fivefold bow destroys all sins, and of all auspicious things it is the first. (The book treats these lines as an appendix that the old commentaries do not explain.)
L2.1 · The Samayik pledge (Karemi Bhante)

करेमि भंते ! सामाइयं सावज्जं जोगं पच्चक्खामि जावज्जीवाए तिविहं तिविहेणं मणेणं वायाए काएणं ण करेमि ण कारवेमि करतंपि अण्णं ण समणुजाणामि तस्स भंते पडिक्कमामि णिंदामि गरिहामि अप्पाणं वोसिरामि ।

Venerable one, I undertake Samayik. I renounce sinful activity for as long as I live, in three ways and by three means: by mind, speech and body I will not do it, will not make others do it, and will not approve of another doing it. From that, venerable one, I turn back; I censure it before my own soul, I confess it before the Guru, and I give up that sinful self.
The print here reads करतंपि; the same pledge in the 4th Avashyak (p. 109) prints करंतं पि.
Introduction (p. 67) · Why it is called Avashyak

समणेण सावएण य, अवस्स कायव्वं हवइ जम्हा ।
अंतो अहो-निसस्स उ, तम्हा आवस्सयं णामं ॥

Because the monk and the householder must necessarily do it within each day and night, it is called Avashyak.
Introduction (p. 69, from the Anuyogadvara Sutra) · The six aims

सावज्जजोगविरई, उक्कित्तण गुणवओ य पडिवत्ती ।
खलियस्स णिंदणा वणतिगिच्छ गुणधारणा चेव ॥१॥

Giving up sinful activity, praise, honour to the virtuous, censure of lapses, healing of wounds, and holding fast to virtues: these are the six aims of the six Avashyaks.
Commentary (p. 83, from the Avashyak Bhashya) · The soul itself is Samayik

सावज्ज जोग विरओ, तिगुत्तो छसु संजओ उवउत्तो जयमाणो आया सामाईयं होइ ॥

When the soul has turned away from sinful activity, is guarded in mind, speech and body, restrained toward the six kinds of living beings, attentive and careful, that soul itself is Samayik.
Checked against the scans: L1.1 · chulika · L2.1 · p. 67 · p. 69 · p. 83

09_modules/avashyak_02_praise_of_the_24.title: Module · Avashyak 2: Praise of the 24
09_modules/avashyak_02_praise_of_the_24.content:
Avashyak 2 · Chaturvimshatistava (બીજો આવશ્યક : ચતુર્વિંશતિસ્તવ): Praise of the 24
In one line: the seeker keeps the 24 Tirthankaras, who reached perfect equanimity, before his eyes by praising their names, and asks of them only health of the soul, right understanding and the highest calm.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 2nd Avashyak (1 sutra: the Logassa, 7 verses), translated pages 86–95 (data/translations/avashyak/). References read v.(verse) of the Logassa, with page numbers for the preface and commentary. 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Praise follows equanimity because the seeker needs a model. Old habits keep pulling him back into sinful activity. As a painter first fixes the picture in his mind, the seeker fixes on the Tirthankaras, who are wholly free of it, and draws strength from remembering their names and virtues. “A person becomes what he has faith in” (p. 86).
Its fruit is purer faith. In the Uttaradhyayan Sutra, Gautama asks what the soul gains from this praise; Mahavira answers that it purifies faith (darshan vishuddhi). Love of their virtues brings those virtues, and in the end the soul becomes like them (p. 86).
How it is recited. Seated in yoga-mudra (hands joined, elbows on the stomach) or standing in jina-mudra (arms hanging straight, as in the Tirthankaras’ meditation). The first verse is in Anushtup metre, the other six in Arya (p. 86).
A name carries its meaning. As the word “lotus” calls up the flower, Mahavira’s name calls up his patience and equanimity. The spoken word can awaken inner knowledge (p. 87).
The first verse names four marks of a Tirthankara. “Illuminator of the world” (light of knowledge that never sets), “founder of the ford of dharma” (the fourfold order of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen), “Jina” (conqueror of attachment and aversion) and “Arihant” (worthy of worship). “Kevali” adds that ordinary omniscients, who found no order, are equal to them in knowledge and conduct (v.1; pp. 90–91).
The 24 names have reasons. Verses 2–4 name the 24 of this age in Bharat. The commentary, following the Niryukti, explains each name from what happened while the mother carried the child: Ajit because she always won at the board game (chopat), Shantinath because plague in the city ceased, Vardhaman because the clan’s wealth grew (v.2–4; pp. 91–93).
They are free of the dust and dirt of karma, and of old age and death. Karma being bound now is “dust”, karma bound before is “dirt”, or loosely and tightly bound karma. Rooting out attachment and aversion, they bind no karma that brings another birth (v.5; pp. 93–94).
“Be pleased with me”, though they are beyond pleasure. A detached being is pleased or displeased with no one. The devotee says it anyway, giving up his ego; it is the purity of his own feeling that sheds karma (v.5; pp. 93–95).
He asks only for spiritual gifts. Praised in name (kirtan), bowed to (vandan) and honoured (puja), they are asked for health of the soul (freedom from the disease of birth and death), bodhi (right understanding, the seed of the three jewels) and the highest samadhi. He asks for nothing material (v.6; pp. 94–95).
Purer than moons, brighter than suns, deeper than the ocean. The moon has a spot, the sun sets, the sea has waves; the Siddhas have none of these. “Grant me perfection” means: with your support may I reach it (v.7; p. 95).

Key passages
v.1 · I will praise the 24

लोगस्स उज्जोयगरे, धम्मतित्थयरे जिणे ।
अरिहंते कित्तइस्सं, चउवीसं पि केवली ॥१॥

I will praise the Arihants who light up the whole world, who found the ford of dharma, the conquerors, the omniscient ones, all twenty-four.
v.5 · Free of karma’s dust, old age and death

एवं मए अभिथुआ, विहुयरयमला पहीणजरमरणा ।
चउवीसं पि जिणवरा, तित्थयरा मे पसीयंतु ॥५॥

Thus praised by me, free of the dust and dirt of karma, rid of old age and death, may the twenty-four supreme Jinas, the Tirthankaras, be pleased with me.
v.6 · The only gifts asked

कित्तिय-वंदिय-महिया, जे ए लोगस्स उत्तमा सिद्धा ।
आरुग्ग-बोहि लाभं, समाहि-वरमुत्तमं दिंतु ॥६॥

Praised, bowed to and honoured, they are the highest in the world, the perfected ones. May they grant health of the soul, the gain of right understanding, and the best, highest calm.
v.7 · Moon, sun and ocean

चंदेसु णिम्मलयरा, आइच्चेसु अहियं पयासयरा ।
सागरवरगंभीरा, सिद्धा सिद्धिं मम दिसंतु ॥७॥

Purer than the moons, shining more than the suns, deep as the greatest ocean: may the Siddhas grant me perfection.
Preface (p. 86, from the Uttaradhyayan Sutra) · What the praise gives

चउव्वीसत्थएणं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ?
चउव्वीसत्थएणं दंसण विसोहिं जणयइ ।

“Venerable one, what does the soul gain by praising the twenty-four?” “By praising the twenty-four, it purifies its faith.”
Commentary (p. 95, from the Avashyak Niryukti) · Devotion brings its own reward

भत्तीइ जिनवराणं परमाए खीणपिज्जदोसाणं ।
आरुग्ग बोहिलाभं समाहि मरणं पावंति ॥१०९७॥

By supreme devotion to the Jinas, whose attachment and aversion are destroyed, devotees gain health of the soul, right understanding, and a calm death.
The translation numbers this Niryukti verse 1017; the print reads १०९७. The print also has जिनवराणं (with न) here, where the Logassa uses जिणवरा.
Checked against the scans: v.1–7 · p. 86 · p. 95

09_modules/avashyak_03_vandana.title: Module · Avashyak 3: Vandana
09_modules/avashyak_03_vandana.content:
Avashyak 3 · Vandana (ત્રીજો આવશ્યક : વંદના): Bowing to the Guru
In one line: the disciple asks leave to come near the Guru, touches his feet, asks after his day and his practice, and begs forgiveness for every disrespect, because humility toward the Guru is the root of every good that follows.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 3rd Avashyak (1 sutra: the Guru-vandana sutra Ichchhami Khamasamano), translated pages 96–105 (data/translations/avashyak/). The sutra is one long passage; the key passages below take it in parts. 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The Guru is bowed to because he is the guide now. After praising the 24, the seeker’s devotion turns to the Guru, who guides the practice in the Tirthankaras’ absence. There are three levels: a quick bow with joined hands when meeting him on the road (matthaena vandami); the Tikkhutto with three turns when he is seated; and the full Ichchhami Khamasamano with twelve turns at the time of Pratikraman (p. 96).
Humility is the root of every good. Bowing destroys ego. Following the Uttaradhyayan, it removes low-status karma and binds high-status karma. The book quotes Acharya Umasvati’s chain: humility brings service, service brings scriptural knowledge, knowledge brings restraint, and so on through stopping karma, austerity and shedding karma, to the end of birth and death and to liberation (p. 96).
It starts with “I wish”. Spiritual practice is voluntary; done under pressure it is forced labour. So the disciple says ichchhami, “I wish to bow.” He calls the Guru khamasamana, the forgiving ascetic, because forgiveness is the monk’s leading quality (pp. 98–99).
He asks leave to come close. The Guru’s space (avagraha) is three and a half cubits on every side. The disciple stays outside it out of respect, and enters only when the Guru says anujanami, “I permit” (p. 99).
He asks after the Guru’s day, his journey of restraint and his senses. “Journey” (jatta) is care in austerity, study, meditation and the daily duties; “provision” (javanijjam) is mastery of the senses and mind, the food for that journey. Asking also opens the chance to serve (pp. 99–100).
He begs forgiveness for every kind of disrespect. The Dashashrutaskandha Sutra lists 33 kinds of disrespect (ashatana); the commentators group them as disrespect in things, place, time and attitude: keeping the better food for oneself, taking the better seat, not answering when called at night, addressing the Guru with a careless “you”. It may come through mind, speech or body, or through anger, pride, deceit or greed, and he asks pardon for all times, past lives included (pp. 100–101).
The Guru may set the form. If the Guru is unwell or busy he says tivihena and the disciple bows briefly from outside; if free he says chhandena. The full bow is done twice, the second time without leaving the Guru’s space. The words “your day has passed” change to “night”, “fortnight”, “four months” or “year” in those Pratikramans (pp. 101–102).
The full bow has 25 parts. Two half-bows, one “as-born” posture (hands joined at the forehead, like a newborn or a monk at initiation), twelve circular turns of the hands, four bowings of the head, the three restraints of mind, speech and body, two entries and one exit (pp. 102–104).
It is a dialogue of six steps. At each step the Guru answers: tivihena or chhandena, anujanami, tatha (“I am well”), “and is your journey going well?”, evam, and finally ahamapi khamayami, “I too ask forgiveness”, for any hurt he caused while guiding and correcting the disciple. The bond between them grows deep (pp. 104–105).

Key passages
1 (opening) · Asking leave and touching the feet

इच्छामि खमासमणो ! वंदिउं जावणिज्जाए णिसीहियाए अणुजाणह मे मि उग्गहं णिसीहि अहोकायं कायसंफासं खमणिज्जो भे ! किलामो

Forgiving ascetic, I wish to bow to you as far as my strength allows, with my body turned away from sinful acts. Give me leave to enter your space. Setting aside all other activity, I touch your feet with my head. Forgive me, venerable one, any discomfort this touch has caused.
1 (middle) · Asking after the Guru

अप्पकिलंताणं बहुसुभेण भे ! दिवसो वइक्कंतो जत्ता भे जवणिज्जं च भे ?

Free of weariness, has your day passed in great well-being? Is your journey of restraint going well, and are your senses and mind at ease?
1 (close) · Forgiveness for every disrespect

खामेमि खमासमणो देवसियं वइक्कमं आवस्सियाए पडिक्कमामि खमासमणाणं देवसियाए आसायणाए तित्तीसण्णयराए जं किंचि मिच्छाए मणदुक्कडाए वयदुक्कडाए कायदुक्कडाए कोहाए माणाए मायाए लोहाए सव्व कालियाए सव्वमिच्छोवयाराए सव्व धम्माइक्कमणाए आसायणाए जो मे देवसिओ अइयारो कओ तस्स खमासमणो पडिक्कमामि णिंदामि गरिहामि अप्पाणं वोसिरामि ।

Forgiving ascetic, I ask pardon for the day’s offences. I turn back from whatever I did wrong in the daily duties. For any of the thirty-three kinds of disrespect to you today, done in a false spirit, with bad mind, bad speech or bad bodily acts, out of anger, pride, deceit or greed, at any time, through any wrong behaviour or any breach of dharma: for whatever fault I committed today, forgiving ascetic, I turn back from it, I censure it in myself, I confess it before you, and I give up that sinful self.
Commentary (p. 102, from the Samavayanga Sutra) · The 25 parts of the bow

दुओ णयं जहाजायं, कितिकम्मं बारसावयं
चउसिरं तिगुत्तं च, दुपवेसं एग-णिक्खमणं

Two bows, the as-born posture, twelve turns in the rite of reverence, four bowings of the head, three restraints, two entries and one exit.
The translation of the sutra (p. 97) prints most of it in Gujarati script and has लोभाए; the scan is in Devanagari throughout and reads लोहाए. The verse on p. 102 is printed without danda marks.
Checked against the scans: 1 · p. 102

09_modules/avashyak_04_pratikraman.title: Module · Avashyak 4: Pratikraman
09_modules/avashyak_04_pratikraman.content:
Avashyak 4 · Pratikraman (ચોથો આવશ્યક : પ્રતિક્રમણ): Turning Back
In one line: each day the monk looks back over everything he did, waking and sleeping, walking, begging and studying, turns back from every lapse with “may that wrong of mine be undone”, renews his faith and vows, and ends by forgiving and asking forgiveness of every living being.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 4th Avashyak (10 lessons, 62 numbered sutras; the 4th Shramana Sutra alone has 45), translated pages 106–191 (data/translations/avashyak/). The brief gave 106–187, but the chapter runs on to the forgiveness sutra and ends on p. 191 (“Avashyak-4 complete”). References read L(esson).sutra. 25 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Ten lessons, and no vows recited. The chapter has: Karemi Bhante, the four auspicious things, the short Pratikraman, the walking sutra, five Shramana Sutras and the forgiveness sutra. The book notes that the Avashyak Sutra itself has no recital of the monk’s five great vows or the householder’s twelve vows; the present custom of adding them before the Shramana Sutras is tradition (pp. 106–108).
First, take refuge. The pledge is repeated (now with savvam, “all” sinful activity), then four things are declared auspicious, highest and the only refuge: the Arihants, the Siddhas, the Sadhus and the dharma taught by the omniscient. Coconut and kumkum are not real auspiciousness; no person or thing in the world can shelter the soul, but dharma is an island for one drowning in the sea of births (L1–L2; pp. 109–113).
The short Pratikraman lists every area of a monk’s life. Body, speech and mind; going against scripture or the path; the three restraints, four passions, five great vows, six kinds of beings, seven ways of seeking alms, eight “mothers of the teaching”, nine fences of celibacy, ten monk’s virtues. A vow partly broken or badly damaged is cleansed by Pratikraman; a vow wholly broken (anachara) needs the Guru’s penance (L3; pp. 113–118).
Harm means much more than killing. The walking sutra (Iriyavahiyam) names ten kinds of harm, from striking a creature in one’s way, covering it, crushing it and frightening it, to moving it from its place and taking its life. Violence is injuring any of the ten life-forces through careless or passionate activity; a surgeon with a pure intention is not violent. The Niryukti reads michchhami dukkadam letter by letter: humility, covering one’s faults, staying within the limits, despising the wrong in oneself, admitting it, and calming it away (L4; pp. 118–123).
Faults in sleep and dreams count too. Sleeping too long or on too soft a bed, turning over without first brushing the bed, yawning without care, and in dreams being stirred by battles and weddings or wanting food at night: the monk is answerable for all of it, and reflects on it on waking (L5; pp. 123–126).
Begging must not burden anyone. The monk takes a little from many houses, like a cow grazing only the tips of the grass or a bee taking nectar without hurting the flower. He turns back from pushing open a closed door, brushing past dogs, calves and children, taking food in doubt or in haste, or food mixed with living seeds or water. Food found impure afterwards must be given up, not eaten (L6; pp. 126–131).
Study and inspection at their proper times. Four periods of study a day and night, inspection of clothes and bowls morning and evening, and careful brushing of any small creature to safety. The commentary’s example of the four grades of fault: accepting an invitation to food cooked for the monk is the first (atikrama), setting out to fetch it the second, taking it the third, eating it the fourth (L7; pp. 131–135).
One to thirty-three: what to know, what to drop, what to practise. The long 4th Shramana Sutra counts from one kind of non-restraint, two bonds (attachment and aversion, “the two seeds of karma”), three thorns (deceit, longing for reward, false belief), four passions (conquer anger with forgiveness, pride with gentleness, deceit with straightness, greed with contentment), up to eight prides, nine fences of celibacy, the 22 hardships and the 33 disrespects. The book’s own table marks each as to be known, given up or adopted (L8.1–45; pp. 135–175).
Disrespect reaches everyone. The second list of 33 disrespects includes householders, men and women, gods, this world and the next, and “all living beings”; mispronouncing or misordering the scripture, or studying it at the wrong time, is disrespect to knowledge. The commentary says monks and Acharyas too must ask pardon each day for any disrespect to laymen and laywomen (L8.45; pp. 168–173).
Then the vow is renewed. The 5th Shramana Sutra praises the teaching of the Nirgranthas as true, complete and the path that ends all sorrow; those who stand in it become perfect. The monk declares faith in it, then gives up eight things and takes their opposites: non-restraint for restraint, unchastity for celibacy, the improper for the proper, ignorance for knowledge, wrong action for right action, false belief for right belief, unawareness for awakening, the wrong path for the right. He turns back from faults remembered and forgotten, and reminds himself: “I am a Shramana.” He bows to every monk in the fifteen lands where dharma can be practised, keepers of the 18,000 limbs of conduct (L9.1–7; pp. 175–190).
It ends in forgiveness. He forgives all beings and asks their forgiveness, declares friendship with all and enmity with none, and bows to the 24 Jinas. Only one who feels friendship toward every living being can become free of attachment (L10.1; pp. 190–191).

Key passages
L2.1 and L2.3 · The four auspicious things, the four refuges

चत्तारि मंगलं-अरिहंता मंगलं, सिद्धा मंगलं, साहू मंगलं, केवलि-पण्णतो धम्मो मंगलं ।
चत्तारि सरणं पवज्जामि- अरिहंते सरणं पवज्जामि, सिद्धे सरणं पवज्जामि, साहू सरणं पवज्जामि, केवलि पण्णत्तं धम्मं सरणं पवज्जामि ।

Four are auspicious: the Arihants, the Siddhas, the Sadhus, and the dharma taught by the omniscient. I take four refuges: I take refuge in the Arihants, in the Siddhas, in the Sadhus, and in the dharma taught by the omniscient.
L4.1 · Turning back from harm done while walking

इच्छामि पडिक्कमिउं इरियावहियाए विराहणाए गमणागमणे पाणक्कमणे बीयक्कमणे हरियक्कमणे ओसा उत्तिंग पणग दग मट्टी मक्कडा संताणा संकमणे जे मे जीवा विराहिया एगिंदिया बेइंदिया तेइंदिया चउरिंदिया पंचिंदिया अभिहया वत्तिया लेसिया संघाइया संघट्टिया परियाविया किलामिया उद्दविया ठाणाओठाणं संक्कामिया जीवियाओ ववरोविया तस्स मिच्छामि दुक्कडम् ।

I wish to turn back from harm done on the path. In going and coming, treading on living creatures, seeds or green plants, on dew, ant-holes, moss, water, wet earth or spiders’ webs: whatever beings I have harmed, with one, two, three, four or five senses, if I struck them, covered them, crushed them, heaped them together, jostled them, tormented them, wearied them, terrified them, moved them from place to place or took their life, may that wrong of mine be undone.
The print writes इरियावहियाए with an older form of the final ए; the word meanings below it spell it इरियावहियाए. It prints संक्कामिया where the translation has संकामिया.
L9.2 · The teaching that ends all sorrow

इणमेव णिग्गंथं पावयणं सच्चं अणुतरं केवलियं पडिपुण्णं णेआउयं संसुद्धं सल्लकत्तणं सिद्धिमग्गं मुत्तिमग्गं णिज्जाणमग्गं णिव्वाणमग्गं अवितहमविसंधि सव्वदुक्खप्पहीणमग्गं ।

This very teaching of the Nirgranthas is true, unsurpassed, taught by the omniscient, complete, leading to liberation, wholly pure, the cutter of the inner thorns, the path to perfection, to release, to leaving the round of births and to nirvana; it is never false, never broken, the path that ends all sorrow.
The print reads अणुतरं (single त) in both the sutra and its word meanings; the translation has अणुत्तरं. The print reads सल्लकत्तणं; the translation has सल्लकरणं.
L9.6 · “I am a Shramana”

समणोऽहं संजय विरय पडिहय पच्चक्खाय पावकम्मो अणियाणो दिट्ठि संपण्णो मायामोसो विवज्जिओ ।

I am a Shramana: restrained, turned away from sin, one who has struck down and renounced sinful karma, free of longing for reward, possessed of right vision, and free of deceitful falsehood.
L10.1 · Forgiveness and friendship

खामेमि सव्वे जीवा, सव्वे जीवा वि खमंतु मे ।
मित्तीमे सव्व भूएसू, वेरं मज्झं ण केणइ ॥१॥
एवमहं आलोइय, णिंदिय गरिहिय दुगंछियं सम्मं ।
तिविहेण पडिक्कंतो, वंदामि जिणे चउव्वीसं ॥२॥

I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none. Having thus rightly reviewed my faults, censured them within, confessed them before the Guru and turned from them in disgust, and having turned back in all three ways, I bow to the twenty-four Jinas.
Checked against the scans: L2.1 · L2.3 · L4.1 · L9.2 · L9.6 · L10.1

09_modules/avashyak_05_kayotsarga.title: Module · Avashyak 5: Letting Go of the Body
09_modules/avashyak_05_kayotsarga.content:
Avashyak 5 · Kayotsarga (કાયોત્સર્ગ): Letting Go of the Body
In one line: after confessing his faults, the practitioner stands still, silent and absorbed in good meditation, giving up attachment to the body, to heal what confession has not yet healed and to destroy sinful karma.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 5th Avashyak (4 lessons: 5 sutras plus the 7 verses of the Logassa), translated pages 192–200. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Kayotsarga means giving up attachment to the body, not the body itself. Kaya is the body, utsarga is letting go. While life lasts the body cannot be dropped, so what is dropped is the sense of “mine” towards it. Speech is stilled into silence and the mind is turned from bad thoughts to one-pointed good ones (introduction, p.192).
It is a treatment for wounds. The Anuyogadvara Sutra calls it “wound-healing” (vranachikitsa): faults in one’s vows are wounds in conduct, and kayotsarga is their ointment. It is a form of atonement (prayashchitta) and an inner austerity. The Niryukti lists its fruits: the body’s dullness goes, the mind is cleared, one learns to bear pleasure and pain, reflection deepens, and the mind becomes one-pointed (introduction, pp.192–193).
Two subjects for the standing meditation. In pratikraman the kayotsarga is used either to reflect on the day’s faults, or (in the night pratikraman) to decide which austerity to take up today. The chapter has four lessons: Karemi Bhante, the short confession, the kayotsarga vow, and the Logassa (p.193).
First the vow of equanimity and a short confession are repeated. Lesson 1 is the Karemi Bhante (giving up all sinful activity for life, in three ways and by mind, speech and body). Lesson 2 is the short pratikraman: whatever fault I committed today, in body, speech or mind, in knowledge, faith, conduct, the three restraints, the five great vows, the six kinds of living beings and so on, “may that wrong of mine be undone” (micchami dukkadam) (l.1–2).
The purpose: four steps to destroy sinful karma. I stand in kayotsarga for further purification, for atonement, for cleansing, and to be free of the three inner thorns (shalya): deceit, craving for a worldly reward, and wrong belief. The commentary compares it to washing a cloth: confession removes the dirt, kayotsarga makes up what is lacking, and the next Avashyak, renunciation, adds the shine (l.3 s.1, pp.194–196).
Twelve natural movements do not break it. Breathing in and out, coughing, sneezing, yawning, belching, passing wind, dizziness, fainting, and tiny movements of the limbs, phlegm and eyes are allowed in advance, because forcing them to stop would disturb the mind. The commentators add four more: sudden fire, an attack on the body, robbers or a king, and a snake bite (l.3 s.2, pp.196–197).
How long, and how. It lasts until it is closed by saying “Namo Arihantanam” aloud. Meanwhile the body stays still in one posture, in silence and in meditation. This practises the three restraints (gupti) of body, speech and mind, so it both stops new karma (samvara) and sheds old karma (nirjara) (l.3 s.3, pp.197–198).
Standing is the rule, but the inner state is what counts. It is normally done standing; the sick or those in their last practice may sit or lie down. The Churni separates outer kayotsarga (stopping bodily movement) from inner kayotsarga (good meditation). Of four kinds, “body up, soul up” and “body seated, soul up” are true kayotsarga; a standing body with a sleeping soul, or a seated body with bad thoughts, is only a show (pp.198–199).
Nineteen faults to avoid. The Niryukti lists them: standing like a horse on one leg, swaying like a creeper, leaning on a pillar or wall, looking around like a crow, shaking the head, moving the lips or fingers to count, and so on. Hemachandra counts 21 (pp.199–200).
It closes with the Logassa. After any kayotsarga the praise of the twenty-four Tirthankaras is said aloud. Bowing to the perfect ones makes faith firm and purifies one’s vision (l.4, v.1–7, p.200).

Key passages
Lesson 3, s.1 · Why I stand in kayotsarga

तस्स उत्तरीकरणेणं पायच्छित्तकरणेणं विसोहीकरणेणं विसल्लीकरणेणं पावाणं कम्माणं णिग्घायणट्ठाए, ठामि काउस्सग्गं ॥

For the further purification of this soul, for atonement, for cleansing it, for freeing it from its thorns, and to destroy sinful karmas completely, I stand in kayotsarga.
Lesson 3, s.2 · What does not break it

उससिएणं, णीससिएणं, खासिएणं, छीएणं, जंभाइएणं, उड्डुएणं, वायणिसग्गेणं, भमलीए, पित्तमुच्छाए, सुहुमेहिं अंगसंचालेहिं, सुहुमेहिं खेल संचालेहिं, सुहुमेहिं दिट्ठि संचालेहिं, एवमाइएहिं आगारेहिं, अभग्गो, अविराहिओ, हुज्ज मे काउस्सग्गो ।

Except for breathing in, breathing out, coughing, sneezing, yawning, belching, passing wind, dizziness, fainting from bile, and slight movements of the limbs, of phlegm and of the eyes, and other such exceptions, may my kayotsarga stay unbroken and unharmed.
Lesson 3, s.3 · The vow of stillness

जाव अरिहंताणं भगवंताणं णमुक्कारेणं ण पारेमि ताव कायं ठाणेणं, मोणेणं, झाणेणं, अप्पाणं वोसिरामि ।

Until I close it by bowing to the Arihanta Bhagavans, I give up my body: I keep it in one place, in silence, in meditation.
Lesson 4, v.1 · I will praise the twenty-four

लोगस्स उज्जोयगरे, धम्मतित्थयरे जिणे ।
अरिहंते कित्तइस्सं, चउवीसं पि केवली ॥

I will praise the Arihantas, the Jinas who light up the world and found the ford of dharma, all twenty-four, the all-knowing ones.
Lesson 4, v.6 · What I ask of them

कित्तिय-वंदिय-महिया, जे ए लोगस्स उत्तमा सिद्धा ।
आरुग्ग-बोहि लाभं, समाहि-वरमुत्तमं दिंतु ॥

They whom I have praised, bowed to and worshipped, the highest perfected ones of the world: may they give me health of soul, the gain of awakening (bodhi), and the best and highest equanimity (samadhi).
Lesson 4, v.7 · Purer than the moons

चंदेसु णिम्मलयरा, आइच्चेसु अहियं पयासयरा ।
सागरवरगंभीरा, सिद्धा सिद्धिं मम दिसंतु ॥

Purer than the moons, brighter than the suns, deep as the greatest ocean: may the perfected ones grant me perfection (liberation).
Checked against the scans: l.3 s.1 · l.3 s.2 · l.3 s.3 · l.4 v.1, 6, 7. The translated page drops the words सागरवरगंभीरा (“deep as the greatest ocean”) from v.7; the scan has them, and they are restored here.

09_modules/avashyak_06_pratyakhyan.title: Module · Avashyak 6: Vows of Renunciation
09_modules/avashyak_06_pratyakhyan.content:
Avashyak 6 · Pratyakhyan (પ્રત્યાખ્યાન): Vows of Renunciation
In one line: having cleaned out past faults, the practitioner closes the door on future karma by taking a time-bound vow to give up food (from one muhurta after sunrise up to a full fast), keeps it pure, closes it properly, and ends the whole Avashyak with the Namotthunam in praise of the Arihantas and Siddhas.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, 6th Avashyak and the closing Namotthunam (10 lessons: 10 renunciation formulas, the closing formula, 1 Niryukti verse, and the Namotthunam), translated pages 201–229. 18 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Renunciation stops what is still to come. The 4th and 5th Avashyaks destroy karma already gathered; the 6th, pratyakhyan, blocks karma that would come in future. It is a firm resolve, made with right knowledge, to give up sinful activity. The commentary sorts vows into root vows (the five great vows of a monk, the five small vows of a layman) and supporting vows, and lists ten kinds of supporting vow; this Avashyak teaches the tenth, the time-bound vows (addha pratyakhyan). The Anuyogadvara Sutra calls this Avashyak “holding on to virtues” (gunadharana) (introduction, p.201).
Navakarshi: the shortest vow. “When the sun has risen” one gives up all four kinds of food (staple food, water, fruit and sweets, and mouth-fresheners) until one muhurta after sunrise has passed and the Navkar has been said. Both conditions are needed. It has only two exceptions (agara): complete forgetfulness and a sudden accident, like a drop of buttermilk splashing into the mouth. The same words, with “a knot” or “a fist” in place of the Navkar, make a vow that ends when one unties the knot or opens the fist (l.1, pp.202–204).
Porisi and two-porisi: the exceptions show the aim. Porisi lasts one prahar, until a man’s shadow equals his height; it adds exceptions for a clouded sky, confusing the directions, and a trusted person’s word. The exception “for the sake of complete equanimity” lets a sudden severe pain be treated, because a vow that produces distress and anger has already lost its purpose. The two-porisi vow (purimaddha) adds “by order of an elder”: serving a sick monk is an inner austerity, greater than the outer austerity of fasting (l.2–3, pp.204–206).
Eating once. Ekasana is one meal a day, after which only boiled water (or nothing) is taken; it has eight exceptions, two of which (a householder arriving, and eating leftover alms that would otherwise be thrown away) are for monks only. Ekatthana is stricter: one meal without moving any limb except the right hand and the mouth, so it has seven exceptions (l.4–5, pp.206–209).
Ayambil conquers the tongue. One meal of dry, bland food such as boiled rice or urad, with no rich foods (vigai: milk, curd, ghee, oil, jaggery, sugar). It ranks above ekasana because in ekasana one may still eat all six tastes. Its extra exceptions cover a trace of ghee left on the giver’s ladle, and similar cases; these are for monks, whose food is given by others (l.6, pp.209–211).
The fast runs from sunrise to sunrise. A fast (upavas) gives up all four foods, or three if water is kept; on a three-food fast six kinds of water are allowed. Names like “fourth meal” for a one-day fast are only old conventional names (l.7, pp.211–212).
The end of the day, the end of life, and a secret resolve. Divas-charim gives up food from evening until the next sunrise; bhav-charim is the same vow taken for the rest of life (santhara). An abhigraha is a private condition: “I will eat only when such-and-such happens, otherwise I will fast so many days.” It is told to no one, and should be taken only after honestly weighing one’s own strength, not to copy others (l.8–9, pp.212–214).
Giving up rich foods. Nirvigai gives up ghee, oil, milk, curd, jaggery and sugar, with nine exceptions. A table in the book shows the count for each vow: Navakarshi 2, Porisi 6, two-porisi 7, ekasana 8, ekatthana 7, ayambil 8, fast 5, divas-charim 4, nirvigai 9, abhigraha 4 (l.10, pp.214–215).
Six purities, and closing the vow properly. A vow must be pure in faith, knowledge, respect, recitation, keeping and inner feeling. When it ends, the closing formula declares it “touched, kept, carried to the end, praised, purified and fulfilled”, and asks that any failure be undone (pp.216–217).
The Namotthunam ends the Avashyak. The text opened with the Navkar, put the Logassa in the middle, and ends with this praise. Each word names a virtue: the Tirthankara builds a ford (tirtha) across worldly life in the fourfold sangha; he is a lamp, not a sun, because a lamp lights other lamps and makes them like itself; he gives fearlessness, the greatest gift; and he has reached the Siddha state, which is free of trouble, unmoving, without end and without return. Said for the Arihanta, the ending changes to “who wishes to reach that place”; a third Namotthunam is said to one’s own teacher. It is also called Shakrastava, because Indra praises the Lord with it (pp.218–229).

Key passages
Lesson 1, s.1 · The Navakarshi vow

उग्गए सूरे णमुक्कारसहियं पच्चक्खामि चउव्विहं पि आहारं-असणं पाणं खाइमं साइमं अण्णत्थणाभोगेणं सहसागारेणं वोसिरामि ।

Now that the sun has risen, I take the vow that ends with the Navkar: I give up all four kinds of food (staple food, water, fruit and sweets, mouth-fresheners), except through forgetfulness or sudden accident. I let them go.
Lesson 7, s.1 · The fast

उग्गए सूरे, अभत्तट्ठं पच्चक्खामि, चउव्विहं पि आहारं-असणं, पाणं, खाइमं, साइमं । अण्णत्थणाभोगेणं, सहसागारेणं, पारिट्ठावणियागारेणं, महत्तरागारेणं, सव्वसमाहिवत्तियागारेणं, वोसिरमि ।

Now that the sun has risen, I take the vow of “no purpose of food” (a fast) and give up all four kinds of food, except through forgetfulness, sudden accident, leftover alms that would be thrown away, an elder’s order, or to keep complete equanimity. I let them go.
Niryukti 1585 (no. 2) · Six purities of a vow

सा पुन सद्दहण जाणणा य विनयानुभासणा चेव ।
अनुपालना विसोही भावविसोही भवे छट्ठा ॥

Its purity lies in faith, knowledge, respect and correct recitation, in keeping it, and sixth, in purity of inner feeling.
No. 3 · Closing the vow

उग्गएसूरे नमुक्कार सहियं… पच्चक्खाणं कयं । तं पच्चक्खाणं सम्मं काएण फासियं, पालियं, तीरियं, किट्टियं, सोहियं, आराहियं । जं च न आराहियं तस्स मिच्छामि दुक्कडम् ।

At sunrise I took the vow that ends with the Navkar. That vow I have properly touched with the body, kept, carried to its end, praised, purified and fulfilled. Whatever I have not fulfilled, may that wrong of mine be undone.
Namotthunam, opening · Salutation to the Arihantas

णमोत्थुणं अरिहंताणं भगवंताणं आइगराणं तित्थयराणं सयंसंबुद्धाणं पुरिसुत्तमाणं पुरिस-सीहाणं पुरिस-वर-पुंडरियाणं पुरिसवर-गंधहत्थीणं लोगुत्तमाणं लोगणाहाणं लोगहियाणं लोगपईवाणं लोगपज्जोयगराणं अभयदयाणं …

Salutation to the Arihanta Bhagavans: the beginners of dharma, the founders of the ford, awakened by themselves; best among men, lions among men, white lotuses among men, scent-elephants among men; highest in the world, lords of the world, friends of the world, lamps of the world, lighters of the world; givers of fearlessness …
Namotthunam, close · Crossed over, and helping others cross

… जिणाणं-जावयाणं तिण्णाणं तारयाणं बुद्धाणं-बोहयाणं मुत्ताणं-मोयगाणं सव्वण्णूणं सव्वदरिसीणं सिव-मयल-मरुय-मणंत-मक्खय-मव्वाबाह-मपुणरावित्ति सिद्धिगइ णामधेयं ठाणं संपत्ताणं णमो जिणाणं जियभयाणं ।

… who have conquered and help others conquer, who have crossed and carry others across, who are awake and awaken others, who are free and free others; all-knowing and all-seeing; who have reached the place called the Siddha state, free of trouble, unmoving, free of disease, endless, imperishable, unhindered and without return. Salutation to the Jinas, who have conquered fear.
Checked against the scans: l.1 · l.7 · no. 2, 3 · Namotthunam. Corrected from the translated pages: अभत्तट्ठं (not अभट्ठं) in l.7; पुंडरियाणं (not पुंडरीयाणं) in the Namotthunam. The print itself reads वोसिरमि at the end of l.7, where every other vow has वोसिरामि (“I let go”); kept as printed, probably a misprint. The translated pages label this lesson “Lesson 9”; the scan has पाठ-७.

09_modules/avashyak_07_householders_vows.title: Module · Avashyak 7: The Householder's Vows
09_modules/avashyak_07_householders_vows.content:
Avashyak 7 · Shravak Vrat (શ્રાવક વ્રત): The Householder’s Vows
In one line: a lay follower first turns from wrong belief to right faith, then takes twelve vows sized to household life (five small vows, three supporting vows, four training vows), learns the faults that weaken each one, and at life’s end may let go of the body in sallekhana.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, “The vows of a Shravaka” section after the 6th Avashyak (15 sutras and 3 Niryukti verses), translated pages 230–264. 22 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

This section comes from the commentary, not the sutra. The sutra’s own lessons (Karemi Bhante and the rest) speak of a monk’s great vows; it does not set out the lay vows. Haribhadra’s commentary, inside the 6th Avashyak on renunciation, adds them, and the book follows it. The lay follower’s five small vows are “partial root vows”; the other seven are “partial supporting vows” (pp.230–231).
Right faith comes first. A shravaka is “one who listens” to dharma. Some take vows (like Ananda); some have only right faith (like King Shrenika). Before any vow, the lay follower turns back from wrong belief and accepts right faith: from now on he does not bow to other sects’ teachers, gods or shrines as a religious act, and does not feed their ascetics as a religious duty. There are six exceptions (king, community, force, a god, elders, hard times for one’s living), and giving out of compassion is not forbidden. The five faults of right faith are doubt, wanting another faith, doubting the fruit of dharma, praising other sects’ teachings, and close religious intimacy with them. Asking questions to strengthen faith, as Gautama did, is not doubt (s.1, pp.231–234).
Non-violence, sized for a household. The layman gives up, for life, intentional violence; he cannot give up the violence of cooking, farming or travel. Tradition puts a monk’s compassion at 20 parts and a layman’s at 1¼: he renounces only intentional, purposeless violence to innocent moving beings. Vows can be taken in 49 combinations of doing, causing and approving by mind, speech and body. The faults are tying up, beating, cutting, overloading and withholding food, and today these include overworking servants and paying wages late (s.2, pp.234–239).
No big lies; no theft. The layman gives up five gross lies: about a bride or groom, cattle, land, a deposit left in trust, and false witness. He gives up stealing by breaking in, opening locks, robbery or picking up what is plainly another’s; its faults include buying stolen goods, smuggling, false weights and passing off bad goods as good. The commentary keeps one test throughout: done by mistake it is a fault (atichara), done on purpose it breaks the vow (anachara) (s.3–4, pp.239–243).
Content with one’s own spouse; a limit on possessions. The fourth vow keeps a man to his own wife (and a woman to her own husband). The fifth sets a limit on nine kinds of outer possessions: wealth, grain, fields, houses, silver, gold, people and animals in one’s keeping, and household goods. Possession is really attachment (murchha); anything that comes beyond the limit should be given away (s.5–6, pp.243–246).
Three supporting vows guard the five. Limit how far you travel in each direction, so no harm is done beyond it. Limit daily things (towels, oils, clothes, foods, vehicles, beds: 26 items), avoid uncooked living foods, and avoid fifteen trades that cause great harm, such as charcoal-making, forest-cutting, dealing in ivory, liquor, poison or weapons, and draining lakes. Give up purposeless harm: brooding and cruel thoughts, careless habits, handing out weapons, and urging others into sin (s.7–9, pp.247–255).
Four training vows are practised again and again. Samayik: 48 minutes of equanimity, spoiled by a wandering mind, harsh speech, a restless body, forgetting one is in samayik, or doing it irregularly. Deshavagasik: shrinking the travel limit for a day, and not getting round it by sending people or signalling. Paushadh: a full day and night lived like a monk, fasting, with no bathing or adornment, celibate, and free of business. Atithi samvibhag: giving monks pure food and fourteen kinds of things, honestly earned, at the right time, with respect and joy (s.10–13, pp.255–262).
Right faith is the root of it all. The five small vows and three supporting vows are taken for life; the four training vows for a set time. Right faith arises either by itself or through teaching. A layman’s vows are “like gold ingots”: he may take one, two or three as his strength allows, and need not take all twelve at once (s.14, pp.262–263).
Sallekhana: the last practice, not suicide. When the body can no longer serve spiritual practice, the layman confesses, gives up the eighteen sins, the four foods and attachment to the body, and waits for death in equanimity. Its faults are wishing for a good next life, for heaven, for longer life, for quick death, or for pleasures. Suicide comes from anger, grief or despair; this “wise death” comes from renunciation, so the two are as different as earth and sky (s.15, pp.263–264).

Key passages
s.1 · Turning to right faith

तत्थ समणोवासओ पुव्वामेव मिच्छत्ताओ पडिक्कमइ, सम्मत्तं उवसंपज्जइ, … सम्मत्तस्स समणोवासएणं इमे पंच अइयारा जाणियव्वा ण समायरियव्वा, तं जहा- संका, कंखा, वितिगिच्छा, परपासंडपसंसा, परपासंडसंथवो ।

There, first of all, the lay follower turns back from wrong belief and takes up right faith. … The lay follower should know these five faults of right faith but not commit them: doubt, longing for another faith, doubting the fruit of dharma, praising other sects, and close association with them.
s.2 · The vow of non-violence

थूलगपाणाइवायं समणोवासओ पच्चक्खाइ, से पाणाइवाए दुविहे पण्णत्ते, तं जहा- संकप्पओ अ आरंभओ अ । तत्थ समणोवासओ संकप्पओ जावज्जीवाए पच्चक्खाइ, नो आरंभओ । थूलगपाणाइवायवेरमणस्स समणोवासएणं इमे पंच अइयारा जाणियव्वा, (ण समायरियव्वा) तं जहा- बंधे, वहे, छविच्छेए, अइभारे, भत्तपाणवुच्छेए ।

The lay follower gives up gross violence to living beings. That violence is of two kinds: intended and arising from work. Of these he gives up intended violence for life, not violence arising from work. He should know, but not commit, five faults of this vow: tying up, beating, cutting the skin, overloading, and withholding food and water.
s.6 · A limit on desire

अपरिमियपरिग्गहं समणोवासओ पच्चक्खाइ इच्छापरिमाणं उवसंपज्जइ, से परिग्गहे दुविहे पण्णत्ते, तं जहा- सचित्तपरिग्गहे अचित्तपरिग्गहे । इच्छापरिमाणस्स समणोवासएणं इमे पंच अइयारा जाणियव्वा, ण समायरिव्वा तं जहा- धणधाण्णपमाणाइक्कमे, खित्तवत्थुपमाणाइक्कमे, हिरण्णसुवण्णपमाणाइक्कमे, दुपयचउप्पयपमाणाइक्कमे, कुवियपमाणाइक्कमे।

The lay follower gives up unlimited possessions and takes up a limit on desire. Possessions are of two kinds, living and non-living. He should know, but not commit, five faults: going beyond the limit set for wealth and grain, for fields and houses, for silver and gold, for two-footed and four-footed beings, and for household goods.
s.10 · Samayik

सामाइयं णाम सावज्जजोगपरिवज्जणं णिरवज्जजोगपडिसेवणं च । सामाइयस्स समणोवासएणं इमे पंच अइयारा जाणियव्वा, (ण समायरियव्वा) तं जहा- मणदुप्पणिहाणे, वइदुप्पणिहाणे, कायदुप्पणिहाणे, सामाइयस्स सइअकरणया, सामाइयस्स अणवट्ठियस्स करणया ।

Samayik means giving up sinful activity and taking up blameless activity. Its five faults, to be known but not committed: misusing the mind, misusing speech, misusing the body, forgetting that one is in samayik, and doing samayik unsteadily.
s.14 · The root is right faith

इत्थं पुण समणोवासगधम्मे पंचाणुव्वयाइं तिण्णि गुणव्वयाइं आवकहियाइं, चत्तारि सिक्खावयाइं इत्तरियाइं । एयस्स पुणो समणोवासगधम्मस्स मूलवत्थुं सम्मत्तं, तं जहा- तं णिसग्गेण वा अभिगमेण वा पंच अइयारविसुद्धं अणुव्वयगुणव्वयाइं च अभिग्गहाअण्णेवि पडिमादओ विसेसकरणजोगा ।

So in the lay follower’s dharma, the five small vows and three supporting vows are for life, and the four training vows are for a time. The root of this dharma is right faith, which comes by itself or through learning. With right faith free of its five faults, and the small and supporting vows kept, other resolves and the lay follower’s stages (pratima) may be taken up for special purification.
s.15 · Sallekhana

अपच्छिमा मारणंतिया संलेहणाझुसणाराहणया । इमीसे समणोवासएणं इमे पंच अइयारा जाणियव्वा, (ण समायरियव्वा) तं जहा- इहलोगासंसप्पओगे, परलोगासंसप्पओगे, जीवियासंसप्पओगे, मरणासंसप्पओगे, कामभोगासंसप्पओगे ।

The last practice, at the approach of death: lovingly following sallekhana, the thinning of body and passions. Its five faults, to be known but not committed: wishing for this world, wishing for the next world, wishing to live, wishing to die, and wishing for pleasures.
Checked against the scans: s.1 · s.2 · s.6 · s.10 · s.14 · s.15. Corrected from the translated pages: मारणंतिया (not मारंतिया) in s.15, धणधाण्ण in s.6. The print reads समायरिव्वा in s.6 where every other vow has समायरियव्वा (“to be practised”); kept as printed, probably a misprint.

09_modules/dashvaikalik_01_the_monk_and_.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 1: The Monk and the Bee
09_modules/dashvaikalik_01_the_monk_and_.content:
Dashvaikalik 1 · Drumapushpika (दुमपुप्फिया): The Monk and the Bee
In one line: dharma, made of non-violence, restraint and austerity, is the highest good, and a monk keeps his body alive the way a bee feeds on flowers: a little from many, taking only what is freely given, and hurting no one.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 1 (5 verses), translated pages 61–75 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 8 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The name means “the tree’s flower”. Duma is a tree and pupphiya a flower. The chapter compares the harmless way monks get their food to a bee drawing nectar from a tree’s flowers, and so is called “the tree’s flower” (introduction, p. 61).
Dharma is the highest good, and even the gods bow to it. Dharma is non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapa). The gods bow to the person whose mind is always set on it. The commentary calls this opening verse the essence of the whole book: it gives what dharma is, how to reach it, and how great it is. Dharma protects the soul from falling into a bad state and sets it in a good one (v.1).
The three parts hold each other up. Non-violence means seeing all beings as equal to yourself and not hurting them. Restraint means turning away from sinful activity; the commentary lists seventeen kinds, from care for earth, water, fire, air and plant beings to restraint of mind, speech and body. Non-violence is the goal and restraint is keeping the rules that reach it, so each needs the other. Austerity “burns” karma, and it is dharma only when done to purify the soul, not for fame here or rewards hereafter (v.1, commentary).
The problem the chapter solves. A monk has a body, the body needs food, and getting food seems impossible without harm. How can he then keep non-violence? The bee is the answer (introduction, p. 61).
Live like the bee. A bee drinks nectar from a tree’s flowers without making them wither, and it is satisfied. In the same way, monks who are free of ties go out seeking food that is given to them (v.2–3).
The monk’s difference from the bee. The bee takes nectar no one gave it. The monk takes only what the householder gives gladly, food the family cooked for itself, free of living things, and within the rules for alms. The commentary lists the bee-like points: he does not cook or have food cooked; takes a little from each house; does not store; does not depend on one house, village or person, but goes to rich, middle and poor homes alike (v.3, commentary; pp. 61–62).
The monk’s vow. “We will get our living so that no one is harmed, taking from what householders made for themselves, as bees go among flowers.” The commentary gives six names for such alms, among them the cow’s way of grazing (gochari: a mouthful here and there, never pulling up the roots, and eyes only on the food, not on the person serving it) and filling a pit or putting out a fire (eat plain food only to quiet hunger) (v.4).
Four marks of a true monk. He is awake to the truth, unattached like the bee, content with whatever varied food he receives from many houses, and in control of his senses and mind. Because of these he is called a monk (sadhu). Sudharma Swami ends: “Thus I say” (v.5).

Key verses
1 · Dharma is the highest good

धम्मो मंगलमुक्किट्ठं, अहिंसा संजमो तवो ।
देवा वि तं णमंसंति, जस्स धम्मे सया मणो ॥

Dharma, which is non-violence, restraint and austerity, is the highest auspiciousness. Even the gods bow to the one whose mind is always in dharma.
2 · The bee does not hurt the flower

जहा दुम्मस्स पुप्फेसु, भमरो आवियइ रसं ।
ण य पुप्फं किलामेइ, सो य पीणेइ अप्पयं ॥

Just as a bee drinks nectar from the flowers of a tree, does not make the flower wither, and still satisfies itself,
3 · So do monks seek their food

एमेए समणा मुत्ता जे लोए संति साहुणो ।
विहंगमा व पुप्फेसु, दाणभत्तेसणे रया ॥

so too the monks in this world, free of ties, are like bees among flowers: they are devoted to seeking food that is given to them.
4 · The monk’s vow

वयं च वित्तिं लब्भामो, ण य कोइ उवहम्मइ ।
अहागडेसु रीयंते, पुप्फेसु भमरा जहा ॥

We will get our living in such a way that no living being is harmed. As bees go among flowers, we will take from food that householders have made for themselves.
5 · Why they are called monks

महुगारसमा बुद्धा, जे भवंति अणिस्सिया ।
णाणापिंडरया दंता, तेण वुच्चंति साहुणो ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Those who know the truth, who are unattached like the bee, content with varied food from many houses, and in control of themselves: because of this they are called monks. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.2–3 · v.4 · v.5

09_modules/dashvaikalik_02_the_groundwor.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 2: The Groundwork of Monkhood
09_modules/dashvaikalik_02_the_groundwor.content:
Dashvaikalik 2 · Shramanyapurvaka (सामण्णपुव्वयं): The Groundwork of Monkhood
In one line: no one can live as a monk without first giving up desire for sense pleasures, and when the mind slips, as Rathanemi’s did, it must be brought back at once, as Rajimati brought him back with a few hard words.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 2 (11 verses), translated pages 76–94 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Giving up desire comes before monkhood. The name means “what comes before the monk’s life”. Its seed is turning away from desire; the commentator adds patience, since only a patient person can drop desire (introduction, p. 76).
A man ruled by desire sinks at every step. How can someone who does not hold back desire live as a monk? Caught in his own plans and longings, he grows downcast at every step. Desire and restraint are like light and dark: they cannot stay together. The commentary quotes: “Desire, I know you; you are born of thought. I will not think of you, so you will not arise.” It tells of a young monk who asked his father-guru for one comfort after another (shoes, socks, a head cloth, a soft bed, a bath) until he finally said he could not live without a woman, and the guru left him (v.1).
Not having is not giving up. A man who does not enjoy clothes, scents, ornaments, women and beds only because he cannot get them is not called a renouncer. The true renouncer turns his back on lovely, wanted pleasures that are in his hands, by his own choice. Two stories make the point: Subandhu, who lived like a monk only out of fear of a poisoned scent left by Chanakya, was no renouncer; and when Abhayakumar offered three heaps of gems to anyone who would give up water, fire and women for life, no one took them, which showed that the woodcutter-monk had given up more than gems (v.2–3).
When the mind wanders: “She is not mine, nor am I hers.” Even a careful monk’s mind may stray. He should remove the attachment with this thought, seeing the woman and every other thing as separate from the soul. The commentary’s picture: when a prince’s pebble cracks a servant girl’s water pot, she plugs it with wet clay at once; plug a bad thought the same way (v.4).
Four remedies. Bear heat (practise austerity), give up softness and comfort, get past desire (and suffering is gone with it), cut off aversion and remove attachment. Do this and you will be happy (v.5).
The story behind the verses. Prince Arishtanemi turned back from his own wedding when he saw animals penned to be killed for the feast, and became a monk. Rajimati, his bride-to-be, also renounced. On her way to Girnar a storm separated her from the other nuns; she entered a cave and spread out her wet clothes. Rathanemi, Arishtanemi’s younger brother and a monk, was meditating there, saw her in a flash of lightning, and his mind turned to desire (introduction, pp. 77–78).
The snake that will not take back its poison. Snakes of the Agandhana family would rather enter a blazing fire than suck back poison they have spat out. “Shame on you, seeker of disgrace, who would drink back what you vomited for the sake of this life. Death would be better” (v.6–7).
Remember who you are. Rajimati reminds him that she is King Ugrasena’s daughter and he is of the Andhaka-Vrishni line: let us not be like the Gandhana snake; steady your mind and live in restraint. If you long for every woman you see, you will drift like the rootless hada plant pushed by the wind (v.8–9).
He came back, as an elephant to the goad. Hearing her well-spoken words, Rathanemi was set firmly back in dharma. The commentary says her words worked because her own conduct was pure. Both later reached liberation (v.10; p. 78).
The wise do the same. The awakened, learned and discerning turn away from pleasures just as that best of men did. The commentary explains why he is still called “best of men”: one who slips but admits the fault, takes good advice and returns to restraint is great; best of all is one who never wavers (v.11).

Key verses
1 · Desire first, or no monkhood

कहं णु कुज्जा सामण्णं, जो कामे ण णिवारए ।
पए पए विसीयंतो, संकप्पस्स वसं गओ ॥

How can one live as a monk who does not hold back desire? Under the sway of his own longings, he sinks into gloom at every step.
3 · The true renouncer

जे य कंते पिए भोए, लद्धे वि पिट्ठि कुव्वइ ।
साहीणे चयइ भोए, से हु चाइ त्ति वुच्चइ ॥

The one who turns his back on lovely and dear pleasures even when he has them, and gives up pleasures that are in his own power, is truly called a renouncer.
4 · She is not mine, nor am I hers

समाइ पेहाइ परिव्वयंतो, सिया मणो णिस्सरइ बहिद्धा ।
ण सा महं णो वि अहं पि तीसे, इच्चेव ताओ विणएज्ज रागं ॥

If, while a monk moves about with care, his mind should wander outside restraint, let him remove his attachment to her with this thought: “She is not mine, nor am I hers.”
6 · The Agandhana snake

पक्खंदे जलियं जोइं, धूमकेउं दुरासयं ।
णेच्छंति वंतयं भोत्तुं, कुले जाया अगंधणे ॥

Snakes born in the Agandhana family leap into a blazing, smoky fire that is hard even to approach, but they will not take back what they have vomited.
7 · Rajimati’s rebuke

धिरत्थु तेऽजसोकामी, जो तं जीवियकारणा ।
वंतं इच्छसि आवेउं, सेयं ते मरणं भवे ॥

Shame on you, seeker of disgrace, who for the sake of this life want to drink back what you have vomited. Death would be better for you.
10 · Like an elephant to the goad

तीसे सो वयणं सोच्चा, संजयाइ सुभासियं ।
अंकुसेण जहा णागो, धम्मे संपडिवाइओ ॥

Hearing the well-spoken words of that restrained nun, he was brought back to dharma, as an elephant is brought back by the goad.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3 · v.4 · v.6–7 · v.10

09_modules/dashvaikalik_03_minor_rules_o.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 3: Minor Rules of Conduct
09_modules/dashvaikalik_03_minor_rules_o.content:
Dashvaikalik 3 · Kshullakachara Katha (क्षुल्लकाचार कथा): Minor Rules of Conduct
In one line: a monk who wants to be free keeps away from a long list of small-looking comforts and habits (the tradition counts fifty-two), because each one brings harm to living beings, attachment to the body or dependence on householders; by keeping clear of them he burns off his karma.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 3 (15 verses), translated pages 95–121 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 14 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Why “minor” rules. Chapter 6 gives the monk’s conduct at length; this chapter gives it in short, by listing what must not be done, so it is called the account of minor (kshullaka) conduct. Conduct is the heart of knowledge, and keeping it pure helps the monk and, the introduction adds, brings peace to society and the world (introduction, p. 95).
Who the rules are for. These things are not done by the great sages, the nirgranthas (those free of every knot of possession), who are firmly set in restraint, free of worldly ties, and protectors of themselves and of all six kinds of living beings. Each quality depends on the others (v.1).
Rules about food. No food made for the monk, bought for him, taken daily from a house that invited him, or carried to him from elsewhere. No food that is stored, eaten from a householder’s dish, prepared for a king, or made after asking “What would you like?” No food from the family that gives him lodging, and no food or water not fully free of life. Behind most of these lies one reason: cooking and buying for a monk harm living beings, and accepting it makes him a party to that harm (v.2–3, 5–6).
No eating at night. For a nirgrantha, giving up night food is part of the great vow. Bringing food by day to eat at night, by night to eat by day, by day to eat the next day, or by night to eat at night are all forbidden (v.2, commentary).
No care and decoration of the body. No bathing, scent, garlands, fanning, massage, cleaning or colouring the teeth, looking at oneself in a mirror, collyrium for the eyes, oiling or adorning the body, or purging and cleansing treatments done for the body’s sake. Adornment, says the commentary, endangers celibacy and binds sticky karma (v.2–3, 5, 9).
No comforts and no worldly ties. No games of dice, no umbrella, no footwear, no lighting fire, no sitting on chairs or beds, no sitting in a householder’s home, no serving householders or asking about their affairs, no getting food by mentioning one’s caste, family, craft, learning or austerity, and no calling on family for refuge when in hardship. The commentary notes allowed exceptions, such as an umbrella or treatment in serious illness, set against the general rule (v.3–6).
Nothing living. Radish, ginger, sugarcane pieces, tubers, roots, fruits and seeds while still living, and six kinds of living (unprocessed) salt, are not to be taken (v.7–8).
The true nirgrantha. He knows and stops the five inflows of karma (ashrava), guards mind, speech and body, protects the six kinds of beings, holds the five senses in check, is steady, and looks only to the straight path. He bears the summer sun, goes without covering in winter, and stays in one place during the rains to protect the many beings born then (v.10–12).
The goal: an end to all suffering. Having conquered hardships as enemies, shaken off delusion and won over the senses, the great sages strive to end all suffering. After doing what is hard and bearing what is hard to bear, some go to the heavens and some, free of karma’s dust, reach liberation (v.13–14).
Restraint closes the inlet, austerity dries the pond. Through restraint and austerity they destroy their past karma, reach the path to liberation and are fully freed. The commentary’s picture: first close the channels feeding a pond, then the sun dries up what is left (v.15).

Key verses
1 · For whom these things are wrong

संजमे सुट्ठिअप्पाणं, विप्पमुक्काण ताइणं ।
तेसिमेयमणाइण्णं णिग्गंथाण महेसिणं ॥

For the great sages, the nirgranthas, whose souls are well set in restraint, who are free of all ties and protect themselves and others, the following things are not to be done.
2 · The first nine wrong practices

उद्देसियं कीयगडं, णियागमभिहडाणि य ।
राइभत्ते सिणाणे य, गंधमल्ले य वीयणे ॥

Food made for the monk, food bought for him, food taken daily from a house by invitation, and food brought to him; eating at night, bathing, scents, garlands and fanning.
11 · Marks of the nirgrantha

पंचासवपरिण्णाया, तिगुत्ता छसु संजया ।
पंचणिग्गहणा धीरा, णिग्गंथा उज्जुदंसिणो ॥

They know the five inflows and give them up, guard themselves in three ways, are careful toward the six kinds of beings, hold the five senses in check, are steady, and see the straight path: these are the nirgranthas.
12 · Through the three seasons

आयावयंति गिम्हेसु, हेमंतेसु अवाउडा ।
वासासु पडिसंलीणा, संजया सुसमाहिया ॥

In summer they stand in the sun’s heat, in winter they stay uncovered, in the rains they stay withdrawn in one place: restrained and well collected.
13 · Striving to end all suffering

परीसह रिऊदंता, धुयमोहा जिइंदिया ।
सव्वदुक्खप्पहीणट्ठा, पक्कमंति महेसिणो ॥

Having tamed hardships as enemies, shaken off delusion and conquered the senses, the great sages strive to put an end to all suffering.
15 · Freed by restraint and austerity

खवित्ता पुव्वकमाइं, संजमेण तवेण य ।
सिद्धिमग्गमणुप्पत्ता, ताइणो परिणिव्वुडा ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Having destroyed their past karma through restraint and austerity, and having reached the path to liberation, the protectors of all beings are fully freed. Thus I say.
(As printed: पुव्वकमाइं. The same page’s word meanings read पुव्वकम्माइं, “past karmas”, so this is a misprint; the English follows the meaning.)
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.2 · v.11–12 · v.13 · v.15

09_modules/dashvaikalik_04_six_kinds_of_.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 4: The Six Kinds of Living Beings
09_modules/dashvaikalik_04_six_kinds_of_.content:
Dashvaikalik 4 · Chhajjivaniya (छज्जीवणिया, Gujarati छ जीवनिकाय): The Six Kinds of Living Beings
In one line: earth, water, fire, air, plants and moving creatures are all alive, so the monk takes the five great vows and the vow against night eating, does everything with care, and grows from knowing the living and non-living all the way to liberation.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 4 (19 prose sutras and 29 verses), translated pages 122–188 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 25 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

This teaching comes straight from Mahavira. Sudharma Swami tells his disciple Jambu: “I heard this from the Lord.” The chapter is called the Six Kinds of Living Beings, and also the Teaching of Dharma (Dharmaprajnapti); it is good for a monk to learn it. The introduction calls it “like the life-breath” of a seeker, because the great vows given at the greater initiation are in it (introduction, s.1–3).
Earth, water, fire, air and plants are alive. Each contains many beings, each with its own separate existence, until it is changed by a “weapon” (something that kills them, such as fire, water, other soil or trampling). The commentary gives signs: a dug-out mine slowly fills like a wound healing, and fire grows with fuel and fades without it. Plants are of eight kinds by how they grow (from tips, roots, joints, stems, seeds, by themselves, grasses, creepers) (s.4, commentary).
The sixth kind is moving beings (trasa). They are born in eight ways (from eggs, from the womb, from sweat, appearing suddenly like gods and hell beings, and so on), and you can tell them because they come forward, go back, curl up, cry out, take fright and run away. Insects and ants, animals, hell beings, humans and gods all belong here, and all of them want happiness (s.5, commentary).
The monk gives up harming all six, in nine ways. He will not harm them himself, have others harm them, or approve of harm, in mind, speech or body (three times three, nine ways), for his whole life. He turns back from past wrongs, condemns them in his own heart, confesses them before the guru, and lets go of the self that did them (s.6, commentary).
The five great vows and the sixth vow. No taking of life, whether beings are tiny or large, moving or still; no false speech, whether from anger, greed, fear or jest; no taking what is not given, little or much, in village, town or forest; no sexual activity, with gods, humans or animals; no possessions, small or large, living or non-living; and no eating at night. Nonviolence comes first, and the others serve it. They are “great” because nothing is left out and they are taken for life. Night eating is given up because tiny creatures cannot be seen in the dark. All six are taken “for the good of my own soul” (s.7–13, commentary).
The vow is lived out in small daily acts. By day or night, alone or with others, asleep or awake, the monk does not scratch or dig the earth or a wall, does not touch or wring out water, dew or a wet cloth, does not feed, kindle or put out fire, does not fan himself or blow on hot food, and does not walk, sit or lie on seeds and sprouts. If an insect or ant climbs onto his body, cloth or bowl, he looks, brushes it gently, and puts it down in a safe, quiet place (s.14–19).
Carelessness binds bad karma; care does not. A seeker who walks, stands, sits, sleeps, eats or speaks carelessly (ayatana) harms living beings and binds bad karma with bitter fruit. The disciple asks how to live, and the answer is one word: with care (yatana). These six acts cannot be given up, but done with care they bind no bad karma. One who sees all beings as equal to himself, watches them rightly, has shut the doors of karmic inflow and controls his senses is like a boat without holes that water cannot enter (v.1–9, commentary).
First knowledge, then compassion. What can an ignorant person do? Only one who knows the living and the non-living can know restraint. By listening to the teaching one learns what is good and what is harmful, and then does the good. People who think only animals and humans are alive keep their compassion that small (v.10–13, commentary).
A ladder from knowledge to liberation. Each verse begins “when” and the next begins “then.” Knowing the living and the non-living, one knows how beings are born into many states; then merit and sin, bondage and liberation; then one loses interest in divine and human pleasures; then one gives up outer and inner ties; then one becomes a homeless monk; then one touches the highest dharma; then one shakes off the dust of karma; then one gains perfect knowledge and perception; then, as a Jina, one knows the world and what lies beyond it; then one stills mind, speech and body (the shaileshi state); then one destroys all karma, and rests forever at the top of the universe as a liberated soul (siddha). The commentary counts thirteen steps (v.14–25).
Who finds a good destiny hard, and who finds it easy. It is hard for a monk who chases comfort, sleeps too much and keeps washing his body. It is easy for one rich in austerity, straightforward, forgiving, restrained and able to bear hardships. Even those who take vows late in life reach the heavens quickly if they love austerity, restraint, forgiveness and celibacy. The last verse tells the monk who has gained rare monkhood not to harm the six kinds by any act (v.26–29, commentary).

Key verses
1 · Careless walking binds karma

अजयं चरमाणो य, पाणभूयाइं हिंसइ ।
बंधई पावयं कम्मं, तं से होइ कडुयं फलं ॥

One who walks carelessly harms living beings, moving and still. He binds bad karma, and it gives him bitter fruit. (Verses 2–6 say the same of standing, sitting, sleeping, eating and speaking.)
8 · With care, no bad karma

जयं चरे जयं चिट्ठे, जयमासे जयं सए ।
जयं भुंजंतो भासंतो पावकम्मं ण बंधइ ॥

Walk with care, stand with care, sit with care, sleep with care. Eating with care and speaking with care, one does not bind bad karma.
9 · All beings as oneself

सव्वभूयप्पभूयस्स, सम्मं भूयाइं पासओ ।
पिहियासवस्स दंतस्स, पावकम्मं ण बंधइ ॥

One who sees all beings as equal to himself, looks at beings rightly, has closed the doors of karmic inflow and controls his senses does not bind bad karma.
10 · First knowledge, then compassion

पढमं णाणं तओ दया, एवं चिट्ठइ सव्वसंजए ।
अण्णाणी किं काही, किं वा णाहीइ सेयपावगं ॥

First knowledge, then compassion: this is how every restrained monk stays firm. What can an ignorant person do? How will he know what is good and what is harmful?
11 · Learn by listening, then choose the good

सोच्चा जाणइ कल्लाणं, सोच्चा जाणइ पावगं ।
उभयंपि जाणइ सोच्चा, जं सेयं तं समायरे ॥

By listening one knows what is good, by listening one knows what is harmful. By listening one knows both; then do what is good.
25 · The top of the ladder

जया कम्मं खवित्ताणं, सिद्धिं गच्छइ णीरओ ।
तया लोगमत्थयत्थो, सिद्धो हवइ सासओ ॥

When he has destroyed his karma and, free of its dust, reaches perfection, then he rests at the top of the universe, a liberated soul forever.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.8 · v.9 · v.10–11 · v.25
