09_modules/dashvaikalik_05_seeking_alms.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 5: Seeking Alms
09_modules/dashvaikalik_05_seeking_alms.content:
Dashvaikalik 5 · Pindaishana (पिंडैषणा): Seeking Alms
In one line: a monk lives only on food he begs, so he must seek it, take it and eat it in a way that hurts no living being, burdens no giver and feeds no craving, and the giver who gives expecting nothing and the monk who takes expecting nothing both reach a good state.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 5 (150 verses in two sub-sections: sub-section (uddesha) 1 has 100 verses, uddesha 2 has 50), translated pages 189–299 (uddesha 1: pp. 189–263; uddesha 2: pp. 264–299). Verse numbers below are given as “1.v” and “2.v” for the two uddeshas. 20 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The name means “the search for food”, and the search has three parts. Pinda is food of all four kinds, eshana is searching: checking that it is free of faults. The introduction lists three searches: finding faultless food (avoiding the faults of how it was made), accepting it without the ten faults of receiving, and eating it without attachment. Begging by a monk who takes only what is naturally there, hurting no one, is called “begging that brings all blessings” (introduction, pp. 189–190).
Go at the right time, calm, and watch the ground. When the time for alms comes, the monk goes without hurry or craving and seeks food “in this order”. He walks slowly with an undistracted mind, looking a yoke’s length (about four cubits) ahead and avoiding seeds, plants, small creatures, raw water and earth. The commentary gives the picture of a calf that the merchant’s daughter-in-law feeds: it looks only at its fodder, never at her jewels; so the monk keeps his mind on the search alone (1.1–3).
Protect yourself and others on the way. Avoid pits, rough ground and mud, and do not cross on loose planks or stones when another path exists, since a fall hurts the monk and living beings. Do not go out in rain, fog, a strong wind or when insects swarm. Keep away from the prostitutes’ quarter, which shakes the vow of celibacy and makes people doubt the monk. Give a wide berth to dogs, a cow that has just calved, a wild bull, horse or elephant, children at play, a quarrel or a fight (1.4–12).
Walk and stand with dignity. Face neither raised in pride nor bent in gloom; not hurrying, talking or laughing; going to rich and poor homes alike. Do not stare at windows, holes or the secret stores of kings. Do not enter houses that are forbidden, that have said “do not come”, or that people distrust. Do not push open a door or curtain without asking, enter a dark room with a low door, step over a goat, child, dog or calf, or go past the part of the house the family allows (1.13–26).
Refuse food if giving it hurts a living being. If the giver spills it, treads on seeds or plants, touches raw water or living things, or washes hands, ladle or bowl in raw water before giving (the “before” fault) or after giving (the “after” fault), the monk says: “Such a thing is not proper for me.” He may accept from a hand already smeared with food, if nothing else is wrong (1.27–36).
Refuse food if giving it causes anyone pain or loss. Food two people share is taken only if both want to give. Food made for a pregnant woman is taken only after she has eaten, and not if a woman near her time stands up or sits down to give. Not if a mother puts her crying baby down to fetch alms. Not if there is any doubt, if a heavy lid or seal must be broken, or if the food was set aside as charity, for merit, or for beggars or other ascetics, since the monk would take it from them (1.37–54).
Ask “for whom was this made, and by whom?” Food made for the monk, bought, borrowed, brought to him or cooked extra for him is refused. So is food mixed with living flowers or seeds, set on water or fire, or given after stoking, damping or lifting a pot off the fire; food fetched down a ladder from a loft (the giver may fall); raw roots, fruit and ginger; dusty food laid out in a shop; fruit with more to throw away than to eat. Washing water is taken only when it has stood long and become lifeless; if he doubts it is drinkable he asks for a little in his hand to taste (1.55–81).
Back at the lodging: confess, give thanks, share, eat without fuss. The monk enters respectfully, recalls every slip on the way and at the houses, and tells his guru plainly what he received and how. Then he reflects with wonder that the Jinas have shown a blameless way to keep alive the body that serves liberation. He invites the other monks in order of seniority and eats with any who accept, carefully, from an open bowl, spilling nothing. Bitter or sweet, dry or moist, plenty or little, he eats it as if it were ghee and sugar, and does not scorn it. The commentary tells of a king who asked five beggars how they lived; only the Jain monk, who took food with no return, impressed him. The uddesha ends: the selfless giver and the monk who lives free of return are both rare, and both go to a good state (1.82–100).
The second uddesha adds more rules for the search. Wipe the bowl clean and leave nothing. If the food was not enough, go again. Go when people in that place eat; going at the wrong time tires you and makes you blame the village, and if you get nothing, do not grieve: call it austerity. Do not walk straight at birds or animals feeding. Do not sit, chat or lean on doors in a house. If another beggar or ascetic is at the door, wait out of sight until they have gone. Refuse alms from a giver who plucks or crushes living flowers, and raw stalks, shoots, pods, fruits and flours. Go to poor and rich homes in turn, never skipping the poor for the rich (2.1–25).
Stay even-minded, and do not deceive. Do not be gloomy when nothing comes or attached when much does; do not be angry if a householder refuses, or ask from someone who has just bowed, or grow proud when honoured. The petty monk who hides good food under plain food, or eats the tasty part on the way so that others will praise his plain diet, piles up sin and the thorn of deceit. The monk who drinks liquor in secret, thinking no one sees, grows more addicted, lies, is blamed by householders and cannot keep restraint even at death; the monk who shuns rich food and liquor is honoured by teachers and householders. One who “steals” austerity, vows, the monk’s appearance or his conduct is reborn among the lowly kilvishi gods, then as a dumb goat, in hell or as an animal, where awakening is very hard. So give up even the slightest deceit, learn the purity of alms from the wise, and live with senses controlled (2.26–50).

Key verses
1.3 · Look a yoke’s length ahead

पुरओ जुगमायाए, पेहमाणो महिं चरे ।
वज्जंतो बीयहरियाइं, पाणे य दगमट्टियं ॥

He should walk looking at the ground a yoke’s length ahead of him, avoiding seeds and green plants, living creatures, and living water and earth.
1.92 · A blameless way to keep the body

अहो जिणेहिं असावज्जा, वित्ती साहूण देसिया ।
मोक्खसाहणहेउस्स, साहुदेहस्स धारणा ॥

How wonderful! The Jinas have shown monks a blameless way of living, to sustain the monk’s body, which is the means of reaching liberation.
1.97 · Eat it as ghee and sugar

तित्तगं च कडुयं च कसायं, अंबिलं च महुरं लवणं वा ।
एयं लद्धमण्णत्थ पउत्तं, महुघयं व भुंजिज्ज संजए ॥

Pungent or bitter, astringent, sour, sweet or salty: whatever he has properly received, made for someone else, the restrained monk should eat as if it were ghee and sugar.
1.100 · The rare giver and the rare taker

दुल्लहा उ मुहादाई, मुहाजीवी वि दुल्लहा ।
मुहादाई मुहाजीवी, दोवि गच्छंति सुग्गइं ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Rare is the one who gives expecting nothing, and rare too is the one who lives without giving anything in return. The selfless giver and the selfless taker both go to a good state. Thus I say.
2.6 · No food today is austerity

सइ काले चरे भिक्खू, कुज्जा पुरिसकारियं ।
अलाभो त्ति ण सोएज्जा, तवो त्ति अहियासए ॥

When the right time comes, the monk should go for alms and make the effort. If he gets nothing, he should not grieve; thinking “this is austerity”, he should bear it.
2.30 · Not angry when ignored, not proud when honoured

जे ण वंदे ण से कुप्पे, वंदिओ ण समुक्कसे ।
एवमण्णेसमाणस्स, सामण्णमणुचिट्ठइ ॥

He should not be angry with one who does not bow to him, nor swell with pride when someone does. For one who seeks in this way, his monkhood stays whole.
Verses checked against the scans: 1.3 · 1.92 · 1.97 · 1.100 · 2.6 · 2.30

09_modules/dashvaikalik_06_the_great_con.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 6: The Great Conduct
09_modules/dashvaikalik_06_the_great_con.content:
Dashvaikalik 6 · Mahachara Katha (महाचार कथा): The Great Conduct
In one line: when kings and others ask a teacher how Jain monks live, he answers with eighteen rules of conduct (the six vows, care for the six classes of living beings, and six more rules), and says that a monk who keeps them all wipes out old karma and reaches liberation.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 6 (69 verses), translated pages 300–347. 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The kings ask, and the teacher answers. Kings, royal ministers, Brahmins and Kshatriyas come with calm minds to a teacher (acharya) staying in a garden, a man rich in knowledge, faith, restraint and austerity, and ask: “What is your conduct, and how do you seek alms?” He says the conduct of the Nirgranthas is hard and fearsome to ordinary people, is taught nowhere else, and must be kept unbroken by everyone, young or old, sick or healthy. The introduction calls it “great” conduct because it explains in detail, with rule and exception, what chapter 3 only listed (introduction, v.1–6).
There are eighteen places of conduct, and breaking one is a fall. The six vows, the six classes of living beings, things not allowed, a householder’s dishes, beds, sitting in a householder’s home, bathing and adornment. A careless monk who breaks any one of them falls from the state of a monk (v.7–8).
Nonviolence comes first, because every being wants to live. Mahavira taught nonviolence first: restraint towards all beings. A monk does not kill, or have killed, anything moving or still, knowingly or unknowingly. “All beings wish to live, not to die,” so the Nirgranthas give up the terrible killing of living beings (v.9–11).
No lies, no taking, no sex. A monk does not tell a hurtful lie for himself or another, from anger or fear; lying is condemned by all good people and makes a person trusted by no one (v.12–13). He takes nothing that is not given, “not even a toothpick” (v.14–15). Unchastity is “the root of unrighteousness” and a heap of great faults, so he keeps away from it and from the places that lead to it (v.16–17).
Possession is attachment, not things. Monks do not store even salt, oil, ghee or jaggery overnight; wanting to store anything is a touch of greed, and one who wants to store is “a householder, not a monk”. The cloth, bowl, blanket and broom a monk keeps are only for restraint and modesty. Mahavira did not call these possession; “attachment is possession”. The wise feel no “mine” even for their own body (v.18–22).
No food at night. Eating once, in the day only, is called a lifelong austerity. At night tiny moving and still beings cannot be seen on the ground, on wet things and on seeds, so food cannot be sought without harm; therefore monks take no food or water of any kind at night (v.23–26).
Care for all six classes of beings. For each class (earth, water, fire, air, plants, moving beings) the chapter says the same three things: the monk does not harm it by mind, speech or body; whoever harms it also harms the many seen and unseen beings that live in it; so he gives up that harm for life. Fire gets special words: it is the sharpest weapon, burning in every direction with no escape, so a monk lights none even for a lamp or warmth. For air, he does not fan himself with a palm leaf or a branch (v.27–46).
Things a monk must refuse. He refuses food, lodging, cloth or a bowl that was bought for him, made for him, brought to him, or given by standing invitation; taking it is approving the killing done for it (v.47–50). He does not eat from a householder’s metal dishes, because they get washed with live water before or after (v.51–53). He does not sit or lie on cots, beds and chairs, because their deep holes cannot be inspected for small creatures (v.54–56).
Do not sit in homes, do not bathe, do not adorn. Sitting in a householder’s home while seeking alms endangers celibacy, harms beings, keeps other beggars waiting and angers the family; only a monk who is very old, sick or a great ascetic may sit (v.57–60). Sick or healthy, a monk does not bathe in cold or hot water, since bath water drowns tiny beings in the cracks of the ground (v.61–63). He uses no powders or scents: what use is adornment to a shaven monk with long nails who has given up sex? Adornment, and even a mind set on it, binds sticky karma (v.64–67).
The fruit. Monks free of delusion, devoted to austerity, restraint and straightforwardness, shake off the sins done before and make no new ones. Calm, owning nothing, they become pure like the autumn moon and reach liberation, or the heavens if some karma is left (v.68–69).

Key verses
9 · Nonviolence is the first rule

तत्थिमं पढमं ठाणं, महावीरेण देसियं ।
अहिंसा णिउणा दिट्ठा, सव्वभूएसु संजमो ॥

Of these eighteen places, the first, taught by Mahavira, who was skilled in explaining the truth, is nonviolence: restraint towards all living beings.
11 · Every being wants to live

सव्वे जीवा वि इच्छंति, जीविउं ण मरिज्जिउं ।
तम्हा पाणिवहं घोरं, णिग्गंथा वज्जयंति णं ॥

All living beings wish to live, not to die. Therefore the Nirgranthas give up the terrible killing of living beings.
21 · Attachment is possession

ण सो परिग्गहो वुत्तो, णायपुत्तेण ताइणा ।
मुच्छा परिग्गहो वुत्तो, इइ वुत्तं महेसिणा ॥

Mahavira, the son of the Jnata clan and protector of beings, did not call these things (cloth, bowl and the like) possession. Attachment (murchha) is possession; so the great sage said.
24 · Why not at night

संतिमे सुहुमा पाणा, तसा अदुव थावरा ।
जाइं राओ अपासंतो, कहमेसणियं चरे ॥

There are tiny living beings, moving and still, that cannot be seen at night. Not seeing them, how could a monk seek pure food? He cannot.
68 · Old sins shaken off, no new ones made

खवेंति अप्पाणममोहदंसिणो, तवे रया संजम अज्जवे गुणे ।
धुणंति पावाइं पुरे कडाइं, णवाइं पावाइं ण ते करेंति ॥

Those who aim at freedom from delusion, devoted to austerity, restraint and straightforwardness, wear away the karma-bound self. They shake off the sins done before and do not make new ones.
69 · Pure like the autumn moon

सओवसंता अममा अकिंचणा, सविज्जविज्जाणुगया जसंसिणो ।
उउप्पसण्णे विमलेव चंदिमा, सिद्धिं विमाणाइं उवेंति ताइणो ॥

Always calm, free of “mine” and owning nothing, following the knowledge of the self, renowned protectors of all beings: pure like the moon in the clear autumn sky, they reach liberation (siddhi), or the heavenly realms if some karma remains.
Verses checked against the scans: v.9 · v.11 · v.21 · v.24 · v.68–69

09_modules/dashvaikalik_07_pure_speech.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 7: Pure Speech
09_modules/dashvaikalik_07_pure_speech.content:
Dashvaikalik 7 · Suvakya Shuddhi (सुवाक्य शुद्धि): Pure Speech
In one line: a monk speaks only what is true or plainly practical, and even then only after thinking, so that his words never hurt anyone, never push anyone towards harm, and never claim more than he knows.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 7 (57 verses), translated pages 348–384. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Of four kinds of speech, use two with care and drop two. Speech is true, false, mixed (part true, part false) or practical (neither true nor false, like an instruction). A wise monk never uses false or mixed speech, and uses true and practical speech only when it is blameless, gentle, well thought out and free of doubt. Even a truth is not to be spoken if it is sinful (v.1–3). The introduction says a monk stays silent as far as he can; careful speech helps both speaker and listener, and it serves nonviolence as much as truth (introduction).
Even a small slip of appearance is a lie. Do not use unclear, double-meaning speech. If someone is dressed as the other sex and you name them by their dress, you are touched by sin; how much more one who lies outright (v.4–5).
Do not speak with certainty about what you do not know. Do not say “We will go”, “I will do it”, “This will happen”. Say only “this is so” about past, present or future things you know without doubt. The commentary gives the monk better phrases: “I intend to come”, “he may be able to do it” (v.6–10).
A harsh truth is still not to be spoken. Do not call a one-eyed man one-eyed, a eunuch a eunuch, a sick man sick or a thief a thief: true words that hurt bring in sinful karma. No insulting names either, like “fool” or “dog” (v.11–14).
How to address people. A monk does not call women or men by family words (“mother”, “aunt”, “grandfather”, “son”) or by rough or servile words; he calls them by name or by family line (gotra), or by a fitting polite word (v.15–20).
Speech about animals. Until he knows whether an animal is male or female, he names only its kind. He does not say a person or animal is “fat, fit to kill, fit to cook”, or that cows are “fit to milk” and bulls “fit to yoke”; he may say “well grown”, “large-bodied”, “a young bull”, “a milking cow” (v.21–25).
Speech about trees, fruit and grain. Seeing big trees, he does not say “good for pillars, boats or a monk’s seat”. Seeing fruit and grain, he does not say “ripe, pick it, cut it, roast it”. He may say “these trees are tall and fine to see”, “these mango trees are bent with fruit”, “the grain has eared” (v.26–35).
No words that praise or prompt harm. He does not call a feast a good deed, a thief someone who deserves death, or a river easy to swim. He does not praise food as “well cooked, well cut”; he does not say “the best”, “priceless”, “nothing like it”; he does not promise “I will tell them all of it”; and in trade he does not say “buy this, sell that” (v.36–46).
No commands, no false titles, no forecasts. He does not tell a householder “sit, come, do this, go”. He calls only a true monk a monk: one rich in knowledge, faith, restraint and austerity. He does not wish victory to one side in a war, or ask when rain, cold or plenty will come. He does not call a cloud, the sky or a great man “a god” (v.47–53).
The fruit of pure speech. A monk who weighs every word, free of anger, greed, fear, pride and joking, is praised among good people. Speaking after examining, with senses calm and the four passions gone, he shakes off old karma and wins both this world and the next (v.54–57).

Key verses
1 · Four kinds of speech

चउण्हं खलु भासाणं, परिसंखाय पण्णवं ।
दोण्हं तु विणयं सिक्खे, दो ण भासिज्ज सव्वसो ॥

Having fully understood the four kinds of speech, a wise monk should learn to use two of them with care, and should never use the other two at all.
3 · Speech that may be spoken

असच्चमोसं सच्चं च, अणवज्जमकक्कसं ।
समुप्पेहमसंदिद्धं, गिरं भासिज्ज पण्णवं ॥

A wise monk should speak true speech and practical speech that is blameless, not harsh, well thought out and free of doubt.
11 · Even a true word can be sinful

तहेव फरुसा भासा, गुरुभूओवघाइणी ।
सच्चा वि सा ण वत्तव्वा, जओ पावस्स आगमो ॥

Likewise, harsh speech that badly hurts living beings should not be spoken even if it is true, because through it sinful karma flows in.
12 · Do not name a wound

तहेव काणं काणे त्ति, पंडगं पंडगे त्ति वा ।
वाहियं वावि रोगि त्ति, तेणं चोरे त्ति णो वए ॥

Likewise, he should not call a one-eyed man “one-eyed”, a eunuch “eunuch”, a sick man “sick”, or a thief “thief”.
55 · Measured words win praise

सुवक्कसुद्धिं समुपेहिया मुणी, गिरं च दुट्ठं परिवज्जए सया ।
मियं अदुट्ठं अणुवीइ भासए, सयाण मज्झे लहइ पसंसणं ॥

Having thought carefully about the purity of good speech, a monk always gives up faulty words. Speaking measured, faultless words after reflection, he wins praise among good people.
57 · Speech that sheds karma

परिक्खभासी सुसमाहिइंदिए, चउक्कसायावगए अणिस्सए ।
स णिद्धुणे धुण्णमलं पुरेकडं, आराहए लोगमिणं तहा परं ॥

One who speaks after examining, whose senses are well controlled, who is rid of the four passions and bound to nothing, shakes off the dirt of karma gathered before, and succeeds in this world and the next.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3 · v.11–12 · v.55 · v.57

09_modules/dashvaikalik_08_the_treasure_.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 8: The Treasure of Conduct
09_modules/dashvaikalik_08_the_treasure_.content:
Dashvaikalik 8 · Achara Pranidhi (आचार प्रणिधि): The Treasure of Conduct
In one line: taking initiation is only entering school; this chapter is a store of practical guidance on how a monk then lives day by day, guarding living beings, his taste, his speech, his passions and his celibacy, until karma clears from him like clouds from the moon.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 8 (64 verses), translated pages 385–440. 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Having got the treasure, learn to use it. “Achara pranidhi” means the store or treasure of conduct. The introduction says the chapter has no single subject; it is a collection of useful teachings gathered one by one. Accepting restraint is like entering school: much is still to be learned (introduction, v.1).
Care for the six classes of beings in daily life. Earth, water, fire, air, plants and moving beings are all living. So a monk does not dig or scratch earth, wall or stone; sits only on lifeless, swept ground with the owner’s leave; drinks only well-boiled or lifeless water; does not wipe his body when rain-wet; does not light, touch or put out fire; does not fan himself or hot food; does not cut grass, trees, fruit or roots, or stand on seeds and green shoots (v.2–12).
Eight tiny things to watch for. Tiny moisture (dew, frost), tiny flowers, tiny creatures, tiny ant-holes, mould, tiny seeds, tiny sprouts and tiny eggs. Knowing them, the monk sits, stands and lies down with care, inspects his bowl, blanket, bed and seat regularly, and disposes of bodily waste only on inspected ground (v.13–18).
In a householder’s home, see much and say little. He stands with care, speaks little and does not let his mind go after beauty. “He hears much with his ears and sees much with his eyes,” but should not tell everything. The commentary tells of a man seen with another’s wife who chased the monk to kill him, and dropped the idea when the monk said a monk sees much but tells little (v.19–21).
Master the tongue, bear hardship. He does not call food tasty or bad, or tell who gave and who did not; he takes a little from many homes, stores nothing, lives on plain food, is content and does not get angry. He bears hunger, thirst, a hard bed, cold, heat, unease and fear without distress, because “suffering of the body brings great fruit” (liberation). After sunset he does not want food even in his mind (v.22–28).
Inner faults to drop. He is not irritable or restless, speaks little, eats moderately, and does not scold the giver when he gets little. He does not look down on others or praise himself, or take pride in learning, birth, austerity or intelligence. If he does wrong, knowingly or not, he checks himself at once, does not repeat it, and neither hides nor denies it before his teacher. He makes his teacher’s words fruitful by saying “yes” and then doing it (v.29–33).
Life is short; act while you can. Knowing life is unsteady and his own span limited, he turns from pleasures. Weighing his strength, firmness, health, place and time, he sets himself to practice “as long as old age does not press, illness does not grow, and the senses do not fail” (v.34–36).
Conquer the four passions. Anger, pride, deceit and greed increase sin. Anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, greed destroys everything. Beat anger with calm, pride with gentleness, deceit with straightforwardness, greed with contentment; left unchecked, the four water the roots of rebirth (v.37–40).
Study, reverence and right speech. Show respect to seniors in the monastic life, keep the daily conduct unbroken, draw in like a tortoise. Do not sleep much, laugh loudly or chat; stay devoted to study; sit near a learned teacher and ask him the meaning. Do not speak unasked or cut in, do not backbite, do not mock even a great scholar’s slip of the tongue, and do not tell householders about stars, dreams, omens, mantras or medicines (v.41–51).
Guard celibacy, keep the first faith, and shine. Live in a lodging free of women and animals; as a chick fears the cat, a celibate fears a woman’s body (and a nun a man’s); turn the eyes from a painted wall or an adorned person as from the sun; avoid even a woman of a hundred with hands and nose cut off; adornment, closeness and rich food are poison to a seeker; all matter changes, so let craving cool (v.52–60). Keep for life the faith with which you left home (v.61). Such a monk is like a well-armed hero, his karma is burned off like the dirt on silver in fire, and he shines like the moon when the clouds are gone (v.62–64).

Key verses
20 · See much, tell little

बहुं सुणेहि कण्णेहिं, बहुं अच्छीहिं पिच्छइ ।
ण य दिट्ठं सुयं सव्वं, भिक्खू अक्खाउमरिहइ ॥

A monk hears much with his ears and sees much with his eyes, but it is not right for him to tell all that he has seen and heard.
27 · Suffering of the body brings great fruit

खुहं पिवासं दुस्सेज्जं, सीउण्हं अरइं भयं ।
अहियासे अव्वहिओ, देहदुक्खं महाफलं ॥

Without distress he should bear hunger, thirst, a hard bed, cold and heat, unease and fear, for bodily suffering borne calmly brings the great fruit of liberation.
36 · Practise while you are able

जरा जाव ण पीडेइ, वाही जाव ण वड्ढइ ।
जाविंदिया ण हायंति, ताव धम्मं समायरे ॥

As long as old age does not press on you, as long as illness does not grow, as long as the senses do not weaken, practise dharma.
38 · What each passion destroys

कोहो पीइं पणासेइ, माणो विणय णासणो ।
माया मित्ताणि णासेइ, लोहो सव्व विणासणो ॥

Anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything.
39 · The four remedies

उवसमेण हणे कोहं, माणं मद्दवया जिणे ।
मायं च अज्जवभावेण, लोभं संतोसओ जिणे ॥

Kill anger with calm, conquer pride with gentleness, deceit with straightforwardness, and greed with contentment.
64 · Like the moon when the clouds part

से तारिसे दुक्खसहे जिइंदिए, सुएण जुत्ते अममे अकिंचणे ।
विरायइ कम्मघणम्मि अवगए, कसिणब्भपुडावगमे व चंदिमे ॥

Such a monk, who bears hardship, has conquered his senses, is rich in scripture, and is free of “mine” and of possessions, shines when the cloud of karma has gone, like the moon when the whole bank of clouds has cleared.
Verses checked against the scans: v.20 · v.27 · v.36 · v.38 · v.39 · v.64

09_modules/dashvaikalik_09_composure_thr.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 9: Composure Through Humility
09_modules/dashvaikalik_09_composure_thr.content:
Dashvaikalik 9 · Vinay Samadhi (विनय समाधि): Composure Through Humility
In one line: humility towards the guru (vinaya) is the root of the tree of dharma and liberation is its fruit; disrespect burns up a disciple’s own virtues, while the humble disciple grows, becomes worthy of honour, and finds composure (samadhi) in humility, learning, austerity and conduct.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 9 (63 verses in four sections, uddeshas: 17, 24, 15 and 7; section 4 also has prose sutras), translated pages 441–506 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 18 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Vinaya is more than politeness: it is the root of Jain dharma. The introduction explains that vinaya means humility but also a particular discipline or duty. Jainism is a religion where vinaya comes first; the chapter (quoting its own verse 9.2.2) calls it the root of dharma. Of its seven kinds (towards knowledge, faith, conduct, and in mind, speech, body and respectful behaviour), the last, outward respect for the guru, is the main subject here. Acceptance of the guru’s discipline must go together with a humble heart (introduction, pp. 441–443).
Section 1: disrespect destroys the disrespecter. A monk who, from stiff pride, anger, conceit or laziness, does not practise humility before his guru ruins his own virtues, as the bamboo’s fruit kills the bamboo. Do not look down on a guru as “slow”, “young” or “of little learning”: such a guru, if scorned, burns the disciple’s virtues to ashes like fire. The fire does not mean to burn; the disciple burns himself (1.1–3, commentary).
Section 1: worse than fire, poison, a snake or a lion. Teasing a small snake, entering fire, angering a cobra, eating poison, butting a mountain with your head, waking a sleeping lion, striking a spear point: by some spell or chance these may do no harm, but there is no liberation through disrespecting the guru. The commentary adds that “no liberation” is said to warn and teach; it means liberation becomes very hard, since confession and repentance can still free even a serious offender (1.4–10).
Section 1: even with infinite knowledge, the disciple still bows. As a fire-priest keeps bowing to his sacred fire all his life, a disciple serves his acharya even after he himself has reached omniscience. Bow with the head, join the hands, and honour the guru in body, speech and mind; thank him for teaching modesty, compassion, restraint (samyama) and celibacy. The acharya shines among monks like the sun at dawn, like Indra among the gods, like the autumn moon among the stars; please him, and you reach the highest state (1.11–17).
Section 2: humility is the root, liberation the fruit. As a tree grows from root to trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruit and juice, so dharma grows from humility, bringing fame, learning and praise, and at last liberation. The undisciplined man (angry, foolish, stiff, harsh-tongued, deceitful) is swept along like wood in a river; one who gets angry when gently urged towards humility is driving away good fortune with a stick (2.1–4).
Section 2: the undisciplined suffer everywhere, the disciplined prosper. Untrained horses and elephants end up in servitude; trained ones are honoured. So with men and women, and even with gods. Learning grows like a watered tree for those who serve the acharya and upadhyaya. Princes put up with binding and beating from their teachers to learn a worldly craft; how much more should one who seeks endless welfare obey his teacher (2.5–16).
Section 2: what humility looks like in practice. Keep your bed, walk, standing place and seat lower than the guru’s; bow low and join your hands low. If you touch him or his things, say “Forgive me; I will not do it again.” Don’t be like a stubborn bullock that moves only when goaded; get up from your seat to answer when called; read the season and the guru’s wishes and act on them. The angry, proud, tale-bearing, rash, disobedient monk who does not share with others has no liberation; those who follow the guru’s instruction cross the flood (2.17–24).
Section 3: who is worthy of honour (pujya). Each verse ends “he is worthy of honour”: the one who reads the guru’s glance and gesture; who respects monks senior in initiation even if younger in age; who is not upset when no alms come and does not boast when they do; who bears harsh words without hope of reward, since an iron thorn is easily pulled out but a harsh word is not; who does not slander, flatter or gossip; who knows that one is a monk by virtues and not by dress; who scorns no one, child or elder, man or woman, monk or householder (3.1–12).
Section 3: the guru raises the disciple as a father raises a daughter. The guru who is honoured carefully settles the disciple in a high place, as a father settles his daughter in a good family. The wise monk who listens to such gurus keeps the five great vows, the three restraints (gupti) and drops the four passions, and serving the guru he shakes off old karma and reaches the radiant, unequalled state (3.13–15).
Section 4: the four kinds of composure. The elders taught four grounds of samadhi. Humility: listen when taught, accept it, follow the scripture, and do not become proud of being humble. Learning: study so as to gain knowledge, to make the mind one-pointed, to steady yourself, and then to steady others. Austerity: not for this world, not for the next, not for fame, only to shed karma. Conduct: likewise not for this world, the next, or fame, only for the purposes the Arhats taught. One who has all four is freed from birth and death and becomes a siddha, or, if a little karma is left, a great god (4.1–7).

Key verses
1.1 · The bamboo’s fruit

थंभा व कोहा व मयप्पमाया, गुरुस्सगासे विणयं ण सिक्खे ।
सो चेव उ तस्स अभूइभावो, फलं व कीयस्स वहाय होइ ॥

A monk who, from stiff pride, anger, conceit or laziness, does not practise humility in his guru’s presence brings about his own ruin by that very lack of humility, as the fruit of the bamboo brings about the bamboo’s death.
1.11 · Even the omniscient disciple bows

जहाहिअग्गी जलणं णमंसे, णाणाहुईमंतपयाभिसित्तं ।
एवायरियं उवचिट्ठएज्जा, अणंतणाणोवगओ वि संतो ॥

As a fire-priest bows to his fire, consecrated with many offerings and mantras, so a disciple should serve his acharya, even when he has attained infinite knowledge.
2.2 · The root of dharma

एवं धम्मस्स विणओ, मूलं परमो से मोक्खो ।
जेण कित्तिं सुयं सिग्घं, णीसेसं चाभिगच्छइ ॥

In the same way, humility is the root of dharma and liberation is its highest fruit. Through humility one gains fame, learning, praise, and everything worth gaining.
2.22 · Know both outcomes

विवत्ती अविणीयस्स, संपत्ती विणियस्स य ।
जस्सेयं दुहओ णायं, सिक्खं से अभिगच्छइ ॥

Ruin comes to the undisciplined, and a wealth of good qualities to the disciplined. Whoever knows both of these receives the teaching.
3.11 · A monk by virtues

गुणेहिं साहू अगुणेहिं असाहु, गिण्हाहि साहूगुण मुंचऽसाहू ।
वियाणिया अप्पगमप्पएणं, जो रागदोसेहिं समो स पुज्जो ॥

One is a monk through virtues and not a monk through faults. Take up the virtues of a monk and let go of the faults. Whoever knows the self by the self and stays even amid attachment and aversion is worthy of honour.
4.4 · Austerity only to shed karma

विविहगुणतवोरए य णिच्चं, भवइ णिरासए णिज्जरट्ठिए ।
तवसा धुणइ पुराणपावगं, जुत्तो सया तवसमाहिए ॥

Always devoted to austerity in its many kinds, wanting nothing in return and seeking only to shed karma, the monk shakes off old sinful karma by austerity and stays always in the composure of austerity.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1.1 · v.1.11 · v.2.2 · v.2.22 · v.3.11 · v.4.4

09_modules/dashvaikalik_10_the_true_monk.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 10: The True Monk
09_modules/dashvaikalik_10_the_true_monk.content:
Dashvaikalik 10 · Sa Bhikkhu (स भिक्खू, Gujarati સ ભિક્ષુ): The True Monk
In one line: living on alms does not make a true monk; he is the one who protects all six kinds of living beings, keeps the great vows, bears every hardship like the earth, gives up pride and craving, and so reaches the state from which there is no return.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, chapter 10 (21 verses), translated pages 507–532 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The touchstone of a true monk. A bhikshu is one who lives on alms, but so do many who still harm living beings and are bound to gold and women. Real and fake gold look alike until rubbed on a touchstone; in the same way, the true monk (sa bhikkhu) is known by his virtues. He begs in order to live without harm, not just to fill his stomach. Every verse ends “he is a monk,” and the chapter gathers up in short form all that the first nine chapters taught (introduction).
His mind stays steady. Having left home at the word of the Jina, he stays calm in mind, does not fall under the sway of women, and does not go back to the pleasures he has given up (v.1).
He protects all six kinds of living beings. He does not dig the earth, drink water that has life in it, or light fire, which is like a sharp weapon; he does not fan the air or cut plants, steps around seeds, and does not take food that has life in it. Cooking harms beings living in earth, grass and wood, so he does not eat food made for him, cook, or have food cooked. Accepting Mahavira’s word, he treats the six kinds as equal to himself, keeps the five great vows and shuts the five doors of karmic inflow (v.2–5, commentary).
He drops passions and possessions. He always throws off anger, pride, deceit and greed, holds steady to the Jina’s word, keeps no wealth, gold or silver, and takes no part in householders’ work. With right vision and a clear mind about knowledge, austerity and restraint, he burns off old karma through austerity and guards mind, speech and body (v.6–7, commentary).
He does not store food, and he shares it. He does not keep food for “tomorrow or the day after,” just as a bird eats what it finds and stores nothing. He first invites his fellow monks to share what he has received, then eats, and after eating turns to study (v.8–9, commentary).
He stays out of quarrels. He tells no stories that stir up strife, does not get angry, keeps his senses still, and never looks down on anyone (v.10, commentary).
He bears hardship like the earth. Abuse, blows and threats prick the senses like thorns; he bears them, and terrifying sounds and mocking laughter too, treating pleasure and pain alike. He stands in meditation in a cremation ground without fear. Insulted, beaten or wounded, he stays like the earth, which bears everything and pushes back on nothing; he wants no reward and no revenge. Overcoming hardships, he lifts himself out of the round of birth and death (v.11–14, commentary).
He is careful with hands, feet and tongue. He is restrained in hands, feet, speech and senses, delights in the inner life, keeps his mind calm, and keeps studying the scripture and its meaning. The commentary notes that even Gautam Swami studied before going for alms (v.15, commentary).
He wants no comfort and no fame, and he is not proud. He is not attached to his few belongings; he takes plain things a little at a time from houses that do not know him, and does not buy, sell or store. He does not crave tastes, honour or worship; the commentary calls praise a fine thorn, hard to pull out. He never says “this monk is lax,” knowing each being’s merit and sin are its own, and never praises himself. He is not proud of birth, looks, gain or learning, but stays in meditation on dharma (v.16–19, commentary).
He helps others and reaches the end. The great sage teaches the noble path, stands firm in dharma and makes others firm, avoids lax ways and does not play the clown. Always holding to what is truly good, he lets go of this impure, passing body, cuts the bond of birth and death, and goes to the state from which there is no return (v.20–21).

Key verses
2 · He harms no earth, water or fire

पुढविं ण खणे ण खणावए, सीओदगं ण पिए ण पियावए ।
अगणिसत्थं जहा सुणिसियं, तं ण जले ण जलावए जे स भिक्खू ॥

He does not dig the earth or have it dug; he does not drink water that has life in it or give it to others to drink; fire is like a well-sharpened weapon, and he does not light it or have it lit. He is a monk.
5 · All six kinds as himself

रोइय णायपुत्तवयणे, अत्तसमे मण्णेज्ज छप्पि काए ।
पंच य फासे महव्वयाइं, पंचासवसंवरे जे स भिक्खू ॥

Taking to heart the words of Jnataputra (Mahavira), he treats all six kinds of living beings as equal to himself, keeps the five great vows and shuts the five doors of karmic inflow. He is a monk.
13 · Like the earth

असइ वोसट्ठचत्तदेहे, अकुट्ठे व हए व लूसिए वा ।
पुढवि समे मुणी हवेज्जा, अणियाणे अकोउहल्ले जे स भिक्खू ॥

Again and again he lets go of the body and his care for it. Insulted, beaten or wounded, the sage stays like the earth, wanting no reward and feeling no stir of curiosity. He is a monk.
15 · Careful in hands, feet and speech

हत्थसंजए पायसंजए, वायसंजए संजइंदिए ।
अज्झप्परए सुसमाहियप्पा, सुत्तत्थं च वियाणइ जे स भिक्खू ॥

He is restrained in hands, restrained in feet, restrained in speech and restrained in the senses; he delights in the inner life, his mind is well settled, and he knows the scripture and its meaning. He is a monk.
18 · He does not call others lax

ण परं वइज्जासि अयं कुसीले, जेणं च कुप्पिज्ज ण तं वइज्जा ।
जाणिय पत्तेयं पुण्णपावं, अत्ताणं ण समुक्कसे जे स भिक्खू ॥

He does not say of another, “This one is of bad conduct,” and he says nothing that would make another angry. Knowing that each being’s merit and sin are its own, he does not raise himself up. He is a monk.
19 · No pride of any kind

ण जाइमत्ते ण य रूवमत्ते, ण लाभमत्ते ण सुएण मत्ते ।
मयाणि सव्वाणि विवज्जइत्ता, धम्मज्झाणरए जे स भिक्खू ॥

He is not proud of his birth, not proud of his looks, not proud of his gains, not proud of his learning. Giving up every kind of pride, he delights in meditation on dharma. He is a monk.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.5 · v.13 · v.15 · v.18–19

09_modules/dashvaikalik_11_delight_in_re.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 11: Delight in Restraint
09_modules/dashvaikalik_11_delight_in_re.content:
Dashvaikalik 11 (Chulika 1) · Rativakya (रतिवाक्या): Delight in Restraint
In one line: for a monk whose mind has turned against restraint and who is thinking of going home, the chulika gives eighteen points to reflect on and a set of pictures of the fallen monk’s regret, so that he finds delight in restraint again and resolves to give up the body rather than the teaching.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, Chulika 1 (2 prose sutras and 18 verses), translated pages 533–560 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A crest on the mountain, written to steady a wavering monk. Chulika means a crest or peak; the two chulikas crown the ten chapters. This one is called Rativakya, “words that awaken delight”, because it is meant for the time when, in good or bad circumstances, a monk loses interest in restraint (samyama) and wants to return to household life (introduction, pp. 533–534).
Bridle, goad and sail. For a monk who has come to dislike restraint because some suffering has arisen, who wants to leave but has not yet left, eighteen points are to be reflected on carefully. They work like a bridle on a horse, a goad on an elephant and a sail on a ship. The commentary adds that the guru or acharya he confides in should use these same points to help him (sutra 1).
The eighteen points. In this hard age life is hard; householders’ pleasures are trivial and brief; people are deceitful; this suffering of mine will not last long; at home one must flatter lowly people; going back is drinking what one has vomited; it is like moving to a lower state of existence; dharma is very hard to practise amid household life; disease and endless worries there bring ruin; household life is full of trouble, bondage and sin, while monastic life is free of trouble, a way to freedom and sinless; householders’ pleasures are shared with many; merit and sin belong to each one alone; human life is as unsteady as a drop of water on the tip of kusha grass; I have done much evil karma; and there is no release from past evil karma except by experiencing it or burning it up through austerity (sutra 2).
The one who leaves for pleasure cannot see the future. When a man of ignoble mind gives up dharma for pleasures, he becomes infatuated, like a child, and does not see what is coming (v.1).
Four pictures of regret. The monk who runs back to household life later burns with regret: like Indra fallen to earth; like a goddess fallen from her place, because he was once bowed to and now is not; like a king who has lost his kingdom, because he was once honoured and now is not; like a city’s chief merchant banished to a small village, because he was once respected and now is not (v.2–5).
Old age, family and the “if only”. When youth has passed he suffers like a fish that swallowed the bait on a hook. Troubled by a bad family, he is like an elephant caught in a pit and bound; surrounded by wife and children, like an elephant stuck in mud, unable to reach water or return to the bank. Then he thinks, “If I had stayed, today I would be a learned acharya” (v.6–9).
Heaven for some, hell for others. For great sages who delight in it, the life of restraint is like the world of the gods; for those who do not, it is like a great hell. Knowing both, the wise monk delights in restraint. The commentary notes that the joy of restraint comes from within, while heavenly joy depends on outer things and ends (v.10–11).
The fallen monk is scorned. Fallen from dharma, without the wealth of austerity, he is treated with contempt even by people of bad conduct, like a sacrificial fire that has gone out or a deadly snake whose fangs have been pulled. He earns disgrace and a bad name here and a low state hereafter; having indulged with an attached mind, he will not easily find awakening (bodhi) again (v.12–14).
What is my small grief? Even beings in hell, whose suffering lasts a palyopama or a sagaropama, see it end; how long can this mental pain of mine last? This suffering will not last; the thirst for pleasure does not last either, and if it does not leave with the body it will leave at the end of life (v.15–16).
Give up the body, not the teaching. The monk whose mind is firm, “I will give up the body but not the Jina’s teaching”, cannot be shaken by the senses, as storm winds cannot shake Mount Sudarshana (Meru). Having weighed all this, the wise person, guarded by the three restraints in body, speech and mind, should follow the Jina’s word (v.17–18).

Key verses
1 · Leaving for pleasure

जया य चयइ धम्मं, अणज्जो भोगकारणा ।
से तत्थ मुच्छिए बालो, आयइं णावबुज्झइ ॥

When a man of ignoble mind gives up dharma for the sake of pleasures, that fool, infatuated with them, does not understand the future.
6 · The fish on the hook

जया य थेरओ होइ, समइक्कंतजुव्वणो ।
मच्छुव्व गलं गिलित्ता, स पच्छा परितप्पइ ॥

When he grows old and his youth has passed, he burns with regret, like a fish that has swallowed the baited hook.
10 · Like heaven, like hell

देवलोगसमाणो उ, परियाओ महेसिणं ।
रयाणं अरयाणं तु, महाणरयसारिसो ॥

For great sages who delight in it, the monk’s life is like the world of the gods; for those who do not delight in it, it is like a great hell.
15 · Even hell comes to an end

इमस्स ता णेरइयस्स जंतुणो, दुहोवणीयस्स किलेसवत्तिणो ।
पलिओवमं झिज्जइ सागरोवमं, किमंग पुण मज्झ इमं मणोदुहं ॥

Even for a being in hell, gripped by suffering and wholly in distress, a palyopama or a sagaropama runs out. What, then, is this mental pain of mine?
17 · Unmoved like Meru

जस्सेवमप्पा उ हविज्ज णिच्छिओ, चइज्ज देहं ण हु धम्मसासणं ।
तं तारिसं णो पइलेंति इंदिया, उवेंत वाया व सुदंसणं गिरिं ॥

One whose mind is firmly resolved, “I will give up the body, but never the teaching of dharma”, cannot be moved by the senses, as rushing winds cannot move Mount Sudarshana.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.6 · v.10 · v.15 · v.17

09_modules/dashvaikalik_12_the_solitary_.title: Module · Dashvaikalik 12: The Solitary Way
09_modules/dashvaikalik_12_the_solitary_.content:
Dashvaikalik 12 (Chulika 2) · Vivikta Charya (विविक्त चर्या): The Solitary Way
In one line: the world swims with the current of the senses and stays in the round of birth and death; the monk swims against it, wandering without attachment, living simply, examining his own faults every night, and always guarding the soul.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra, Chulika 2 (16 verses), translated pages 561–581 (data/translations/dashvaikalik/). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

With the current and against it. Vivikta means separate, pure, secluded; charya means way of life. Most beings go with the current of worldly life: body, senses, family and comfort. That is easy, but it increases birth and death. Vows, austerity and restraint go against the current: hard, but they lead out of birth and death (introduction, pp. 561–562).
Heard from the omniscient. The author will speak the chulika as he heard it, spoken by the omniscient Lord; hearing it, those with merit come to have faith in dharma (v.1).
Turn yourself against the current. When most people are flowing with the current, the one who wants liberation should set himself against it. The world finds going with the current pleasant; going against it is the refuge of the well-disciplined. With the current is the round of births (samsara); against it is the crossing out. So monks should keep their conduct, virtues and rules always in view (v.2–4).
The sages’ way of wandering. Not living in a fixed place, collecting alms from many houses, taking a little from households that did not prepare for him, staying in a secluded place, keeping few belongings and avoiding quarrels: this is the praised way of the sages (v.5).
Simple food, much study. Avoid crowded feasts; generally accept only food brought within sight. Take no intoxicants, meat or fish; often go without rich foods; often stand in kayotsarga (letting go of the body); and be devoted to study (v.6–7).
Own nothing, belong nowhere. Do not bind yourself to a bed, seat, lodging or food, nor feel “mine” about any village, family, town or country. Do not serve or bow to householders; live with monks who are free of trouble, so your conduct does not decline (v.8–9).
Alone, if need be. If you cannot find a capable companion better or equal in virtues, wander alone, avoiding sin and unattached to pleasures. The commentary stresses that for an ordinary monk staying in the group is safest; going alone is for unavoidable circumstances, and even then he must not give up restraint (v.10).
Limits on staying, and the sutra as guide. After a rainy-season stay, do not return to stay in the same place within a year (the commentary gives the rule: not before twice the period of the stay has passed). Walk by the path of the sutra, as its meaning commands (v.11).
Look at yourself every night. In the first and last parts of the night, examine yourself by yourself: “What have I done? What is left to do? What can I do that I am not doing? What faults of mine do others see, what do I see, and which do I still not give up?” Whenever you see yourself going wrong in body, speech or mind, pull back at once, as a fine horse answers the bridle (v.12–14).
The awakened life and the guarded soul. One who lives like this, senses conquered, steady and good, is called in the world “one who lives awake” (padibuddhajivi); he lives the life of restraint. The soul must always be guarded with all the senses well controlled: unguarded it goes the way of birth and death, well guarded it is freed from all suffering (v.15–16).

Key verses
2 · Against the current

अणुसोयपट्ठिए बहुजणम्मि, पडिसोयलद्धलक्खेणं ।
पडिसोयमेव अप्पा, दायव्वो होउकामेणं ॥

While most people are flowing with the current, one who has made going against it his aim, and who wants liberation, should set himself against the current.
3 · The current is samsara

अणुसोयसुहो लोगो, पडिसोओ आसवो(मो) सुविहियाणं ।
अणुसोओ संसारो, पडिसोओ तस्स उत्तारो ॥

The world finds going with the current pleasant; going against it is the refuge of the well-disciplined. Going with the current is samsara; going against it is the crossing out of it.
5 · The sages’ way of wandering

अणिएयवासो समुयाण चरिया, अण्णायउंछं पइरिक्कया य ।
अप्पोवही कलहविवज्जणा य, विहारचरिया इसिणं पसत्था ॥

No fixed home, alms gathered from many houses, a little food from households that did not expect him, a secluded dwelling, few belongings and no quarrels: this way of wandering is praised for sages.
10 · Better alone than in bad company

ण वा लभेज्जा णिउणं सहायं, गुणाहियं वा गुणओ समं वा ।
एक्को वि पावाइं विवज्जयंतो, विहरेज्ज कामेसु असज्जमाणो ॥

If he cannot find a capable companion who is greater or equal in virtues, let him wander even alone, avoiding sinful acts and not clinging to sense pleasures.
12 · The nightly self-examination

जो पुव्वरत्तावररत्तकाले, संपेहए अप्पगमप्पएणं ।
किं मे कडं किं च मे किच्चसेसं, किं सक्कणिज्जं ण समायरामि ॥

In the first and last parts of the night he looks at himself by himself: “What have I done? What remains for me to do? What am I able to do that I am not doing?”
16 · Guard the soul

अप्पा खलु सययं रक्खियव्वो, सव्विंदिएहिं सुसमाहिएहिं ।
अरक्खिओ जाइपहं उवेइ, सुरक्खिओ सव्वदुहाण मुच्चइ ॥

The soul must always be guarded, with all the senses well composed. Unguarded, it goes the way of birth and death; well guarded, it is freed from all suffering.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2, v.3 · v.5 · v.10 · v.12 · v.16

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_01_humility.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 1: Humility
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_01_humility.content:
Uttaradhyayan 1 · Vinayashruta: Humility
In one line: humility (vinaya) towards the teacher is the root of dharma: the humble disciple who obeys, restrains himself and welcomes correction gains knowledge, honour, and in the end liberation or a high heaven.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 1 (48 verses), translated pages 71–99. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Humility shows in how a disciple behaves. The humble one carries out the teacher’s commands, stays near him and reads his gestures and expressions; the one who does the opposite is “unhumble”. Like a dog with festering ears he is driven out everywhere, and like a pig that leaves grain to eat dung he leaves good conduct for bad. Seeing this, one who wants his own good should settle himself in humility (v.1–6).
Ten habits of the humble disciple. Practise humility, and you will gain good conduct and never be sent away. Stay calm near the wise and say little. Learn what is meaningful and drop idle talk. Do not get angry when corrected; forgive. Keep away from base company, joking and games. Study at the proper time, then meditate alone. If you did wrong in anger, never hide it: say “I did it”, or “I did not” (v.7–11).
Don’t wait for the whip. A bad horse keeps needing the whip, while a good horse turns from the wrong path at the mere sight of it. Disobedient, careless disciples make even a gentle teacher angry, while one who follows the teacher’s mind soon calms even an angry one. The commentary tells of Acharya Chandrarudra, who struck his new disciple’s head in anger. The disciple bore it calmly and gained omniscience, and the teacher then asked his forgiveness (v.12–13).
Speak only when asked, and truthfully. Do not speak unasked; when asked, never lie. If anger arises, make it fruitless, and accept the teacher’s words whether pleasant or not. In the commentary’s story, a nobleman’s son catches his brother’s killer, but his mother tells him that his greatness lies in calming his anger, and he lets the man go (v.14).
Tame yourself before others tame you. The self is hard to tame, but the one who tames it is happy here and hereafter. It is better to subdue oneself by restraint (samyama) and austerity than to be subdued by others with chains and blows. In the commentary, the elephant Sechanaka walks into King Shrenika’s stable of his own accord rather than be captured, and is honoured there (v.15–16).
Respect with the body. Never oppose the teacher, in public or private, in word or deed. Do not sit pressed against him, in front of him or behind him, knee to knee, cross-legged or with legs stretched out. When he calls, do not stay silent or seated; rise, come near, squat and ask with joined hands. Asked in this way, the teacher should explain the sutra and its meaning just as he himself heard them (v.17–23).
Guard your speech, and welcome correction. Avoid falsehood, sweeping statements, sinful, pointless or hurtful words, and deceit. A monk alone should not stand or talk with a woman who is alone. Whether the teacher corrects gently or harshly, the wise disciple thinks “this is my gain”; the fool hears the same words with hatred (v.24–29).
Daily life at the right time and place. Sit on a lower, steady, quiet seat and do not fidget. Go out for alms and come back at the proper time. Don’t push into a queue or past other monks. Stand neither too near nor too far from the giver, accept only suitable food made for the household, and eat a limited amount at the proper time. Eat carefully, in a covered place free of living beings, and don’t praise the food (“well cooked!”, “nicely done!”), since such words approve of harm (v.30–36).
The teacher and the two kinds of disciple. The teacher rejoices in teaching a good disciple, as a rider enjoys a good horse, and suffers with a foolish one. The disciple with wrong outlook thinks of correction as kicks, slaps and abuse, and feels like a slave. The good disciple feels treated like a son, brother or kinsman. He does not anger the teacher or look for his faults. If the teacher is angry he calms him with joined hands, saying “I will not do it again”. He reads the teacher’s wishes and acts on them without being prompted (v.37–44).
The fruits of humility. The humble disciple becomes famous, and a support for all good practice as the earth supports all beings. The pleased teachers give him vast scriptural knowledge. His doubts vanish, he lives in his teacher’s heart, and keeping the five great vows he shines. Honoured by gods and men, he leaves this body and becomes an eternal siddha, or a mighty god if a little karma remains (v.45–48).

Key verses
2 · Who is humble

आणाणिद्देसकरे, गुरुणमुववायकारए ।
इंगियागारसंपण्णे, से विणीए त्ति वुच्चइ ॥२॥

One who acts on the teacher’s commands and directions, stays near him, and understands his gestures and expressions is called humble.
15 · Tame the self

अप्पा चेव दमेयव्वो, अप्पा हु खलु दुद्दमो ।
अप्पा दंतो सुही होइ, अस्सिं लोए परत्थ य ॥१५॥

The self alone should be tamed, for the self is truly hard to tame. One who tames the self is happy in this world and in the next.
16 · Better by my own hand

वरं मे अप्पा दंतो, संजमेण तवेण य ।
माहं परेहिं दम्मंतो बंधणेहि वहेहि य ॥१६॥

It is better that I tame my own self through restraint and austerity than be tamed by others with chains and blows.
29 · Harsh words, two hearers

हियं विगयभया बुद्धा, फरुसं पि अणुसासणं ।
वेस्सं तं होइ मूढाणं, खंति-सोहिकरं पयं ॥२९॥

The fearless and wise take even harsh instruction as being for their good. To fools, those same words, which bring forgiveness and purity, become a cause of hatred.
45 · Like the earth

णच्चा णमइ मेहावी, लोए कित्ती से जायए ।
हवइ किच्चाणं सरणं, भूयाणं जगई जहा ॥४५॥

Knowing this, the wise disciple bows in humility, and his fame spreads in the world. He becomes a refuge for all good practices, as the earth is for all living beings.
48 · The end of the path

स देवगंधव्व-मणुस्सपूइए, चइत्तु देहं मलपंकपुव्वयं ।
सिद्धे वा हवइ सासए, देवे वा अप्परए महिड्ढिए ॥४८॥

Honoured by gods, gandharvas and humans, he leaves this body born of filth and mire and becomes an eternal siddha; or, if a little karma remains, a god of great power.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.15 · v.16 · v.29 · v.45 · v.48

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_02_enduring_har.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 2: Enduring Hardships
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_02_enduring_har.content:
Uttaradhyayan 2 · Parishaha: Enduring Hardships
In one line: a monk will meet twenty-two kinds of hardship, from hunger and insults to doubt about the faith, and he bears each one calmly, inside his vows, as a way of shedding karma.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 2 (an opening prose passage and 46 verses), translated pages 100–132 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Mahavira named twenty-two hardships (parishaha). A monk hears them, understands them, gets used to them by practice and overcomes them, so that he does not waver when they come. The introduction adds that hardships are not obstacles but help in destroying karma. They differ from bodily austerity, which a monk chooses; a hardship is what arises on its own while he keeps his restraint (prose passage, v.1).
Hunger and thirst do not break the rules. However hungry, a monk does not cut or cook food or have it done. His body may grow thin “like a crow’s leg”, with the veins showing, and still he goes on without gloom. When thirsty he does not drink unboiled, living water; he looks for water that is lifeless and allowed. The commentary tells of Hastibhuta, who would not even take fallen fruit in the forest because no one had given it, and of the young monk Dhanasharma, who died of thirst rather than drink from a river, though his own father told him to (v.2–5).
Cold, heat and insects are borne without comfort-seeking. He does not warm himself at a fire, bathe, sprinkle water on himself or fan himself. Bitten by flies and mosquitoes, he stands firm “like an elephant at the front of a battle”. He does not kill or drive them off, and bears them no ill will even in his mind. The story of Arhannaka tells of a pampered young monk who left the order in the summer heat. His mother’s grieving cries brought him back, and he died at peace on a burning rock (v.6–11).
With clothes or without, and when restraint feels dull. Sometimes a monk has clothes, sometimes not; both are good for the dharma, so he does not grieve. If dislike of restraint (arati) creeps in, he puts it behind him and delights in “the garden of dharma” (v.12–15).
Women as mud. For men, women in the world are a bond. The wise monk sees this, does not get stuck in that mud, and seeks the self. The commentary tells how Sthulibhadra spent the rains in the house of the courtesan Kosha and stayed pure, which his guru called “difficult, difficult” (v.16–17).
Wandering, sitting and lodging. He wanders alone, settles nowhere, owns nothing and stays unattached to householders. He sits still in a cremation ground, an empty house or under a tree, and does not run away from danger. Given a good or bad room, he thinks, “What can one night do?” (v.18–23).
Abuse and beating are not answered. If someone abuses him, he does not flare up, for then he becomes like the fool. Harsh words are “village thorns”, and he lets them pass in silence. If someone strikes him, he thinks, “The soul is not destroyed.” The commentary adds that the one who hits him is only an occasion; his own past karma is the cause (v.24–27).
Begging, getting nothing, illness, grass and dirt. Everything a monk has must be asked for, and holding out the hand is hard. Still he never thinks, “Home life was better.” Given nothing, he thinks, “Perhaps tomorrow.” When ill he bears the pain and does not seek treatment. The commentary says this is strict for monks of the Jina’s mode of conduct, while elder (sthavira) monks may take treatment with the guru’s permission. Grass pricks his body and sweat and dust coat it; he bears both until death, for the sake of shedding karma (v.28–37).
Honour is also a hardship. When kings and the wealthy greet and invite him, he does not crave it. He keeps his passions few and his wants few, and does not hunger for tasty food. The commentary calls this a favourable hardship, like that of women (v.38–39).
Slow learning, no special knowledge, doubt. If he cannot answer questions, he thinks, “Past karma brings this; knowledge will come later,” and consoles himself. He must not think that his celibacy and austerity were wasted because no higher knowledge has come. Nor may he think that there is no next world, that ascetics have no powers, or that talk of past, present and future Jinas is false. All twenty-two were taught by Mahavira, and a monk must not be beaten by any of them (v.40–46).

Key verses
2 · Hunger

दिगिंछा-परिगए देहे, तवस्सी भिक्खू थामवं ।
ण छिंदे, ण छिंदावए, ण पए ण पयावए ॥२॥

Even when his body is gripped by hunger, the strong, austere monk does not cut, or have anything cut; he does not cook, or have anything cooked.
24 · Abuse

अक्कोसेज्जा परे भिक्खुं, ण तेसिं पडिसंजले ।
सरिसो होइ बालाणं, तम्हा भिक्खू ण संजले ॥२४॥

If others abuse a monk, he should not flare up at them. One who does becomes like the ignorant; so a monk does not flare up.
27 · The soul is not destroyed

समणं संजयं दंतं, हणिज्जा कोई कत्थई ।
णत्थि जीवस्स णासु त्ति, एवं पेहेज्ज संजए ॥२७॥

If anyone, anywhere, should strike a restrained and self-controlled monk, the monk should reflect: “The soul cannot be destroyed.”
31 · Perhaps tomorrow

अज्जेवाहं ण लब्भामि, अवि लाभो सुए सिया ।
जो एवं पडिसंचिक्खे, अलाभो तं ण तज्जए ॥३१॥

“Today I have received nothing; perhaps tomorrow I will.” The hardship of getting nothing does not trouble the one who reflects like this.
45 · Do not doubt the Jinas

अभू जिणा अत्थि जिणा, अदुवा वि भविस्सइ ।
मुसं ते एवमाहंसु, इइ भिक्खू ण चिंतए ॥४५॥

“There were Jinas, there are Jinas, there will be Jinas: those who say this speak falsely.” A monk should not think this.
46 · Not beaten by any

एए परीसहा सव्वे, कासवेण पवेइया ।
जे भिक्खू ण विहण्णेज्जा, पुट्ठो केणइ कण्हुइ ॥४६॥

All these hardships were taught by the Kashyapa, Mahavira. When any one of them strikes him, anywhere, a monk should not be overcome by it.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.24 · v.27 · v.31 · v.45, v.46

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_03_four_rare_th.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 3: The Four Rare Things
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_03_four_rare_th.content:
Uttaradhyayan 3 · Chaturangiya: The Four Rare Things
In one line: four things are hard to get, each harder than the one before: a human life, hearing the dharma, believing it, and actually living it. The one who gets all four ends suffering for good.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 3 (20 verses), translated pages 136–150 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The soul has been everywhere. Driven by its own karma, a being is born sometimes among the gods, sometimes in hell; a king now, then an outcast, then an insect or an ant. It never tires of this wandering (v.3–6).
Human birth comes rarely, only when the karma blocking it wears away little by little (v.7).
Then, hearing the dharma is rare. Those who hear it take up austerity, forgiveness and non-violence (v.8).
Then, faith is rarer still. Many hear the true path and still drift away from it (v.9).
Rarest of all is effort. Many like the dharma but never put it into practice (v.10).
The one who has all four sheds karma like dust. Purity stays only in a straight, honest heart, and such a soul blazes up to liberation “like a fire fed with ghee” (v.11–12).
Even the detour is good. Some rise to the heavens first, are reborn as humans with every good thing (family, health, wisdom, wealth), wake up again, and finish the path (v.14–19).
Know the four are rare, and act (v.20).

Key verses
1 · The four rare things

चत्तारि परमंगाणि, दुल्लहाणीह जंतुणो ।
माणुसत्तं सुई सद्धा, संजमम्मि य वीरियं ॥

For a living being in this world, four supreme things are hard to attain: human life, hearing the dharma, faith, and effort in self-restraint.
3 · Where the soul has been

एगया देवलोएसु, णरएसु वि एगया ।
एगया आसुरे काये, अहाकम्मेहिं गच्छइ ॥

According to its own actions, a being goes sometimes to the heavens, sometimes to hell, sometimes among the asuras.
9 · Faith is rarer

आहच्च सवणं लद्धुं, सद्धा परमदुल्लहा ।
सोच्चा णेयाउयं मग्गं, बहवे परिभंसइ ॥

Even when one happens to hear it, faith is extremely rare. Many hear the path that leads out, and still fall away.
12 · Like a fire fed with ghee

सोही उज्जुयभूयस्स, धम्मो सुद्धस्स चिट्ठइ ।
णिव्वाणं परमं जाइ, घय-सित्तिव्व पावए ॥

Purity belongs to the straightforward; dharma stays in the pure. Such a one reaches supreme nirvana, like a fire fed with ghee.
20 · Know it, and act

चउरंगं दुल्लहं णच्चा संजमं पडिवज्जिया ।
तवसा धुयकम्मंसे, सिद्धे हवइ सासए ॥

Knowing the four to be rare, taking up restraint and shaking off karma by austerity, one becomes an eternal siddha.
Verse 1 checked against the scan by hand; the others are from the machine translation and may have a small spelling slip. Scan of v.1
Song (English): Four Rare Things
Simple words for students (class 9). Bright, gentle folk-pop; warm young voice, acoustic guitar, light tabla. About 3 minutes.
▶ Listen
Intro
Mahavira said to his student one day:
“Four things are rare. Don’t throw them away.”
Verse 1: we have been everything
Life after life, we’ve come and gone,
Our own actions move us on.
Sometimes in heaven, sometimes in pain,
A king, a beggar, then born again.
We’ve been a tiny insect, an ant,
Still we want more, and stop? We can’t!
Chorus
Four rare things, count them with me:
One, a human life, like we have, you see.
Two, to hear what’s true. Three, to believe.
Four, to really do it. That’s the key.
Verse 2: one and two
A human life is hard to win,
It comes when lots of bad karma’s thin.
And even then, few get to hear
The good teachings, simple and clear:
Be patient, forgive, don’t hurt anyone,
Control yourself, and the work is begun.
Chorus
Verse 3: three and four
Some people hear, but don’t believe,
Some believe, then turn and leave.
Lots of people like what’s right,
But never try with all their might.
Hearing is good, believing is great,
But doing it is how you become great.
Bridge: an honest heart
Keep your heart honest, simple and clean,
That’s where goodness can be seen.
Like a fire when you add some ghee,
It burns bright and sets you free.
Verse 4: the goal
So now you know these four are rare,
Use them well, with love and care.
Control yourself, let bad karma go,
And become a free soul, forever so.
Final chorus
Four rare things, count them with me:
A human life, we’ve got it, see?
Now listen, believe, and really try,
And one day your soul will fly.
गीत (हिंदी): चार अनमोल चीज़ें
कक्षा 9 के लिए सरल भाषा। मधुर भजन-पॉप; युवा मीठी आवाज़, हारमोनियम, तबला, गिटार। लगभग 3 मिनट।
▶ सुनें
शुरुआत
भगवान महावीर ने कहा प्यार से,
चार चीज़ें मुश्किल से मिलती हैं संसार में।
अंतरा 1: हम सब कुछ बन चुके हैं
जन्म पे जन्म, हम आते-जाते,
अपने ही कर्म हमें घुमाते।
कभी स्वर्ग में, कभी दुख भारी,
कभी राजा बने, कभी भिखारी।
कभी कीड़ा, कभी चींटी बनकर,
फिर भी ना थके, इस चक्कर में फँसकर।
मुखड़ा
चार चीज़ें अनमोल हैं, गिन लो मेरे साथ,
पहला, मानव जीवन, जो है हमारे हाथ।
दूसरा, सच्ची बात सुनना, तीसरा, उस पर विश्वास,
चौथा, सच में करके दिखाना, यही है सबसे ख़ास।
अंतरा 2: पहला और दूसरा
मानव जीवन आसान नहीं,
बुरे कर्म घटें, तब मिलता यहीं।
फिर भी बहुत कम लोग सुनते,
अच्छी बातें जो गुरु चुनते:
धीरज रखो, माफ़ करो सबको,
किसी को दुख ना दो, संभालो खुद को।
(मुखड़ा)
अंतरा 3: तीसरा और चौथा
कुछ सुनते हैं, पर मानें नहीं,
कुछ मानें, फिर छोड़ें वहीं।
अच्छाई सबको अच्छी लगे,
पर करने में कोई ना आगे बढ़े।
सुनना अच्छा, मानना बढ़िया,
पर करना ही है सच्चा ज़रिया।
(मुखड़ा)
अंतरा 4: सच्चा दिल
सच्चा दिल हो, सीधा-सादा,
वहीं धर्म रहता, सबसे ज़्यादा।
जैसे आग में घी डालो तो,
तेज़ जले वो, वैसे आत्मा चमके।
अंतरा 5: मंज़िल
अब जानो, ये चारों अनमोल,
इनको ना खोना, समझो इनका मोल।
खुद को संभालो, बुरे कर्म छोड़ो,
आत्मा को हमेशा के लिए मुक्त कर लो।
(मुखड़ा)

Lyrics are original, written from this chapter’s teaching; they are not a translation of the verses.

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_04_life_cannot_.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 4: Life Cannot Be Mended
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_04_life_cannot_.content:
Uttaradhyayan 4 · Asamskrita: Life Cannot Be Mended
In one line: a broken life cannot be joined again, and neither wealth nor family can save you from your own karma, so do not put dharma off: live awake, without negligence (pramada), until the body ends.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 4 (13 verses), translated pages 152–162. 7 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Life cannot be mended, so don’t be careless. Once life breaks, no one can join it again. Even hundreds of Indras, mantras and medicines cannot stop death. In old age there is no protector, so where will the careless, violent and unrestrained go for refuge? In the commentary, the wrestler Attanamalla loses to a young fisherman, realises he is old, and takes initiation, seeing that in old age only dharma is a refuge (v.1).
Wealth won by sin leads to hell. People who gather wealth by sinful deeds, treating it like nectar, leave it all behind. Bound by enmity, they go to hell (v.2).
No escape from what you have done, and family will not share it. A thief is caught in the very hole he cut in the wall and suffers for his own act; in the same way no being escapes the fruit of its own karma, in this world or the next. A person may do karma for the sake of relatives, but when the fruit comes those relatives do not step in to share it (v.3–4).
Wealth gives no shelter, and blinds. The careless find no protection in wealth, here or hereafter. Like a man in a cave whose lamp has gone out, a soul lost in endless delusion cannot see even the path to liberation it once saw (v.5).
Stay awake like the bharanda bird. Among those asleep in delusion, the wise stay awake and never trust negligence. The moments are merciless and the body is weak, so move with care, like the ever-watchful bharanda bird (v.6).
Use the body, then let it go. Walk carefully, seeing even small ties as a snare. Keep the body going while it helps you gain virtue. When it can no longer serve restraint, know this and give it up through a final fast that destroys karma (v.7).
Give up your own will. A trained, armoured horse wins by obeying the rider, and a monk who lets go of self-will and stays alert reaches liberation quickly (v.8).
“Later” is a trap. One who does not practise dharma earlier will not manage it later either. When life weakens and death comes, he grieves. Discernment cannot be gained in a hurry at death, so give up sense pleasures now, see the world with equanimity, guard the self and live alert (v.9–10).
Bear hardship and calm the passions. Many painful touches will come to a monk on the path; he must not hate them, even in his mind. Sense pleasures are alluring and dull the mind, so do not set the mind on them. Calm anger, remove pride, give up deceit and let go of greed (v.11–12).
Turn away from the undisciplined. Some people are uncultivated, petty and full of talk about others’ faults, and live by likes and dislikes. Seeing this as unrighteous, keep away from it and seek virtue until the body falls (v.13). The commentary notes the word play: in v.1 asamskrita means “cannot be mended”, while here it means “uncultivated”, an undisciplined life.

Key verses
1 · Life cannot be mended

असंखयं जीविय मा पमायए, जरोवणीयस्स हु णत्थि ताणं ।
एवं वियाणाहि जणे पमत्ते, किण्णू विहिंसा अजया गहिंति ॥१॥

Life cannot be mended, so do not be careless. For one who has reached old age there is truly no protector. Know this: where will careless, violent, unrestrained people go for refuge?
3 · The thief in his own hole

तेणे जहा संधिमुहे गहीए, सकम्मुणा किच्चइ पावकारी ।
एवं पया पेच्च इहं च लोए, कडाण कम्माण ण मोक्ख अत्थि ॥३॥

As a sinful thief caught at the hole he cut suffers through his own deed, so beings, here and hereafter, find no release from the karma they have done.
5 · The lamp gone out

वित्तेण ताणं ण लभे पमत्ते, इमम्मि लोए अदुवा परत्था ।
दीवप्पणट्ठे व अणंत मोहे, णेयाउयं दट्ठुमदट्ठुमेव ॥५॥

The careless find no protection in wealth, in this world or the next. Like one whose lamp has gone out, the soul in endless delusion, having seen the right path, is as if it had never seen it.
6 · Awake like the bharanda bird

सुत्तेसु यावि पडिबुद्धजीवी, णो वीससे पंडिए आसुपण्णे ।
घोरा मुहुत्ता अबलं सरीरं, भारंड-पक्खी व चरेऽप्पमत्तो ॥६॥

Even among the sleeping, the wise and quick-minded one lives awake and does not trust negligence. The moments are fierce and the body is weak, so move without negligence, like the bharanda bird.
10 · No sudden wisdom at death

खिप्पं ण सक्केइ विवेगमेउं, तम्हा समुट्ठाय पहाय कामे ।
समिच्च लोयं समया महेसी, आयाणरक्खी चरेऽप्पमत्तो ॥१०॥

No one can gain discernment in a hurry. So rise up now and give up sense pleasures. The great sage, seeing the world with equanimity and guarding the self, should live without negligence.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3 · v.5–6 · v.10
