09_modules/uttaradhyayan_05_two_kinds_of.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 5: Two Kinds of Death
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_05_two_kinds_of.content:
Uttaradhyayan 5 · Akamamaraniya: Two Kinds of Death
In one line: everyone dies, but the fool dies unwillingly, in fear, again and again, while the one who lives with restraint meets death calmly, by choice, and so cuts the round of births short.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 5 (32 verses), translated pages 163–180 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

There are only two ways to die. Mahavira, the greatly wise one who crossed the ocean of worldly life, named them: death against one’s will (akama-marana) and death with one’s will (sakama-marana). The immature die the first way again and again; the wise die the second way, at best only once (v.1–3).
The fool lives for pleasure now. Attached to the pleasures of the senses, he says: “I have not seen the next world, but these pleasures are right before my eyes. Who knows if there is a next world? Whatever happens to everyone will happen to me” (v.4–7).
So he harms, lies and grabs. He hurts moving and non-moving beings, with or without a reason; he is violent, lying, deceitful and cunning, takes liquor and meat and calls it good. He gathers karma from both attachment and aversion, as an earthworm gathers soil both inside and on its body (v.8–10).
At the end, fear arrives. Struck by a fatal illness, he remembers his own deeds and dreads the next world. He has heard of hell, where the cruel suffer terribly, and he goes there by his own karma (v.11–13).
The cart driver and the gambler. Like a driver who knowingly leaves the smooth highway for a rough track and weeps when his axle breaks, the fool who leaves dharma for its opposite weeps in the mouth of death. Trembling, he dies unwillingly, like a gambler who loses everything on one throw (v.14–16).
The death of the wise is calm. For the restrained who hold knowledge, faith and conduct, death is serene and free of distress (v.17–18).
Clothes do not decide it. Not every monk or every householder gets this death. Some householders are better in restraint than some monks, but true monks surpass all householders. Bark cloth, deer skin, nakedness, matted hair, a patched robe or a shaved head cannot save a person of bad conduct. A beggar of bad conduct does not escape hell; monk or householder, whoever keeps the vows well goes to heaven (v.19–22). The commentary tells of a beggar at Rajagriha who, refused food at a feast, tried to roll a rock down on the people, was crushed by it himself and went to the seventh hell.
The good householder. A faithful lay follower keeps samayika and the other lay practices with the body, and does not miss the fasting-day observance (paushadha) in either half of the month, not even for one night. Such a one, though living at home, leaves this body of skin and joints and goes to the world of the gods (v.23–24).
The restrained monk has two destinies: freedom from all suffering, or birth as a god of great power, in shining heavens that grow finer and less deluded one above another. Monk or householder, those who have cooled the fire of the passions by restraint and austerity go there (v.25–28).
Prepare, then die willingly. Hearing of these, the virtuous and learned do not tremble at death. The wise one weighs the two deaths, chooses the better, and stays serene through compassion and forbearance. When death comes near, near the teacher he puts away fear and waits for the body to fall away, then dies one of the three willing deaths: giving up food (bhakta-parijna), fasting within a fixed space (ingini-marana), or lying still like a fallen tree (padapopagamana) (v.29–32).

Key verses
3 · Many times, or once

बालाणं तु अकामं तु, मरणं असइं भवे ।
पंडियाणं सकामं, तु उक्कोसेण सइं भवे ॥

For the immature, death against their will happens again and again. For the wise, willing death, at its highest, happens only once.
15 · The broken axle

एवं धम्मं विउक्कम्म, अहम्मं पडिवज्जिया ।
बाले मच्चुमुहं पत्ते, अक्खे भग्गे व सोयइ ॥

(Like the cart driver of v.14, who leaves the smooth highway for a rough road.) So the fool who leaves dharma and takes up what is against it grieves when he reaches the mouth of death, like the driver whose axle has broken.
16 · The gambler’s last throw

तओ से मरणंतम्मि, बाले संतस्सइ भया ।
अकाममरणं मरइ, धुत्ते व कलिणा जिए ॥

Then, at the moment of death, the fool trembles with fear and dies an unwilling death, like a gambler beaten in a single throw.
20 · Who is higher in restraint

संति एगेहिं भिक्खूहिं, गारत्था संजमुत्तरा ।
गारत्थेहि य सव्वेहिं, साहवो संजमुत्तरा ॥

Some householders are higher in restraint (samyama) than some monks; but true monks are higher in restraint than all householders.
21 · Outward signs do not save

चीराजिणं णगिणिणं, जडी संघाडी मुंडिणं ।
एयाणि वि ण तायंति, दुस्सीलं परियागयं ॥

Bark cloth and deer skin, nakedness, matted hair, a patched robe, a shaved head: none of these protects a person of bad conduct, however long he has been an ascetic.
29 · No fear at the end

तेसिं सोच्चा सपुज्जाणं, संजयाण वुसीमओ ।
ण संतसंति मरणंते, सीलवंता बहुस्सुया ॥

Having heard of these honoured, restrained ones who hold the three jewels, the virtuous and learned do not tremble when death comes.
Verses checked against the scans: v.3 · v.15 · v.16 · v.20, v.21 · v.29

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_06_the_young_mo.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 6: The Monk Free of Knots
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_06_the_young_mo.content:
Uttaradhyayan 6 · Kshullaka-Nirgranthiya: The Monk Free of Knots
In one line: ignorance ties us in knots, and neither family, wealth nor clever words can untie them; only a monk who drops every possession and attachment, and stays watchful, becomes truly free of knots (nirgrantha).
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 6 (18 verses), translated pages 181–192 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 8 minutes.
About the name: there are two chapters on the nirgrantha, the one “without knots”. This short one (kshullaka, “lesser”) has 18 verses; the great one is chapter 20. Outer knots are things like hoarding and taking what is not given. Inner knots are wrong belief, attachment, deceit and the passions (introduction).
What the chapter teaches

Ignorance is the root of suffering. All who lack true knowledge bring suffering on themselves and are crushed again and again in endless worldly existence. The commentary tells of a poor man who was offered either a wishing-pot or the skill to make one. Too lazy to learn, he took the pot, broke it while dancing drunk, and was poor again (v.1).
So seek the truth yourself. Seeing the many paths of birth and death, the wise one seeks truth by his own effort, taking up restraint, and holds friendship for all beings (v.2).
No one can save you from your own karma. Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife and sons cannot protect you. Neither can land, goods, wealth or grain. So the one with right faith cuts greed and affection and does not long for old ties. By giving up cattle, jewels and servants, one can even become a god able to take any form (v.3–6).
Life is dear to every being. Seeing this, one does not take any life, and turns away from fear and enmity. Knowing that possessions lead to hell, a monk does not keep even a blade of grass, and eats only what is given into his own bowl (v.7–8).
Knowing is not enough. Some think that just knowing the noble teaching frees them, without giving up sin. They talk of bondage and liberation, do nothing, and comfort themselves with words. Many languages cannot protect you, and no learning in the sciences can either. Fools who think themselves learned sink in their own sinful acts (v.9–11).
Attachment to the body brings suffering. Those attached to body, colour and beauty in thought, word and deed all suffer. The road through worldly existence is long, so wander watchfully, without carelessness (v.12–13).
Keep the body only to burn off old karma. Aim at liberation and want nothing else. Remove the causes of karma, such as wrong belief. Eat a measured amount of the food and water that householders made for themselves (v.14–15).
Store nothing, like a bird. A monk keeps no food, not even a smear, and moves on free of need “as a bird goes with only its wings”. He wanders with no fixed home, modest and careful, seeking pure alms (v.16–17).
This is Mahavira’s own teaching. The Arhat, son of the Jnata clan, of unsurpassed knowledge and vision, taught it. The conclusion adds that a change of clothes is not enough; there must also be a change of heart (v.18).

Key verses
1 · The fruit of ignorance

जावंतऽविज्जापुरिसा, सव्वे ते दुक्खसंभवा ।
लुप्पंति बहुसो मूढा, संसारम्मि अणंतए ॥१॥

All those without true knowledge bring suffering on themselves. Deluded, they are crushed again and again in endless worldly existence.
3 · No one can protect you

माया पिया ण्हुसा भाया, भज्जा पुत्ता य ओरसा ।
णालं ते तव ताणाय, लुप्पंतस्स सकम्मुणा ॥३॥

Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife and your own sons: none of them can protect you when you suffer through your own karma.
7 · Every life is dear

अज्झत्थं सव्वओ सव्वं, दिस्स पाणे पियाउए ।
ण हणे पाणिणो पाणे, भयवेराओ उवरए ॥७॥

Seeing every being’s inner state, and that every being holds its life dear, one should not take the life of any living being, and should turn away from fear and enmity.
10 · Talk without practice

भणंता अकरेंता य, बंध मोक्खपइण्णिणो ।
वाया विरियमित्तेण, समासासेंति अप्पयं ॥१०॥

Those who profess bondage and liberation talk but do not act. By the mere power of words, they reassure themselves.
11 · Learning does not save

ण चित्ता तायए भासा, कुओ विज्जाणुसासणं ।
विसण्णा पावकम्मेहिं, बाला पंडियमाणिणो ॥११॥

Many languages do not protect you; how could learning in the sciences? Fools who think themselves learned sink in their own sinful acts.
16 · Like a bird with its wings

सण्णिहिं च ण कुव्विज्जा, लेवमायाए संजए ।
पक्खीपत्तं समादाय, णिरवेक्खो परिव्वए ॥१६॥

A restrained monk should not store anything, not even a smear. Like a bird that takes only its wings, he should wander free of need.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3 · v.7 · v.10, v.11 · v.16

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_07_the_fattened.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 7: The Fattened Ram
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_07_the_fattened.content:
Uttaradhyayan 7 · Urabhriya: The Fattened Ram
In one line: the one who fattens on pleasure is like a ram fed well only for the guest’s table: he trades a long, bright future for a few short years of enjoyment, so keep your human birth as capital and grow it.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 7 (30 verses), translated pages 193–208 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The fattened ram. A man raises a ram (elaka) for a guest, feeding it rice and grain in his courtyard until it is plump and big-bellied. It lives only until the guest arrives; then its head is cut off and it is eaten. The introduction tells it as a calf asking its mother why the ram gets green fodder and they get dry grass; she answers that its death is near, and soon the ram is killed for a guest (v.1–3).
The pleasure-seeker is that ram. So the fool who does wrong is, in truth, waiting for a lifetime in hell (v.4). Violent, lying, robbing on the road, stealing, always thinking “whom shall I rob next?”, deceitful, greedy for women and pleasures, busy with big undertakings and possessions, eating meat and drinking liquor, fat and full of blood, oppressing others: he longs for hell as the ram’s owner waits for the guest (v.5–7).
At the end he grieves. Having enjoyed seats, beds, vehicles, wealth and pleasures, he leaves behind his hard-won wealth and carries only a heavy load of karma. Living only for the present, he grieves at death like the ram when the guest has come, and goes, helpless, to the dark realm of hell (v.8–10).
The coin and the mango. A man loses a thousand gold coins for one tiny coin (kakini); a king, forbidden mangoes by his doctor, eats one and loses his kingdom and his life. So the fool loses a precious human birth for small pleasures (v.11).
Human pleasure is small. Compared with the pleasures of the gods, human pleasures are nothing; divine life and pleasure are thousands of times greater. The fool loses a divine life of countless years for a human life of under a hundred (v.12–13).
The three merchants. Three traders set out with capital: one comes back with profit, one with only his capital, one having lost it. In dharma, a human birth is the capital, birth as a god is the profit, and hell or animal birth is losing the capital (v.14–16).
Losing the capital is hard to undo. The fool, through greed and deceit, loses both the god and the human state and falls into the two miserable states, rooted in killing. From there it is hard to rise even after a very long time (v.17–18).
Keeping and growing the capital. Householders of good nature, trained in many ways, are born human again, for beings reap exactly what their karma brings. Those whose training is wide and whose conduct grows go beyond the capital to the state of the gods, undaunted. Knowing this, who would throw such a gain away? (v.19–22)
A drop on a blade of grass. Human pleasures are like a drop of water on the tip of kusa grass beside the ocean, and life is very short. One who does not turn from pleasure loses his true aim and falls away even after hearing the path; one who does turn away leaves this impure body and becomes a god, then is born again among humans with wealth, beauty, fame, long life and happiness (v.23–27).
See both, and choose. See the folly of the fool, who drops dharma and goes to hell, and the steadiness of the wise, who drops wrong and goes to the gods. The wise monk weighs the two, leaves folly and lives by wisdom (v.28–30).

Key verses
1 · Raised for the guest

जहाएसं समुद्दिस्स, कोइ पोसेज्ज एलयं ।
ओयणं जवसं देज्जा, पोसेज्जा वि सयंगणे ॥

Just as someone, with a guest in mind, raises a ram, gives it rice and grain, and fattens it in his own courtyard.
11 · The coin and the mango

जहा कागिणिए हेउं, सहस्सं हारए णरो ।
अपत्थं अंबगं भोच्चा, राया रज्जं तु हारए ॥

Just as a man loses a thousand coins for the sake of one kakini, and a king who eats a mango forbidden to him loses his kingdom.
16 · Human birth is the capital

माणुसत्तं भवे मूलं, लाभो देवगई भवे ।
मूलच्छेएण जीवाणं, णरग-तिरिक्खत्तणं धुवं ॥

Human birth is the capital; birth among the gods is the profit. When the capital is lost, beings surely go to hell or to animal birth.
23 · A drop beside the ocean

जहा कुसग्गे उदगं, समुद्देण समं मिणे ।
एवं माणुस्सगा कामा, देवकामाण अंतिए ॥

Like a drop of water on the tip of a blade of kusa grass measured against the ocean: so are human pleasures beside the pleasures of the gods.
26 · Turning away is not a loss

इह कामाणियट्टस्स, अत्तट्ठे णावरज्झइ ।
पूइदेह-णिरोहेणं, भवे देवे त्ति मे सुयं ॥

Here, one who turns away from sensual pleasures does not lose the soul’s true aim. Leaving this impure body, he becomes a god: so I have heard.
30 · Weigh, and choose wisdom

तुलियाण बालभावं, अबालं चेव पंडिए ।
चइऊण बालभावं, अबालं सेवए मुणी ॥

The wise monk weighs folly against wisdom, gives up folly, and lives by wisdom.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.11 · v.16 · v.23 · v.26 · v.30

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_08_kapila_and_g.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 8: Kapila and Greed
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_08_kapila_and_g.content:
Uttaradhyayan 8 · Kapiliya: Kapila and Greed
In one line: to escape a bad rebirth, let go of attachments, harm no living being, eat only to keep up restraint, and see through greed, which grows with every gain, as Kapila found when two grams of gold turned into a wish for millions.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 8 (20 verses), translated pages 209–221. 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Kapila’s story: greed has no end. Kapila, son of a royal priest, was sent to study in Shravasti, fell in love with a maidservant, and went out at midnight to be the first to greet a rich merchant, who gave two mashas of gold to whoever came first. Guards arrested him as a thief. The king, pleased by his honesty, offered him anything. Sitting in a grove, Kapila’s wish grew from two mashas to crores of gold coins, and still he was not satisfied. Then his thinking turned: he asked for nothing, became a monk, and in six months reached perfect knowledge and liberation (introduction, pp. 209–210).
The question. In this unstable, impermanent world full of suffering, what conduct keeps a person from falling into a bad rebirth (durgati)? (v.1).
Let go of old ties. Having left parents and other worldly ties, a monk should form no attachment to anyone, not even to those who show him affection. Free of attachment, he is freed from faults and their results (v.2–3).
Drop possessions and quarrels. A monk gives up all possessions and strife. Seeing the bitter results of sense pleasures, he is not stained by them. The fool stuck in pleasures is trapped like a fly in phlegm. Pleasures are hard to give up for the weak, but monks of good vows cross over, like a merchant crossing the sea (v.4–6).
Harm no living being. Some call themselves ascetics yet do not even understand what killing is; such fools go to hell. One who even approves of killing is never freed from suffering. One who harms no being, moving or still, by mind, speech or body, sheds sinful karma like water running off high ground (v.7–10). The commentary tells of a shravaka’s son, sold to a hunter, who would not kill a bird even when he was crushed under an elephant for refusing.
Eat to live, not for taste. A monk seeks pure alms and eats only to sustain his life of restraint, never greedy for flavour; plain, cold, old or coarse food is enough (v.11–12).
No fortune-telling. Those who read bodily marks, dreams or twitching limbs for householders are not true monks (shramanas). Those who let their life run loose and fall from calm and restraint, greedy for pleasures, are reborn among the asuras, then wander long, and right understanding (bodhi) becomes very hard to gain (v.13–15).
Greed cannot be filled. Give one person the whole world full of wealth and grain, and he would still not be content. As gain grows, greed grows: what two mashas of gold would have done was not done by crores (v.16–17).
Keep clear of attachment to women. A homeless monk should not be attached to women, who can lure a man and make him dance like a servant; he should set his soul in the dharma instead. The commentary adds that a man is equally a cause of desire for a woman, so nuns too must stay alert; the verse speaks from a man’s side only (v.18–19).
Kapila’s dharma carries you across. This is the dharma taught by Kapila of pure wisdom. Those who practise it cross worldly existence and succeed in both this world and the next (v.20).

Key verses
1 · The question

अधुवे असासयम्मि, संसारम्मि दुक्खपउराए ।
किं णाम होज्ज तं कम्मयं, जेणाऽहं दुग्गइं ण गच्छेज्जा ॥१॥

In this unstable, impermanent world full of suffering, what conduct is there by which I will not go to a bad rebirth?
2 · No attachment, even to those who love you

विजहित्तु पुव्वसंजोगं, ण सिणेहं कहिंचि कुव्वेज्जा ।
असिणेह सिणेहकरेहिं, दोसपओसेहिं मुच्चए भिक्खू ॥२॥

Having left his former ties, a monk should form attachment to nothing. Unattached even to those who are attached to him, he is freed from faults and their results.
9 · Like water off high ground

पाणे य णाइवाएज्जा, से समिए त्ति वुच्चइ ताई ।
तओ से पावयं कम्मं, णिज्जाइ उदगं व थलाओ ॥९॥

One who does not harm living beings is called careful (samita) and a protector of all beings. His sinful karma runs off him like water off high ground.
16 · The self is hard to fill

कसिणं पि जो इमं लोयं, पडिपुण्णं दलेज्ज इक्कस्स ।
तेणावि से ण संतुस्से, इइ दुप्पूरए इमे आया ॥१६॥

Even if someone gave one person this whole world, full of wealth and grain, he would not be satisfied with it. So hard is this self to fill.
17 · Greed grows with gain

जहा लाहो तहा लोहो, लाहा लोहो पवड्ढइ ।
दोमास-कयं कज्जं, कोडीए वि ण णिट्ठियं ॥१७॥

As gain grows, so grows greed; gain makes greed increase. A need that two mashas of gold would have met was not met even by crores.
20 · Kapila’s dharma

इइ एस धम्मे अक्खाए, कविलेणं च विसुद्धपण्णेणं ।
तरिहिंति जे उ काहिंति, तेहिं आराहिया दुवे लोगा ॥२०॥

Thus this dharma has been taught by Kapila of pure wisdom. Those who practise it will cross over; by them both worlds, this life and the next, are won.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1–2 · v.9 · v.16 · v.17 · v.20

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_09_namis_renunc.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 9: Nami's Renunciation
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_09_namis_renunc.content:
Uttaradhyayan 9 · Namipravrajya (नमिप्रव्रज्या): Nami’s Renunciation
In one line: when King Nami leaves his kingdom, Indra comes disguised as a Brahmin and tests him with ten worldly duties, and Nami answers each one by turning it inward: the real city, fort, war and wealth are inside the soul.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 9 (62 verses), translated pages 222–250 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Nami woke up through a small sound. The introduction tells his story. King Nami of Mithila (Videha) had a burning fever for six months. When the queens ground sandalwood for him, their bangles clinked and he could not bear the noise, so they kept one bangle each and the sound stopped. Nami saw it: “Where there are many, there is conflict and sorrow; where there is one, there is peace.” He is one of four kings in the book who were awakened by an outside event (individually awakened, pratyekabuddha) (introduction, pp. 222–223).
He remembered his past life and left everything. Come down from the heavens and born a man, with his deluding karma calmed, Nami remembered his previous birth, put his son on the throne, and left Mithila, its army, palace and people for a solitary place. The city filled with an uproar (v.1–5).
Indra tests him: “Why is the city crying?” Nami answers with a picture: a great tree in a garden gave shade and fruit to many birds; a storm has uprooted it, and the birds cry because they have lost their shelter. His going forth harms no one; self-restraint protects all six kinds of living beings (v.6–10, commentary).
“Your palace is burning.” Nami: “I live happily, for I own nothing. When Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.” For a monk who has left wife and children, nothing is dear and nothing is hateful, and great well-being comes from seeing that he is alone (v.11–16).
“First build a fort and palaces.” Nami builds a different fort: faith is the city, austerity and restraint its bolt, forgiveness its wall, the three restraints (gupti) its guard; valour is the bow and austerity the arrow that pierces the armour of karma. And only a man who doubts he will arrive builds his house on the road; build your lasting home where you are going (v.17–26).
“First punish the thieves and conquer the kings.” In this world the innocent are often punished and the guilty go free, Nami says, so catch the thieves inside. And the victory over one’s own self is greater than defeating a million warriors; conquer the self and the senses, anger, pride, deceit and greed are all conquered (v.27–36).
“First give gifts, hold sacrifices, stay a householder.” Self-restraint, even in one who gives nothing, is better than giving a million cows every month. A month-long fast done without right understanding is not worth a sixteenth of the well-taught dharma (v.37–44).
“First fill your treasury.” Mountains of gold and silver as many as Kailash would not satisfy a greedy man; desire is endless like the sky. Knowing this, practise austerity (v.45–49).
“You are giving up the pleasures you have for ones you don’t.” Nami: pleasures are a thorn, poison, a cobra; even wanting them without enjoying them leads to a bad birth. Anger takes you down, pride lowers you, deceit blocks a good state, greed brings fear in both worlds (v.50–54).
Indra bows. Indra drops his disguise and praises Nami: he has conquered anger, pride, deceit and greed, and so has forgiveness, gentleness, straightforwardness and freedom from greed. He will reach liberation. The wise turn away from pleasures as Nami did (v.55–62).

Key verses
14 · Nothing of mine burns

सुहं वसामो जीवामो, जेसिं मो णत्थि किंचणं ।
मिहिलाए डज्झमाणीए, ण मे डज्झइ किंचणं ॥

We live and dwell happily, we who own nothing. When Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
20 · The city of faith

सद्धं णगरं किच्चा, तव संवरमग्गलं ।
खंति णिउणपागारं, तिगुत्तं दुप्पधंसयं ॥

Make faith your city, austerity and restraint its bolt, and forgiveness its strong wall, guarded by the three restraints, so that the enemy, karma, cannot break it.
34 · The greatest victory

जो सहस्सं सहस्साणं, संगामे दुज्जए जिणे ।
एगं जिणेज्ज अप्पाणं, एस से परमो जओ ॥

One man may defeat a million warriors in a hard battle; another conquers only his own self. That is the supreme victory.
36 · Conquer the self, conquer all

पंचिंदियाणि कोहं, माणं मायं तहेव लोहं च ।
दुज्जयं चेव अप्पाणं, सव्वं अप्पे जिए जियं ॥

The five senses, anger, pride, deceit and greed, and the self (the mind) are hard to conquer. When the self is conquered, all of them are conquered.
48 · Desire is endless like the sky

सुवण्ण-रुव्वस्स उ पव्वया भवे, सिया हु केलाससमा असंखया ।
णरस्स लुद्धस्स ण तेहिं किंचि, इच्छा उ आगाससमा अणंतिया ॥

Even if there were countless mountains of gold and silver as big as Kailash, they would be nothing to a greedy man, for desire is endless like the sky.
53 · Pleasures are a thorn, a poison, a cobra

सल्लं कामा विसं कामा, कामा आसीविसोवमा ।
कामे य पत्थेमाणा वि, अकामा जंति दुग्गइं ॥

Sense pleasures are a thorn, sense pleasures are poison, sense pleasures are like a venomous snake. Even those who only long for them, without enjoying them, go to a bad state of birth.
Verses checked against the scans: v.14 · v.20 · v.34 · v.36 · v.48 · v.53

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_10_the_falling_.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 10: The Falling Leaf
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_10_the_falling_.content:
Uttaradhyayan 10 · Drumapatraka: The Falling Leaf
In one line: life falls like a yellow leaf from a tree, and a human birth with everything needed for dharma is very hard to get, so do not be careless (pramada) even for a moment.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 10 (37 verses), translated pages 251–266. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches
Lord Mahavira speaks to Gautama, but the book says the teaching is meant for every seeker. Every verse except the last ends with the same line: “Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.”

Life is short and can end at any time. It is like a yellowed leaf that drops as nights and days pass, and like a dewdrop that hangs on the tip of a blade of grass for only a little while. A short life is also full of dangers, so shake off the karma already gathered (v.1–3).
A human birth is hard to get. Even over a very long time, the effects of karma are so strong that a being rarely gets a human birth (v.4).
Without it, a soul can be stuck for ages. As an earth, water, fire or air being, a soul can keep being born in that same kind of body for countless time; as a plant, for endless time; as a two-, three- or four-sensed being, for a long but countable time; as a five-sensed animal or human, for seven or eight births in a row; in heaven or hell, one birth at a time. The commentary calls these the “eleven valleys” a soul crosses before reaching human life. A careless soul wanders like this because of its good and bad karma (v.5–15).
Even as a human, five more things are rare, each harder than the last: birth in a land where right and wrong are known (an “Aryan” land), all five senses whole, the chance to hear the highest dharma, faith in it, and actually living it with the body, since many who believe stay caught in sense pleasures (v.16–20).
Old age takes the senses one by one. Your body is wearing out, your hair is turning white, and your hearing, sight, smell, taste, touch and all your strength are failing. The commentary explains why: without hearing you cannot listen to dharma, without sight you cannot look out for living beings or study, and without strength you cannot bear hardship or do austerity (v.21–26).
Disease can break the body. Boils, cholera and many sudden, deadly illnesses can strike and destroy it. The book notes Gautama himself had no illness; the warning is for everyone (v.27).
Cut attachment and do not take back what you gave up. Be like the autumn lotus that grows in water but stays apart from it. You left wealth and wife to become a monk; do not swallow again what you have vomited. Do not go looking again for the friends, relatives and riches you left (v.28–30).
The path is here now; walk it bravely. The Jina is not seen today, but the path he showed is. You have left the thorny road for the great highway. Do not be like the weak porter who drops his precious load on a rough road and regrets it all his life. You have crossed the great ocean, so why stand at the shore? Hurry across (v.31–34).
Liberation is sure for the one who keeps going. Climbing the ladder that leads beyond the body, you will reach the world of the liberated, safe and blissful. Awake, calm and restrained, wander through villages and towns and spread the path of peace (v.35–36).
Gautama did it. Hearing the Lord’s well-spoken words, Gautama cut off attachment and aversion and reached liberation (siddhi). The book ends by saying that “our Gautama is our mind”, which must be trained by these teachings (v.37).

Key verses
1 · The yellow leaf

दुमपत्तए पंडुयए जहा, णिवडइ राइगणाण अच्चए ।
एवं मणुयाण जीवियं, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥१॥

Just as a tree’s leaf turns yellow and falls as nights and days go by, so does human life. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
4 · A human birth is rare

दुल्लहे खलु माणुसे भवे, चिरकालेण वि सव्वपाणिणं ।
गाढा य विवाग कम्मुणो, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥४॥

For all living beings, a human birth is truly hard to get, even after a very long time, because the effects of karma are so strong. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
20 · Living it is rarer still

धम्मं पि हु सद्दहंतया, दुल्लहया काएण फासया ।
इह कामगुणेहिं मुच्छिया, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥२०॥

Even when people have faith in dharma, it is rare to practise it with the body, because here people are lost in sense pleasures. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
28 · Like the autumn lotus

वुच्छिंद सिणेहमप्पणो, कुमुयं सारइयं व पाणियं ।
से सव्वसिणेह वज्जिए, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥२८॥

As the autumn lotus stays apart from the water it grows in, cut your attachment away from yourself and be free of every attachment. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
34 · Why stand at the shore?

तिण्णो हु सि अण्णवं महं, किं पुण चिट्ठसि तीरमागओ ।
अभितुर पारं गमित्तए, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥३४॥

You have crossed the great ocean. Why then do you stand still, having reached the shore? Hurry to get across to the other side. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
37 · Gautama reaches liberation

बुद्धस्स णिसम्म भासियं, सुकहिय-मट्ठपओवसोहियं ।
रागं दोसं च छिंदिया, सिद्धिगइं गए गोयमे ॥३७॥

Having heard the words of the Enlightened One, well spoken and rich with meaningful words, Gautama cut off attachment and aversion and went to the state of liberation. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.4 · v.20 · v.28 · v.34 · v.37

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_11_glory_of_the.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 11: The Glory of the Learned
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_11_glory_of_the.content:
Uttaradhyayan 11 · Bahushrut Puja (બહુશ્રુત પૂજા): The Glory of the Learned
In one line: a monk becomes deeply learned (bahushrut) only through humility, self-control and staying with his teacher; such a learned monk shines above all others, and his learning carries him and others to liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 11 (32 verses), translated pages 267–283 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

This chapter is about the conduct that makes a monk learned. The teacher promises to set out, in order, the conduct of a homeless monk who is free from all outer and inner ties. “Conduct” here means restraint, humility and the gaining of scriptural knowledge (v.1).
First, what the unlearned monk is like. He has no scriptural knowledge, is proud, greedy for tastes, does not control his senses, keeps talking without sense, and lacks humility. The commentary calls these six faults that must never be let into the soul (v.2).
Five things block learning: pride, anger, carelessness (pramada), illness and laziness. No one teaches a proud person, because he shows no respect (v.3).
Eight qualities make one fit to learn. One who does not laugh and joke all the time, always controls the senses, does not expose another’s weak points, does not lack good conduct, does not stain his vows, is not greedy, does not get angry, and loves truth (v.4–5).
Fourteen faults make a monk ill-disciplined (avinita), and he does not reach liberation. He is often angry and stays angry long, pushes away those who are friendly, becomes vain on gaining knowledge, blames others, gets angry even with friends, speaks ill of a dear friend behind his back, talks rashly, betrays friends, is proud, greedy, uncontrolled, does not share food with fellow monks, and makes everyone dislike him (v.6–9).
Fifteen qualities make a monk well-disciplined (suvinita). He is humble, steady, free of deceit and of craving for shows; he is slow to rebuke and quick to cool down; he keeps friendships, is not vain about his learning, does not dwell on others’ slips, is not angry with friends, and speaks well even of a friend who has displeased him, behind his back; he avoids quarrels, is wise, cultured, modest and keeps his senses withdrawn (v.10–13).
The ground for becoming learned is living with the teacher. One who always lives in the teacher’s household (gurukul), keeps mind, speech and body wholesome, does austerity, does what is pleasing and speaks pleasantly, deserves to receive teaching (v.14).
Sixteen pictures show how the learned monk shines. Like milk in a conch, which shines twice over; like Kanthaka, the finest horse of Kamboja; like a brave warrior on a fine horse with victory music before and behind; like a sixty-year-old elephant at full strength that no one can defeat; like the sharp-horned bull that leads the herd; like the young lion, first among animals; like Vasudeva with conch, discus and mace; like the universal monarch (chakravarti) with his fourteen jewels; like Shakra, lord of the gods; like the rising sun that drives out darkness; like the full moon among the stars; like a well-guarded granary full of many grains; like Sudarshana, the best of trees; like the Sita, best of rivers; like Mount Mandara (Meru), best of mountains; like the Svayambhuramana ocean, full of jewels and never drained (v.15–30).
The fruit of great learning is liberation. Deep as the ocean, unshakable, full of vast knowledge and protecting all six kinds of living beings, the learned destroy their karma and reach the highest state (v.31).
So, study. One who seeks the highest goal should take up the scriptures, by which he reaches liberation himself and helps others reach it too (v.32).

Key verses
2 · The unlearned monk

जे यावि होइ णिव्विज्जे, थद्धे लुद्धे अणिग्गहे ।
अभिक्खणं उल्लवइ, अविणीए अबहुस्सुए ॥

The monk who has no learning, is proud, greedy for tastes, does not control his senses, keeps talking without sense, and lacks humility, is not learned.
3 · Five things that block learning

अह पंचहिं ठाणेहिं, जेहिं सिक्खा ण लब्भइ ।
थंभा कोहा पमाएणं, रोगेणाऽऽलस्सएण य ॥

There are five reasons why learning is not gained: pride, anger, carelessness, illness and laziness.
14 · Live with the teacher

वसे गुरुकुले णिच्चं, जोगवं उवहाणवं ।
पियंकरे पियंवाई, से सिक्खं लद्धुमरिहइ ॥

One who always lives with the teacher, keeps mind, speech and body wholesome, practises austerity, does what is pleasing and speaks pleasantly, is worthy of receiving teaching.
15 · Milk in a conch

जहा संखम्मि पयं णिहियं, दुहओ वि विरायइ ।
एवं बहुस्सुए भिक्खू, धम्मो कित्ती तहा सुयं ॥

Milk placed in a conch shines in two ways, by its own whiteness and by the conch’s. So in a learned monk, dharma, good name and scriptural learning all shine.
31 · The fruit of learning

समुद्द-गंभीरसमा दुरासया, अचक्किया केणइ दुप्पहंसया ।
सुयस्स पुण्णा विउलस्स ताइणो, खवित्तु कम्मं गइमुत्तमं गया ॥

Deep as the ocean, unconquerable, never overpowered by anyone, full of vast scriptural knowledge and protectors of all living beings, they destroyed their karma and reached the highest state.
32 · So, study the scriptures

तम्हा सुयमहिट्ठिज्जा, उत्तमट्ठगवेसए ।
जेणऽप्पाणं परं चेव, सिद्धिं संपाउणेज्जासि ॥

Therefore one who seeks the highest goal should study and hold on to the scriptures, by which he can reach liberation (siddhi) himself and help others reach it.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.3 · v.14 · v.15 · v.31 · v.32

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_12_the_true_sac.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 12: The True Sacrifice
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_12_the_true_sac.content:
Uttaradhyayan 12 · Harikeshiya (હરિકેશીય): The True Sacrifice
In one line: a monk born among outcastes shows the proud Brahmins at a sacrifice that a person is made high by conduct, not by birth, and that the true sacrifice and the true bath happen inside the soul, through austerity, restraint and dharma.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 12 (47 verses), translated pages 284–308 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Birth does not make a monk; conduct does. The commentary tells the background. In a past life the Brahmin Somadatta became a monk but never repented his pride in caste and looks. So he was reborn in a Chandala (outcaste) family as Harikeshbal: ugly, angry and shunned. One day he watched his people kill a venomous snake and spare a harmless one. He saw that beings suffer for their own faults and are loved for their virtues. He remembered his past life, took initiation, and began fierce austerities in a tinduka grove near Varanasi, where a yaksha came to serve him. When Princess Bhadra spat on him, the yaksha drove her mad until the king offered her to the monk as a wife. The monk calmly refused: for a monk, all women are like mothers, sisters and daughters. She was then married to the royal priest Rudradeva (pp.284–286).
The monk was real in practice, not only in name. Born in a Chandala family, he had excellent virtues and had conquered his senses. He kept the five careful practices (samitis) and the three restraints (guptis). On the day he broke a month-long fast, he came for alms to Rudradeva’s sacrificial hall (v.1–3).
The proud mock what they cannot see. Seeing his body thin from austerity and his clothes worn and dirty, the Brahmins, proud of their caste, laughed at him. They called him black, terrifying and flat-nosed, a dusty ghost in rubbish-heap rags, and told him to get out (v.4–7).
The yaksha speaks for the silent monk. The yaksha entered the monk’s body and said: I am a shramana, restrained and celibate, living on alms; give this ascetic a little of what is left over. The Brahmins said the food was for Brahmins only (v.8–11).
Who is the worthy field for a gift? Farmers sow seed on high ground and low ground alike, the yaksha said, so give to me too. The Brahmins answered that Brahmins with birth and learning are the best fields. The yaksha replied that anyone with anger, pride, violence, lies, theft and possessiveness has neither birth nor learning: such fields are fields of sin. You carry the Vedas like a load but do not know their meaning; monks who beg from high and low homes alike are the true fields (v.12–17).
Violence meets the power of austerity. Rudradeva ordered the young men to beat the monk with sticks, canes and whips. Bhadra recognised him as the monk who had refused her even in his mind. She warned them: insulting him is digging a mountain with your nails, chewing iron with your teeth, kicking fire. Do not let him burn you all. The yaksha struck the young men from the sky until they lay twisted and vomiting blood (v.18–29).
The monk has no anger. Rudradeva and Bhadra begged forgiveness. The monk said there was no ill will in his mind before, now, or in the future: it was the yaksha, serving him, who struck the boys. The Brahmins took refuge at his feet. He accepted their food to break his month-long fast. The gods showered flowers, fragrant water and wealth and cried “Oh, what a gift!” (v.30–36).
The lesson spoken aloud. The greatness of austerity is seen with one’s own eyes; no greatness of caste is seen. The son of a Chandala has such power. The commentary adds that the door to liberation is open to anyone, of any caste, country or sex, who practises the three jewels purely (v.37).
The true sacrifice is inside. Kindling fire and washing with water seeks only outer purity, and harms countless living beings. The Brahmins asked how to sacrifice rightly. The monk answered: the restrained harm none of the six kinds of living beings and give up lies, theft, possessions, women, pride and deceit. Closed against karma by the five restraints, careless of the body, they perform the best sacrifice. Austerity is the fire, the soul its altar, karma the fuel (v.38–44).
The true bath is inside too. Dharma is the lake and celibacy (brahmacharya) the holy bathing place. Bathing there, one becomes clean and cool and throws off the dust of karma. In this “great bath” the great sages reached the highest state. The commentary ends: by the strength of his conduct, Harikeshbal himself attained liberation (v.45–47, p.308).

Key verses
1 · A monk from an outcaste family

सोवाग-कुल-संभूओ, गुणुत्तरधरो मुणी ।
हरिएसबलो णाम, आसी भिक्खू जिइंदिओ ॥१॥

There was a monk named Harikeshbal, born in a Chandala family, who held the highest virtues and had conquered his senses.
14 · Who is a fit field for a gift

कोहो य माणो य वहो य जेसिं, मोसं अदत्तं च परिग्गहं च ।
ते माहणा जाइविज्जाविहूणा, ताइं तु खेत्ताइं सुपावयाइं ॥१४॥

Brahmins whose lives hold anger and pride, violence and lies, taking what is not given and possessiveness, are empty of birth and learning. Such fields are fields of sin, not good fields for a gift.
32 · No anger in the monk’s mind

पुव्विं च इण्हिं च अणागयं च, मणप्पओसो ण मे अत्थि कोई ।
जक्खा हु वेयावडियं करेंति, तम्हा हु एए णिहया कुमारा ॥३२॥

There was no ill will in my mind before, there is none now, and there will be none in the future. The yaksha serves me, and it is he who has struck these young men down.
37 · Austerity is seen, caste is not

सक्खं खु दीसइ तवोविसेसो, ण दीसइ जाइविसेस कोई ।
सोवागपुत्तं हरिएस साहुं, जस्सेरिस्सा इड्ढि महाणुभागा ॥३७॥

The greatness of austerity is plainly seen before our eyes; no greatness of caste is seen at all. Look at the monk Harikesh, son of a Chandala, whose spiritual power is so great.
44 · The inner fire sacrifice

तवो जोई जीवो जोइठाणं, जोगा सुया सरीरं कारिसंगं ।
कम्मेहा संजमजोग संति, होमं हुणामि इसिणं पसत्थं ॥४४॥

Austerity is my fire, the soul is its altar, my good acts of mind, speech and body are the ladle, and the body is the dung-cake that kindles it. Karma is the fuel, and the practice of restraint (samyama) is the prayer for peace. I offer the sacrifice the sages praise.
46 · The inner bath

धम्मे हरए बंभे संतितित्थे, अणाविले अत्तपसण्णलेसे ।
जहिंसि ण्हाओ विमलो विसुद्धो, सुसीइभूओ पजहामि दोसं ॥४६॥

Dharma is my lake, and celibacy my holy bathing place of peace: unclouded, and bringing the soul to a pure state. Bathing there I become spotless, purified and wholly cool, and I cast off my faults.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.14 · v.32 · v.37 · v.44 · v.46

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_13_two_brothers.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 13: Two Brothers, Two Paths
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_13_two_brothers.content:
Uttaradhyayan 13 · Chitta-Sambhutiya: Two Brothers, Two Paths
In one line: two brothers who were together for five lives meet again in the sixth, one a monk and one an emperor; the monk urges the emperor to let go of pleasures, the emperor cannot, and so one reaches liberation and the other the lowest hell.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 13 (35 verses), translated pages 309–326 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The story behind the chapter. The introduction tells it. Chitta and Sambhuta were brothers in five births: servants in Dasharna, deer on Mount Kalinjara, swans on the Mritaganga, sons of a Chandala (outcaste) chief in Kashi, and then gods. As Chandala boys they were gifted singers and dancers, but were beaten and driven out of Varanasi for their caste. About to kill themselves, they met a monk who told them suicide only adds to suffering, and they became monks. Later, in Hastinapura, Sambhuta was beaten on the orders of the minister Namuchi and in anger let loose his fiery power (tejoleshya); Chitta calmed him. Then, when Queen Sunanda bowed and her soft hair touched his feet, Sambhuta made a wish, a binding resolve (niyana), that his austerities should make him an emperor. Chitta could not turn him from it (pages 309–311).
The resolve came true. Sambhuta, humiliated for his caste, made his resolve in Hastinapura and was born as Brahmadatta, son of Queen Chulani, in Kampilya. Chitta was born into a great merchant family in Purimatala, heard the dharma and became a monk (v.1–2). The emperor found his brother again with a half-verse that only Chitta could complete (pages 311–312).
The brothers meet and look back. In Kampilya they met and told each other the fruits of their good and bad deeds. Brahmadatta recalls their five lives together; this sixth is the one in which they are apart (v.3–7).
Separation came from desire. The monk says the karma the king made out of desire (his resolve) is what pulled them apart (v.8). The king answers that good deeds always bear fruit and there is no escape from what one has done; his wealth and pleasures are that fruit. Is Chitta enjoying his? (v.9–10)
The monk had wealth too, and gave it up. Chitta says he too had great prosperity and splendour, but hearing the elders’ teaching, he became a monk (v.11–12).
The emperor’s invitation. Brahmadatta offers his palaces, his wealth, women, drama, music and song: “enjoy these; renunciation is painful” (v.13–14).
Pleasures are not what they seem. Songs are lamentation, dance is mockery, ornaments are burdens, all sense pleasures bring suffering. The happiness of monks rich in austerity is not found in pleasures, which only charm the ignorant. Their high birth now is the fruit of the restraint they practised as outcaste monks, so the king should give up passing pleasures and go forth (v.15–20).
Death comes alone. As a lion carries off a deer, death carries off a person. No relative can share the suffering; karma follows the doer alone. The body is burned and the family turns to the next provider. Life runs out, old age takes beauty: do not do deeds that bind heavy karma (v.21–26).
The emperor knows but cannot act. Brahmadatta admits it: because of the resolve he never repented of, he knows the dharma yet stays stuck in pleasures, like an elephant sunk in mud that sees the dry bank and cannot reach it (v.27–30).
A lesser path, then parting. Time runs, pleasures leave a person like birds leaving a tree with no fruit. If you cannot give them up, at least stay in dharma, do noble deeds and have compassion for all beings, and you will become a god. Seeing the king has no wish to renounce, Chitta says he has spoken in vain and leaves (v.31–33).
Two ends. Brahmadatta enjoyed the highest pleasures and went to the lowest hell; Chitta kept the highest restraint and reached the highest state, liberation (v.34–35). The commentary’s lesson: a longing for pleasure, made into a resolve, causes the soul’s great downfall, so a seeker should stay free of desire for worldly happiness (page 326).

Key verses
6–7 · Six births

दासा दसण्णे आसी, मिया कालिंजरे णगे ।
हंसा मयंगतीरे य, सोवागा कासिभूमिए ॥६॥
देवा य देवलोगम्मि, आसि अम्हे महिड्ढिया ।
इमा णो छट्ठिया जाई, अण्णमण्णेण जा विणा ॥७॥

We were servants in Dasharna, deer on Mount Kalinjara, swans on the bank of the Mritaganga, and outcastes (Chandalas) in the land of Kashi. Then we were gods of great power in the heavens. This is our sixth birth, the one in which we are apart from each other.
16 · What pleasures really are

सव्वं विलवियं गीयं, सव्वं णट्टं विडंबियं ।
सव्वे आभरणा भारा, सव्वे कामा दुहावहा ॥१६॥

All song is lamentation, all dance is mockery, all ornaments are burdens, all sense pleasures bring suffering.
23 · Karma follows the doer

ण तस्स दुक्खं विभयंति णाइओ, ण मित्तवग्गा ण सुया ण बंधवा ।
इक्को सयं पच्चणुहोइ दुक्खं, कत्तारमेव अणुजाइ कम्मं ॥२३॥

Relatives, friends, sons and kin cannot share his suffering. He bears it himself, alone, for karma follows only the one who did it.
30 · The elephant in the mud

णागो जहा पंकजलावसण्णो, दट्ठुं थलं णाभिसमेइ तीरं ।
एवं वयं कामगुणेसु गिद्धा, ण भिक्खुणो मग्गमणुव्वयामो ॥३०॥

As an elephant sunk in mud sees the dry ground and still cannot reach the bank, so I, gripped by sense pleasures, cannot follow the monk’s path.
31 · Like birds leaving a bare tree

अच्चेइ कालो तूरंति राइओ, ण यावि भोगा पुरिसाण णिच्चा ।
उविच्च भोगा पुरिसं चयंति, दुमं जहा खीणफलं व पक्खी ॥३१॥

Time passes, the nights hurry by, and a person’s pleasures do not last. They come on their own and then leave him, as birds leave a tree whose fruit is gone.
34–35 · Two ends

पंचालराया वि य बंभदत्तो, साहुस्स तस्स वयणं अकाउं ।
अणुत्तरे भुंजिय कामभोगे, अणुत्तरे सो णरए पविट्ठो ॥३४॥
चित्तो वि कामेहिं विरत्तकामो, उदग्ग चारित्ततवो महेसी ।
अणुत्तरं संजम पालइत्ता, अणुत्तरं सिद्धिगइं गओ ॥३५॥

Brahmadatta, king of Panchala, did not follow that monk’s words. Having enjoyed the highest pleasures, he entered the deepest hell. And Chitta, the great sage, free of desire for pleasures, rich in conduct and austerity, kept the highest restraint (samyama) and reached the highest state, liberation (siddhi).
Verses checked against the scans: v.6–7 · v.16 · v.23 · v.30–31 · v.34–35

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_14_king_ishukar.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 14: King Ishukara
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_14_king_ishukar.content:
Uttaradhyayan 14 · Ishukariya: King Ishukara
In one line: two boys wake to their past life and leave home, and their reasons, that the soul is real, life is short and only dharma protects, win over their father, their mother, the queen and at last the king, until all six reach liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 14 (53 verses), translated pages 327–354. 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Six souls meet again. In an earlier life six friends kept restraint (samyama) together and were reborn as gods in one heavenly dwelling. Four of them were born first in the city of Ishukara: King Ishukara, Queen Kamalavati, the priest Bhrigu and his wife Yasha. The other two came later as the priest’s two sons. The commentary tells how the parents, warned that the sons would become monks, taught them to fear monks; but the boys, hidden in a tree, watched a monk eat his simple food with care, remembered their past life, and turned to the path (v.1–5).
“Life is short; let us go.” Free of desire for human or divine pleasures, the sons ask their father’s leave: this life does not last, has many obstacles and is brief, so they find no joy at home (v.6–7).
The father argues from the Vedas. Men without sons, he says, reach no good state; first study the Vedas, feed the Brahmins, marry, hand the house to your sons, and only then go to the forest. Burning with grief, he offers them wealth and pleasures (v.8–11).
The sons answer point by point. Study of the Vedas does not protect; feeding Brahmins leads into darkness; sons are no refuge. Pleasures give a moment of happiness and long suffering, and a man chasing wealth for his kin meets old age and death still saying “this is done, that is still to do” (v.12–15). Wealth, family and pleasures have no part in dharma; they will become monks living on alms (v.16–17).
Is there a soul at all? The father says a living being appears in the body like fire in fire-sticks, ghee in milk or oil in sesame, and perishes with it. The sons reply: the soul is formless, so the senses cannot grasp it, and being formless it is eternal; its own inner faults bind it, and that bondage is the cause of worldly life (v.18–19).
The world is under attack. Death strikes the world, old age surrounds it, and the nights are arrows that never miss. Nights that pass never come back: fruitless for one who does wrong, fruitful for one who lives dharma (v.20–25).
“Not later: today.” The father asks them to stay together as lay followers and become monks in old age. The sons say only one who is friends with death, can run from it, or knows he will not die may put dharma off till tomorrow; nothing in this world is new to the soul, so they will take it up today (v.26–28).
The priest and his wife follow. Bhrigu says a tree without branches is a stump, and he is like a wingless bird without his sons. Yasha urges him to enjoy pleasures first; he answers that youth is passing and, as a snake leaves its old skin, the sons are leaving pleasures, so how can he stay behind? Yasha then sees her sons and husband breaking free like cranes and swans through a net, and decides to go too (v.29–36).
The queen wakes the king. When the king begins taking the priest’s abandoned wealth into his treasury, Queen Kamalavati tells him one who eats what was vomited is not praised; even the whole world’s wealth would not be enough nor protect him; dharma alone is a refuge at death. Like a bird in a cage she finds no joy, and with examples of a forest fire, a bird with a scrap of meat, and an elephant breaking its chains, she resolves to renounce (v.37–48).
All six are freed. The king and queen give up the kingdom, take up severe austerity, and all six, awakened one after another, reach the end of suffering in a short time (v.49–53).

Key verses
7 · Asking leave to go

असासयं दट्ठु इमं विहारं, बहुअंतरायं ण य दीहमाउं ।
तम्हा गिहंसि ण रइं लभामो, आमंतयामो चरिस्सामु मोणं ॥७॥

Seeing that this human life does not last, is full of obstacles, and is not long, we find no joy in the household. We ask your leave: we shall live the life of a monk.
12 · No protection in these

वेया अहीया ण हवंति ताणं, भुत्ता दिया णिंति तमं तमेणं ।
जाया य पुत्ता ण हवंति ताणं, को णाम ते अणुमण्णेज्ज एयं ॥१२॥

The Vedas, merely studied, do not protect. Brahmins who are fed lead one into deeper and deeper darkness. Sons who are born do not protect either. Who would accept what you say?
13 · What pleasures really give

खणमित्तसुक्खा बहुकालदुक्खा, पगामदुक्खा अणिगामसुक्खा ।
संसारमोक्खस्स विपक्खभूया, खाणी अणत्थाण उ कामभोगा ॥१३॥

Pleasures of the senses give a moment of happiness and a long time of suffering; much suffering and little happiness. They stand against freedom from worldly life, and they are a mine of harm.
27 · Who may say “tomorrow”

जस्सत्थि मच्चुणा सक्खं, जस्स वऽत्थि पलायणं ।
जो जाणे ण मरिस्सामि, सो हु कंखे सुए सिया ॥२७॥

Only one who is a friend of death, or who can run away from it, or who knows “I shall not die,” can wish to leave dharma for tomorrow.
38 · Eating what was vomited

वंतासी पुरिसो रायं, ण सो होइ पसंसिओ ।
माहणेण परिच्चत्तं, धणं आदाउमिच्छसि ॥३८॥

O king, a man who eats what has been vomited is not praised. Yet you wish to take the wealth the Brahmin has thrown away.
40 · Dharma alone is a refuge

मरिहिसि रायं जया तया वा, मणोरमे कामगुणे पहाय ।
इक्को हु धम्मो णरदेव ताणं, ण विज्जइ अण्णमिहेह किंचि ॥४०॥

O king, sooner or later you will die and leave these lovely pleasures behind. Then, lord of men, dharma alone is a refuge; nothing else here is.
Verses checked against the scans: v.7 · v.12 · v.13 · v.27 · v.38 · v.40

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_15_the_true_mon.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 15: The True Monk
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_15_the_true_mon.content:
Uttaradhyayan 15 · Sabhikshuka: The True Monk
In one line: begging does not make a monk. A true monk (bhikshu) lives for liberation alone: he wants no honour, bears every hardship calmly, earns nothing by magic or medicine, flatters no one, fears nothing, and wanders free and alone. Each verse ends with the same words, “he is a monk”.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 15 (16 verses), translated pages 355–367 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 8 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A monk is more than his robe. The introduction says a monk is not just someone who lives by begging. He works at knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity. Someone who gives up his restraint for comfort, position or fame is a monk “only in dress and name”. The phrase “he is a monk” (sa bhikkhu) is not there to judge who is a monk. It sets out the qualities a monk should live by (intro; commentary).
He starts by resolving to live as a muni. He thinks the dharma through and resolves, “I shall live the life of a muni.” He is straightforward and free of any wish for a reward (nidana). He gives up close ties with his relatives, wants no sense pleasures, and takes alms from homes that are not expecting him (v.1).
He clings to nothing. He does not eat or travel at night, keeps away from wrongdoing, knows the scriptures, guards his soul, sees all living beings as like himself, and is attached to nothing, living or non-living (v.2).
He bears hardship evenly. If someone abuses or beats him, he takes it as the fruit of his own past karma. He makes do with poor bedding and seats and bears cold, heat, flies and mosquitoes. Hardship does not upset him and comfort does not excite him (v.3–4).
He wants no honour. He does not want respect, worship or bows, much less praise. He is restrained, keeps his vows, does austerities and seeks the self (v.5). He also keeps away from any man or woman whose company would break his restraint, and he stays free of idle curiosity (v.6).
He does not earn his living with magic or medicine. He does not make a living from ten kinds of fortune-telling: reading cuts in cloth, sounds, the earth, the sky, dreams, body marks, staffs, buildings, twitching limbs, and animal and bird cries. He also gives up mantras, herbal roots, medical treatment, emetics, purges, nose-cleansing, bathing, and turning to householders for shelter when he is ill (v.7–8). The commentary explains each of these arts (pp. 364–366).
He flatters no one. He does not praise warriors, princes, Brahmins, chiefs or artisans. He does not build friendships for worldly gain with householders he knew before or after taking vows (v.9–10).
He does not mind what he is given. If a householder refuses him food, water, a bed or a seat, he does not feel even the slightest ill will. He does not praise the food he gets, in mind, speech or body. He does not look down on plain food such as rice-water, barley or sour gruel, and he goes for alms to ordinary homes too (v.11–13).
He is fearless and calm. He hears terrible sounds from gods, humans and animals and is not afraid. He knows the many doctrines in the world, yet stays steady and peaceful and hurts no living being (v.14–15).
He wanders alone. He has no trade, no home and no friends that bind him. He has conquered his senses, is free of every bond, and has only mild passions. He eats a little plain food, leaves his home, and wanders alone, both in body and at heart (v.16).

Key verses
1 · The resolve

मोणं चरिस्सामि समिच्च धम्मं, सहिए उज्जुकडे णियाणछिण्णे ।
संथवं जहिज्ज अकामकामे, अण्णायएसी परिव्वए स भिक्खू ॥१॥

Having thought the dharma through, he resolves, “I shall live the life of a muni.” He has right faith and the other virtues. He is straightforward and has cut off all wish for a reward. He gives up close ties with his relatives and wants no sense pleasures. He keeps wandering and takes alms from homes that are not expecting him. He is a monk.
3 · Abuse is the fruit of one’s own karma

अक्कोस वहं विइत्तु धीरे, मुणी चरे लाढे णिच्चमायगुत्ते ।
अव्वग्गमणे असंपहिट्ठे, जे कसिणं अहियासए स भिक्खू ॥३॥

When he is abused or beaten, the steady sage knows it as the fruit of his own actions. He wanders in suitable lands and always guards his soul. Neither upset nor elated, he bears every hardship evenly. He is a monk.
5 · No wish for honour

णो सक्कियमिच्छइ ण पूयं, णो वि य वंदणगं कुओ पसंसं ।
से संजए सुव्वए तवस्सी, सहिए आयगवेसए स भिक्खू ॥५॥

He does not want respect or worship, not even bows, and praise still less. He is restrained, keeps his vows, does austerities, has right knowledge, and seeks the self. He is a monk.
12 · No praise for the food he gets

जं किंचि आहारपाणगं, विविहं खाइमं साइमं परेसिं लद्धुं ।
जो तं तिविहेण णाणुकंपे, मण वय कायसुसंवुडे स भिक्खू ॥१२॥

Whatever food and drink, snacks and mouth-fresheners he gets from householders, he does not praise them, in mind, speech or body. He keeps mind, speech and body well guarded. He is a monk.
14 · Not afraid

सद्दा विविहा भवंति लोए, दिव्वा माणुस्सगा तहा तिरिच्छा ।
भीमा भयभेरवा उराला, जो सोच्चा ण विहिज्जइ स भिक्खू ॥१४॥

The world is full of sounds made by gods, humans and animals, some of them terrible, frightening and enormous. The one who hears them and is not afraid is a monk.
16 · Alone and free

असिप्पजीवी अगिहे अमित्ते, जिइंदिए सव्वओ विप्पमुक्के ।
अणुक्कसाई लहुअप्पभक्खी, चिच्चा गिहं एगचरे स भिक्खू ॥१६॥
त्ति बेमि ।

He does not live by a trade. He has no home and no friends or enemies. He has conquered his senses and is free of every bond. His passions are mild and he eats a little plain food. He has left home and wanders alone. He is a monk. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.3, v.5 · v.12, v.14 · v.16

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_16_supports_of_.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 16: The Supports of Celibacy
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_16_supports_of_.content:
Uttaradhyayan 16 · Brahmacharya Samadhisthan: The Supports of Celibacy
In one line: celibacy is the heart of a monk’s practice, and ten simple guards (where he lives, what he says, sees, hears, remembers, eats and wears, and how he treats the senses) keep it safe; the one who keeps it is honoured even by the gods and reaches liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 16 (12 prose sutras, then 17 verses), translated pages 368–390. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Celibacy holds up the whole practice. The introduction calls celibacy (brahmacharya) the backbone of a monk’s life: austerity, study, meditation and the rest “revolve around” it like planets round the sun. Rules alone do not finish the work, since the seeds of desire lie within; but they are watchful guards that keep the seeker from drifting (pp.368, 370).
The elders taught ten supports. Sudharma tells Jambu what he heard from the Lord: the elders gave ten supports for steadiness in celibacy (samadhi-sthana). Hearing them and taking them to heart, a monk grows in restraint (samyama), in stopping karma (samvara) and in calm, guards mind, speech and body, and lives always without carelessness (sutras 1–2).
Each support comes with a reason. The chapter first gives the ten in prose. Each says “one who does not do this is a nirgrantha”, asks “why?”, and the teacher gives the same answer each time: doubt, longing or wavering about celibacy may arise; the vow may break; he may lose his balance of mind, fall into long illness, or fall away from the dharma taught by the omniscient ones (sutras 3–12).
The ten supports in prose. (1) Live and sit in a secluded place, not one shared with women, animals or eunuchs. (2) Do not talk about women. (3) Do not sit on the same seat with women. (4) Do not gaze at and dwell on their charming features. (5) Do not listen to their sounds (singing, laughing, weeping, lamenting) from behind a wall or curtain. (6) Do not recall past pleasures and play from household life. (7) Do not eat rich food. (8) Do not eat or drink beyond measure. (9) Do not adorn the body, since an adorned monk becomes desirable to women. (10) Do not chase sound, form, taste, smell and touch (sutras 3–12).
The commentary spells out the harm. It lists seven steps of decline: doubt, then desire, then doubt about the fruit of celibacy, then breaking the vow, then mental frenzy, then illness, and finally falling from the faith altogether (pp.373–374).
The same ten in verse. The verses repeat the ten: a secluded, uncrowded lodging (v.1), no pleasing talk about women (v.2), no close acquaintance or frequent chat (v.3), no looking at their limbs and glances (v.4), no listening to their sounds (v.5), no recalling past laughter, play and pleasure (v.6), no rich food that quickly inflames desire (v.7), measured food, gained rightly, eaten at the right time, only to keep the disciplined life going (v.8), no adornment (v.9), and giving up the five kinds of sense pleasure (v.10).
Together they are swift poison. Verses 11–13 list the ten again as things to avoid and say they are like talaputa poison to a man seeking the self. The commentary explains that this poison kills as soon as it touches the palate (v.11–13).
Avoid every place of doubt. A wise monk always gives up hard-to-conquer pleasures and every situation that could put celibacy at risk, not only the ten named (v.14).
Live in the garden of dharma. Steady, a charioteer of dharma who also guides others, he walks and delights in the garden of dharma, senses tamed, settled in celibacy (v.15).
Gods bow to the celibate, and the path is eternal. Gods, demons, gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas and kinnaras all bow to the one who does this hard thing. This dharma is steady, lasting and eternal, taught by the Jina; by it beings have become perfected (siddha), are becoming so, and will become so (v.16–17).

Key verses
Sutra 1 · The ten supports were taught

सुयं मे आउसं ! तेणं भगवया एवमक्खायं इह खलु थेरेहिं भगवंतेहिं
दस बंभचेर समाहिठाणा पण्णत्ता, जे भिक्खू सोच्चा, णिसम्म, संजमबहुले,
संवरबहुले, समाहिबहुले, गुत्ते, गुत्तिंदिए, गुत्तबंभयारी सया अप्पमत्ते विहरेज्जा।

O long-lived one, I have heard the Blessed One say this: here the venerable elders have taught ten supports for steadiness in celibacy. Having heard them and taken them to heart, a monk should live full of restraint, of stopping karma and of calm; guarded in mind, speech and body, with senses guarded, his celibacy guarded, always free from carelessness.
Verse 1 · A secluded lodging

जं विवित्तमणाइण्णं, रहियं इत्थी जणेण य ।
बंभचेरस्स रक्खट्ठा, आलयं तु णिसेवए ॥१॥

To protect celibacy, a monk should live in a lodging that is secluded, not crowded, and free of women (and of animals and eunuchs).
Verse 13 · Like talaputa poison

गत्तभूसणमिट्ठं च, कामभोगा य दुज्जया ।
णरस्सऽत्त गवेसिस्स, विसं तालउडं जहा ॥१३॥

(Together with the things in verses 11–12:) adorning the body, pleasing sense objects, and sensual pleasures that are hard to conquer: to a man who seeks the self, all these are like talaputa poison.
Verse 15 · The garden of dharma

धम्मारामे चरे भिक्खू, धिइमं धम्मसारही ।
धम्मारामे रए दंते, बंभचेर समाहिए ॥१५॥

A steady monk, a charioteer of dharma, should walk in the garden of dharma. Delighting in that garden, senses tamed, he stays settled in celibacy.
Verse 16 · The gods bow

देव-दाणव-गंधव्वा, जक्ख-रक्खस-किण्णरा ।
बंभयारिं णमंसंति, दुक्करं जे करंति तं ॥१६॥

Gods, demons (danavas), gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas and kinnaras all bow to the celibate who does this difficult thing.
Verse 17 · An eternal path

एस धम्मे धुवे णिच्चे, सासए जिणदेसिए ।
सिद्धा सिज्झंति चाणेणं, सिज्झिस्संति तहावरे ॥१७॥
–त्ति बेमि ।

This dharma is steady, lasting and eternal, taught by the Jina. Through it beings have become perfected, are becoming perfected, and others too will become perfected. So I say.
Verses checked against the scans: sutra 1 · v.1 · v.13 · v.15, v.16 · v.17

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_17_the_bad_monk.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 17: The Bad Monk
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_17_the_bad_monk.content:
Uttaradhyayan 17 · Papashramaniya: The Bad Monk
In one line: a monk who takes his vows “like a lion” but then lives “like a jackal”, for comfort, sleep, tasty food and his own way, is called a bad monk (papa-shramana); the one who drops all these faults is honoured like nectar.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 17 (21 verses), translated pages 391–403 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 8 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Taking the vows is not the end of the work. Someone hears the dharma, gains the very rare gift of understanding, and becomes a monk, but afterwards lives just as he pleases. The commentary says he took initiation like a lion and then lives like a jackal (v.1).
“Why should I study?” The bad monk says: I have a safe place to stay, a cloth to cover me, food and drink; I can see what is happening now, so what will scripture do for me? (v.2).
Eat, drink, sleep. The one who sleeps a great deal and, after eating and drinking, sleeps in comfort “is called a bad monk”, the line that closes almost every verse of the chapter (v.3).
He turns on his teachers. He learned scripture and good conduct from the acharya and upadhyaya, then speaks ill of those same teachers. He does not serve them, forgets their kindness, and stays stiff with pride (v.4–5).
Carelessness in walking, sitting and checking. He walks over living beings, seeds and green plants and still thinks himself restrained. He sits on bedding, plank or stool without looking and brushing it first. He walks fast and heavily, breaks the rules and flares up when corrected. He checks his things carelessly while listening to talk, and answers his guru back (v.6–10). The commentary gives the guru-insulting reply: “You taught me this way yourself; the mistake is yours, not ours.”
The passions show in him. He is deceitful, talkative, proud, greedy, uncontrolled, does not share his food, and is unkind to fellow monks. He stirs up quarrels that had died down and spoils his own understanding with bad reasoning (v.11–12). The commentary sets this against the seven marks of a good monk: straight, sparing in speech, humble, content, master of the senses, sharing, devoted to the guru.
Restless in sitting and sleeping. He cannot sit still, fidgets, sits anywhere without care for the seat, and goes to bed with dusty feet without checking the bed (v.13–14).
Greed for food, no austerity. He keeps eating rich foods such as milk and curd (vigai) and has no taste for austerity (tapas). He eats all day until sunset, and when a guru urges him to change, he lectures the guru back: “Why don’t you do austerity yourself?” (v.15–16).
He cannot stay put. He leaves his acharya, goes over to another faith, and keeps changing groups and teachers. The commentary says this means moving to another group within six months, without permission and without a reason such as study (v.17).
He slides back into household life. He gives up his own home but busies himself in other people’s homes, tells omens, takes food only from his own relatives instead of begging from all homes, rich and poor (samudanika alms), and sits on householders’ seats (v.18–19).
The two endings. Such a one, only wearing the monk’s dress, falls into the five kinds of misconduct, is shunned in this world like poison, and is well in neither this world nor the next. The monk who always avoids these faults is honoured like nectar and succeeds in both worlds (v.20–21).

Key verses
2 · “What will I do with scripture?”

सेज्जा दढा पाउरणं मे अत्थि, उप्पज्जइ भोत्तुं तहेव पाउं ।
जाणामि जं वट्टइ आउसु त्ति, किं णाम काहामि सुएण भंते ॥२॥

“Revered sir, I have a safe place to stay and a cloth to cover me; food to eat and water to drink come to me. I know what is happening now. So what will I do by studying scripture?”
3 · Eat, drink and sleep

जे केइ उ पव्वइए, णिद्दासीले पगामसो ।
भोच्चा पेच्चा सुहं सुवइ, पावसमणे त्ति वुच्चइ ॥३॥

Whoever, after becoming a monk, takes to sleeping a great deal, and after eating and drinking sleeps at ease, is called a bad monk.
11 · The passions in a monk

बहुमाई पमुहरे, थद्धे लुद्धे अणिग्गहे ।
असंविभागी अचियत्ते, पावसमणे त्ति वुच्चइ ॥११॥

One who is very deceitful, talkative, proud, greedy and uncontrolled, who does not share his food and is unkind to fellow monks, is called a bad monk.
17 · The one who cannot stay

आयरिय परिच्चाई, परपासंड सेवए ।
गाणंगणिए दुब्भूए, पावसमणे त्ति वुच्चइ ॥१७॥

One who abandons his acharya, goes over to another faith, keeps changing groups and teachers, and lives a blameworthy life, is called a bad monk.
20 · Shunned like poison

एयारिसे पंचकुसीलसंवुडे, रूवंधरे मुणिपवराण हेट्ठिमे ।
अयंसि लोए विसमेव गरहिए, ण से इहं णेव परत्थ लोए ॥२०॥

Such a one, caught in the five kinds of misconduct and only wearing a monk’s dress, falls below the best of monks. In this world he is condemned like poison; it is well with him neither here nor in the next world.
21 · Honoured like nectar

जे वज्जए एए सया उ दोसे, से सुव्वए होइ मुणीण मज्झे ।
अयंसि लोए अमयं व पूइए, आराहए लोगमिणं तहा परं ॥२१॥
त्ति बेमि ।

The monk who always avoids these faults is a monk of good vows among monks. In this world he is honoured like nectar, and he succeeds in this world and the next. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.3 · v.11 · v.17 · v.20–21

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_18_king_sanjaya.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 18: King Sanjaya
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_18_king_sanjaya.content:
Uttaradhyayan 18 · Sanjayiya (Samyatiya): King Sanjaya
In one line: a hunting king meets a silent monk, learns that he too must give others the fearlessness he begged for, and renounces; a fellow monk then shows him that the great kings of old all won liberation by leaving one-sided views behind and walking the Jina’s path of knowledge and conduct.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 18 (54 verses), translated pages 404–440 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A king goes hunting. King Sanjaya of Kampilya rides out with his fourfold army of horses, elephants, chariots and foot soldiers. Greedy for the taste of meat, he drives the frightened, tired deer into the Kesara garden and shoots them down (v.1–3).
A monk sits in the middle of it. In a bower of creepers in that garden sits an ascetic monk, rich in austerity, absorbed in study and in meditation on dharma (dharma-dhyana). The commentary names him Gardabhali. The wounded deer fall near him (v.4–5).
The king is terrified of what he has done. Seeing the dead deer beside the monk, the king thinks: “How unlucky I am! Greedy for taste, I have hurt this monk’s heart.” He gets off his horse, bows at the monk’s feet and asks forgiveness. The monk stays silent in meditation, and the king grows more afraid, because he has heard that an angry monk can burn millions with his power. “I am King Sanjaya,” he says, “speak to me” (v.6–10).
The monk’s answer: fear nothing, and give fearlessness. “You have nothing to fear from me, O king. Now you too become a giver of fearlessness (abhaya) to other beings. In this passing world, why cling to violence, or to a kingdom you must one day leave behind? Life and beauty flicker like lightning” (v.11–13).
No one goes with you. Wife, sons, friends and relatives follow a man while he lives, but none follows him in death. Sons carry out a dead father, a father carries out dead sons; then others enjoy the wealth he gathered. Only his good and bad deeds go with him into the next life. “So, O king, practise austerity” (v.14–17).
Sanjaya renounces. Hearing this, the king is filled with longing for liberation (samvega) and turning away from the world (nirveda). He gives up his kingdom and is initiated into the Jina’s order under Gardabhali (v.18–19).
A second monk, the Kshatriya sage, meets him. A royal sage who had left his own kingdom sees Sanjaya and says, “As your face is calm, so your mind seems.” He asks his name, clan, why he became a monk, and how he serves his teacher. Sanjaya answers: name Sanjaya, clan Gautama, teacher Gardabhali, master of knowledge and conduct (v.20–22). The book notes the later verses are not clear about who says what; following the old commentator Shantyacharya, it takes v.23 onward as the Kshatriya sage teaching Sanjaya.
One-sided views are empty talk. There are four one-sided doctrines: action, non-action, mere humility, and ignorance. Mahavira, the truthful one, taught plainly that wrongdoers fall to hell and those who practise the noble dharma reach a divine state. The rest is deceit and empty words; the sage keeps himself restrained. He recalls his own past life as a god in the Brahma heaven, gives up fortune-telling and household dealings, and urges Sanjaya: hold to right action, drop false views, and with right vision practise the hard dharma (v.23–33).
The great kings who walked this path. The sage lists those who left power for restraint and reached liberation: the chakravartis Bharata, Sagara, Maghava, Sanatkumara, Shantinatha, Kunthu, Ara, Mahapadma, Harishena and Jaya; King Dasharnabhadra, humbled when Indra’s splendour outshone his own; the four self-awakened kings Karakandu, Dvimukha, Nami and Naggati, each woken by a small sight (a wasted bull, a fallen festival pole, a stripped mango tree); and Udayana, the king of Kashi, Vijaya and Mahabala (v.34–51). The commentary notes that two chakravartis, Subhuma and Brahmadatta, clung to pleasure and went to hell, and are not named here.
So why would a wise person wander after bad reasoning? These heroes took up the Jina’s distinctive teaching. This truth has carried beings across in the past, carries them now and will carry them in the future. Free of every attachment, the wise one becomes a siddha (v.52–54).

Key verses
11 · Be fearless, and give fearlessness

अभओ पत्थिवा तुब्भं, अभयदाया भवाहि य ।
अणिच्चे जीवलोगम्मि, किं हिंसाए पसज्जसि ॥११॥

O king, you are safe from me; now you too become a giver of safety to other beings. In this impermanent world of living beings, why are you so attached to violence?
13 · Like a flash of lightning

जीवियं चेव रूवं च, विज्जुसंपाय चंचलं ।
जत्थ तं मुज्झसि रायं, पेच्चत्थं णावबुज्झसे ॥१३॥

O king, this life and this beauty that you are so taken with are as fleeting as a flash of lightning. Why do you not think about your good in the next world?
14 · Only the living are followed

दाराणि य सुया चेव, मित्ता य तह बंधवा ।
जीवंतमणुजीवंति, मयं णाणुव्वयंति य ॥१४॥

Wives and sons, friends and relatives follow a person while he is alive, but no one follows him when he dies.
17 · Only deeds go along

तेणावि जं कयं कम्मं, सुहं वा जइ वा दुहं ।
कम्मुणा तेण संजुत्तो, गच्छइ उ परं भवं ॥१७॥

Whatever deeds he has done, bringing happiness or suffering, he goes on to the next life bound up with those deeds alone.
33 · Choose right action, practise the hard dharma

किरियं च रोयए धीरे, अकिरियं परिवज्जए ।
दिट्ठिए दिट्ठिसंपण्णे, धम्मं चर सुदुच्चरं ॥३३॥

The steadfast person takes delight in right action and turns away from the denial of it. With right vision, having gained true insight, practise this dharma that is so hard to practise.
54 · Free of every tie

कहं धीरे अहेऊहिं, अत्ताणं परियावसे ।
सव्वसंग विणिम्मुक्के, सिद्धे हवइ णीरए ॥५४॥

How could a wise person let his soul dwell among false reasons? Freed from every attachment and cleansed of karma, he becomes a siddha.
Verses checked against the scans: v.11 · v.13, v.14 · v.17 · v.33 · v.54
