09_modules/uttaradhyayan_19_mrigaputra.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 19: Mrigaputra
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_19_mrigaputra.content:
Uttaradhyayan 19 · Mrigaputriya: Mrigaputra
In one line: a pampered prince sees a monk, remembers that he was once a monk himself, and answers every warning his parents give about the hard monk’s life with the far worse pains he has already suffered in hell, until they let him go to live “like a deer” and he reaches liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 19 (99 verses), translated pages 441–479 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 20 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A prince who has everything. In the lovely city of Sugriva, King Balabhadra and Queen Mriga have a son, Balashri, known as Mrigaputra (“Mriga’s son”). He is the crown prince, dear to his parents, and he lives in a palace like a garden of the gods, always enjoying himself with his wives (v.1–3).
One look at a monk wakes him up. From a palace window he sees a monk walking along the road, a man of austerity, restraint and good character. Gazing at him without blinking, he thinks, “I have seen such a form before.” His mind becomes pure, delusion thins, and he remembers his past life: he came here from the world of the gods, and before that he had lived as a monk (v.4–9).
He asks to leave. Turning away from pleasures, he tells his parents: “I have known the five great vows, and the suffering of hell and animal life. I am tired of this great ocean. Let me become a monk” (v.10–11).
Why the world holds nothing for him. Pleasures are like poison fruit: sweet now, bitter later, and they keep suffering going. The body is impermanent and impure, a home of disease, a bubble that must burst sooner or later. Birth, old age, disease and death are all suffering. Fields, house, gold, wife, sons and this body must all be left behind (v.12–18).
Dharma is food for the journey. Whoever sets out on a long road without provisions suffers hunger and thirst; whoever goes to the next life without practising dharma suffers. Whoever takes provisions travels happily. When a house is on fire the owner saves the valuables and leaves the junk; in a world burning with old age and death, “I will save my soul, if you permit me” (v.19–24).
The parents: the monk’s life is too hard for you. A monk must keep thousands of virtues: equal regard for friend and enemy, no harm, no lies, not even a toothpick untaken, celibacy, owning nothing, no food at night; he must bear hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insects, abuse, beatings, begging and plucking out his hair. “You are delicate. It is like carrying a load of iron, swimming the ocean with your arms, eating a mouthful of sand, walking a sword’s edge, chewing iron grains, drinking a flame. Enjoy pleasures first, and practise dharma when you are old” (v.25–44).
Mrigaputra: nothing is hard for one without craving, and I have known worse. He agrees the path is hard, but for one free of thirst for this world nothing is hard. Then he describes, in a long vivid passage, the hell he has suffered countless times: heat and cold endlessly greater than any here; being boiled in pots, burned in sand, sawn, crushed like sugarcane, torn by beings in the form of dogs and pigs, yoked to a red-hot chariot, pecked by iron-beaked birds, cut by the razor waters of the Vaitarani and the sword-leaves of the forest, fed his own roasted flesh and made to drink molten metal because he had loved meat and liquor. “Not for the blink of an eye was there any comfort there” (v.45–75). The commentary explains that the tormentors are the paramadharmika asuras, who take these forms by their powers.
“Who treats the deer in the forest?” The parents give in, but ask: “As a monk you may not seek treatment when you fall ill.” He answers: when a deer falls sick in the forest, who gives it medicine, food or water? It rests under a tree, and when it recovers it goes and finds its own grass and water. “So I too will live the deer’s way (miga-chariya).” Like the deer, the monk wanders alone, lives in many places, lives on what he finds, and never scorns what he is given (v.76–84).
He goes, and lives as a true monk. With his parents’ blessing (“go, son, as you wish”) he drops all attachment as a snake sheds its skin, shaking off wealth, friends, wife, son and family like dust from a cloth. He keeps the five great vows, the five carefulnesses (samiti) and three guards (gupti); free of “mine” and of ego, he is even-minded in gain and loss, pleasure and pain, life and death, praise and blame, honour and insult (v.85–94).
The end, and the lesson. After practising knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity for many years, he ends his life with a month’s fast and reaches supreme liberation. The wise turn back from pleasures as the sage Mrigaputra did: knowing that wealth increases suffering and binds with fear, take up the yoke of dharma, which brings the joys of nirvana (v.95–99).

Key verses
16 · Birth is suffering

जम्मं दुक्खं जरा दुक्खं, रोगाणि मरणाणि य ।
अहो दुक्खो हु संसारो, जत्थ कीसंति जंतवो ॥१६॥

Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, and so are disease and death. Alas, the whole round of births (samsara) is suffering, where living beings are tormented.
20 · No provisions for the road

एवं धम्मं अकाऊणं, जो गच्छइ परं भवं ।
गच्छंतो सो दुही होइ, वाहीरोगेहिं पीडिओ ॥२०॥

In the same way, whoever goes on to the next life without having practised dharma suffers on the way, afflicted by sickness and disease.
45 · Nothing is hard for the one without craving

सो बिंतऽम्मा पियरो, एवमेयं जहा फुडं ।
इह लोए णिप्पिवासस्स, णत्थि किंचि वि दुक्करं ॥४५॥

He said, “Mother and father, it is just as you say, the monk’s life is hard. But for one who has no thirst for the things of this world, nothing at all is hard.”
78 · Like a deer in the forest

एगब्भूओ अरण्णे वा, जहा उ चरइ मिगो ।
एवं धम्मं चरिस्सामि, संजमेण तणेव य ॥७८॥

Just as a deer wanders alone in the forest, so I will live the dharma, by restraint and by austerity.
(As printed: तणेव. This is a misprint for तवेण, “by austerity”, as the book’s own word meanings show; the English follows the meaning.)
91 · Even-minded in all things

लाभालाभे सुहे दुक्खे, जीविए मरणे तहा ।
समो णिंदा पसंसासु, तहा माणावमाणओ ॥९१॥

He stayed the same in gain and loss, in pleasure and pain, in life and death, in blame and praise, and in honour and insult.
99 · Take up the yoke of dharma

वियाणिया दुक्खविवद्धणं धणं, ममत्तबंधं च महाभयावहं ।
सुहावहं धम्मधुरं अणुत्तरं, धारेज्ज णिव्वाण गुणावहं महं ॥९९॥

Knowing that wealth only increases suffering, and that the bond of “mine” brings great fear, take up the great, unsurpassed yoke of dharma, which brings happiness and the qualities of nirvana.
Verses checked against the scans: v.16 · v.20 · v.45 · v.78 · v.91 · v.99

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_20_the_great_ni.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 20: The Great Nirgrantha
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_20_the_great_ni.content:
Uttaradhyayan 20 · Mahanirgranthiya: The Great Nirgrantha
In one line: no wealth, family or doctor can protect us from suffering; only the soul that takes up restraint and keeps it truly has a protector, and a monk who lets his restraint slip becomes unprotected again.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 1, chapter 20 (60 verses), translated pages 480–507 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-1/). 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A teaching on what is real, how to practise, and where it leads. The chapter opens with homage to the Siddhas and the self-restrained, and promises a true teaching on the nature of things, on dharma, and on liberation (v.1).
A king meets a young monk. King Shrenik of Magadha, out on a walk in the Mandikukshi garden, sees a young, delicate monk deep in meditation under a tree. Amazed by his beauty, calm and detachment, he bows and asks why he became a monk at the age for pleasure (v.2–8).
“I had no protector.” The monk answers that he was without a protector (anatha) and found no friend to care for him. The king laughs and offers to be his protector, so that he can enjoy life among friends, “for human birth is rare” (v.9–11).
“You have none yourself.” The monk replies that the king, being without a protector himself, cannot protect anyone. The king, stunned, lists his horses, elephants, city, palace and power; the monk says he does not know what “protector” really means (v.12–17).
The monk’s story: no one could take the pain away. In Kaushambi, the son of a very rich man, he was struck in youth by burning pain in his eyes and body, like an enemy’s sharp weapon. The best healers gave fourfold treatment; his father would have given all his wealth; his mother, brothers and sisters tried; his wife wept at his side, did not eat or bathe, and never left him. None could free him from suffering: “this was my helplessness” (v.18–30).
The resolve, and the cure. Seeing that he would have to bear such pain again and again in endless worldly life, he resolved: if freed from this pain even once, he would become forgiving, self-controlled, free of harmful activity, and a homeless monk. He fell asleep; the pain faded through the night; next morning he took leave of his family and became a monk (v.31–34).
The soul is its own protector, friend and enemy. By taking initiation he became the protector of himself, of others, and of all moving and still beings. The soul itself is hell’s Vaitarani river and thorn tree, and also the wish-granting cow and the Nandana grove; it makes and unmakes its own joy and sorrow (v.35–37). The commentary: one who can protect himself and others has a protector; the means are to see that nothing outside can remove suffering, to reflect on karma, and to resolve on renunciation.
The second kind of helplessness: the slack monk. Some take the Nirgrantha path and then grow lax: they do not keep the great vows with care, are greedy for tastes, careless in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling things and disposing of waste, live off the monk’s dress, tell fortunes from marks, dreams and omens, and accept any food at all, “all-consuming like fire”. Such a one is an empty fist, a counterfeit coin, glass passing as a gem; his dharma, joined to sense-pleasure, kills like poison, a weapon held wrongly, or an untamed spirit. He loses both this world and the next (v.38–50).
Leave the bad path, walk the great one. The wise one who hears this abandons the way of the ill-conducted, keeps the highest restraint, stops the inflow of karma, destroys karma, and reaches the eternal, supreme place (v.51–53).
The king is won over. Shrenik says the monk has explained being without a protector exactly as it is; the monk’s human birth is truly fruitful and he truly has a protector and kin. He asks forgiveness for disturbing his meditation and tempting him with pleasures, and with his household and kin becomes devoted to the dharma. The monk wanders on, free as a bird, rid of delusion (v.54–60).

Key verses
12 · “You are without a protector yourself”

अप्पणा वि अणाहो सि, सेणिया मगहाहिवा ।
अप्पणा अणाहो संतो, कहं णाहो भविस्ससि ॥

O Shrenik, lord of Magadha, you yourself are without a protector. Being without a protector yourself, how can you be anyone else’s protector?
32 · The resolve in the night

सइं च जइ मुच्चेज्जा, वेयणा विउला इओ ।
खंतो दंतो णिरारंभो, पव्वइए अणगारियं ॥

If I am freed even once from this terrible pain, I will become forgiving, master of my senses, free of harmful activity, and take up the homeless life.
35 · Protector of all beings

तओऽहं णाहो जाओ, अप्पणो य परस्स य ।
सव्वेसिं चेव भूयाणं, तसाणं थावराण य ॥

Then I became a protector: of myself and of others, and of all living beings, moving and still.
36 · The soul is hell and heaven to itself

अप्पा णई वेयरणी, अप्पा मे कूडसामली ।
अप्पा कामदुहा धेणू, अप्पा मे णंदणं वणं ॥

The soul itself is my Vaitarani river and my Kutasalmali tree (the torments of hell); the soul itself is the wish-granting cow and my Nandana grove.
37 · The soul is its own friend and enemy

अप्पा कत्ता विकत्ता य, दुहाण य सुहाण य ।
अप्पा मित्तममित्तं च, दुप्पट्ठिय-सुपट्ठिओ ॥

The soul itself makes and unmakes its sorrows and joys. The soul set on the right path is its own friend; set on the wrong path, its own enemy.
48 · Worse than an enemy with a knife

ण तं अरी कंठछेत्ता करेइ, जं से करे अप्पणिया दुरप्पा ।
से णाहइ मच्चुमुहं तु पत्ते, पच्छाणुतावेण दयाविहूणो ॥

An enemy who cuts one’s throat cannot do the harm that one’s own soul does when it goes wrong. The one without compassion realises this only at the mouth of death, in regret.
Verses checked against the scans: v.12 · v.32 (translation’s सईं corrected to सइं) · v.35–37 (v.35: सव्वेसिं, भूयाणं, तसाणं restored) · v.48

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_21_samudrapala.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 21: Samudrapala
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_21_samudrapala.content:
Uttaradhyayan 21 · Samudrapaliya: Samudrapala
In one line: a rich young merchant sees a condemned man led to execution, understands that every bad deed bears its fruit, becomes a monk, bears every hardship with an even mind, and crosses the ocean of birth and death.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 21 (24 verses), translated pages 55–65 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 7 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

A layman who knew the teaching. Palita, a merchant of Champa and a lay disciple (shravaka) of Lord Mahavira, was learned in the Nirgrantha teaching. Trading by ship, he came to the city of Pihunda, where a merchant gave him his daughter in marriage (v.1–3).
A child born at sea. Sailing home with his pregnant wife, she gave birth on the sea, so the boy was named Samudrapala (“guarded by the sea”). He grew up happily in Champa, learned the seventy-two arts, became skilled in conduct of affairs, handsome and pleasing to all; his father married him to the beautiful Rupini, and he lived in a lovely palace like a carefree god (v.4–7).
One sight at the window. One day, sitting at his palace window, he saw a condemned man, dressed in the marks of execution, being led to the place of death. The commentary describes the custom: red sandal paste, a garland of red oleander, a donkey, and the crime cried aloud (v.8).
“This is how bad karma ends.” Shaken, he said: “Ah, this is the bitter result of bad deeds.” Right there he woke up, felt a deep longing for liberation (samvega), took his parents’ leave, and became a homeless monk (v.9–10). The commentary adds that he remembered his past births.
What a monk lets go of and takes up. He gave up all clinging to possessions and kin, which brings great pain, great delusion and fear; he took the five great vows (non-violence, truth, not stealing, celibacy, non-possession) and lived the dharma taught by the Jina, kind to all beings, forgiving, with his senses in hand (v.11–13).
How he wandered. At the right time, knowing his own strength; unafraid of frightening sounds, like a lion; answering harsh words with no harsh word; bearing pleasant and unpleasant alike; wanting nothing everywhere; untouched by honour or blame (v.14–15).
Hardships do not break him. People have countless moods and opinions; fearful trials come from gods, humans and animals. Where many cowards go slack, he stays like a royal elephant at the front of battle. Cold, heat, gnats and mosquitoes, illness: he bears them without complaint, and so burns away old karma (v.16–18).
Steady as Mount Meru. Dropping attachment, aversion and delusion, unshaken like Meru in the wind, not lifted by praise nor cast down by blame, straightforward, he takes the road to nirvana. He keeps away from close ties with householders, owns nothing, calls nothing “mine”, and lives in quiet, uncrowded places used by the great sages (v.19–22).
He shines, and is free. With true knowledge and the highest virtues he shone like the sun in the sky. Destroying both kinds of karma, merit and demerit, free of all bonds, he crossed the great ocean of rebirth and went to the state from which there is no return (v.23–24).

Key verses
9 · The window moment

तं पासिऊण संविग्गो, समुद्दपालो इणमब्बवी ।
अहो असुभाणं कम्माणं, णिज्जाणं पावगं इमं ॥

Seeing him, Samudrapala was stirred with longing for freedom and said: “Ah! This is the bitter end of bad deeds.”
12 · The five great vows

अहिंस सच्चं च अतेणगं च, तत्तो य बंभं अपरिग्गहं च ।
पडिवज्जिया पंच महव्वयाणि, चरिज्ज धम्मं जिणदेसियं विदू ॥

Taking up the five great vows (non-violence, truth, not stealing, then celibacy and non-possession), the wise monk lived the dharma taught by the Jina.
17 · Like an elephant at the front of battle

परीसहा दुव्विसहा अणेगे, सीयंति जत्थ बहु कायरा णरा ।
से तत्थ पत्ते ण वहिज्ज भिक्खू, संगामसीसे इव णागराया ॥

Many hardships are hard to bear, and there many cowardly men go slack. When they come, the monk is not shaken, like a royal elephant at the head of the battle.
19 · Unshaken like Meru

पहाय रागं च तहेव दोसं, मोहं च भिक्खू सययं वियक्खणो ।
मेरुव्व वाएण अकंपमाणो, परीसहे आयगुत्ते सहेज्जा ॥

Always giving up attachment, aversion and delusion, the wise monk, unshaken like Mount Meru in the wind and guarding himself, should bear hardships.
20 · Neither raised by praise nor lowered by blame

अणुण्णए णावणए महेसी, ण यावि पूयं गरहं च संजए ।
स उज्जुभावं पडिवज्ज संजए, णिव्वाणमग्गं विरए उवेइ ॥

The great sage is not puffed up by honour or cast down by blame, and seeks neither. Taking up straightforwardness and turning away from pleasures, the restrained one reaches the path to nirvana.
24 · Across the ocean

दुविहं खवेऊण य पुण्णपावं, णिरंगणे सव्वओ विप्पमुक्के ।
तरित्ता समुद्दं च महाभवोघं, समुद्दपाले अपुणागमं गए ॥

Destroying both kinds of karma, merit and demerit, stainless and freed from every bond, Samudrapala crossed the ocean, the great flood of rebirth, and reached the state of no return.
Verses checked against the scans: v.9 (translation’s समुदपालो, असुहाणं corrected to समुद्दपालो, असुभाणं) · v.12 (अतेणं, ततो corrected to अतेणगं, तत्तो) · v.17 (बहू corrected to बहु) · v.19–20 · v.24 (समुंदं, समुद्धपाले corrected to समुद्दं, समुद्दपाले)

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_22_rathanemi.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 22: Rathanemi
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_22_rathanemi.content:
Uttaradhyayan 22 · Rathanemiya: Rathanemi
In one line: Prince Arishtanemi turns back from his own wedding out of compassion for the animals penned up for the feast; Rajemati follows him into renunciation, and later, alone in a cave, her firm words bring the wavering monk Rathanemi back to restraint.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 22 (51 verses), translated pages 66–85 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 13 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Two royal families. In Shauryapura ruled two brothers. Vasudeva had two queens, Rohini and Devaki, and two sons, Rama (Baladeva) and Keshava (Krishna). Samudravijaya and his queen Shiva had the renowned Arishtanemi, master of his senses, dark-skinned, of the Gautama clan, with a sweet voice and the 1,008 auspicious marks (v.1–5).
The match with Rajemati. Krishna asked King Ugrasena for his daughter Rajemati, virtuous, beautiful and bright as lightning, as a bride for Arishtanemi. Ugrasena agreed on one condition: the prince must come to his house as a bridegroom (v.6–8). The commentary adds why Krishna wanted him married: Arishtanemi had blown Krishna’s conch and outdone him in strength.
The wedding procession. Bathed in herbal water, dressed in a divine pair of garments and decked with ornaments, Arishtanemi rode Krishna’s great scent-elephant like a crest-jewel, under a raised parasol and waving whisks, with the ten Dasharha brothers, a fourfold army and music filling the sky (v.9–13).
The cries in the pens. On the way he saw terrified animals and birds shut in pens and cages, near death, kept to be eaten. He asked the charioteer why these creatures, who all want happiness, were shut in. “To feed the many guests at your wedding.” (v.14–17)
His compassion decides. Moved by compassion for living beings, he thought: “If so many beings are killed because of me, it will not be good for me in the next world.” He gave his earrings, waist-cord and all his ornaments to the charioteer (v.18–20). The commentary says he had the animals freed.
His renunciation. The gods came to celebrate. In a palanquin he left Dwaraka for Mount Raivataka; in the garden, under the Chitra star, with a thousand others, he took initiation and pulled out his fragrant hair in five handfuls. Krishna and the others blessed him: may you soon reach your goal and grow in knowledge, faith, conduct, austerity, forgiveness and freedom from greed (v.21–27).
Rajemati’s renunciation. Hearing it, Rajemati lost all laughter and joy and fainted with grief. Then she thought: “Shame on my life, since he has left me; it is better for me to renounce.” She pulled out her own hair; Krishna blessed her to cross the terrible ocean of worldly life quickly; and as a nun, learned and virtuous, she brought many of her kin into renunciation (v.28–32).
The cave. On the way to Mount Raivataka she was soaked by rain and, in the dark, took shelter in a cave. As she spread her clothes to dry, the monk Rathanemi, Arishtanemi’s brother, who was meditating there, saw her and his mind was shaken; she saw him only afterwards, and sat trembling, covering herself with her arms (v.33–35).
Rathanemi’s offer. He said: “I am Rathanemi; accept me, you will come to no harm. Human birth is rare; let us enjoy pleasures, and afterwards we will follow the Jina’s path.” (v.36–38)
Rajemati’s answer. Calm, she covered herself and, guarding her birth, family and virtue, said: “Even if you were Vaishramana in looks, Nalakubara in charm, or Indra himself, I would not want you. A snake of the Agandhana kind would rather enter a blazing fire than take back the poison it has spat out. Shame on you, that you want to swallow again what you have vomited out; death would be better. We are born of noble families; be steady in restraint. If you lose your heart to every woman you see, you will be like a rootless reed in the wind; like a cowherd who does not own the cows, you will not own your monkhood. Master anger, pride, deceit and greed, and your senses, and bring yourself under control.” (v.39–47)
He is brought back. Hearing her well-spoken words, he was set firm in dharma like an elephant turned by the goad. Guarded in mind, speech and body, he kept his monkhood unshaken all his life. Both did fierce austerities, became omniscient (kevali), destroyed all karma and reached liberation. The wise turn from pleasures, as did “that best of men” (v.48–51). The commentary: Rathanemi wavered in mind and speech but not in body, and never lost his faith, which is why he is still called “best of men”.

Key verses
16 · “Why are they shut in?”

कस्स अट्ठा इमे पाणा, एए सव्वे सुहेसिणो ।
वाडेहिं पंजरेहिं च, सण्णिरुद्धा य अच्छहि ॥

For whose sake are all these creatures, who all want happiness, kept shut in pens and cages?
19 · “Not because of me”

जइ मज्झ कारणा एए, हम्मंति सुबहू जिया ।
ण मे एयं तु णिस्सेसं, परलोगे भविस्सइ ॥

If so many living beings are to be killed because of me, this will not be for my good in the next world.
42 · The proud snake

पक्खंदे जलियं जोइं, धूमकेउं दुरासयं ।
णेच्छंति वंतयं भोत्तुं, कुले जाया अगंधणे ॥

Snakes born in the Agandhana family will leap into a blazing, smoking, unbearable fire, but will not take back the poison they have spat out.
43 · “Death would be better”

धिरत्थु ते जसोकामी, जो तं जीवियकारणा ।
वंतं इच्छसि आवेउं, सेयं ते मरणं भवे ॥

Shame on you, seeker of renown (the word can also mean “seeker of disgrace”), who for the sake of this life want to drink again what you have vomited out. It would be better for you to die.
48 · The elephant and the goad

तीसे सो वयणं सोच्चा, संजयाए सुभासियं ।
अंकुसेण जहा णागो, धम्मे संपडिवाइओ ॥

Hearing the well-spoken words of that nun, he was brought back to dharma, as an elephant is by the goad.
51 · How the wise act

एवं करेंति संबुद्धा, पंडिया पवियक्खणा ।
विणियट्टंति भोगेसु, जहा से पुरिसुत्तमो ॥

So do the awakened, the wise and the discerning: they turn away from pleasures, as did that best of men.
Verses checked against the scans: v.16 (translation’s पंजरहिं, सणिरुद्धा corrected to पंजरेहिं, सण्णिरुद्धा) · v.19 (सुब्बहू corrected to सुबहू) · v.42 (णेच्छति corrected to णेच्छंति) · v.43 (सेय corrected to सेयं) · v.48 (संजया, नागो, संपडिबोहिओ corrected to संजयाए, णागो, संपडिवाइओ) · v.51

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_23_keshi_and_ga.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 23: Keshi and Gautama
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_23_keshi_and_ga.content:
Uttaradhyayan 23 · Keshi-Gautamiya: Keshi and Gautama
In one line: two great monks, one from Parshvanatha’s line and one from Mahavira’s, meet to settle why their rules differ; through twelve questions they show that the goal is one, the outer rules suit different people, and the real path is inner: conquering the mind, cutting craving, cooling the passions.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 23 (89 verses), translated pages 86–117 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Two teachers in one city. Keshi Kumara, a renowned monk in the line of Parshva (the 23rd Tirthankara), with three kinds of knowledge, came to Shravasti and stayed in the Tinduka garden. Gautama, Mahavira’s chief disciple, knower of the twelve Angas, came to the same city and stayed in the Koshthaka garden (v.1–9).
The disciples’ doubt. Seeing each other on alms rounds, both groups wondered: Parshva taught four great vows (chaujjama), Vardhamana five; Mahavira’s monks wear plain, limited white cloth (achelaka), Parshva’s may wear any cloth (santaruttara). If the aim is the same, why the difference? (v.10–13)
Courtesy first. Knowing their disciples’ minds, the two decided to meet. Gautama, honouring the older lineage, went to Keshi; Keshi welcomed him and offered him clean straw and kusha grass to sit on. Seated, they shone like moon and sun, while curious people, followers of other creeds, thousands of householders, and unseen gods gathered (v.14–20). The commentary calls this setting aside sectarian insistence the heart of the Jina’s teaching.
Four vows or five: it depends on the people. Wisdom examines dharma. The first Tirthankara’s monks were straight but slow, the last one’s are crooked and slow, the middle ones’ were straight and wise; so the rule was hard to understand for the first, hard to keep for the last, easy for the middle. That is why dharma was taught in two ways (v.21–28). Parshva’s monks counted celibacy within non-possession.
Dress is a means, not the goal. Outer marks and implements were set by the omniscient for people’s trust, to support the life of restraint, and so the monk remembers “I am a monk”. In truth, the real means of liberation are knowledge, faith and conduct, and on this both Tirthankaras agree (v.29–34).
Then ten more questions, each a riddle with an inner answer. Each time Keshi says “well said, Gautama, your wisdom is fine; I have another doubt”.

Enemies: the one unconquered self, then the four passions and the five senses; conquer one and you conquer five, then ten, then all (v.35–39).
Snares: intense attachment, aversion and the bonds of affection, cut by the right method (v.40–44).
The creeper in the heart: craving for worldly life, which bears poisonous fruit, pulled up by the root (v.45–49).
The fire inside the body: the passions, put out by the water of scripture, good conduct and austerity, which comes from the great cloud, the Tirthankara (v.50–54).
The wild horse: the mind, held by the reins of scripture and trained by dharma (v.55–59).
Wrong roads: all false teachings are wrong roads; the path told by the Jina is the right one (v.60–64).


The island and the boat. For beings swept along by the flood of old age and death, dharma is the island, the support, the goal and the best refuge. The body is the boat, the soul the sailor, worldly life the ocean; a leaking boat (one that lets in karma) sinks, a sound one reaches the far shore (v.65–74).
The sun and the safe place. The sun that lights up a world in darkness is the omniscient Jina. The safe, blissful, untroubled place for beings in bodily and mental pain is at the top of the universe, hard to climb to, with no old age, death, illness or pain: nirvana, siddhi; those who reach it grieve no more (v.75–84).
Keshi joins Mahavira’s order. Keshi bowed to Gautama as “beyond doubt, an ocean of all scripture”, and from the earlier Tirthankara’s order entered the later one, taking the five great vows. The meeting raised learning and conduct, settled matters of great weight, and the whole assembly turned to the right path (v.85–89).

Key verses
25 · Wisdom examines dharma

तओ केसिं बुवंतं तु, गोयमो इणमब्बवी ।
पण्णा समिक्खए धम्मं, तत्तं तत्तविणिच्छियं ॥

Then Gautama said to Keshi: it is wisdom that examines dharma, the truth in which the realities are settled.
26 · Three kinds of disciples

पुरिमा उज्जुजडा उ, वंकजडा य पच्छिमा ।
मज्झिमा उज्जुपण्णा उ, तेण धम्मे दुहा कए ॥

The first Tirthankara’s monks were straight but slow, the last one’s crooked and slow, the middle ones’ straight and wise; that is why dharma was taught in two ways.
38 · The real enemy

एगप्पा अजिए सत्तू, कसाया इंदियाणि य ।
ते जिणित्तु जहाणायं, विहरामि अहं मुणी ॥

The one self, unconquered, is the enemy; so are the passions and the senses. Having conquered them in the right way, O sage, I live freely.
58 · The mind is a wild horse

मणो साहस्सिओ भीमो, दुट्ठस्सो परिधावइ ।
तं सम्मं तु णिगिण्हामि, धम्मसिक्खाए कंथगं ॥

The mind is a rash, fearsome, wicked horse that runs everywhere. I hold it well in check, and by the training of dharma it becomes a noble horse.
68 · Dharma is the island

जरामरणवेगेण, वुज्झमाणाण पाणिणं ।
धम्मो दीवो पइट्ठा य, गई सरणमुत्तमं ॥

For beings swept away by the flood of old age and death, dharma is the island, the firm ground, the goal and the highest refuge.
73 · Body, sailor, ocean

सरीरमाहु णावत्ति, जीवो वुच्चइ णाविओ ।
संसारो अण्णवो वुत्तो, जं तरंति महेसिणो ॥

The body is called the boat, the soul the sailor, and worldly life the ocean, which the great sages cross.
Verses checked against the scans: v.25–26 (v.25: translation’s तंतं तत्तविणिच्छयं corrected to तत्तं तत्तविणिच्छियं) · v.38 (जहाणाय, अह मुणि corrected to जहाणायं, अहं मुणी) · v.58 (दुद्दसो corrected to दुट्ठस्सो) · v.68 · v.73

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_24_mothers_of_t.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 24: Mothers of the Teaching
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_24_mothers_of_t.content:
Uttaradhyayan 24 · Pravachanamata: Mothers of the Teaching
In one line: the whole of a monk’s life rests on eight “mothers”: five kinds of careful action (samiti) in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling things and disposing of waste, and three restraints (gupti) of mind, speech and body; whoever keeps them well is soon free.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 24 (27 verses), translated pages 118–131 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 8 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Eight mothers. The mothers of the teaching (pravachana-mata) are five careful actions and three restraints (v.1–2). The commentary: like a mother caring for her child, they protect the practitioner; the Tirthankaras became omniscient by keeping them and only then taught the twelve Angas.
The whole teaching fits inside them. These eight, stated briefly, contain the Jina’s entire twelve-part teaching (v.3). Samiti and gupti are conduct, and conduct already rests on knowledge and faith.
Careful walking (irya samiti), pure in four ways. Its support is knowledge, faith and conduct; its time is daytime; its path avoids wrong paths; and its care is fourfold: watch living beings with the eyes, look a yoke’s length (about three and a half cubits) ahead, walk only while it is day, and walk attentively (v.4–7).
Walk with the mind on walking. Leave aside the sense-objects and even the five kinds of study; make walking itself your whole attention (v.8). The commentary: study is excellent, but while walking it divides attention.
Careful speech (bhasha samiti). Stay watchful of anger, pride, deceit, greed, laughter, fear, chatter and idle talk. Giving up these eight, the wise monk speaks blameless, measured words at the right time (v.9–10). The commentary: words spoken in any agitation are faulty, so do not speak under a passion.
Careful seeking (eshana samiti). For food, requisites and lodging, keep three stages pure: searching, receiving and using, avoiding the faults of origin and production, the faults of acceptance, and the four faults of eating (v.11–12).
Careful handling (adana samiti). Whether everyday things or things taken for a special need, look at them with the eyes and clean them gently before picking them up or putting them down (v.13–14).
Careful disposal. Waste, urine, phlegm, unwanted food, worn-out things, even a dead body: put them down only on ground that no one passes or watches, that harms no one, is level, not hollow, recently made lifeless, wide enough, lifeless deep down, away from villages and gardens, and free of burrows, creatures and seeds (v.15–18). The commentary notes the care this shows for others, for hygiene and for the good name of dharma.
The three restraints. The mind is restrained in all four of its modes (true, false, mixed, neither), and turned back whenever it plans harm, gathers the means for it, or begins it (samrambha, samarambha, arambha). Speech is restrained the same way. The body is restrained in standing, sitting, lying down, crossing over ground, and in the use of the senses (v.19–25).
Samiti and gupti differ. The careful actions are for going about right conduct; the restraints are for turning fully away from what is harmful (v.26). The commentary calls them two sides of one coin: samiti tells you how to act, gupti tells you what to stop.
The fruit. The wise monk who keeps these mothers of the teaching well is quickly freed from the whole round of birth and death (v.27).

Key verses
1 · Eight mothers

अट्ठ पवयणमायाओ, समिई गुत्ती तहेव य ।
पंचेव य समिईओ, तओ गुत्तीउ आहिया ॥

The eight mothers of the teaching are the careful actions and the restraints: five careful actions and three restraints, it is said.
2 · Their names

ईरिया भासेसणादाणे, उच्चारे समिई इय ।
मणगुत्ती वयगुत्ती, कायगुत्ती य अट्ठमा ॥

Care in walking, speaking, seeking, picking up and putting down, and in disposal: these are the careful actions. Restraint of mind, restraint of speech, and restraint of body, the eighth.
7 · Fourfold care in walking

दव्वओ चक्खुसा पेहे, जुगमित्तं च खेत्तओ ।
कालओ जाव रीएज्जा, उवउत्ते य भावओ ॥

As to things, watch with the eyes; as to place, a yoke’s length ahead; as to time, walk only while it is day; as to the mind, walk with full attention.
10 · Measured, blameless speech

एयाइं अट्ठ ठाणाइं, परिवज्जित्तु संजए ।
असावज्जं मियं काले, भासं भासिज्ज पण्णवं ॥

Giving up these eight (anger, pride, deceit, greed, laughter, fear, chatter, idle talk), the wise and restrained monk should speak blameless, measured words at the right time.
26 · How samiti and gupti differ

एयाओ पंच समिईओ, चरणस्स य पवत्तणे ।
गुत्ती णियत्तणे वुत्ता, असुभत्थेसु सव्वसो ॥

These five careful actions are for carrying out right conduct; the restraints are for turning back completely from everything harmful.
27 · Quickly free

एसा पवयणमाया, जे सम्मं आयरे मुणी ।
सो खिप्पं सव्वसंसारा, विप्पमुच्चइ पंडिए ॥

The wise monk who keeps these mothers of the teaching well is quickly released from all of worldly existence.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1–2 (v.2’s first line is missing in the translation and was read from the scan) · v.7 · v.10 (translation’s पण्डवं corrected to पण्णवं) · v.26 · v.27

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_25_the_true_bra.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 25: The True Brahmin
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_25_the_true_bra.content:
Uttaradhyayan 25 · Yajniya: The True Brahmin
In one line: a monk turned away from his brother’s sacrificial hall answers with a teaching, not anger: a true brahmin is made by inner qualities and deeds, not by birth or ritual, and the real sacrifice is restraint; the brother is won over and both reach liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 25 (45 verses), translated pages 132–150 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 11 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Two brothers, two kinds of sacrifice. Jayaghosha, born a brahmin, had become a monk who performed the “sacrifice of restraint” (yama-yajna). Wandering, he came to a garden outside Varanasi. In the city his brother Vijayaghosha, learned in the Vedas, was performing a sacrifice (v.1–4). The introduction tells what turned Jayaghosha: at the Ganga he saw a snake eating a frog, a peacock eating the snake, a hunter aiming at the peacock and a lion leaping at the hunter, and he saw that every creature is someone’s next meal.
Refused at the door. On the day he broke a month-long fast, Jayaghosha came to the sacrificial hall for alms. Vijayaghosha refused: this rich food is only for brahmins who know the Vedas, perform sacrifices, know astrology and the scriptures, and can lift up themselves and others (v.5–8).
Neither angry nor pleased. The monk, seeking only the highest good, felt neither anger nor pleasure (v.9). Not for food or water or a living, but to free his brother from wrong belief, he asked: do you know what is foremost in the Vedas, in sacrifice, among the stars, and in religion? Do you know who can lift up themselves and others? (v.10–12)
The answers. Unable to reply, Vijayaghosha and his assembly asked with joined hands. The monk said: the fire-offering (agnihotra) is foremost in the Vedas, the sacrificer in sacrifice, the moon among the stars, and Kashyapa (Mahavira) among religions; as stars bow to the moon, gods bow to him. Those who only talk of sacrifice do not know true learning; they are like fire covered by ashes, calm outside and burning within (v.13–18).
“Him we call a brahmin.” A long refrain describes the true brahmin: honoured like fire; not clinging when people come or grieving when they go; pure as gold refined in fire, free of attachment, aversion and fear; lean with austerity, self-controlled, at peace; harming no being, moving or still; never lying from anger, laughter, greed or fear; taking nothing not given; chaste in mind, speech and body; untouched by pleasures like a lotus in water; free of greed, owning nothing, living on alms given freely, apart from householders; not attached to old ties or pleasures (v.19–29).
Ritual cannot save. The Vedas that call for animal killing and sacrifices tied to sinful acts cannot protect the wrongdoer, because karma is strong (v.30). The commentary: “karma follows the doer alone.”
Inner qualities, not outer marks. A shaven head does not make a shramana, saying “Om” does not make a brahmin, living in the forest does not make a sage, bark clothes do not make an ascetic. Equanimity, celibacy, knowledge and austerity do (v.31–32).
By deeds, not birth. One becomes a brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya or shudra by one’s actions (v.33). Whoever lives these qualities, taught by the awakened ones, and is freed from all karma is the true brahmin; such people can lift up themselves and others (v.34–35).
The brother is won. His doubt cleared, Vijayaghosha recognised the monk as his brother and said: you are the true sacrificer, knower of the Vedas and of dharma; please accept alms (v.36–39).
“I need no alms; leave the world quickly.” The monk replied that he needed no alms; his brother should renounce quickly and not wander in the ocean of rebirth. Pleasures make karma stick; a wet clay ball sticks to the wall, a dry one does not (v.40–43). Vijayaghosha became a monk, and through restraint and austerity both brothers destroyed their karma and reached liberation (v.44–45).

Key verses
27 · Like a lotus in water

जहा पोमं जले जायं, णोवलिप्पइ वारिणा ।
एवं अलित्तं कामेहिं, तं वयं बूम माहणं ॥

As a lotus born in water is not wetted by the water, so one untouched by pleasures: him we call a brahmin.
31 · Outer marks do not make it

ण वि मुंडिएण समणो, ण ओंकारेण बंभणो ।
ण मुणी रण्णवासेणं, कुसचीरेण ण तावसो ॥

A shaven head does not make a shramana, nor the sound “Om” a brahmin; living in the forest does not make a sage, nor clothes of bark an ascetic.
32 · Inner qualities do

समयाए समणो होइ, बंभचेरेण बंभणो ।
णाणेण य मुणी होइ, तवेण होइ तावसो ॥

By equanimity one becomes a shramana, by celibacy a brahmin, by knowledge a sage, by austerity an ascetic.
33 · By deeds, not birth

कम्मुणा बंभणो होइ, कम्मुणा होइ खत्तिओ ।
वइस्सो कम्मुणा होइ, सुद्दो हवइ कम्मुणा ॥

By one’s actions one is a brahmin, by actions a kshatriya, by actions a vaishya, and by actions a shudra.
42 · Two clay balls

उल्लो सुक्को य दो छूढा, गोलया मट्टियामया ।
दो वि आवडिया कुड्डे, जो उल्लो सोत्थ लग्गइ ॥

Two balls of clay, one wet and one dry, are thrown at a wall. Both hit it; the wet one sticks.
43 · The dry ball does not stick

एवं लग्गंति दुम्मेहा, जे णरा कामलालसा ।
विरत्ता उ ण लग्गंति, जहा से सुक्कगोलए ॥

So the foolish, who crave pleasures, get stuck; the detached do not stick, like the dry ball.
Verses checked against the scans: v.27 · v.31 (translation’s रन्नवासेणं corrected to रण्णवासेणं) · v.32 · v.33 (हवे corrected to हवइ) · v.42–43 (v.43: लग्गति corrected to लग्गंति, twice)

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_26_proper_condu.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 26: Proper Conduct
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_26_proper_condu.content:
Uttaradhyayan 26 · Samachari: Proper Conduct
In one line: a monk’s whole day and night, from the ten courtesies he shows his teacher and fellow monks to the hours of study, meditation, alms, sleep and confession, is laid out as one careful routine, and living it frees him from all suffering.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 26 (53 verses), translated pages 151–178 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Proper conduct (samachari) frees one from all suffering. Sudharma Swami tells Jambu he will describe it; by living it, monks free of bonds (nirgranthas) have crossed the ocean of worldly life (v.1).
There are ten courtesies. Saying “avassahi” on going out and “nissihi” on coming back in; asking the teacher before one’s own task, and asking again before a task for another monk; inviting fellow monks to share the food one has brought; asking others’ wishes rather than ordering them; saying “micchami dukkadam” for one’s own fault; answering the teacher’s words with “tahatti” (“it is true”); rising to receive elders and serving the young, old and sick; and staying under another monk’s guidance when the teacher allows it (v.2–7). The commentary says they train humility, generosity, unity and alertness to even small faults.
The day starts with a question to the teacher. At sunrise the monk inspects his things, bows, and asks with joined hands whether he should serve or study. Service he does without tiring; study he does with devotion. The commentary notes that the sutra puts service before study (v.8–10).
The day and the night each have four watches. Day: study, meditation, alms, study. Night: study, meditation, sleep, study (v.11–12, 17–18). Time is told by the length of a shadow by day (v.13–16) and by the movement of a constellation across the sky by night (v.19–20).
Inspection (padilehana) is an act of compassion. Mouth-cloth first, then the brush, then the clothes: held up, steady, without hurry, shaken gently and then brushed only if a creature is on them, and any creature is moved to a safe place. The chapter lists twelve right ways and thirteen faults (v.21–28).
Inspection needs full attention. A monk who chats, tells stories, teaches or studies while inspecting harms all six kinds of living beings; one who stays attentive protects all six (v.29–31).
Eat for a reason, and fast for a reason. Food is sought in the third watch for six reasons: hunger, serving others, walking with care, restraint, staying alive and reflecting on the dharma. It is given up for six reasons: illness, an attack or hardship, guarding celibacy, compassion for living beings (for example in rain or mist), austerity, and giving up the body at the end (santharo). Alms are sought within half a yojana (v.32–36).
The day ends with confession. In the fourth watch the monk puts away his bowls, studies, inspects his sleeping place and the place for relieving himself, and then does the evening pratikraman: he reflects on his lapses in knowledge, faith and conduct, confesses them to the teacher, becomes free of hidden faults, and praises the perfected ones (v.37–43).
The night ends the same way. He studies quietly in the fourth watch so as not to wake householders, then does the night pratikraman, adds austerity to his reflection (“What austerity shall I take up?”), takes up a fast before the teacher, and praises the Jinas and the Siddhas (v.44–52).
Many have crossed by this conduct (v.53).

Key verses
1 · Conduct that frees from all suffering

सामायारिं पवक्खामि, सव्व दुक्ख विमोक्खणिं ।
जं चरित्ताण णिग्गंथा, तिण्णा संसार सागरं ॥

I shall describe proper conduct, which frees one from all suffering; by living it, the nirgrantha monks have crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
12 · The four watches of the day

पढमं पोरिसी सज्झायं, बीयं झाणं झियायइ ।
तइयाए भिक्खायरियं, पुणो चउत्थीइ सज्झायं ॥

In the first watch he studies the scriptures, in the second he meditates (on the meaning of what he studied), in the third he goes for alms, and in the fourth he studies again.
31 · Attentive inspection protects life

पुढवी आउक्काए, तेऊ वाऊ वणस्सइ तसाणं ।
पडिलेहणा आउत्तो, छण्हं पि संरक्खओ होइ ॥

One who stays attentive while inspecting becomes a protector of all six kinds of beings: earth, water, fire, air, plant and moving beings.
51 · What austerity shall I take up?

किं तवं पडिवज्जामि, एवं तत्थ विचिंतए ।
काउस्सग्गं तु पारित्ता, करिज्जा जिणसंथवं ॥

In the standing meditation (kayotsarga) he reflects, “What austerity shall I take up today?” Having completed it, he praises the Jinas.
53 · Many have crossed

एसा सामायारी, समासेण वियाहिया ।
जं चरित्ता बहू जीवा, तिण्णा संसार सागरं ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

This proper conduct has been described in brief. By living it, many souls have crossed the ocean of worldly existence. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.12 · v.31 · v.51 · v.53

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_27_the_unruly_b.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 27: The Unruly Bullocks
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_27_the_unruly_b.content:
Uttaradhyayan 27 · Khalunkiya: The Unruly Bullocks
In one line: a good disciple carries the cart of dharma like a willing ox, but bad disciples behave like unruly bullocks, and the elder Garga, unable to set his own disciples right, left them and went on alone, calm and steady.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 27 (17 verses), translated pages 179–186 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 7 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Garga was a true teacher. The elder monk Garga, learned in the scriptures and with an acharya’s qualities, led a group of disciples (the commentary says 500) and kept both himself and others in equanimity (samadhi) (v.1).
A good ox crosses the forest; a good disciple crosses worldly life. An ox that pulls the cart willingly takes its owner through the forest, and a disciple who carries the work of restraint crosses the cycle of births (v.2).
An unruly bullock wears out its driver. The driver tires from beating it, grows upset, and even his whip breaks (v.3).
Every bullock goes wrong in its own way. One is bitten on the tail, one is pricked again and again; one breaks the yoke, one takes the wrong path; one falls on its side, sits, lies down; one jumps, one bolts after a young cow; one drops its head deceitfully, one turns back in anger, one plays dead, one runs off at speed; one snaps the rope, one breaks the yoke and runs away snorting (v.4–7).
Bad disciples are the same. Yoked to the cart of dharma, disciples weak in steadfastness break their restraint (v.8).
The faults of bad disciples. Some are proud of their wealthy followers and possessions, some of tasty food, some of comfort; some stay angry for a long time; some are lazy about alms or afraid of being insulted when they beg; some stay stubborn however carefully they are reasoned with (v.9–10).
They answer back and make excuses. They interrupt, find fault with the teacher, and keep acting against his words. Sent for alms, they say, “She doesn’t know me, she won’t give, she must be out; send another monk.” Sent on a task, they come back without doing it, wander off, and frown as if it were a king’s forced labour (v.11–13).
Garga reflects. “I taught them, initiated them and fed them, yet like swans whose wings have grown they fly off in every direction. What use are these bad disciples to me? My own soul is suffering. They are like lazy donkeys” (v.14–16).
He leaves them and goes on. Garga gave them up, took up austerity firmly, and wandered the earth gentle, deep, composed and of good conduct (v.16–17). The commentary adds that he lived in Mahavira’s time and was to reach liberation in that very life.

Key verses
2 · The willing ox

वहणे वहमाणस्स, कंतारं अइवत्तइ ।
जोए वहमाणस्स, संसारो अइवत्तइ ॥

An ox that pulls the cart well gets across the forest; one who carries the work of restraint (yoga) gets across worldly existence.
8 · Disciples like unruly bullocks

खलुंका जारिसा जुज्जा, दुस्सीसा वि हु तारिसा ।
जोइया धम्मजाणम्मि, भज्जंति धिइदुब्बला ॥

Bad disciples are just like unruly bullocks yoked to a cart: yoked to the cart of dharma, those weak in steadfastness break down.
14 · Like swans whose wings have grown

वाइया संगहिया चेव, भत्तपाणेण पोसिया ।
जायपक्खा जहा हंसा, पक्कमंति दिसोदिसिं ॥

I taught them, took them in and fed them with food and water; yet, like swans whose wings have grown, they fly off in every direction.
15 · The driver reflects

अह सारही विचिंतेइ, खलुंकेहिं समागओ ।
किं मज्झ दुट्ठसीसेहिं, अप्पा मे अवसीयइ ॥

Then the driver, stuck with unruly bullocks, reflects: “What use are these bad disciples to me? My soul only sinks into distress.”
16 · He leaves the lazy donkeys

जारिसा मम सीसाओ, तारिसा गलिगद्दहा ।
गलिगद्दहे जहित्ताणं, दढं पगिण्हइ तवं ॥

“My disciples are like lazy donkeys.” Leaving those lazy donkeys behind, he took up austerity firmly.
17 · Garga goes on alone

मिउमद्दवसंपण्णो, गंभीरो सुसमाहिओ ।
विहरइ महिं महप्पा, सीलभूएण अप्पणा ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Gentle and soft, deep and well composed, the great soul wandered the earth, his self grounded in good conduct. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.8 · v.14–17

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_28_the_path_to_.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 28: The Path to Liberation
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_28_the_path_to_.content:
Uttaradhyayan 28 · Mokshamarga Gati: The Path to Liberation
In one line: the path to liberation has four parts: knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity. Knowledge shows what is true, faith holds to it, conduct stops new karma coming in, and austerity burns up the old.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 28 (36 verses), translated pages 187–211 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The path has four parts. The all-seeing Jinas taught that the path to liberation is knowledge, faith (darshana), conduct and austerity, and beings who follow it reach the good state. Knowledge and faith are named as its marks because they stay with the liberated soul, while conduct and austerity depend on the body (v.1–3).
Knowledge is of five kinds: sensory knowledge (mati), scriptural knowledge (shruta), clairvoyance (avadhi), knowing the thoughts of others (manahparyava) and omniscience (kevala). It knows substances, their qualities and their changing states (paryaya). A substance carries qualities, a quality lives in a substance, and a state depends on both (v.4–6).
The universe is six substances. They are the medium of motion (dharmastikaya), the medium of rest (adharmastikaya), space, time, matter (pudgala) and living beings. The first three are one each; time, matter and souls are infinite in number. Motion, rest, room, the passing of time and awareness (upayoga) are what mark each of them. The soul is known by knowledge, faith, conduct, austerity, energy and awareness. Matter shows as sound, darkness, light, shadow, heat, colour, smell, taste and touch (v.7–13).
Right faith means believing the nine truths as they are. The nine are soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, sin, inflow of karma (ashrava), stopping it (samvara), shedding it (nirjara) and liberation. Faith in them, whether it rises by itself or through teaching, is right faith (samyaktva) (v.14–15).
Faith can be reached by ten roads. It may come naturally; or through teaching; or through the command of a Jina or teacher, once attachment and aversion have thinned; or through study of the scriptures. It may spread from one idea to many “like a drop of oil on water”; or come from understanding the scriptures, or from detailed study by every method; or from love of practice. It may also come with little learning but no attachment to false views, or from faith in the substances, the scriptures and conduct (v.16–27).
Faith is kept strong by three habits: getting to know the highest truth, serving those who have understood it, and keeping away from those who have fallen from right faith or hold false views (v.28).
Faith comes first. Without right faith there is no conduct, though one can have faith without conduct; the two may come together, or faith first. Without faith, knowledge is not right knowledge, and without right knowledge, conduct does not arise. Without conduct there is no freedom from karma, and without that there is no nirvana (v.29–30).
Faith has eight limbs. They are freedom from doubt, freedom from wanting other paths or rewards, no disgust or doubt about the fruit of dharma, and clear, undeluded vision. Then come encouraging virtue, steadying those who waver, affection for fellow followers, and spreading the dharma (v.31).
Conduct is of five kinds: equanimity (samayika), re-initiation (chhedopasthapaniya), purification by special austerity (parihara-vishuddhi), the stage of only subtle greed (sukshma-samparaya), and conduct entirely free of passion (yathakhyata). Conduct (charitra) is so called because it empties out the store of karma (v.32–33).
Austerity is of twelve kinds, six outer and six inner. The outer are fasting, eating less, limits in begging alms, giving up rich food, bodily hardship and withdrawing the senses. The inner are atonement, humility, service, study, meditation and letting go (v.34).
Each part does its own work. Knowledge knows, faith believes, conduct restrains, and austerity purifies. Burning up old karma by restraint and austerity, great sages strive to end all suffering (v.35–36). The commentary compares this to a patient, who must understand the illness, trust the doctor, take the medicine and keep the diet.

Key verses
2 · The fourfold path

णाणं च दंसणं चेव, चरित्तं च तवो तहा ।
एस मग्गो त्ति पण्णत्तो, जिणेहिं वरदंसीहिं ॥

Knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity: this is the path, as proclaimed by the all-seeing Jinas.
15 · What right faith is

तहियाणं तु भावाणं, सब्भावे उवएसणं ।
भावेण सद्दहंतस्स, सम्मत्तं तं वियाहियं ॥

The Jinas call it right faith when a person, from within or through teaching, truly believes in the existence of these real principles.
30 · Faith comes before everything

णादंसणिस्स णाणं, णाणेण विणा ण हुंति चरणगुणा ।
अगुणिस्स णत्थि मोक्खो, णत्थि अमोक्खस्स णिव्वाणं ॥

Without faith there is no right knowledge; without knowledge the virtues of conduct do not arise. Without those virtues there is no freedom from karma, and without that freedom there is no nirvana.
35 · What each part does

णाणेण जाणइ भावे, दंसणेण य सद्दहे ।
चरित्तेण णिगिण्हाइ, तवेण परिसुज्झइ ॥

By knowledge one knows things as they are, and by faith one believes them. By conduct one holds karma back, and by austerity one is made pure.
36 · The sages’ effort

खवित्ता पुव्वकम्माइं, संजमेण तवेण य ।
सव्वदुक्खपहीणट्ठा, पक्कमंति महेसिणो ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Having destroyed their past karma by restraint and austerity, the great sages press on to be free of all suffering. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.15 · v.30 · v.35 · v.36

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_29_right_effort.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 29: Right Effort
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_29_right_effort.content:
Uttaradhyayan 29 · Samyak Parakram (Sammatta-parakkame): Right Effort
In one line: for each of 73 practices, from longing for liberation to the final stillness, the disciple asks “Lord, what does the soul gain by this?”, and each answer shows how that one practice, done rightly, carries the soul all the way to freedom.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 29 (76 prose sutras: an opening, a list of 73 topics, one question and answer for each of the 73, and a closing), translated pages 212–277 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 35 minutes.
How the chapter works. Almost every sutra has the same shape. ”___-eṇaṃ bhante! jīve kiṃ jaṇayai?”: “Lord, what does the soul gain through ___?” Then comes the answer. Effort turned outward, toward possessions and success, is not right effort; effort turned inward, toward purifying the soul, is (commentary, s.1). The introduction says any one practice can be a starting point. Each topic stands on its own, and all of them lead to the soul’s purity. Sutra numbers below are the book’s: the first topic is s.3, so topic n is sutra n+2.
What the chapter teaches

Ten steps turn a teaching into freedom. Sudharma tells Jambu that Mahavira taught this chapter. Whoever, in order, trusts it, is convinced of it, comes to like it, takes it up, keeps it, sees it through, praises it, purifies it, practises it and follows it as commanded becomes perfected and ends all suffering. Sutra 2 then lists the 73 topics (s.1–2).
It begins with longing, letting go and trust. Longing for liberation (samvega) brings the highest faith, and that faith brings longing back quickly. Such a soul destroys the worst passions, the ones that bind without end; it may be freed in this very life and will not need more than three lives. Weariness with the world (nirveda) turns the soul from heavenly, human and animal pleasures and cuts off the road of rebirth. Faith in dharma loosens the hold of comfort; the soul leaves household life and gains unobstructed happiness. Serving the guru and fellow followers brings humility, which closes off bad births. Confession pulls out three thorns: deceit, wanting rewards for one’s practice, and wrong belief. Self-reproach brings remorse, and that remorse leads the soul up toward destroying deluding karma. Confessing before others breaks pride and turns the soul to wholesome activity (s.3–9).
The daily essentials each have a fruit. Equanimity (samayika) stops sinful activity. Praising the 24 Tirthankaras purifies faith. Bowing to the guru removes low-status karma and brings goodwill. Pratikramana mends the holes in one’s vows. Kayotsarga lifts off faults “like a porter who has put down his load”. Taking a vow of renunciation (pratyakhyana) shuts the doors through which karma flows in and quiets desire. Hymns of praise bring awakening in knowledge, faith and conduct. Keeping the right times for study removes knowledge-obscuring karma. Atonement cleans sinful karma. Asking forgiveness brings gladness, friendship with all beings and fearlessness (s.10–19).
Study has five parts, and each one helps. Self-study (svadhyaya) destroys knowledge-obscuring karma. Then come its five parts. Reading and teaching keep the scriptures alive and shed karma. Asking questions clears doubts. Repeating lessons keeps the words in memory. Deep reflection (anupreksha) loosens all karma except lifespan karma, and makes it shorter, milder and lighter. Teaching dharma to others spreads the faith. Honouring scripture ends ignorance, and fixing the mind on one point stills its wandering (s.20–27).
Restraint stops new karma, austerity burns the old, and the last purification ends activity. Restraint (samyama) makes one free of sin; austerity (tapa) purifies; full purification (vodana) brings the inactive state and then liberation. The commentary calls these three successive steps. Turning away from pleasure makes one gentle and sorrowless; non-attachment lets one move “alone, one-pointed, day and night”. Secluded lodging guards conduct, and turning back from sense objects carries one across the forest of rebirth (s.28–34).
The renunciations go deeper one by one. Eating apart from the group makes a monk content with his own alms. Giving up equipment frees time for study. Giving up food cuts the craving to live, and giving up the passions makes pleasure and pain equal. Giving up the activity of mind, speech and body stops all new bondage. Giving up the body brings the qualities of the perfected ones at the top of the universe. Giving up help from others brings few quarrels and much calm. A lifelong fast cuts off many hundreds of births. The final renunciation, of all activity in the fourteenth stage, destroys the last four karmas (s.35–43). The commentary notes that possessions, food, passions, activity and body are given up in that order.
Outer form and inner virtue go together. Wearing the true monk’s marks makes one light, careful and trusted by all beings. Service (vaiyavritya) binds the karma of a future Tirthankara. Having all the virtues means never returning to suffering. Freedom from attachment cuts the bonds of affection and craving. Forgiveness conquers hardships, and freedom from greed leaves one owning nothing, of no interest to the greedy. Straightforwardness makes body, mind and speech honest, and gentleness destroys the eight kinds of pride (s.44–51).
Truth, guarding and steadying lead to the three jewels made full. Truth in thought, action and activity purifies the soul. A truthful soul “does as it says”. Guarding the mind gives one-pointedness, guarding speech gives a mind free of agitation, and guarding the body stops sinful inflow. Steadying the mind purifies faith; steadying speech makes awakening easy to reach again in later lives; steadying the body leads to perfect conduct and liberation. Fullness of knowledge keeps the soul from getting lost, like a threaded needle. Fullness of faith keeps its light from going out. Fullness of conduct brings the rock-still state (shaileshi) (s.52–63).
Master the five senses, then the four passions. Restraining hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch stops attachment and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant sounds, forms, smells, tastes and touches; no new karma is bound and old karma falls away. Conquering anger brings forgiveness, pride brings softness, deceit brings straightforwardness, and greed brings contentment. Conquering attachment, aversion and wrong belief destroys deluding karma and then the other destructive karmas, and brings omniscience. While still active, the omniscient one binds only a karma that lasts two instants and is shed in the third (s.64–73).
The end is stillness and an upward flight. With less than a muhurta of life left, the omniscient one stops mind, then speech, then body, then breath. In the time it takes to say five short vowels (a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ) he destroys the last four karmas. Leaving all three bodies, the soul rises straight up, in a single instant and without turning, to the top of the universe and is perfected (s.74–75). Sudharma closes: this is the meaning of the chapter as Mahavira explained it (s.76).

Key passages
s.3 · Longing for liberation, the first step

संवेगेणं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ?
संवेगेणं अणुत्तरं धम्मसद्धं जणयइ, अणुत्तराए धम्मसद्धाए संवेगं हव्वमागच्छइ, अणंताणुबंधी कोह-माण-माया-लोभे खवेइ, णवं च कम्मं ण बंधइ, तप्पच्चइयं च मिच्छत्त-विसोहिं काऊण दंसणाराहए भवइ, दंसणविसोहिए य णं विसुद्धाए अत्थेगइए जीवे तेणेव भवग्गहणेणं सिज्झइ बुज्झइ मुच्चइ परिणिव्वायइ सव्वदुक्खाणमंतं करेइ, विसोहिए य णं विसुद्धाए तच्चं पुणो भवग्गहणं णाइक्कमइ ।

Lord, what does the soul gain through longing for liberation? It gains the highest faith in dharma, and through that faith the longing quickly grows. It destroys the anger, pride, deceit and greed that bind without end, and binds no new karma. Clearing away wrong belief, it becomes a true keeper of faith. Purified by that faith, some souls are perfected in this very life. Even the rest do not go beyond a third birth.
s.19 · Asking forgiveness

खमावणयाए णं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ?
खमावणयाए णं पल्हायणभावं जणयइ । पल्हायण भावमुवगए य सव्वपाण-भूय-जीव-सत्तेसु मित्तीभावमुप्पाएइ । मित्तीभावमुवगए यावि जीवे भावविसोहिं काऊण णिब्भए भवइ ।

Lord, what does the soul gain by asking forgiveness? It gains gladness of heart. Glad at heart, it feels friendship for all living beings. In friendship, it purifies its feelings and becomes fearless.
s.20 · Self-study

सज्झाएणं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ? सज्झाएणं णाणावरणिज्जं कम्मं खवेइ ।

Lord, what does the soul gain through self-study? Through self-study it destroys the karma that covers knowledge.
s.61 · The threaded needle

जहा सूई ससुत्ता, पडिया वि ण विणस्सइ ।
तहा जीवे ससुत्ते, संसारे ण विणस्सइ ॥

A needle with its thread is not lost, even when it falls. In the same way, a soul that holds the scripture is not lost in the world.
s.75 · The flight to the top of the universe

तओ ओरालिय-तेयकम्माइं सव्वाहिं विप्पजहणाहिं विप्पजहित्ता उज्जुसेढिपत्ते अफुसमाणगईए उड्ढं एगसमएणं अविग्गहेणं तत्थ गंता सागारोवउत्ते सिज्झइ बुज्झइ मुच्चइ परिणिव्वायइ सव्वादुक्खाणमंतं करेइ ।

Then, casting off completely the physical, fiery and karmic bodies, the soul takes the straight path. Without touching anything on the way, it rises in a single instant, without turning, and goes there. Fully aware, it is perfected, awakened and freed, reaches final peace and ends all suffering. (The scan prints सव्वादुक्खाणमंतं here, where the other sutras have सव्वदुक्खाणमंतं.)

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_30_the_path_of_.content:
Uttaradhyayan 30 · Tapomarga Gati: The Path of Austerity
In one line: first close the channels through which karma flows in. Then dry up what has gathered over countless lives with twelve kinds of austerity: six outer, which work through the body, and six inner, which work through the mind and heart.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 30 (37 verses), translated pages 278–306 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Stop the inflow first. A soul that gives up killing, lying, stealing, sex, possessions and eating at night lets no new karma in. So does one that keeps the five careful practices (samiti) and three guards (gupti), is free of passion, masters the senses, and is free of the three kinds of pride (in powers, in tasty food, in comfort) and the three thorns (deceit, wanting rewards, wrong belief) (v.1–4).
The lake. When the streams feeding a great lake are blocked, its water is drawn off and dries in the sun. In the same way, once a restrained monk stops sinful karma flowing in, karma gathered over crores of births is burned away by austerity (tapa) (v.5–6).
Austerity is outer and inner, six of each (v.7). The commentary defines austerity as “restraining desire”. Outer austerity works mainly on the body and others can see it. Inner austerity works on the soul’s own states.
Fasting (anashana) is either for a set time, with the thought of eating again, or until death. The set-time fasts come in six patterns. The first five are the row (shreni), the layer (pratara), the block (ghana), the block multiplied by itself (varga), and that multiplied by itself again (varga-varga). Each is a rising run of fasts; built on a three-step row, the last lasts over 25,000 years. The sixth is any fast chosen freely. Fasting until death has three ways of being divided. It may be with or without movement, with or without care of the body, and with the body later carried out for last rites or left where it lies. In every form, food is given up (v.8–13).
Eating less (unodari) is done in five ways. By amount: even one mouthful less. By place: begging only in a chosen area or in a chosen pattern, such as a box, a zigzag “like an ox’s urine” or a conch-spiral. By time: only in a chosen part of the day. By the giver: only from, say, a woman or a man, adorned or not, of a certain age or dress. Or by all four together (v.14–24).
The other outer austerities. Begging alms under vows means the eight patterns of alms round, seven kinds of acceptable food and other resolves. Giving up rich foods means milk, curd, ghee and the like. Bodily hardship means hard postures such as the hero’s pose, “harsh to the body, happy for the soul”. Withdrawal means a secluded lodging free of crowds, women, animals and eunuchs (v.25–28). This ends the outer austerities (v.29).
Inner austerity: atonement, humility and service. Atonement (prayashchitta) is of ten kinds, from simply confessing to the guru up to full re-initiation. Humility (vinaya) means standing up when elders come, joining hands, offering a seat, devotion and heartfelt service. Service (vaiyavritya) is given to ten: the acharya, the teacher, elders, ascetics, the sick, new monks, the family of disciples, the group, the whole order and fellow followers (v.30–33).
Inner austerity: study, meditation and letting go of the body. Study (svadhyaya) is reading, asking, repeating, reflecting and teaching. Meditation (dhyana) means giving up distressed and cruel thinking and resting in righteous meditation (dharma) and pure meditation (shukla). The commentary explains all four kinds of meditation with their marks and supports. Letting go of the body (vyutsarga) means not moving the body, whether lying, sitting or standing (v.34–36).
The fruit. The wise monk who practises both kinds of austerity rightly is quickly freed from all of worldly existence. The commentary says “wise” (pandita) means one who sees what helps and what harms, and does only what helps (v.37).

Key verses
5–6 · The lake that dries up

जहा महातलायस्स, सण्णिरुद्धे जलागमे ।
उस्सिंचणाए तवणाए, कमेणं सोसणा भवे ॥
एवं तु संजयस्सावि, पावकम्म णिरासवे ।
भवकोडी संचियं कम्मं, तवसा णिज्जरिज्जइ ॥

When the water flowing into a great lake is blocked, it slowly dries up as it is drawn out and heated by the sun. In the same way, when a restrained monk stops sinful karma from coming in, the karma gathered over crores of births is shed through austerity.
8 · The six outer austerities

अणसणमूणोयरिया, भिक्खायरिया य रसपरिच्चाओ ।
कायकिलेसो संलीणया, य बज्झो तवो होइ ॥

Fasting, eating less, limits in begging alms, giving up rich food, bodily hardship and withdrawal: these are the outer austerities.
30 · The six inner austerities

पायच्छित्तं विणओ, वेयावच्चं तहेव सज्झाओ ।
झाणं च विउस्सग्गो, एसो अब्भिंतरो तवो ॥

Atonement, humility, service, study, meditation and letting go of the body: these are the inner austerities.
35 · True meditation

अट्टरुद्दाणि वज्जित्ता, झाएज्जा सुसमाहिए ।
धम्म-सुक्काइं झाणाइं, झाणं तं तु बुहा वए ॥

Giving up distressed and cruel thinking, well composed, one should meditate in righteous and pure meditation. This, say the wise, is meditation.
37 · The fruit of austerity

एयं तवं तु दुविहं, जे सम्मं आयरे मुणी ।
सो खिप्पं सव्वसंसारा, विप्पमुच्चइ पंडिए ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

The wise monk who rightly practises this twofold austerity is quickly freed from all of worldly existence. Thus I say.

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_31_rules_of_con.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 31: Rules of Conduct
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_31_rules_of_con.content:
Uttaradhyayan 31 · Charan Vidhi: Rules of Conduct
In one line: conduct comes down to one rule: turn away from lack of restraint and turn toward restraint. The chapter then counts up from one to thirty-three, naming what a monk must give up, take up or simply know. Each verse ends with the same promise: “that monk does not stay in the round of rebirth.”
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 31 (21 verses), translated pages 307–328 (data/translations/uttaradhyayan-2/). 15 minutes.
How the chapter works. After an opening verse, each verse names one or more numbered groups (“the twos”, “the threes” … “the thirty-threes”). Each ends with the refrain je bhikkhū jayaī ṇiccaṃ, se ṇa acchaī maṃḍale: “the monk who always takes care over these does not stay in the round.” The commentary sorts every group into what to abandon, what to adopt and what to know. The book closes with a table of all 33 (pages 326–328).
What the chapter teaches

This conduct brings happiness and has carried many across. Mahavira’s way of conduct (charan vidhi) is happy for the soul, and by living it many souls have crossed the ocean of rebirth (v.1). The commentary adds that knowledge and faith show the way, but conduct stops new karma and austerity sheds the old.
One: leave lack of restraint, enter restraint (v.2). The commentary explains this as giving up the 17 kinds of lack of restraint and keeping the 17 kinds of restraint.
Two: attachment and aversion. These two sins set all sinful action going; the commentary calls them seeds from which a whole banyan tree of sin grows. The monk who always holds them back does not wander (v.3).
Three and four: things to drop and things to bear. Drop the three ways of harming oneself (mind, speech, body misused), the three prides (in powers, tasty food, comfort) and the three thorns (deceit, wanting rewards, wrong belief). Bear calmly the troubles that come from gods, animals and humans (v.4–5). Avoid the four kinds of idle talk (about women, food, countries, kings), the four passions, the four instincts (food, fear, sex, possession) and the two bad kinds of meditation, distressed and cruel (v.6).
Five to seven: the working tools of a monk’s life. Take care over the five great vows, the five senses, the five careful practices (samiti) and the five kinds of karma-binding activity (v.7). Take care over the six soul-colours (leshya), keeping to the three bright ones. Protect the six classes of living beings, and keep the six reasons for eating and the six for not eating (v.8). Keep the seven vows about accepting alms and the seven about lodging, and stay clear of the seven fears (v.9).
Eight to twelve: pride, celibacy, the ten virtues and the vowed stages. Drop the eight kinds of pride (birth, family, strength, beauty, austerity, learning, gain, wealth). Keep the nine fences of celibacy and the ten virtues of a monk: forgiveness, freedom from greed, straightforwardness, gentleness, lightness, truth, restraint, austerity, giving and celibacy (v.10). Know and teach the eleven vowed stages (pratima) of a lay follower and the twelve of a monk (v.11).
Thirteen to twenty: what to avoid and what to study. Avoid the thirteen kinds of activity that bind karma, except careful walking. Protect the fourteen groups of living beings. Never become like the fifteen cruel gods who torment hell-beings, and do not hate them either (v.12). Follow the sixteen chapters of the Sutrakritanga’s first part and the seventeen kinds of restraint (v.13). Keep the eighteen-fold celibacy, learn from the nineteen chapters of the Jnata Sutra, and avoid the twenty things that disturb a monk’s calm, such as rushing, repeated anger, stirring up old quarrels and studying at the wrong time (v.14).
Twenty-one to twenty-eight: serious faults, hardships and the texts on conduct. Avoid the twenty-one serious faults (shabala), such as eating at night or knowingly lying. Bear the twenty-two hardships taught in chapter 2 (v.15). Take care over the twenty-three chapters of the Sutrakritanga and the twenty-four kinds of gods, toward whom one stays neutral, wanting nothing from them (v.16). Use the twenty-five supporting practices of the great vows and the twenty-six sections of the three books on conduct (v.17). Grow the twenty-seven qualities of a monk, and follow the twenty-eight chapters of the Acharanga and Nishitha (v.18).
Twenty-nine to thirty-three: the darkest wrongs and the highest goal. Avoid the twenty-nine kinds of “sinful learning” (omens, palmistry, spells and the like) and the thirty acts that bind the heaviest deluding karma. These include killing living beings by drowning or smoke, falsely claiming celibacy or learning, and slandering one’s teachers (v.19). Aim at the thirty-one qualities of the perfected ones and the thirty-two good practices (yoga-sangraha), and avoid the thirty-three kinds of disrespect toward the guru, such as walking ahead of him or interrupting his teaching (v.20).
The wise monk who keeps all this is quickly freed from the whole round of rebirth (v.21).

Key verses
1 · The rule that carries across

चरणविहिं पवक्खामि, जीवस्स उ सुहावहं ।
जं चरित्ता बहू जीवा, तिण्णा संसार-सागरं ॥

I shall tell the rule of conduct, which brings happiness to the soul. By living it, many souls have crossed the ocean of rebirth.
2 · One thing to leave, one to take up

एगओ विरइं कुज्जा, एगओ य पवत्तणं ।
असंजमे णियत्तिं च, संजमे य पवत्तणं ॥

Turn away from one thing and toward another: turn away from lack of restraint, and toward restraint.
3 · The two sins

रागदोसे य दो पावे, पावकम्म-पवत्तणे ।
जे भिक्खू रुंभइ णिच्चं, से ण अच्छइ मंडले ॥

Attachment and aversion are the two sins that set sinful action going. The monk who always holds them back does not stay in the round of rebirth.
20 · The highest numbers

सिद्धाइगुण जोगेसु, तेत्तीसासायणासु य ।
जे भिक्खू जयइ णिच्चं, से ण अच्छइ मंडले ॥

The monk who always takes care over the thirty-one qualities of the perfected ones, the thirty-two good practices and the thirty-three kinds of disrespect does not stay in the round of rebirth.
21 · Quickly freed

इइ एएसु ठाणेसु, जे भिक्खू जयइ सया ।
खिप्पं सो सव्व संसारा, विप्पमुच्चइ पंडिओ ॥ त्तिबेमि ॥

The wise monk who always takes care over these points is quickly freed from the whole of worldly existence. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1–2 · v.3 · v.20 · v.21
