09_modules/uttaradhyayan_32_sources_of_n.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 32: Sources of Negligence
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_32_sources_of_n.content:
Uttaradhyayan 32 · Pramadasthana: Sources of Negligence
In one line: suffering does not come from the objects of the senses but from our attachment and aversion toward them; the one who stays even-minded among them, like a lotus leaf in water, is freed from all suffering.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 32 (111 verses), translated pages 329–365. 15 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

There is a way out of all suffering, root and all. Liberation, which is complete happiness, comes from the light of full knowledge, the removal of ignorance and delusion, and the end of attachment and aversion (raga and dvesha). The path: serve the teacher and the elder monks, stay far from the spiritually immature, study alone, reflect on the scriptures, and be steady (v.1–3).
Three supports for a calm mind (samadhi). Measured, faultless food; a companion who understands the teaching; a place fit for solitude. If no companion better than or equal to oneself is found, one may wander alone, avoiding wrong and unattached to pleasures. The commentary warns this is an exception, only for a monk with the eight qualities the scriptures name (v.4–5).
The chain of suffering. As the heron comes from the egg and the egg from the heron, craving gives rise to delusion and delusion to craving. Attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma; karma is the root of birth and death; birth and death are suffering. Break the chain from the bottom: no possessions, no greed; no greed, no craving; no craving, no delusion; no delusion, no suffering (v.6–8).
How to uproot attachment, aversion and delusion. Do not eat rich food to excess, for it inflames the senses as wind feeds a forest fire. Keep secluded lodging, eat little, guard the senses. A celibate should not live among women, as mice should not live by a cat’s den, nor dwell on their beauty, words or glances. Even monks whom adorned goddesses could not shake are told to live in seclusion (v.9–16).
The hardest bond. For one who seeks liberation, nothing is as hard to cross as attachment to women; once that is crossed, the rest is easy, as a river like the Ganges is easy after the ocean. All suffering of body and mind, even among the gods, grows from craving for pleasure. Sense pleasures are like the kimpaka fruit, lovely and sweet but deadly when they ripen (v.17–20).
Even-mindedness toward all five senses. The heart of the chapter: thirteen verses for each sense, all built the same way. Each sense has its object; a pleasing object becomes a cause of attachment, a displeasing one a cause of aversion; one who stays even toward both is free of passion (vitaraga) (v.21–23).
Five examples of death by one sense. The moth dies for light (sight), the deer for music (hearing), the snake drawn out by the scent of herbs (smell), the fish caught on the hook for flesh (taste), the buffalo seized by a crocodile in cool water (touch). In each set the same chain follows: the attached person harms living beings, is never satisfied, steals, lies, and suffers before, during and after; the one who hates suffers at once by his own hatred, and “the object is in no way at fault” (v.22–86).
The mind is the sixth. The mind grasps feelings (bhava) as the eye grasps form. The elephant mad for a female elephant meets his end. The detached person, though living in the world, is untouched by this flood of suffering, like a lotus leaf by water (v.87–99).
Objects are neutral; the mind decides. Sense pleasures in themselves bring neither calm nor disturbance. Whoever clings to them falls into anger, pride, deceit, greed, disgust, fear, sorrow and sexual feeling, and becomes pitiable. A monk should not long for a helper or disciples, should not regret his restraint, and should not do austerity for a reward; the uncontrolled senses are “thieves” that pull him into the ocean of delusion (v.100–105).
The fruit of detachment. For the detached, sound and the other objects cause neither liking nor disliking; craving dies. He destroys in a moment the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring and obstructing karmas, knows and sees everything, and at the end of life is liberated, wholly happy. This is the path out of the suffering that has no beginning (v.106–111).

Key verses
7 · The root of birth and death

रागो य दोसो वि य कम्मबीयं, कम्मं च मोहप्पभवं वयंति ।
कम्मं च जाईमरणस्स मूलं, दुक्खं च जाईमरणं वयंति ॥

Attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma; karma, the wise say, arises from delusion. Karma is the root of birth and death, and birth and death, they say, are suffering.
8 · Breaking the chain

दुक्खं हयं जस्स ण होइ मोहो, मोहो हओ जस्स ण होइ तण्हा ।
तण्हा हया जस्स ण होइ लोहो, लोहो हओ जस्स ण किंचणाइं ॥

Suffering is gone for one who has no delusion; delusion is gone for one who has no craving; craving is gone for one who has no greed; greed is gone for one who owns nothing.
24 · The moth and the flame

रूवेसु जो गिद्धिमुवेइ तिव्वं, अकालियं पावइ से विणासं ।
रागाउरे से जह वा पयंगे, आलोयलोले समुवेइ मच्चुं ॥

One who is intensely attached to forms meets an untimely end, like the moth, sick with longing and greedy for light, that rushes to its death.
34 · The lotus leaf

रूवे विरत्तो मणुओ विसोगो, एएण दुक्खोह परंपरेण ।
ण लिप्पइ भवमज्झे वि संतो, जलेण वा पोक्खरिणी पलासं ॥

A person detached from form is free of sorrow. Though living in the middle of worldly existence, he is not touched by this stream of suffering, as a lotus leaf in a pond is not touched by water.
100 · Not the object, but attachment

एविंदियत्था य मणस्स अत्था, दुक्खस्स हेउं मणुयस्स रागिणो ।
ते चेव थोवं पि कयाइ दुक्खं, ण वीयरागस्स करेंति किंचि ॥

So the objects of the senses and of the mind are a cause of suffering for a person with attachment. Those very objects never cause even the least suffering to one free of attachment.
Verses checked against the scans: v.7 · v.8 · v.24 · v.34 · v.100

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_33_nature_of_ka.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 33: The Nature of Karma
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_33_nature_of_ka.content:
Uttaradhyayan 33 · Karma Prakriti: The Nature of Karma
In one line: the soul wanders because it is bound by eight kinds of karma; know their kinds, their length and their strength, and then stop new karma coming in and destroy the old.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 33 (25 verses), translated pages 366–383. 10 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Karma is why the soul wanders. The soul is in itself pure consciousness, but it has been mixed with lifeless karma since beginningless time, as gold and earth lie mixed in a mine. Attachment and aversion bind karma, karma brings birth and death, and in living out karma the soul binds more (v.1).
The eight karmas. Knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, lifespan, body-making (nama), status-determining (gotra) and obstructing (antaraya). The commentary gives a picture for each: a cloud over the sun (or a blindfold), a king’s gatekeeper, a honey-smeared sword, liquor, a fetter, a painter, a potter, a king’s treasurer (v.2–3).
Four ways karma is bound. By nature, by duration, by intensity and by quantity of particles. The commentary explains with a sweet ball (modak): what it is made of, how long it keeps, how strong its taste is, how big it is. Nature and quantity come from activity (yoga); duration and intensity come from the passions (kashaya) (introduction, v.2–3 commentary).
The sub-kinds. Knowledge-obscuring 5; perception-obscuring 9 (four kinds of perception covered, plus five kinds of sleep); feeling-producing 2, pleasant and unpleasant; deluding 28 (3 that delude faith, 16 passions, 7 or 9 quasi-passions such as laughter, fear and sexual feeling); lifespan 4 (hell, animal, human, god); body-making 2, auspicious and inauspicious, each with many kinds; status 2, high and low, eight kinds each; obstructing 5 (giving, gaining, enjoying once, enjoying repeatedly, energy). The chapter names 71 in all (v.4–15).
How much karma is bound. In a single instant a soul takes in infinitely many karmic particles: more than the souls that never break the knot, fewer than the liberated souls. It draws them from all six directions, and they bind to every space-point of the soul (v.16–18).
How long karma stays. At most: 30 crore-crore sagaropamas for the two obscuring karmas, feeling-producing and obstructing; 70 for deluding (the longest); 33 sagaropamas for lifespan; 20 crore-crore for body-making and status. At least: less than a muhurta, except body-making and status, at least eight muhurtas (v.19–23).
How strongly it acts. The intensity (anubhaga) depends on how strong or mild the passions were at the moment of binding (v.24).
Therefore, act. Knowing all this, the wise person strives to stop the inflow of karma (samvara) and to destroy what is already bound. The commentary: “the fruit of knowledge is renunciation”; good and bad karma alike are bondage (v.25).

Key verses
1 · Why the soul wanders

अट्ठ कम्माइं वोच्छामि, आणुपुव्विं जहक्कमं ।
जेहिं बद्धो अयं जीवो, संसारे परिवट्टइ ॥

I shall describe the eight karmas in their proper order, bound by which this soul wanders through worldly existence.
2–3 · The eight karmas

णाणस्सावरणिज्जं, दंसणावरणं तहा ।
वेयणिज्जं तहा मोहं, आउकम्मं तहेव य ॥
णामकम्मं च गोयं च, अंतरायं तहेव य ।
एवमेयाइं कम्माइं, अट्ठेव उ समासओ ॥

Knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, lifespan, body-making, status-determining and obstructing karma: these, in brief, are the eight karmas.
21 · Delusion lasts longest

उदहिसरिसणामाणं, सत्तरिं कोडिकोडीओ ।
मोहणिज्जस्स उक्कोसा, अंतोमुहुत्तं जहण्णिया ॥

The longest duration of deluding karma is seventy crore-crore sagaropamas; the shortest is less than a muhurta.
25 · Stop it and destroy it

तम्हा एएसिं कम्माणं, अणुभागा वियाणिया ।
एएसिं संवरे चेव, खवणे य जए बुहो ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Therefore, knowing the strength of these karmas, the wise person should strive to stop them and to destroy them. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.2–3 · v.21 · v.25

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_34_leshya.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 34: The Colours of the Soul
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_34_leshya.content:
Uttaradhyayan 34 · Leshya: The Colours of the Soul
In one line: the soul’s states, coloured by the passions, come in six shades from black to white; the dark three lead to a bad birth and the bright three to a good one, so a monk should leave the dark and hold to the bright.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 34 (61 verses), translated pages 384–407. 12 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

What leshya is. Here leshya means the states of the soul coloured by the passions. There is a material leshya (physical, with colour, smell, taste and touch) and an inner leshya (formless), and each arises along with the other. The leshya at the moment the next life’s lifespan is bound is the one present at death and at the next birth (introduction).
Eleven doors. The chapter describes leshya through eleven headings: name, colour, taste, smell, touch, gradations, marks, places, duration, destiny and lifespan (v.1–2).
Names and colours. Black (krishna), blue (nila), grey (kapota), fiery red (tejo), lotus yellow (padma) and white (shukla). Black is like a rain cloud, a buffalo’s horn or lampblack; blue like a blue jay’s feather or beryl; grey like a pigeon’s neck; red like the rising sun or a parrot’s beak; yellow like turmeric; white like a conch, a stream of milk or a silver necklace (v.3–9).
Taste, smell and touch. Each is “infinitely more” than its example: black more bitter than neem, blue more pungent than dry ginger and pepper, grey more sour than an unripe mango, red sweet-sour like a ripe mango, yellow like fine wine, white sweeter than dates, milk and sugar. The dark three smell worse than a dead cow, dog or snake, and feel rougher than a saw or a cow’s tongue; the bright three are more fragrant than crushed flowers and softer than butter (v.10–19).
Gradations. Each leshya has 3, 9, 27, 81 or 243 grades; in truth they are countless (v.20).
The marks of each person. Black: one who indulges in the five sins, is unguarded, harms the six kinds of beings, is cruel, rash and has not conquered the senses. Blue: envious, resentful, deceitful, shameless, greedy for taste and comfort. Grey: crooked in speech and act, hiding faults, wrong in belief, harsh, thieving, jealous. Red: humble, steady, without deceit, disciplined, loving and firm in dharma, fearing wrong. Yellow: little anger, pride, deceit and greed, a calm mind, speaking little. White: gives up the troubled and cruel meditations, meditates on dharma and the pure, calm, careful and guarded, with little or no attachment (v.21–32).
Places and durations. The places of leshya are as many as the instants in countless cycles of time. The chapter then gives the shortest and longest time each leshya can last, in general and for hell beings, humans and animals, and gods. For humans and animals any leshya lasts less than a muhurta, except the white leshya of an omniscient one, which can last almost a crore of purvas (v.33–55).
Where they lead. Black, blue and grey are leshyas of non-dharma and lead to a bad destiny; red, yellow and white are leshyas of dharma and lead to a good one (v.56–57).
Leshya at death. No being is reborn at the first or last instant of a leshya; it goes to the next world only when part of a muhurta of that leshya has passed and part remains (v.58–60).
So choose. Knowing all this, a monk gives up the dark leshyas and stays in the bright ones. The commentary: a person needs no effort for the dark states, which come by long habit; the bright ones are taken up by his own free effort (v.61).

Key verses
3 · The six names

किण्हा णीला य काऊ य, तेऊ पम्हा तहेव य ।
सुक्कलेसा य छट्ठा य, णामाइं तु जहक्कमं ॥

In order, the names are black, blue, grey, fiery, lotus, and sixth, white leshya.
31–32 · The white leshya

अट्टरुद्दाणि वज्जित्ता, धम्मसुक्काणि झायए ।
पसंतचित्ते दंतप्पा, समिए गुत्ते य गुत्तिसु ॥
सरागे वीयरागे वा, उवसंते जिइंदिए ।
एयजोगसमाउत्तो, सुक्कलेसं तु परिणमे ॥

Giving up the troubled and the cruel meditations, he meditates on dharma and on the pure; calm in mind, self-controlled, careful in conduct and guarded; whether still with some attachment or free of it, peaceful and master of the senses. One with these qualities takes on the white leshya.
56 · The dark three

किण्हा णीला काऊ, तिण्णि वि एयाओ अहम्मलेसाओ ।
एयाहि तिहि वि जीवो, दुग्गइं उववज्जइ ॥

Black, blue and grey: these three are leshyas of non-dharma. Through them a soul is born into a bad destiny.
57 · The bright three

तेऊ पम्हा सुक्का, तिण्णि वि एयाओ धम्मलेसाओ ।
एयाहि तिहि वि जीवो, सुग्गइं उववज्जइ ॥

Fiery, lotus and white: these three are leshyas of dharma. Through them a soul is born into a good destiny.
61 · Leave the dark, hold the bright

तम्हा एयासिं लेसाणं, आणुभावे वियाणिया ।
अप्पसत्थाओ वज्जित्ता, पसत्थाओ अहिट्ठए मुणी ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Therefore, knowing the nature of these leshyas, the monk should give up the inauspicious ones and stand firm in the auspicious ones. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.3 · v.31–32 · v.56–57 · v.61

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_35_the_homeless.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 35: The Homeless Monk's Path
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_35_the_homeless.content:
Uttaradhyayan 35 · Anagara Marga Gati: The Homeless Monk’s Path
In one line: a monk who has left home must not let home’s bonds creep back; he lives in a simple place, does not build, cook, buy or sell, eats only to keep going, wants no honour, and so ends all suffering.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 35 (21 verses), translated pages 408–417. 7 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

Why this chapter. Even after leaving home, old habits and deluding karma pull a monk back through three kinds of bonds: family, society, and the wish for position, prestige and wealth. The chapter gives rules to keep him free of all three (introduction).
Listen: this path ends suffering. It is the path taught by the omniscient ones; a monk who walks it brings suffering to an end (v.1).
Know the bonds and drop the five faults. Having left home, the sage should see mother, father, wife and son as bonds in which many get stuck. He gives up violence, falsehood, stealing, sexual conduct, desire and greed (v.2–3).
Where to live. He should not even wish in his mind for a lovely lodging with pictures, garlands, incense and fine doors; in such a place the senses are very hard to hold back. He prefers a cremation ground, an empty house, the foot of a tree, or a place a householder built for himself, free of women, animals and eunuchs, free of living creatures and disturbance (v.4–7).
No building, no cooking, no fire. Building a house harms moving and still beings, subtle and gross, so a monk neither builds nor has others build. Cooking harms the beings living in water, grain, earth and wood, so he neither cooks nor has others cook. There is no weapon like fire, which spreads in every direction, so he lights no fire (v.8–12).
No gold, no trade. Seeing a lump of earth and gold as equal, he does not want silver or gold even in thought. One who buys is a customer and one who sells is a merchant, not a monk. A monk who lives on alms should beg, not buy; trade is a great fault, alms bring happiness (v.13–15).
How to eat. He gathers a little food from many blameless houses, content whether he gets it or not. Not greedy, not attached to taste, he eats “not for taste, but to keep going” in the life of restraint (v.16–17).
No honour, only meditation. He does not wish, even in his mind, for welcome marks, worship, gifts or respect. Free of possessions, of wishes for reward (nidana) and of care for the body, he meditates on the pure until death comes (v.18–19).
The end. When death comes he gives up food (the commentary: through sallekhana and santhara), leaves the human body, and is freed from suffering. Without “mine”, without ego, free of passion and of inflowing karma, he reaches omniscience and lasting nirvana (v.20–21).

Key verses
1 · The path that ends suffering

सुणेह मे एगग्गमणा, मग्गं बुद्धेहिं देसियं ।
जमायरंतो भिक्खू, दुक्खाणंतकरे भवे ॥

Listen to me with a one-pointed mind to the path taught by the enlightened ones. The monk who follows it puts an end to suffering.
8 · No house of one’s own

ण सयं गिहाइं कुव्विज्जा, णेव अण्णेहिं कारए ।
गिहकम्मसमारंभे, भूयाणं दिस्सए वहो ॥

A monk should not build a house himself, nor have others build one, for in house-building the killing of living beings is plainly seen.
13 · Earth and gold alike

हिरण्णं जायरूवं च, मणसा वि ण पत्थए ।
समलेट्ठुकंचणे भिक्खू, विरए कयविक्कए ॥

The monk, to whom a clod of earth and gold are the same, should not wish for silver or gold even in his mind, and keeps away from buying and selling.
17 · Eating to keep going

अलोले ण रसे गिद्धे, जिब्भादंते अमुच्छिए ।
ण रसट्ठाए भुंजिज्जा, जवणट्ठाए महामुणी ॥

Free of greed, not hungry for flavour, his tongue tamed, unattached, the great sage should eat not for taste but to sustain his life of restraint.
21 · The goal

णिम्ममो णिरहंकारो, वीयरागो अणासवो ।
संपत्तो केवलं णाणं, सासयं परिणिव्वुए ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Without possessiveness, without ego, free of passion and of the inflow of karma, he attains perfect knowledge and is liberated for ever. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.1 · v.8 · v.13 · v.17 · v.21

09_modules/uttaradhyayan_36_living_and_n.title: Module · Uttaradhyayan 36: The Living and the Non-living
09_modules/uttaradhyayan_36_living_and_n.content:
Uttaradhyayan 36 · Jivajiva-Vibhakti: The Living and the Non-living
In one line: the whole world is made of the living and the non-living; the chapter maps every kind of each, from atoms to the siddhas, so that a monk who knows and trusts this map delights in restraint, dies well, and reaches liberation.
Source: Uttaradhyayan Sutra Part 2, chapter 36 (274 verses, the last chapter of the sutra), translated pages 418–505. 25 minutes.
What the chapter teaches

The world and the non-world. Where living and non-living things exist is the world (loka); beyond it, where there is only space, is the non-world (aloka). Both have no beginning and no end, so no creator, keeper or destroyer. Everything is described by substance, place, time and state. Knowing the difference between living and non-living is the reason for the chapter: “knowing it, a monk strives rightly in restraint” (v.1–3).
The non-living (ajiva): 14 kinds. Formless are the medium of motion (dharmastikaya, which helps beings and matter move, as water helps a fish), the medium of rest (adharmastikaya, like shade for a tired traveller), and space (akasha), each counted as whole, part and smallest point, plus time: 10 kinds. The first two fill the world, space fills world and non-world, time is counted only in the human region. Matter (pudgala) alone has form: aggregate, part, point and atom, 4 kinds (v.4–10).
Matter and its 530 modes. Atoms join into aggregates and aggregates break into atoms. Matter has 5 colours, 2 smells, 5 tastes, 8 touches and 5 shapes; because these always occur together, their combinations give the 530 modes the commentary counts out (v.11–48).
The liberated (siddhas). Living beings are worldly or liberated. Liberation can come in a female, male or neuter body; in a monk’s own dress, another dress, or a householder’s; from above, below or the middle world, even from the ocean. The verses give how many can be liberated in one instant, for example 108 men, 20 women, 4 householders. Liberated souls are stopped by the non-world and rest at the top of the world, above Siddhashila: an umbrella-shaped earth of white gold, 45 lakh yojanas wide, 8 yojanas thick at the centre and thinner than a fly’s wing at the edge. There they are formless, all knowledge and perception, in a happiness that has no comparison (v.49–68).
Worldly beings: the immobile and the “moving” elements. Worldly beings are mobile or immobile. Earth, water and plant beings are immobile; fire and air are counted with the mobile because they move. Each kind is subtle (filling the whole world) or gross (in one part), developed or undeveloped. Gross earth includes soft clays and 36 hard kinds, from sand and salt to gold, diamond and gems. Plants are either one soul per body (trees, creepers, grasses) or many souls sharing one body (potato, radish, ginger, onion, garlic and other root plants). Fire includes embers, flames, lightning; air includes whirlwinds and pure wind (v.69–126).
Beings with two, three and four senses. Two senses: worms, earthworms, shells, conches, cowries, leeches. Three: ants, termites, lice and other small insects. Four: flies, mosquitoes, bees, moths, scorpions (most four-sensed names are unclear in the source, v.147–149). All live in only part of the world (v.127–155).
Five-sensed beings: hell, animals, humans, gods. Hell beings live in seven earths, from Ratnaprabha to Tamastamahprabha. Animals are born of a womb or spontaneously, and live in water (fish, turtles, crocodiles), on land (one-hoofed, two-hoofed, round-footed and clawed four-footed beasts, and creatures that crawl on limbs or on the belly), or in the air (birds with leathery or feathered wings, and two kinds not seen here). Humans live in the 15 lands of action, 30 lands without action and 56 islands between. Gods are of four classes: 10 kinds of mansion gods, 8 kinds of forest gods, 5 kinds of luminaries (moons, suns, lunar mansions, planets, stars), and the heavenly gods of the 12 heavens, 9 Graiveyakas and 5 Anuttara abodes, the highest being Sarvarthasiddha (v.156–253).
Every kind has its clock. For each group the chapter states the lifespan, how long a soul can keep being reborn in that same group, and the gap before it returns. Each group also has “thousands of varieties” by colour, smell, taste, touch and shape. The maximum lifespans, as the verses give them:






































BeingsLongest lifeEarth / water / plant / air22,000 / 7,000 / 10,000 / 3,000 yearsFire3 days and nightsTwo- / three- / four-sensed12 years / 49 days / 6 monthsHell beings33 sagaropamas (7th hell)Water animals; land animals; birds1 crore purvas; 3 palyopamas; a countless fraction of a palyopamaHumans3 palyopamasGods33 sagaropamas (Sarvarthasiddha)

From knowing to restraint, and a good death. Having heard and believed this account, the monk should delight in restraint. After many years of monk’s life he thins body and passions by sallekhana: at best 12 years (four years without rich foods, four of varied fasts, then alternate-day fasts with ayambil, and a final year of ayambil before giving up food), at middle one year, at least six months (v.254–261).
What spoils the end. Five dispositions lead to a low birth even among gods: frivolous joking and lewd talk (kandarpa), using mantras and charms for comfort (abhiyogiki), deceitfully slandering knowledge, the omniscient, the teacher and the community (kilvishi), nursing anger (asuri), and suicide or gross misconduct (moha). Those who die in wrong belief, with wishes for reward (nidana), violence or the black leshya find awakening (bodhi) hard to regain; those who die in right belief, without nidana and in the white leshya find it easily. Those devoted to the Jina’s word have few births left. A confession should be made to a monk who knows the Agamas, brings peace and sees virtue (v.262–273).
The close of the whole sutra. Thus the enlightened Lord Mahavira, son of the Jnata clan, made known these thirty-six chapters, prized by those fit for liberation (v.274).

Key verses
2 · World and non-world

जीवा चेव अजीवा य, एस लोए वियाहिए ।
अजीव देसमागासे, अलोए से वियाहिए ॥

This world is said to consist of the living and the non-living. Where there is only space, a part of the non-living, that is called the non-world.
57 · Where the liberated rest

अलोए पडिहया सिद्धा, लोयग्गे य पइट्ठिया ।
इहं बोंदिं चइत्ताणं, तत्थ गंतूण सिज्झइ ॥

The liberated are stopped by the non-world and established at the top of the world. Leaving the body here, the soul goes there and attains liberation.
255 · Knowing leads to restraint

इय जीवमजीवे य, सोच्चा सद्दहिऊण य ।
सव्व णयाणमणुमए, रमेज्ज संजमे मुणी ॥

Having thus heard about the living and the non-living and believed it, the monk should delight in restraint, which is approved from every point of view.
264 · Dying in the light

सम्मदंसणरत्ता, अणियाणा सुक्कलेसमोगाढा ।
इय जे मरंति जीवा, तेसिं सुलहा भवे बोही ॥

Those who die devoted to right belief, free of wishes for reward and steeped in the white leshya will find awakening easy to attain.
274 · The end of the sutra

इइ पाउकरे बुद्धे, णायए परिणिव्वुए ॥
छत्तीसं उत्तरज्झाए, भवसिद्धिय सम्मए ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Thus the enlightened one of the Jnata clan, who reached nirvana, made known the thirty-six chapters of the Uttaradhyayan, held dear by souls fit for liberation. Thus I say.
Verses checked against the scans: v.2 · v.57 · v.255 · v.264 · v.274

10_course/00_course_home.title: Course: Learning Jainism from the Agamas
10_course/00_course_home.content:
Learning Jainism from the Agamas
38 lessons in 6 units · one lesson a day takes about six weeks; one a week, about nine months
This course teaches Jain dharma from the scriptures themselves. Every verse it quotes was checked by hand against the printed page of the Gujarati edition (jainaagam.org). Nothing comes from outside the books.
How each lesson works

Read the module or learning-path page it points to (the source).
Key ideas: the three things to take away.
Reflect: three questions about your own life. Write a line or two for each.
Practice this week: one small thing to do.
Self-check: open each question only after you have tried to answer it.

Keep the concept pages open: karma, the six substances, the nine tattvas, leshya, ahimsa and the rest are explained there, each from the source.
Unit 1 · Foundations
What Jainism is, what is real, and how that turns into daily living. Start here.

Lesson 1 · What Jainism Is (30 min): You will be able to say in your own words whom a Jain bows to, what dharma is, and what the goal of the path is and how it is reached.
Lesson 2 · Soul, Matter and Karma (35 min): You will be able to explain what the soul is, what the world is made of, and how karma binds the soul and is shed, and why that makes your joys and sufferings your own.
Lesson 3 · Non-violence and Awareness (30 min): You will understand why harming none is the centre of the Jain path, and how care, simplicity, evenness and humility turn it into daily living.
Lesson 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions (40 min): You will understand how a householder’s twelve vows scale down the monk’s great vows, what makes speech right, and how each of the four passions is met by its opposite.
Lesson 5 · Forgiveness and Friendship (30 min): You will understand why the Agamas ask for friendship toward every being and forgiveness in both directions, and how humility, careful words and judging by deeds follow from that.

Unit 2 · Waking up (Uttaradhyayan)
The great wake-up chapters and stories: the rare human life, the falling leaf, Nami, Harikeshi, Mrigaputra, Keshi and Gautama.

Lesson 6 · Four Rare Things, a Falling Leaf (35 min): You will see why the Uttaradhyayan calls this human life rare and short, and why its answer is not fear but wakefulness: do not be careless (pramada), even for a moment.
Lesson 7 · Life Cannot Be Mended; Two Kinds of Death (35 min): You will understand why the Uttaradhyayan says dharma cannot be put off, and how the way you live decides whether you meet death in fear or in calm.
Lesson 8 · Free of Knots; the Ram; Kapila's Greed (45 min): You will understand three warnings: knowing without doing does not untie the knots, a human life is capital not to be spent on small pleasures, and greed only grows as it is fed.
Lesson 9 · Nami's Renunciation (30 min): You will be able to follow King Nami’s dialogue with Indra and see how each worldly duty he is pressed with is turned inward: the real city, fort, war and wealth are inside the soul.
Lesson 10 · Worth Is in Deeds, Not Birth (40 min): You will understand, through two stories of monks turned away at a sacrifice, why the Uttaradhyayan judges a person by conduct and not by birth, and why it calls the true sacrifice and the true bath inner ones.
Lesson 11 · Bonds of Family and Past Lives (30 min): You will see how two chapters treat family love: as a real bond that can carry souls across many lives, but not a refuge at death, where only your own deeds and dharma go with you.
Lesson 12 · Kings and Princes Who Woke (45 min): You will understand, through three royal stories, what it means in the texts to be “protected”: not by power, money or family, but by your own soul set on the right path.
Lesson 13 · Samudrapala and Rathanemi (30 min): You will see two ways the path is kept: by being woken once and then staying steady through hardship (Samudrapala), and by being pulled back by a good friend’s firm words when you waver (Rathanemi and Rajemati).
Lesson 14 · Keshi and Gautama (30 min): You will understand how two great monks with different rules settled their differences with courtesy, and why the texts say the real path is inner: conquering the self, the mind and the passions.

Unit 3 · The disciple’s life (Uttaradhyayan)
How a disciple lives: humility, bearing hardship, guarding the mind, and a day lived well.

Lesson 15 · Humility and Learning (35 min): You will understand why the Uttaradhyayan begins with humility (vinaya), how humility opens the door to learning, and what kind of student makes a teacher’s work light or heavy.
Lesson 16 · Hardship and the True Monk (40 min): You will understand the twenty-two hardships (parishaha) a monk learns to bear, and the marks that separate a true monk from one who is a monk “only in dress and name”.
Lesson 17 · Guarding the Mind: Celibacy, the Eight Mothers, the Homeless Path (40 min): You will understand how a monk guards his practice from the outside in: ten supports for celibacy, the eight “mothers of the teaching” (five careful actions and three restraints), and the rules that keep home’s bonds from creeping back.
Lesson 18 · A Day Lived Well (35 min): You will see how a monk’s whole day and night is laid out as one careful routine, and how all of conduct comes down to a single rule: turn away from lack of restraint and turn toward restraint.

Unit 4 · The path and reality (Uttaradhyayan)
The path to liberation, right effort, austerity, karma, the colours of the soul, and the map of the living and non-living.

Lesson 19 · The Path to Liberation (35 min): You will be able to name the four parts of the path to liberation (knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity), say what each one does, and explain why faith comes first.
Lesson 20 · Right Effort: 73 Questions (50 min): You will understand how one simple question, “Lord, what does the soul gain by this?”, turns 73 practices into a map of the path, and you will be able to pick one practice and say what it brings.
Lesson 21 · Austerity and the Roots of Negligence (35 min): You will understand how austerity (tapa) dries up old karma once the inflow is stopped, and why the texts say suffering comes from our attachment and aversion, not from the things we see, hear, smell, taste and touch.
Lesson 22 · Karma and the Colours of the Soul (30 min): You will be able to name the eight kinds of karma, say what decides how long and how strongly karma acts, and recognise the six “colours” (leshya) of the soul in ordinary moods and actions.
Lesson 23 · The Living and the Non-living (35 min): You will be able to sketch the Jain map of the world, from atoms to the liberated souls, and say why the Uttaradhyayan ends its teaching with this map: knowing what is alive is what makes restraint possible.

Unit 5 · Careful living (Dashvaikalik)
The Dashvaikalik’s guide to careful living: the six kinds of living beings, alms, speech, the passions and humility.

Lesson 24 · Dharma and the Bee (40 min): You will understand the Dashvaikalik’s opening definition of dharma, the bee as the picture of harmless living, and why giving up desire, not just going without, is the ground of a monk’s life.
Lesson 25 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings (35 min): You will be able to name the six kinds of living beings, explain the monk’s six vows and the “nine ways” of giving up harm, and see why the Dashvaikalik’s answer to “how should I live?” is one word: with care.
Lesson 26 · Alms and the Great Conduct (40 min): You will understand how a monk seeks, receives and eats food without harming anyone, what the eighteen points of “great conduct” are built on, and what the texts ask of the giver as well as the taker.
Lesson 27 · Pure Speech and the Treasure of Conduct (35 min): You will be able to test your words the way the Dashvaikalik tests a monk’s, and use its plain remedies for anger, pride, deceit and greed in daily life.
Lesson 28 · Humility's Composure; the True Monk (35 min): You will understand why the Dashvaikalik calls humility (vinaya) the root of dharma, what four kinds of composure it leads to, and how a true monk is known by his virtues rather than his dress.
Lesson 29 · Staying the Course (30 min): You will know what the Dashvaikalik offers when the wish to keep going fades, and you will be able to use its nightly self-examination to steady your own practice.

Unit 6 · The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak)

Lesson 30 · Knowing the Weapon: Harm to the Six Kinds of Life (30 min): You will understand why the Acharang begins with the soul and then walks through earth, water, fire, plants, moving creatures and air, and what it means to “know the weapon” and put it down.
Lesson 31 · Conquering the World; Cold and Heat (30 min): You will see that the “world” the Acharang asks you to conquer is the sense of “mine” inside you, and how to meet pleasant and painful things with the same even, wakeful mind.
Lesson 32 · Right Faith and the Essence of the World (30 min): You will be able to state the one dharma the Acharang says every Tirthankara teaches, explain why bondage and freedom depend on your inner state, and say what the book calls the essence of the world.
Lesson 33 · Shaking Off, Liberation, and Mahavira's Own Practice (35 min): You will understand how the last chapters of Acharang Book 1 describe a monk shaking off karma and growing lighter step by step, and how Mahavira himself lived every one of these teachings.
Lesson 34 · The Careful Monk: Alms, Lodging, Walking, Speech (70 min): You will see how Book 2 of the Acharang turns the non-violence of Book 1 into everyday detail (how a monk seeks food, finds a place to stay, walks the road and speaks) and you will be able to apply its rules of speech to your own talk.
Lesson 35 · Few Possessions; the Five Great Vows and Their Bhavanas (70 min): You will understand how little a monk keeps and how he holds it, how Mahavira’s own life leads into the five great vows with their twenty-five supporting reflections (bhavana), and what “release” means in the last chapter of the Acharang.
Lesson 36 · Samayik, Praise of the 24, and Bowing (45 min): You will know what the six daily essentials (avashyak) are and why they come in their order, understand the words of the Namaskar Mantra, the Samayik pledge, the Logassa and the bow to the Guru, and be able to sit one samayik of your own.
Lesson 37 · Pratikraman, Kayotsarga, Pratyakhyan (65 min): You will understand the last three daily essentials as one movement (look back at the day’s faults, heal them in stillness, then close the door on new ones) and be able to keep one small time-bound vow of your own.
Lesson 38 · The Householder's Twelve Vows (40 min): You will know the twelve vows of a lay follower (five small vows, three supporting vows, four training vows), see how each is sized to household life, and be able to choose one vow, or one part of one, to try for yourself.

10_course/concepts/00_concepts.title: Concepts
10_course/concepts/00_concepts.content:
Concepts
Short reference pages for the ideas that come up again and again in the course. Each page says what the idea is in plain words, where the sources teach it, gives one checked verse, and links to the lessons that use it.
Reality

Six Substances: motion, rest, space, time, matter and souls; the whole world, with no creator (Utt 28, 36)
Nine Realities (Tattvas): soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, sin, inflow, stopping, shedding, liberation (Utt 28, 30)
Karma: fine matter bound by attachment and aversion; eight kinds; stopped and shed (Utt 32, 33)
Leshya: the six colours of the soul, three dark and three bright (Utt 34)
Five Knowledges: sensory, scriptural, clairvoyant, mind-reading and omniscient knowledge (Utt 28, 29, 33)

The path

Ratnatraya (the Three Jewels): right faith, knowledge and conduct, with austerity as a fourth (Utt 28, 23)
Ahimsa: non-violence, the first part of dharma (Dash 1, 4, 6)
Samyama: restraint of senses, speech, body and mind (Dash 1, Utt 1, 5)
Tapas: twelve austerities, outer and inner, that burn karma (Utt 30, Dash 9)

Inner work

Kashaya: anger, pride, deceit and greed, and their four antidotes (Dash 8, Utt 23, 33)
Vinaya: humility, the root of the tree of dharma (Dash 9, Utt 1)
Parishaha: the twenty-two hardships, borne calmly (Utt 2, 15, 21)

Careful living

Samiti and Gupti: the eight mothers of the teaching, five careful actions and three restraints (Utt 24)
Bhramar Vritti (the Bee's Way): taking a little from many, harming none (Dash 1, 5)


Course home

10_course/concepts/ahimsa.title: Concept · Ahimsa
10_course/concepts/ahimsa.content:
Concept · Ahimsa
What it is
Non-violence (ahimsa) is the first part of Jain dharma and the centre of its conduct. It rests on one plain fact: every living being, from an earth-being to a human, loves its life and does not want pain. So ahimsa means not killing, but also not bullying, enslaving, tormenting or harassing any being, in mind, speech or body. The Dashvaikalik’s commentary defines it as seeing all beings as equal to yourself. It is not passive: it needs knowledge of what is alive, and care in every act.
In the sources

The first word of dharma. Dharma is non-violence, restraint and austerity (Dash 1.1). See Dash 1 · The Monk and the Bee and Foundations §3.
The first of the eighteen places of conduct. Mahavira taught non-violence first, “restraint towards all living beings”; all beings wish to live, not to die (Dash 6.9–11). See Dash 6 · The Great Conduct.
Six kinds of beings. Earth, water, fire, air, plants and moving beings are all alive; the monk gives up harming all six in nine ways (doing, causing, approving, by mind, speech and body) (Dash 4, s.4–6). See Dash 4.
The householder’s version. Ananda renounces gross harm, in two ways and three modes; the monk renounces all harm in three ways (Upasakdashang 1.16; Dash 4 s.7). See Conduct §2 and §6.
Every life is dear. Seeing that every being holds its life dear, do not take life, and turn from fear and enmity (Utt 6.7). See Utt 6. Prince Arishtanemi turns back from his own wedding when he sees the animals penned for the feast (Utt 22.16–19). See Utt 22.
Give fearlessness. The sage tells the hunting king: you are safe from me; now become a giver of safety to others (Utt 18.11). See Utt 18.
First knowledge, then compassion. You cannot protect life you do not know is there (Dash 4.10). See Way of Life §5.

One verse

सव्वे जीवा वि इच्छंति, जीविउं ण मरिज्जिउं ।
तम्हा पाणिवहं घोरं, णिग्गंथा वज्जयंति णं ॥

All living beings wish to live, not to die. Therefore the Nirgranthas give up the terrible killing of living beings.
Source: Dashvaikalik 6.11 · module (verse checked against the scan)
Related

Concepts: Restraint · Austerity · Samiti and gupti · The bee's way · Six substances
Lessons: 1 · What Jainism Is · 3 · Non-violence and Awareness · 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions · 8 · Free of Knots; the Ram; Kapila's Greed · 12 · Kings and Princes Who Woke · 13 · Samudrapala and Rathanemi · 24 · Dharma and the Bee · 25 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings · 26 · Alms and the Great Conduct

10_course/concepts/bhramar_vritti.title: Concept · Bhramar_Vritti
10_course/concepts/bhramar_vritti.content:
Concept · Bhramar Vritti (the Bee’s Way)
What it is
Bhramar vritti, “the bee’s way of living”, is the Dashvaikalik’s picture for how a monk gets his food without harm. A bee (bhamara) drinks a little nectar from many flowers and does not make any of them wither. In the same way the monk takes a little from many homes, only food the family cooked for itself and gives gladly, stores nothing, and depends on no one house. It answers a real problem: the body needs food, and getting food seems impossible without harm. The bee’s way is non-violence applied to eating, and the monk eats only to keep up his life of restraint, not for taste. The term “bhramar vritti” itself is not used in the modules; they speak of the bee (Dash 1.2–5).
In the sources

The bee and the flower. The bee drinks nectar without making the flower wither; so monks, free of ties, seek food that is given to them (Dash 1.2–3). See Dash 1 · The Monk and the Bee.
Where the monk differs from the bee. The bee takes nectar no one gave it; the monk takes only what is given gladly, does not cook or have food cooked, takes a little from each house and goes to rich, middle and poor homes alike (Dash 1.3 commentary). The commentary also gives gochari, the cow’s way of grazing: a mouthful here and there, never pulling up the roots (Dash 1.4 commentary).
Made into rules. Food made, bought or brought for the monk is refused; food is refused if giving it hurts a living being or causes anyone pain or loss (Dash 5.1.27–81). Whatever he receives, he eats “as if it were ghee and sugar” (Dash 5.1.97). See Dash 5 · Seeking Alms.
Giver and taker. The one who gives expecting nothing and the one who lives without giving anything in return are both rare, and both reach a good state (Dash 5.1.100).
The same way elsewhere. He takes a little from many homes and stores nothing (Dash 8, v.22–28); alms gathered from many houses, a little from households that did not expect him (Dash 12.5). See Dash 12. He should eat “not for taste but to sustain his life of restraint” (Utt 35.17). See Utt 35.

One verse

वयं च वित्तिं लब्भामो, ण य कोइ उवहम्मइ ।
अहागडेसु रीयंते, पुप्फेसु भमरा जहा ॥

We will get our living in such a way that no living being is harmed. As bees go among flowers, we will take from food that householders have made for themselves.
Source: Dashvaikalik 1.4 · module (verse checked against the scan)
Related

Concepts: Non-violence · Samiti and gupti (careful seeking, eshana samiti) · Restraint · Austerity
Lessons: 17 · Guarding the Mind: Celibacy, the Eight Mothers, the Homeless Path · 24 · Dharma and the Bee · 26 · Alms and the Great Conduct · 27 · Pure Speech and the Treasure of Conduct · 29 · Staying the Course

10_course/concepts/five_knowledges.title: Concept · Five_Knowledges
10_course/concepts/five_knowledges.content:
Concept · Five Knowledges
What it is
Knowledge (jnana) is the soul’s own nature, and the Uttaradhyayan names five kinds of it: sensory knowledge (mati), scriptural knowledge (shruta), clairvoyance (avadhi), knowing the thoughts of others (manahparyava) and omniscience (kevala). Most of the time this knowledge is covered over by knowledge-obscuring karma, which itself comes in five kinds, one for each. Study, reflection and the end of attachment wear that covering away, until the soul knows and sees everything. The sources name the five but say little about each one; what they stress is how knowledge is uncovered and what it is for.
In the sources

The five, named. Knowledge is of five kinds, and it knows substances, their qualities and their changing states (Utt 28.4–6). See Utt 28 · The Path to Liberation.
Covered by karma. The first of the eight karmas is knowledge-obscuring, “a cloud over the sun”, with five sub-kinds (Utt 33.2–4). See Utt 33 · The Nature of Karma.
A teacher with three. Keshi came to Shravasti “with three kinds of knowledge” (Utt 23.3); the commentary names them as sensory, scriptural and clairvoyant. See Utt 23 · Keshi and Gautama.
How it is uncovered. Keeping the times for study and self-study (svadhyaya) destroy knowledge-obscuring karma (Utt 29 s.17, s.20); a soul that holds the scripture is like a threaded needle that is not lost (s.61). See Utt 29 · Right Effort.
Omniscience. Conquering attachment, aversion and wrong belief brings omniscience (Utt 29 s.73); the detached soul destroys the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring and obstructing karmas “in a moment” and knows and sees everything (Utt 32.106–111). See Utt 32.
What knowledge is for. First knowledge, then compassion (Dash 4.10); on the ladder of Dash 4, knowing the living and non-living leads at last to perfect knowledge and perception (Dash 4.14–25). See Dash 4. The essence of knowledge is to harm no one (Way of Life §4).

One verse

जहा सूई ससुत्ता, पडिया वि ण विणस्सइ ।
तहा जीवे ससुत्ते, संसारे ण विणस्सइ ॥

A needle with its thread is not lost, even when it falls. In the same way, a soul that holds the scripture is not lost in the world.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 29, sutra 61 · module (passage checked against the scan). No verse naming the five kinds (Utt 28.4) is among the checked verses, so it is not quoted here.
Related

Concepts: The three jewels · Karma · Six substances · Austerity (study is an inner austerity)
Lessons: 2 · Soul, Matter and Karma · 14 · Keshi and Gautama · 19 · The Path to Liberation · 20 · Right Effort: 73 Questions · 21 · Austerity and the Roots of Negligence · 22 · Karma and the Colours of the Soul · 25 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings

10_course/concepts/karma.title: Concept · Karma
10_course/concepts/karma.content:
Concept · Karma
What it is
In the Agamas, karma is not fate and not a moral score kept by a god. It is fine, lifeless matter that sticks to the soul whenever the soul acts with attachment and aversion (raga and dvesha). The soul is in itself pure consciousness, but it has been mixed with karma since beginningless time, “as gold and earth lie mixed in a mine”. Karma does not add anything new to the soul; it covers and limits what the soul already has: its knowledge, perception, happiness and energy. Because you bind it, you can also stop it and wear it away, which is what the whole path is for.
In the sources

Why the soul wanders. Bound by eight kinds of karma, the soul goes round in samsara: knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, lifespan, body-making (nama), status (gotra) and obstructing (antaraya) (Utt 33.1–3). See Utt 33 · The Nature of Karma and Reality §7.
Four ways it binds. Karma is bound by nature, duration, intensity and quantity. Nature and quantity come from activity (yoga); duration and intensity come from the passions (kashaya). Deluding karma can last longest, seventy crore-crore sagaropamas (Utt 33.2–3 commentary, 33.21).
The chain. Attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma, karma is the root of birth and death, and birth and death are suffering (Utt 32.7). See Utt 32 · Sources of Negligence.
No one can carry it for you. Mother, father, wife and sons cannot protect you “when you suffer from your own karma”; karma follows only the one who did it (Utt 6.3, 13.23). See Relationships §11.
You are your own friend or enemy. The soul is the maker and unmaker of its own sufferings and joys (Utt 20.37). See Utt 20 · The Great Nirgrantha.
How it ends. Stop the inflow, then dry up what is stored, like a lake whose streams are blocked (Utt 30.5–6); knowing karma, the wise strive “to stop them and to destroy them” (Utt 33.25). See Utt 30 · The Path of Austerity.

One verse

रागो य दोसो वि य कम्मबीयं, कम्मं च मोहप्पभवं वयंति ।
कम्मं च जाईमरणस्स मूलं, दुक्खं च जाईमरणं वयंति ॥

Attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma; karma, the wise say, arises from delusion. Karma is the root of birth and death, and birth and death, they say, are suffering.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 32.7 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/kashaya.title: Concept · Kashaya
10_course/concepts/kashaya.content:
Concept · Kashaya
What it is
The passions (kashaya) are four: anger (krodha), pride (mana), deceit (maya) and greed (lobha). They are what make karma stick hard and long: the strength of the passions at the moment of acting sets how long a karma stays bound and how strongly it acts. Each passion has its own casualty in daily life, and each has an antidote: calm for anger, gentleness for pride, straightforwardness for deceit, contentment for greed. Conquering them, together with the senses, is what the texts call conquering yourself.
In the sources

What each destroys, and the cure. Anger destroys love, pride humility, deceit friendship, greed everything; kill anger with calm, pride with gentleness, deceit with straightforwardness, greed with contentment; unchecked, the four “water the roots of rebirth” (Dash 8.37–40). See Dash 8 · The Treasure of Conduct and Conduct §9–10.
They set karma’s length and strength. Duration and intensity of karma come from the passions; deluding karma includes sixteen passions (Utt 33.2–3 commentary, 33.4–15, 33.24). See Utt 33 · The Nature of Karma.
The real enemy. The one unconquered self is the enemy, and so are the passions and the senses; the fire inside the body is the passions, put out by scripture, good conduct and austerity (Utt 23.38, 23.50–54). See Utt 23 · Keshi and Gautama.
Conquer the self, conquer all. The five senses, anger, pride, deceit and greed: when the self is conquered, all are conquered (Utt 9.36). See Utt 9 · Nami's Renunciation.
Greed grows with gain. What two mashas of gold would have done was not done by crores (Utt 8.17). See Utt 8 · Kapila and Greed.
Each conquest has its fruit. Conquering anger brings forgiveness, pride softness, deceit straightforwardness, greed contentment (Utt 29 s.69–72); longing for liberation destroys the passions “that bind without end” (s.3). See Utt 29.
Do not speak under a passion. Careful speech stays watchful of anger, pride, deceit and greed (Utt 24.9–10). See Utt 24.

One verse

उवसमेण हणे कोहं, माणं मद्दवया जिणे ।
मायं च अज्जवभावेण, लोभं संतोसओ जिणे ॥

Kill anger with calm, conquer pride with gentleness, deceit with straightforwardness, and greed with contentment.
Source: Dashvaikalik 8.39 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/leshya.title: Concept · Leshya
10_course/concepts/leshya.content:
Concept · Leshya
What it is
Leshya is the “colour” of the soul: its states as they are coloured by the passions. The Uttaradhyayan names six, from dark to bright: black (krishna), blue (nila), grey (kapota), fiery red (tejo), lotus yellow (padma) and white (shukla). The first three are leshyas of non-dharma and lead to a bad birth; the last three are leshyas of dharma and lead to a good one. Each person’s leshya shows in how they live: the cruel and careless in the dark ones, the calm, humble and guarded in the bright ones. The commentary’s point is hopeful: the dark states come by long habit, the bright ones are taken up by your own effort.
In the sources

What it is. There is a material leshya with colour, smell, taste and touch, and an inner, formless one, and each arises with the other (Utt 34, introduction). See Utt 34 · The Colours of the Soul.
The six names and colours. Black like a rain cloud, blue like a blue jay’s feather, grey like a pigeon’s neck, red like the rising sun, yellow like turmeric, white like a conch or a stream of milk (Utt 34.3–9).
The marks of each. Black: one who harms the six kinds of beings and has not conquered the senses. Yellow: little anger, pride, deceit and greed, a calm mind. White: one who meditates on dharma and the pure, careful (samita) and guarded (gupta) (Utt 34.21–32).
Where they lead. Black, blue and grey lead to a bad destiny; fiery, lotus and white to a good one (Utt 34.56–57).
The leshya at death. Those who die in right belief, without wishes for reward and in the white leshya find awakening easy; those who die in the black leshya find it hard (Utt 36.264). See Utt 36.
In the monk’s daily list. Among the rules of conduct: take care over the six leshyas, keeping to the three bright ones (Utt 31.8). See Utt 31 · Rules of Conduct.

One verse

तम्हा एयासिं लेसाणं, आणुभावे वियाणिया ।
अप्पसत्थाओ वज्जित्ता, पसत्थाओ अहिट्ठए मुणी ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Therefore, knowing the nature of these leshyas, the monk should give up the inauspicious ones and stand firm in the auspicious ones. Thus I say.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 34.61 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/nine_tattvas.title: Concept · Nine_Tattvas
10_course/concepts/nine_tattvas.content:
Concept · Nine Realities (Tattvas)
What it is
The nine realities (tattva) tell the whole story of the soul in one list: soul (jiva), non-soul (ajiva), bondage (bandha), merit (punya), demerit or sin (papa), inflow of karma (ashrava), stopping the inflow (samvara), shedding karma (nirjara) and liberation (moksha). Soul meets matter, karma flows in and binds, then the inflow is stopped and the old karma is shed until the soul is free. The Uttaradhyayan says that truly believing in these nine is right faith (samyaktva). They are less a theory than a map for action: close the door, then clear the room.
In the sources

The list. The nine are named in Utt 28.14, and the next verse says faith in them, “from within or through teaching”, is right faith (Utt 28.15). See Utt 28 · The Path to Liberation and Reality §6.
Inflow and stopping it. A soul that gives up killing, lying, stealing, sex, possessions and eating at night, and keeps the samitis and guptis, lets no new karma in (Utt 30.1–4). See Utt 30 · The Path of Austerity.
Samvara before nirjara. The lake dries up only once its streams are blocked; then austerity sheds the karma of crores of births (Utt 30.5–6). See Reality §9.
Merit is bondage too. The commentary on Utt 33.25 says good and bad karma alike are bondage; the wise strive to stop karma and destroy it. See Utt 33 · The Nature of Karma.
The closed boat. One who sees all beings as himself “has closed the doors of karmic inflow” and binds no bad karma, like a boat without holes (Dash 4.9). The same chapter’s ladder runs from knowing the living and non-living, to merit and sin, bondage and liberation, to the siddha at the top of the universe (Dash 4.14–25). See Dash 4 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings.
Liberation. The liberated are stopped by the non-world and rest at the top of the world (Utt 36.57). See Utt 36.

One verse

जहा महातलायस्स, सण्णिरुद्धे जलागमे ।
उस्सिंचणाए तवणाए, कमेणं सोसणा भवे ॥
एवं तु संजयस्सावि, पावकम्म णिरासवे ।
भवकोडी संचियं कम्मं, तवसा णिज्जरिज्जइ ॥

When the water flowing into a great lake is blocked, it slowly dries up as it is drawn out and heated by the sun. In the same way, when a restrained monk stops sinful karma from coming in, the karma gathered over crores of births is shed through austerity.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 30.5–6 · module (verses checked against the scan). The verse listing the nine (Utt 28.14) is quoted in Reality §6.

10_course/concepts/parishaha.title: Concept · Parishaha
10_course/concepts/parishaha.content:
Concept · Parishaha
What it is
Parishaha means a hardship that comes by itself while one keeps one’s vows: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insects, abuse, a beating, getting nothing, illness, even honour and doubt. Mahavira named twenty-two of them, and the monk learns them in advance so that he does not waver when they arrive. They differ from austerity, which a monk chooses; a hardship simply happens. Borne calmly, inside the rules, it is not an obstacle but a help in shedding karma. The key move is in the mind: “the soul is not destroyed”, “perhaps tomorrow”, “this is the fruit of my own karma”.
In the sources

Twenty-two hardships. Mahavira named them; a monk hears, understands and practises bearing them so that he is not beaten by any (Utt 2, prose and v.1, v.46). See Utt 2 · Enduring Hardships.
Inside the rules. Even gripped by hunger, the monk does not cut or cook food; thirsty, he drinks no living water (Utt 2.2–5).
Abuse and blows. He does not flare up, for then he becomes like the fool; struck, he reflects that the soul cannot be destroyed (Utt 2.24, 2.27). The true monk takes abuse and beating as the fruit of his own actions (Utt 15.3). See Utt 15 · The True Monk.
Honour is a hardship too. Greetings from kings and the wealthy are a “favourable hardship” not to be craved (Utt 2.38–39).
Like an elephant, like Meru. When hardships come, the monk is unshaken like a royal elephant at the head of battle, or like Mount Meru in the wind (Utt 21.17, 21.19). See Utt 21 · Samudrapala.
Like the earth. Insulted, beaten or wounded, he stays like the earth, wanting no reward and no revenge (Dash 10.13). See Dash 10 · The True Monk. Bodily suffering borne calmly “brings great fruit” (Dash 8.27). See Dash 8.
What helps. Forgiveness conquers hardships (Utt 29 s.48). See Utt 29.

One verse

अज्जेवाहं ण लब्भामि, अवि लाभो सुए सिया ।
जो एवं पडिसंचिक्खे, अलाभो तं ण तज्जए ॥३१॥

“Today I have received nothing; perhaps tomorrow I will.” The hardship of getting nothing does not trouble the one who reflects like this.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 2.31 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/ratnatraya.title: Concept · Ratnatraya
10_course/concepts/ratnatraya.content:
Concept · Ratnatraya (the Three Jewels)
What it is
The three jewels (ratnatraya) are right faith (samyak darshana), right knowledge (samyak jnana) and right conduct (samyak charitra), practised together as one path to liberation. Faith comes first: without seeing things rightly, knowledge is not right knowledge, and without right knowledge, conduct does not arise. The Uttaradhyayan often counts the path as four, adding austerity (tapa) to the three, and says each part does its own work. The word “ratnatraya” itself does not appear in the module texts; the commentaries call these “the three jewels”.
In the sources

The path in four parts. Knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity: this is the path taught by the Jinas (Utt 28.2–3). See Utt 28 · The Path to Liberation and Foundations §7.
The order matters. No right knowledge without faith, no conduct without knowledge, no freedom without conduct (Utt 28.29–30). See Foundations §8.
What each does. Knowledge knows, faith believes, conduct holds karma back, austerity purifies (Utt 28.35); the commentary compares it to a patient who must understand the illness, trust the doctor, take the medicine and keep the diet.
The real means of liberation. Dress and outer marks are only aids; on knowledge, faith and conduct both Tirthankaras agree (Utt 23.29–34). The commentary on Utt 23.2 calls Keshi a master of “the three jewels”. See Utt 23 · Keshi and Gautama.
Open to anyone. The commentary on Utt 12.37 says the door to liberation is open to anyone, of any caste, country or sex, who practises the three jewels purely. See Utt 12. The restrained “who hold the three jewels” do not tremble at death (Utt 5.29). See Utt 5.
Made full. Fullness of knowledge keeps the soul from getting lost, like a threaded needle; fullness of faith keeps its light from going out; fullness of conduct brings the rock-still state (Utt 29 s.61–63). See Utt 29.
Conduct as the third jewel for a householder: the twelve vows (see Conduct, introduction).

One verse

णादंसणिस्स णाणं, णाणेण विणा ण हुंति चरणगुणा ।
अगुणिस्स णत्थि मोक्खो, णत्थि अमोक्खस्स णिव्वाणं ॥

Without faith there is no right knowledge; without knowledge the virtues of conduct do not arise. Without those virtues there is no freedom from karma, and without that freedom there is no nirvana.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 28.30 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/samiti_gupti.title: Concept · Samiti_Gupti
10_course/concepts/samiti_gupti.content:
Concept · Samiti and Gupti
What it is
Samiti and gupti together are the “eight mothers of the teaching” (pravachana-mata). The five samitis are kinds of careful action: careful walking, speaking, seeking (food and other needs), picking up and putting down things, and disposing of waste. The three guptis are restraints of mind, speech and body. The commentary calls them two sides of one coin: samiti tells you how to act, gupti tells you what to stop. Like a mother caring for her child, they protect the one who keeps them, and the whole of the Jina’s teaching is said to fit inside them.
In the sources

The eight mothers. Five careful actions and three restraints; stated briefly, they contain the Jina’s whole twelve-part teaching (Utt 24.1–3). See Utt 24 · Mothers of the Teaching.
Careful walking. Watch living beings with the eyes, look a yoke’s length ahead, walk only by day, and walk with full attention, even setting study aside while walking (Utt 24.4–8). The same rule appears in the alms round: walk looking a yoke’s length ahead, avoiding seeds, plants and creatures (Dash 5.1.3). See Dash 5.
Careful speech. Give up anger, pride, deceit, greed, laughter, fear, chatter and idle talk, and speak blameless, measured words at the right time (Utt 24.9–10).
The three restraints. Mind and speech are turned back whenever they plan harm, gather the means for it, or begin it; the body is restrained in standing, sitting, lying and moving (Utt 24.19–25). Guarding the mind gives one-pointedness, guarding speech a mind free of agitation, guarding the body stops sinful inflow (Utt 29 s.55–57). See Utt 29.
They stop the inflow. A soul that keeps the five samitis and three guptis lets no new karma in (Utt 30.1–4). See Utt 30. The white leshya belongs to one “careful in conduct and guarded” (Utt 34.31–32). See Utt 34.
In the stories. Harikesha (Utt 12), Mrigaputra (Utt 19) and Nami, whose fort of faith is guarded by the three restraints (Utt 9.20), all keep them. See Utt 9.
The root idea: care. Walk, stand, sit, lie, eat and speak with care (yatana), and you bind no bad karma (Dash 4.8). See Way of Life §6.

One verse

एयाओ पंच समिईओ, चरणस्स य पवत्तणे ।
गुत्ती णियत्तणे वुत्ता, असुभत्थेसु सव्वसो ॥

These five careful actions are for carrying out right conduct; the restraints are for turning back completely from everything harmful.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 24.26 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/samyama.title: Concept · Samyama
10_course/concepts/samyama.content:
Concept · Samyama
What it is
Restraint (samyama) means turning away from harmful activity and holding yourself back: your senses, your speech, your body and your mind. It is the second part of dharma, next to non-violence and austerity, and the Dashvaikalik’s commentary says the two need each other: non-violence is the goal, and restraint is keeping the rules that reach it. Restraint is what stops new karma coming in. The texts insist it is better chosen than imposed: tame yourself, or others will.
In the sources

Part of dharma itself. Dharma is non-violence, restraint and austerity; the commentary lists seventeen kinds of restraint, from care for earth, water, fire, air and plant beings to restraint of mind, speech and body (Dash 1.1 and commentary). See Dash 1 · The Monk and the Bee.
The rarest of the four rare things. Human birth, hearing the dharma, faith, and energy for restraint (Utt 3.1). See Foundations §4.
Better by my own hand. It is better to tame myself through restraint and austerity than be tamed by others with chains and blows (Utt 1.15–16). See Utt 1 · Humility.
Not only for monks. Some householders are higher in restraint than some monks (Utt 5.20). See Utt 5 · Two Kinds of Death.
What it does. Restraint makes one free of sin and stops the inflow; austerity then purifies (Utt 29 s.28–29). Restraint and austerity together destroy past karma (Utt 28.36; Dash 3.15). See Utt 29 · Right Effort.
Knowing leads to restraint. Having heard and believed the account of the living and non-living, the monk should delight in restraint (Utt 36.255). See Utt 36.
When restraint feels dull. For the monk who wants to go home, the first chulika gives eighteen points to reflect on, and says restraint is like heaven for those who delight in it and like hell for those who do not (Dash 11, sutra 2, v.10). See Dash 11 · Delight in Restraint.

One verse

संति एगेहिं भिक्खूहिं, गारत्था संजमुत्तरा ।
गारत्थेहि य सव्वेहिं, साहवो संजमुत्तरा ॥

Some householders are higher in restraint (samyama) than some monks; but true monks are higher in restraint than all householders.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 5.20 · module (verse checked against the scan)

10_course/concepts/six_substances.title: Concept · Six_Substances
10_course/concepts/six_substances.content:
Concept · Six Substances
What it is
The Agamas describe the whole world (loka) as made of six substances (dravya): the medium of motion (dharmastikaya), the medium of rest (adharmastikaya), space (akasha), time (kala), matter (pudgala) and souls (jiva). The first three are each a single substance; time, matter and souls are infinite in number. Only souls know and feel; only matter has form, colour, smell, taste and touch. Nothing in this list is a creator: world and non-world have no beginning and no end.
In the sources

The list. The all-seeing Jinas taught that the world is these six; the first three are one each, the last three infinite (Utt 28.7–8). See Utt 28 · The Path to Liberation and Reality §4.
Each has its mark. Dharma helps things move, adharma helps them stay still, space gives them room, time’s mark is change, and the soul’s mark is awareness (upayoga) (Utt 28.9–10).
What marks the soul and what marks matter. The soul is known by knowledge, faith, conduct, austerity, energy and awareness; matter shows as sound, darkness, light, shadow, heat, colour, smell, taste and touch (Utt 28.11–13). See Reality §5.
Living and non-living. The world is the living and the non-living; where there is only space, that is the non-world (aloka) (Utt 36.2). The non-living come in 14 kinds; the medium of motion helps beings move “as water helps a fish”, the medium of rest is “like shade for a tired traveller” (Utt 36.4–10). See Utt 36 · The Living and the Non-living.
Matter in detail. Atoms join into aggregates and aggregates break into atoms; matter has 5 colours, 2 smells, 5 tastes, 8 touches and 5 shapes (Utt 36.11–48).
Why it matters. Knowing the difference between living and non-living is the reason for the map: “knowing it, a monk strives rightly in restraint” (Utt 36.1–3, 36.255).

One verse

जीवा चेव अजीवा य, एस लोए वियाहिए ।
अजीव देसमागासे, अलोए से वियाहिए ॥

This world is said to consist of the living and the non-living. Where there is only space, a part of the non-living, that is called the non-world.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 36.2 · module (verse checked against the scan). The six-substance verses themselves (Utt 28.7–9) are quoted in Reality §4.
Related

Concepts: Nine realities · Karma · Non-violence · Five knowledges

10_course/concepts/tapas.title: Concept · Tapas
10_course/concepts/tapas.content:
Concept · Tapas
What it is
Austerity (tapas, tapa) is the discipline that “burns” karma already bound to the soul. The Uttaradhyayan’s commentary defines it simply as restraining desire. It has twelve kinds: six outer ones that work through the body and can be seen (fasting, eating less, limits on alms, giving up rich food, bodily hardship, withdrawal), and six inner ones that work on the mind (atonement, humility, service, study, meditation, letting go of the body). Austerity counts as dharma only when it is done to purify the soul, not for fame here or rewards hereafter. And it works best once the inflow of new karma has been stopped.
In the sources

The fourth part of the path. Knowledge knows, faith believes, conduct restrains, and austerity purifies (Utt 28.35). Its twelve kinds are listed in Utt 28.34. See Utt 28 · The Path to Liberation.
Outer and inner. Utt 30.8 names the six outer austerities and 30.30 the six inner; 30.35 defines true meditation as leaving distressed and cruel thinking for righteous and pure meditation. See Utt 30 · The Path of Austerity.
Close the channels first. The lake dries up only when its streams are blocked (Utt 30.5–6). See Reality §9.
Only to shed karma. Austerity is not for this world, not for the next, not for fame, only to shed karma (Dash 9.4.4). See Dash 9 · Composure Through Humility. The same point is made of austerity in Dash 1.1’s commentary.
The inner sacrifice. Harikesha, born a Chandala, shows that the greatness of austerity is seen and caste is not; he calls austerity his fire and karma its fuel (Utt 12.37, 12.44). See Utt 12 · The True Sacrifice.
An everyday form. A monk who gets no alms should not grieve: “this is austerity” (Dash 5.2.6). See Dash 5 · Seeking Alms.

One verse

तवो जोई जीवो जोइठाणं, जोगा सुया सरीरं कारिसंगं ।
कम्मेहा संजमजोग संति, होमं हुणामि इसिणं पसत्थं ॥४४॥

Austerity is my fire, the soul is its altar, my good acts of mind, speech and body are the ladle, and the body is the dung-cake that kindles it. Karma is the fuel, and the practice of restraint (samyama) is the prayer for peace. I offer the sacrifice the sages praise.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 12.44 · module (verse checked against the scan)
Related

10_course/concepts/vinaya.title: Concept · Vinaya
10_course/concepts/vinaya.content:
Concept · Vinaya
What it is
Vinaya means humility, but also discipline: readiness to be taught, and the respect that shows it. The Dashvaikalik calls it the root of the tree of dharma, with liberation as its highest fruit. It is shown towards the teacher (guru, acharya) by listening, staying near, reading his wishes, taking correction without anger, and saying “I will not do it again” when you have done wrong. It is also counted as one of the six inner austerities. Its enemy is pride (mana): “pride destroys humility”.
In the sources

The root of dharma. As a tree grows from root to trunk, branches, leaves, flowers and fruit, so dharma grows from humility, and its highest fruit is liberation (Dash 9.2.1–2). See Dash 9 · Composure Through Humility and Relationships §5.
More than politeness. The introduction to Dash 9 gives seven kinds of vinaya: towards knowledge, faith and conduct, and in mind, speech, body and respectful behaviour.
Who is humble. One who acts on the teacher’s word, stays near him and understands his gestures and expressions (Utt 1.2). See Utt 1 · Humility.
Two hearers of harsh words. The wise take even harsh instruction as for their good; to fools the same words become a cause of hatred (Utt 1.29).
Disrespect burns the disrespecter. From pride, anger or laziness, the monk who will not learn humility ruins himself, as the bamboo’s fruit kills the bamboo (Dash 9.1.1).
An inner austerity. Humility means standing up when elders come, joining hands, offering a seat, devotion and heartfelt service (Utt 30.32). See Utt 30.
Its enemy. Anger destroys love, pride destroys humility (Dash 8.38). Serving the guru and fellow followers brings humility, which closes off bad births (Utt 29 s.6). See Utt 29.

One verse

एवं धम्मस्स विणओ, मूलं परमो से मोक्खो ।
जेण कित्तिं सुयं सिग्घं, णीसेसं चाभिगच्छइ ॥

In the same way, humility is the root of dharma and liberation is its highest fruit. Through humility one gains fame, learning, praise, and everything worth gaining.
Source: Dashvaikalik 9.2.2 · module (verse checked against the scan)
Related

Concepts: The four passions · Austerity · The three jewels
Lessons: 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions · 5 · Forgiveness and Friendship · 15 · Humility and Learning · 20 · Right Effort: 73 Questions · 21 · Austerity and the Roots of Negligence · 28 · Humility's Composure; the True Monk

10_course/lesson_01_what_jainism_is.title: Lesson 1 · What Jainism Is
10_course/lesson_01_what_jainism_is.content:
Lesson 1 · What Jainism Is
Unit 1: Foundations · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will be able to say in your own words whom a Jain bows to, what dharma is, and what the goal of the path is and how it is reached.
Read

Start Here: how to read the path (one file at a time, the verse aloud, then the English) and the five books it draws on.
Foundations: What Jainism Is: the ten verses a Jain lives by; notice that almost every one is about qualities, not about persons.

Key ideas


A Jain bows to qualities, not to a person or a god. A Jain is a follower of the Jinas, the “conquerors”, souls who defeated attachment and aversion inside themselves and then taught the way they had found. The Navkar mantra bows to five kinds of soul: the Arihantas who have destroyed the inner enemies, the liberated Siddhas, and the Acharyas, Upadhyayas and Sadhus who lead, teach and walk the path (Avashyak 1, sutra 1). The fourfold refuge turns to the Arihantas, the Siddhas, the Sadhus and the dharma taught by the all-knowing ones (kevalis) (Avashyak 4, Path 2).


Dharma is non-violence, restraint and austerity. The first verse of the Dashvaikalik gives the shortest definition of Jain dharma: not rituals, but not harming, holding yourself back, and disciplining yourself (Dash 1.1).

धम्मो मंगलमुक्किट्ठं, अहिंसा संजमो तवो, ।
देवा वि तं णमंसंति, जस्स धम्मे सया मणो ॥

Dharma is the highest good (mangal). It is non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapa). Even the gods bow to the one whose mind is always set on dharma.
Source: Dashvaikalik Sutra 1.1 (Drumapushpika) · scan (printed page 3)


The goal is the end of all suffering, and the path is four things practised together. The path is knowledge (jnana), faith or right seeing (darshana), conduct (charitra) and austerity (tapa) (Utt 28.2–3). It is a chain: without right faith there is no right knowledge, without knowledge no virtues of conduct, and without them no freedom from karma (Utt 28.30). Knowledge shows the realities, faith accepts them, conduct stops new karma from flowing in, and austerity purifies the karma already bound (Utt 28.35), until the sages, free of past karma, go forth to the end of all suffering (Utt 28.36).


Connect
This is the base for everything that follows. The next lesson asks what the soul is and what karma is, which is the “seeing rightly” that the chain in Utt 28.30 starts from. The four rare things and the falling leaf (Utt 3.1, 10.1, 10.4), which you met in this reading, come back in full in Lesson 6. The three words of Dash 1.1 each have their own page: non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapas); the path itself is on the three jewels (ratnatraya).
Reflect

When you say or hear the Navkar, what do you picture? Would anything change if you thought of it as bowing to qualities you could grow in yourself?
Of non-violence, restraint and austerity, which is already part of your days, and which is mostly missing?
Think of a time your life felt unsafe or uncertain. Where did you turn for refuge, and did it hold?

Practice this week
These verses are the ones a Jain says every day (Foundations, opening). Each morning this week, say the Navkar once, slowly. After each line, name to yourself the quality it honours: the one who conquered the inner enemies, the one who is free, the one who leads, the one who teaches, the ones who walk the path. It takes two minutes.
Self-check
Question

Does the Navkar mantra name any particular person or god?

No. It bows to five kinds of soul by their qualities: Arihantas, Siddhas, Acharyas, Upadhyayas and all Sadhus (Avashyak 1, sutra 1; Foundations §1).

Question

What three things make up dharma in the first verse of the Dashvaikalik?

Non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapa) (Dash 1.1).

Question

What are the four parts of the path to liberation?

Knowledge, faith (right seeing), conduct and austerity, practised together (Utt 28.2–3).

Question

According to Utt 28.35, what does conduct do, and what does austerity do?

Conduct stops new karma from flowing in; austerity purifies the soul of karma already bound (Utt 28.35).
