10_course/lesson_02_soul_matter_and_karm.title: Lesson 2 · Soul, Matter and Karma
10_course/lesson_02_soul_matter_and_karm.content:
Lesson 2 · Soul, Matter and Karma
Unit 1: Foundations · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will be able to explain what the soul is, what the world is made of, and how karma binds the soul and is shed, and why that makes your joys and sufferings your own.
Read

Reality: Soul, Matter and Karma: follow the order of the ten sections, from “who am I?” to the lake that dries up; notice that nothing in the list of what exists is a creator.

Key ideas


The first question is about you: are you a soul that goes on? The Acharang opens not with God or the world but with the question “Who was I before, and what will I become next?” (Acharang 1.1.1.1). The one who comes to know “the one who wanders through all these directions, that one am I” also accepts a real world, karma, and action that creates karma (Acharang 1.1.1.2).


The world is souls and non-souls, and only the soul knows and feels. Everything is either living (jiva) or non-living (ajiva) (Utt 36.2). The world is made of six substances: the medium of motion, the medium of rest, space, time, matter and souls, and souls are infinite in number (Utt 28.7–9). The soul’s mark is awareness (upayoga), shown in knowledge, perception, conduct, austerity, energy, happiness and suffering (Utt 28.10–11).


Karma binds the soul, and the soul can free itself. The whole story is told in the nine realities:

जीवाजीवा य बंधो य, पुण्णं पावासवो तहा ।
संवरो णिज्जरा मोक्खो, संतेए तहिया णव ॥ १४ ॥

Soul (jiva), non-soul (ajiva), bondage (bandha), merit (punna, punya), demerit (pava, papa), inflow of karma (asava, ashrava), stopping the inflow (samvara), shedding karma (nijjara, nirjara) and liberation (mokkha, moksha): these nine are the true realities.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 28.14 · scan (printed page 142)
Eight kinds of karma cover what the soul already has, such as knowledge, perception and energy, and keep it going round in samsara (Utt 33.1–3). Like a lake that dries once its inflowing channels are blocked, karma is shed by austerity once the inflow has been stopped (Utt 30.5–6). So “the soul is the maker and the unmaker of its own sufferings and joys” (Utt 20.37).


Connect
Lesson 1 said that conduct stops new karma and austerity purifies the old (Utt 28.35). This lesson gives those two jobs their names: stopping the inflow (samvara) and shedding (nirjara), the seventh and eighth of the nine realities. The pages Six Substances, Nine Tattvas and Karma gather what the sources say on each; the lake image belongs to austerity (tapas).
Reflect

Think of a recent hurt you blamed on someone else. Looking again, what part of it came from your own reaction?
If you truly believed you carry on after this life, what is one thing you would start or stop doing?
Is there a habit you keep apologising for and keep repeating? What would “closing the channel” look like for it?

Practice this week
The lake verse (Utt 30.5–6) says: first close the channels, then dry out what is there. Each evening this week, take one thing that upset you or that you regret from the day and ask two questions: “What let this in: what did I do, say or think?” and “What one small thing can I do tomorrow to close that channel?” Write the answer in one line.
Self-check
Question

What are the six substances that make up the world?

The medium of motion (dhamma), the medium of rest (adhamma), space, time, matter (pudgala) and souls (Utt 28.7).

Question

What is the mark of the soul?

Awareness (upayoga), known through knowledge, perception, happiness and suffering; no other substance has it (Utt 28.10–11).

Question

In the image of the lake, what has to happen before austerity can dry out the stored karma?

The inflow must be stopped first, like blocking the channels that feed the lake (samvara before nirjara) (Utt 30.5–6).

Question

Does karma add something new to the soul?

No. The learning path’s note on Utt 33.1–3 says karma covers and limits what the soul already has: knowledge, perception, happiness and energy.

10_course/lesson_03_non_violence_and_awa.title: Lesson 3 · Non-violence and Awareness
10_course/lesson_03_non_violence_and_awa.content:
Lesson 3 · Non-violence and Awareness
Unit 1: Foundations · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will understand why harming none is the centre of the Jain path, and how care, simplicity, evenness and humility turn it into daily living.
Read

Way of Life: Non-violence, Awareness, Simplicity: look for the one plain fact the whole chapter rests on, and then for the small daily acts (walking, eating, speaking, owning) it changes.

Key ideas


Every being wants to live, and that is the whole reason for non-violence. All living beings love their life, want happiness and do not want pain; to all, life is dear (Acharang 1.2.3, sutra 4).

सव्वे जीवा वि इच्छंति, जीविउं ण मरिज्जिउं ।
तम्हा पाणिवहं घोरं, णिग्गंथा वज्जयंति णं ॥

All beings wish to live, not to die. Therefore the unattached ones (nirgranthas) give up the terrible act of killing living beings.
Source: Dashvaikalik 6.11 (numbered 6.10 in some editions) · scan (printed page 249)
The rule taught by all the Arhats, past, present and future, covers not only killing but ordering beings about by force, enslaving, tormenting and harassing them (Acharang 1.4.1). And “the one you think should be killed is in truth you” (Acharang 1.5.5).


First knowledge, then care in every act. “First knowledge, then compassion”: you cannot protect life you do not know is there (Dash 4.10). Life cannot stop walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating and speaking, but one who does each of these with care (yatana) does not bind harmful karma (Dash 4.8). However much you learn, its essence is that you harm no one (Sutrakritang 1.1.4.10).


Hold things lightly, stay even, and stay humble about your own view. Mahavira called clinging (murchha) possession, not the things themselves (Dash 6.21). The even-minded monk Mrigaputra stayed the same in gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame (Utt 19.90–91). And those who praise only their own view and condemn others’ stay bound to samsara (Sutrakritang 1.1.2.23).


Connect
In Lesson 2 you learned that every soul knows and feels, and that souls are countless; that is why harming any of them matters. Lesson 1’s first word of dharma, non-violence, is filled out here: see Ahimsa. The care in walking, eating and speaking is the everyday face of the careful practices (samiti) and restraints (gupti), and holding back from harm is restraint (samyama).
Reflect

When did you last hurt a small creature without thinking? What would you have needed to notice to avoid it?
Which of your possessions do you grip hardest? Is it the thing, or the clinging, that troubles you?
In an argument, do you listen for the part of the other person’s view that may be true, or only for a weak point?

Practice this week
“Walk with care, eat with care, speak with care” (Dash 4.8) is written for monks, who keep it in every act. A householder’s version: choose one daily act this week (switching on the stove, walking in the garden, or dealing with an insect at home) and before doing it, stop and look for living beings first. When you find an insect indoors, carry it out instead of killing it.
Self-check
Question

Why do the unattached ones give up killing, according to Dash 6.11?

Because all beings wish to live and not to die (Dash 6.11).

Question

Which comes first, knowledge or compassion?

Knowledge, then compassion: the ignorant cannot know what is good and what is harmful (Dash 4.10).

Question

According to Dash 6.21, what is “possession” (parigraha)?

Clinging (murchha), not the objects themselves such as a monk’s clothes and bowl (Dash 6.21).

Question

Does the eternal dharma of Acharang 1.4.1 forbid only killing?

No. It also forbids ordering beings about by force, enslaving, tormenting and harassing them (Acharang 1.4.1).

10_course/lesson_04_vows_speech_and_pass.title: Lesson 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions
10_course/lesson_04_vows_speech_and_pass.content:
Lesson 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions
Unit 1: Foundations · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand how a householder’s twelve vows scale down the monk’s great vows, what makes speech right, and how each of the four passions is met by its opposite.
Read

Conduct: Vows, Speech and Inner Discipline: compare Ananda’s vows (§2–3) with the monk’s first great vow (§6), then read the passions and their antidotes (§9–10) slowly.

Key ideas


A householder walks the same path with smaller vows. Ananda told Mahavira he could not leave home, and took the twelve-fold householder’s dharma of five small vows and seven training vows; Mahavira said, “Do as brings you happiness. Do not delay” (Upasakdashang 1.15). Ananda renounced gross harm, lying and stealing in two ways, not doing and not having it done (Upasakdashang 1.16–18), and set limits on sex and wealth (1.19–20). The monk renounces all harm, even to the smallest beings, in three ways, adding “I will not approve another doing it” (Dash 4, sutra 7).


Right speech passes four tests, and kindness limits even the truth. Speak what is true or plainly practical, and only what is harmless, not harsh, thought over and clear (Dash 7.3). Harsh words that deeply wound should not be spoken even if true, so do not call a one-eyed man “one-eyed” or a sick man “diseased” (Dash 7.11–12).


Each passion has a casualty and an antidote; conquering yourself is the real victory. Anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything (Dash 8.38).

३९ उवसमेण हणे कोहं, माणं मद्दवया जिणे ।
मायं च अज्जवभावेण, लोभं संतोसओ जिणे ॥

Destroy anger by calm (upashama), conquer pride by gentleness (mardava), deceit by straightforwardness (arjava), and greed by contentment (santosha).
Source: Dashvaikalik 8.39-40 · scan (printed page 355)
Left unchecked, these four “water the roots of rebirth” (Dash 8.40). The self must be tamed (Utt 1.15), and conquering it is greater than conquering a million warriors (Utt 9.34).


Connect
Lessons 1 and 3 named non-violence as the heart of dharma; here it becomes a vow you can actually take, sized to your life. The passions are the inner source of the inflow of karma from Lesson 2, and the page Kashaya collects what the sources say about them. The vows themselves are restraint (samyama) in practice, and the first vow is ahimsa made concrete. You will meet King Nami’s “greatest victory” again in Lesson 9.
Reflect

Ananda chose ceilings he would not cross. Is there one area of your life (money, food, screens, travel) where a chosen limit would free you?
Which passion shows up in you most often, and which relationship or quality is it eating away?
Think of a true thing you said recently that hurt someone. Did it pass the four tests of Dash 7.3?

Practice this week
Pick the one passion you notice most in yourself. Each time it rises this week, try its antidote once, on purpose: calm for anger, gentleness for pride, straightforwardness for deceit, contentment for greed (Dash 8.39). Each night, note in one line when it came and whether you tried the antidote. This is a householder’s practice; no vow is needed for it.
Self-check
Question

How does the householder’s first small vow differ from the monk’s first great vow?

The householder gives up gross, deliberate harm in two ways (not doing, not causing); the monk gives up all harm to every being in three ways, also not approving it (Upasakdashang 1.16; Dash 4, sutra 7).

Question

What does each of the four passions destroy?

Anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility (vinaya), deceit destroys friendships, and greed destroys everything (Dash 8.38).

Question

Should you speak a hurtful word if it is true?

No. Harsh speech that wounds should not be spoken even if true, because it brings in sin (Dash 7.11).

Question

What does Nami call the supreme victory?

Conquering one’s own self, which is greater than defeating ten lakh warriors in battle (Utt 9.34).

10_course/lesson_05_forgiveness_and_frie.title: Lesson 5 · Forgiveness and Friendship
10_course/lesson_05_forgiveness_and_frie.content:
Lesson 5 · Forgiveness and Friendship
Unit 1: Foundations · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will understand why the Agamas ask for friendship toward every being and forgiveness in both directions, and how humility, careful words and judging by deeds follow from that.
Read

Relationships: Forgiveness, Friendship, Respect: look for how far forgiveness reaches (even an ant you did not see), and for what asking forgiveness does to the one who asks.

Key ideas


Friendship toward every being, and forgiveness given and asked at once. The wise person, seeing the many paths of birth that all beings share, holds friendship (maitri) toward all of them (Utt 6.2).

खामेमि सव्वे जीवा, सव्वे जीवा वि खमंतु मे ।
मित्तीमे सव्व भूएसू, वेरं मज्झं ण केणइ ॥१॥

I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship toward all beings; I have enmity toward none.
Source: Avashyak Sutra, Avashyak 4, Path 10 (Kshamapana Sutra) v.1 · scan (printed page 126)


Forgiveness is owed even for harm you did not notice, and it frees you from fear. The Iriyavahiya asks pardon from every being harmed while walking, from one-sensed to five-sensed, ending “may that wrong of mine be fruitless” (micchami dukkadam) (Avashyak 4, Path 4). Asking forgiveness brings gladness, then friendship toward all, then purer feeling and freedom from fear (Utt 29.19). When an elder is upset with you, win back their good will with gentle words and say, “I will not do it again” (Utt 1.41).


Humility is the root, people are worth what they do, and no one can carry your karma. As a tree grows from its root to its fruit, humility (vinaya) is the root of dharma and liberation its fruit (Dash 9.2.1–2). One becomes a brahmin or a shudra by one’s actions, not by birth (Utt 25.32–33). Family is dear, but none of them can protect you from your own karma; it follows only the one who did it (Utt 6.3, 13.23).


Connect
Lesson 3 showed that every being wants to live; friendship toward all beings is the warm side of the same fact. Lesson 4’s caution about wounding words returns here (Dash 7.11–12), and the passions you studied there are what forgiveness dissolves. See Vinaya for humility and Karma for why karma follows only the doer. Lesson 10 tells the full stories behind “worth by deeds, not birth”.
Reflect

Is there someone you have not forgiven? What would it cost you, and what would you gain, to let it go?
Is there someone you owe an apology but have been waiting for them to apologise first?
When someone who means you well corrects you, do you take it as a gift or as an insult?

Practice this week
Choose one person you have hurt, even in a small way. This week, ask their forgiveness in plain words, for one specific thing, without excuses, and if it fits, add “I will not do it again” (Utt 1.41). If no one comes to mind, say the Kshamapana verse each night and picture one person as you say “may all living beings forgive me”.
Self-check
Question

What does “micchami dukkadam” mean?

“May that wrong of mine be fruitless”: a real apology, owed even to small beings harmed without noticing (Avashyak 4, Path 4).

Question

According to Utt 29.19, what does the soul gain by asking forgiveness?

Gladness of mind, then friendship toward all beings, then purified feeling and freedom from fear (Utt 29.19).

Question

What is the root of dharma, and what is its highest fruit?

Humility (vinaya) is the root; liberation (moksha) is the highest fruit (Dash 9.2.1–2).

Question

Can your family share the suffering that comes from your own karma?

No. Kinsmen, friends and sons cannot share it; karma follows only the one who did it (Utt 13.23; also Utt 6.3).


Previous: Lesson 4 · Vows, Speech, the Four Passions · Next: Lesson 6 · Four Rare Things, a Falling Leaf · Course home

10_course/lesson_06_four_rare_things.title: Lesson 6 · Four Rare Things, a Falling Leaf
10_course/lesson_06_four_rare_things.content:
Lesson 6 · Four Rare Things, a Falling Leaf
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will see why the Uttaradhyayan calls this human life rare and short, and why its answer is not fear but wakefulness: do not be careless (pramada), even for a moment.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 3: The Four Rare Things: look for the ladder of four, each rung harder than the one before, and which rung is the rarest.
Uttaradhyayan 10: The Falling Leaf: listen for the refrain at the end of every verse, and for what old age takes away.

Key ideas


Four things are rare, each rarer than the last. For a living being, four supreme things are hard to gain: a human life, hearing the dharma, faith in it, and effort in restraint (Utt 3.1). Driven by its own karma the soul has been god, hell-being, king, outcast, insect and ant, and a human birth comes only when the karma blocking it wears thin (Utt 3.3–7). Many hear and still fall away, and many like the dharma but never practise it (Utt 3.9–10); the one with all four, with a straight and honest heart, blazes up to liberation “like a fire fed with ghee” (Utt 3.11–12).


Life falls like a yellow leaf, and a human birth is hard to come by.

दुमपत्तए पंडुयए जहा, णिवडइ राइगणाण अच्चए ।
एवं मणुयाण जीवियं, समयं गोयम मा पमायए ॥१॥

Just as a tree’s leaf turns yellow and falls as nights and days go by, so does human life. Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 10.1 (Drumapatraka) · verse checked against the scan, as given in the module
Outside a human body a soul can be stuck for countless time as an earth, water, fire, air or plant being (Utt 10.5–15). Even as a human, five more things are rare: a land where right and wrong are known, whole senses, hearing the highest dharma, faith, and living it with the body (Utt 10.16–20).


So act now, while the senses and strength are still yours. Old age takes hearing, sight and strength one by one, and the commentary explains the loss: without hearing you cannot listen to dharma, without sight you cannot watch for living beings or study, without strength you cannot do austerity (Utt 10.21–26). “You have crossed the great ocean; why stand at the shore?” (Utt 10.34). Gautama heard, cut off attachment and aversion and reached liberation, and the book says “our Gautama is our mind” (Utt 10.37).


Connect
You met Utt 3.1, 10.1 and 10.4 briefly in Lesson 1; here they open out into whole chapters. The fourth rare thing, effort in restraint, is where Samyama begins, and the soul’s long wandering by its own deeds is Karma at work, as in Lesson 2. The ladder of hearing, faith and practice matches the chain of the three jewels: seeing rightly first, then living it.
Reflect

Of the four rare things, which do you already have? Which is weakest in you now: hearing, faith or effort?
What good thing have you been putting off “until later”, until retirement, until the children are grown?
If your hearing or eyesight faded next year, what would you be sorry not to have done while you could?

Practice this week
Choose one small act of dharma that you already believe in but do not do: reading one module, saying the Navkar slowly, sitting quietly for ten minutes. Do it every day this week at a fixed time. When you feel like skipping it, say the refrain to yourself, “samayam goyama ma pamayae”: do not be careless even for a moment.
Self-check
Question

Name the four rare things, in order.

A human life, hearing the dharma, faith in it, and effort in self-restraint (Utt 3.1).

Question

Which of the four does Chapter 3 call rarest of all?

Effort: many people like the dharma but never put it into practice (Utt 3.10).

Question

What line ends every verse of Chapter 10 but the last?

“Gautama, do not be careless even for a moment” (samayam goyama ma pamayae) (Utt 10.1–36).

Question

Why does losing the senses in old age matter for dharma, according to the commentary?

Without hearing one cannot listen to dharma, without sight one cannot look out for living beings or study, and without strength one cannot bear hardship or do austerity (Utt 10.21–26).

10_course/lesson_07_life_cannot_be_mende.title: Lesson 7 · Life Cannot Be Mended; Two Kinds of Death
10_course/lesson_07_life_cannot_be_mende.content:
Lesson 7 · Life Cannot Be Mended; Two Kinds of Death
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will understand why the Uttaradhyayan says dharma cannot be put off, and how the way you live decides whether you meet death in fear or in calm.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 4: Life Cannot Be Mended: look for the thief caught in his own hole, the lamp gone out, and the ever-watchful bharanda bird.
Uttaradhyayan 5: Two Kinds of Death: look for the two deaths, the cart driver and the gambler, and what the chapter says about the good householder.

Key ideas


A broken life cannot be joined again, and no one can carry your karma.

असंखयं जीविय मा पमायए, जरोवणीयस्स हु णत्थि ताणं ।
एवं वियाणाहि जणे पमत्ते, किण्णू विहिंसा अजया गहिंति ॥१॥

Life cannot be mended, so do not be careless. For one who has reached old age there is truly no protector. Know this: where will careless, violent, unrestrained people go for refuge?
Source: Uttaradhyayan 4.1 (Asamskrita) · verse checked against the scan, as given in the module
As a thief is caught in the very hole he cut, no being escapes the fruit of its own karma, and the relatives one did it for do not share the fruit (Utt 4.3–4). Wealth gives no shelter either (Utt 4.5).


“Later” is a trap; stay awake now. Among those asleep in delusion, the wise live awake, like the bharanda bird, because the moments are fierce and the body is weak (Utt 4.6). One who does not practise dharma earlier will not manage it later, and discernment cannot be gained in a hurry at death (Utt 4.9–10). So calm anger, remove pride, give up deceit and let go of greed (Utt 4.12).


There are two deaths, and your life chooses between them. The immature die unwillingly (akama-marana), again and again; the wise die willingly (sakama-marana), at best only once (Utt 5.2–3). The fool who says “who knows if there is a next world?” trembles at the end like a gambler beaten in one throw (Utt 5.5–7, 5.16). Outward signs such as a shaved head or bark clothes do not save a person of bad conduct, and some householders are higher in restraint than some monks (Utt 5.20–21); a householder who keeps samayika and the fasting-day observance goes to the world of the gods (Utt 5.23–24).


Connect
Lesson 6 said life is short and rare; this lesson adds that it cannot be repaired once it breaks, so the time for dharma is now. “Karma follows the doer” was in Lesson 5 (Utt 6.3, 13.23) and is the heart of Karma. The four passions to be calmed in Utt 4.12 are those of Lesson 4 and Kashaya, and the calm death of those who hold knowledge, faith and conduct (Utt 5.17–18, 5.29) rests on the three jewels.
Reflect

What is one thing you have been saying you will do “later” for dharma? What makes you sure later will come?
If you had to face death this year, what would you fear most, and what would steady you?
Is there a “lamp” in your life, a clear understanding you once had, that has gone out through busyness?

Practice this week
Chapter 5 praises the householder who keeps samayika (Utt 5.23). Samayika is a set period of sitting in equanimity, giving up all harmful activity, traditionally forty-eight minutes (Conduct §5). Once this week, sit one samayika: phone off, no work or chatter, mind and tongue as still as you can, reading or reflecting on this lesson. If forty-eight minutes is too much as a first step, sit for a shorter time and say honestly to yourself that it is a beginning. (The three willing deaths at the end of Chapter 5, by fasting near death, are monks’ practices and are not part of this week’s work.)
Self-check
Question

Why does Chapter 4 say life “cannot be mended”?

Once life breaks no one can join it again, and in old age there is no protector; even Indras, mantras and medicines cannot stop death (Utt 4.1).

Question

What are the two kinds of death, and how often does each happen?

Death against one’s will (akama-marana), which the immature die again and again, and death with one’s will (sakama-marana), which the wise die at best only once (Utt 5.2–3).

Question

Can a shaved head, matted hair or bark clothes protect a person of bad conduct?

No. None of these outward signs protects one of bad conduct, however long he has been an ascetic (Utt 5.21).

Question

What does the good householder of Chapter 5 do?

Keeps samayika and the other lay practices and does not miss the fasting-day observance (paushadha) in either half of the month, not even for one night (Utt 5.23–24).

10_course/lesson_08_knots_ram_and_greed.title: Lesson 8 · Free of Knots; the Ram; Kapila's Greed
10_course/lesson_08_knots_ram_and_greed.content:
Lesson 8 · Free of Knots; the Ram; Kapila’s Greed
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 45 minutes
Aim: You will understand three warnings: knowing without doing does not untie the knots, a human life is capital not to be spent on small pleasures, and greed only grows as it is fed.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 6: The Monk Free of Knots: look for the outer and inner knots, and the people who “talk but do not act”.
Uttaradhyayan 7: The Fattened Ram: look for the ram, the coin and the mango, and the three merchants.
Uttaradhyayan 8: Kapila and Greed: look for how Kapila’s wish grew in the grove, and what turned it.

Key ideas


Ignorance ties the knots, and words alone do not untie them. A nirgrantha is one “without knots”; the outer knots are things like hoarding, the inner ones are wrong belief, attachment, deceit and the passions (Utt 6, introduction). All who lack true knowledge bring suffering on themselves (Utt 6.1), and neither family nor wealth can protect you from your own karma (Utt 6.3–5). Some talk of bondage and liberation but do nothing and comfort themselves with words; many languages and much learning cannot save them (Utt 6.10–11).


A human birth is capital; do not trade it for small pleasures. The ram is fattened only for the guest’s table, and the pleasure-seeker is like it (Utt 7.1–7). A man loses a thousand coins for one kakini, a king loses his kingdom for a forbidden mango (Utt 7.11).

माणुसत्तं भवे मूलं, लाभो देवगई भवे ।
मूलच्छेएण जीवाणं, णरग-तिरिक्खत्तणं धुवं ॥

Human birth is the capital; birth among the gods is the profit. When the capital is lost, beings surely go to hell or to animal birth.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 7.16 (Urabhriya) · verse checked against the scan, as given in the module
Human pleasures beside a god’s are like a drop on a blade of kusa grass beside the ocean (Utt 7.23), and householders of good nature keep their capital and are born human again (Utt 7.19–22).


Greed grows with every gain. Kapila set out at midnight for two mashas of gold; offered anything by the king, his wish grew to crores and still was not satisfied, until his thinking turned and he asked for nothing (Utt 8, introduction). “As gain grows, so grows greed” (Utt 8.17); give one person the whole world and he would still not be content (Utt 8.16). The one who harms no living being sheds sinful karma like water running off high ground (Utt 8.9).


Connect
Lesson 7 warned that life cannot be mended; these chapters show what people waste it on. Kapila’s greed and Nami’s answer in the next lesson (“desire is endless like the sky”, Utt 9.48) both show the fourth passion of Kashaya, and contentment, its antidote from Lesson 4. Ananda’s fifth vow, a chosen limit on wealth (Lesson 4), is the householder’s way through. Utt 6.3 and 6.7 also came up in Lessons 3 and 5: see Ahimsa and Karma.
Reflect

Is there something you know well about dharma but do not do? What keeps the knowing from becoming doing?
What is your “kakini”, a small pleasure you keep trading something bigger for?
Think of something you wanted badly and then got. Did the wanting stop, or move on to the next thing?

Practice this week
Kapila’s lesson, put into Ananda’s householder vow of a limit on wealth (Lesson 4): before you buy anything this week that is not a need, write down what it costs and ask, “What was my two mashas here: what did I actually need?” Choose one category (clothes, gadgets, eating out) and set a ceiling for the week that you will not cross. Keep it.
Self-check
Question

What does “nirgrantha” mean, and what are the inner knots?

“One without knots”. The inner knots are wrong belief, attachment, deceit and the passions (Utt 6, introduction).

Question

In the parable of the three merchants, what stand for the capital, the profit and the loss?

Human birth is the capital, birth as a god is the profit, and birth in hell or as an animal is losing the capital (Utt 7.14–16).

Question

What happened to Kapila’s wish as he sat in the grove?

It grew from two mashas of gold to crores of coins and still was not satisfied; then he turned, asked for nothing and became a monk (Utt 8, introduction; Utt 8.17).

Question

Is knowing the noble teaching enough to be free, according to Chapter 6?

No. Those who only talk of bondage and liberation, without giving up sin, merely reassure themselves with words (Utt 6.9–10).

10_course/lesson_09_namis_renunciation.title: Lesson 9 · Nami's Renunciation
10_course/lesson_09_namis_renunciation.content:
Lesson 9 · Nami’s Renunciation
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will be able to follow King Nami’s dialogue with Indra and see how each worldly duty he is pressed with is turned inward: the real city, fort, war and wealth are inside the soul.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 9: Nami's Renunciation: read the story of the bangles first, then take Indra’s tests one at a time and notice how Nami turns each one around.

Key ideas


A small sound woke a king. Burning with fever, King Nami could not bear the clink of the queens’ bangles as they ground sandalwood; when each kept only one bangle, the sound stopped, and he saw: “Where there are many, there is conflict and sorrow; where there is one, there is peace” (Utt 9, introduction). He remembered his past life, put his son on the throne and left Mithila for a solitary place (Utt 9.1–5). He is one of four kings in the book awakened by an outside event (pratyekabuddha).


Every duty Indra names, Nami turns inward. Asked why the city cries, he says the birds cry for a fallen tree, and his going harms no one (Utt 9.6–10). Told his palace is burning, he answers:

सुहं वसामो जीवामो, जेसिं मो णत्थि किंचणं ।
मिहिलाए डज्झमाणीए, ण मे डज्झइ किंचणं ॥

We live and dwell happily, we who own nothing. When Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 9.14 (Namipravrajya) · verse checked against the scan, as given in the module
Told to build forts, he makes faith the city, austerity and restraint its bolt and forgiveness its wall (Utt 9.20). Told to fill his treasury, he says mountains of gold like Kailash would not satisfy a greedy man, for desire is endless like the sky (Utt 9.48).


The battle that matters is with yourself. Conquering one’s own self is greater than defeating a million warriors, and when the self is conquered, the five senses and the four passions are conquered with it (Utt 9.34–36). Restraint, even in one who gives nothing, is better than giving a million cows every month (Utt 9.37–44). In the end Indra drops his disguise and bows, praising Nami’s forgiveness, gentleness, straightforwardness and freedom from greed (Utt 9.55–62).


Connect
The “greatest victory” verses you read in Lesson 4 come from this chapter, and Indra’s praise lists the very antidotes of Dash 8.39 from that lesson: see Kashaya. Nami’s “desire is endless like the sky” answers Kapila’s greed in Lesson 8. The fort guarded by the three restraints (gupti) points to Samiti and Gupti, and austerity as the arrow that pierces karma (Utt 9.17–26) to Tapas.
Reflect

Where in your life does “many” bring noise and conflict: too many commitments, possessions, screens, opinions?
If your house burned tonight, what would still be yours?
Which “duty” do you use as a reason to put off dharma, as Indra urged Nami to first build, punish, give and earn?

Practice this week
Nami’s waking came from one bangle instead of many. Monks give up everything; a householder’s version: pick one area where you have many of something and use only one this week. For example, one news source instead of five, one device in the evening, one task at a time at work. At the end of each day, notice whether the “sound” grew quieter.
Self-check
Question

What woke King Nami?

The clinking of the queens’ bangles while he had a fever; when each kept one bangle the sound stopped, and he saw that where there are many there is conflict, where there is one there is peace (Utt 9, introduction).

Question

How does Nami answer when told his palace is burning?

“We live happily, we who own nothing. When Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns” (Utt 9.14).

Question

In Nami’s city of faith, what are the bolt and the wall?

Austerity and restraint are the bolt, forgiveness is the wall, and the three restraints (gupti) guard it (Utt 9.20).

Question

Why does Nami say filling the treasury will not help?

Because even countless mountains of gold and silver as big as Kailash would not satisfy a greedy man; desire is endless like the sky (Utt 9.48).

10_course/lesson_10_worth_is_in_deeds.title: Lesson 10 · Worth Is in Deeds, Not Birth
10_course/lesson_10_worth_is_in_deeds.content:
Lesson 10 · Worth Is in Deeds, Not Birth
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand, through two stories of monks turned away at a sacrifice, why the Uttaradhyayan judges a person by conduct and not by birth, and why it calls the true sacrifice and the true bath inner ones.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 12: The True Sacrifice: look for how the proud Brahmins see Harikeshbal, what the monk himself feels, and his inner fire and inner bath.
Uttaradhyayan 25: The True Brahmin: look for the refrain “him we call a brahmin” and the two balls of clay.

Key ideas


A monk born among outcastes shows what makes a person high. Harikeshbal was born in a Chandala family because, the commentary says, in a past life he never repented his pride in caste and looks; as a monk he held the highest virtues and had conquered his senses (Utt 12.1, pp.284–286). The Brahmins mocked his thin body and dirty clothes, and the yaksha told them that anyone full of anger, pride, violence, lies, theft and possessiveness has neither birth nor learning (Utt 12.4–7, 12.14). When they had seen his power, the lesson was spoken aloud:

सक्खं खु दीसइ तवोविसेसो, ण दीसइ जाइविसेस कोई ।
सोवागपुत्तं हरिएस साहुं, जस्सेरिस्सा इड्ढि महाणुभागा ॥३७॥

The greatness of austerity is plainly seen before our eyes; no greatness of caste is seen at all. Look at the monk Harikesh, son of a Chandala, whose spiritual power is so great.
Source: Uttaradhyayan 12.37 (Harikeshiya) · verse checked against the scan, as given in the module
The commentary adds that the door to liberation is open to anyone, of any caste, country or sex, who practises the three jewels purely.


The true sacrifice and the true bath are inside, and they are done without anger. Harikeshbal says there was no ill will in his mind before, now or in the future (Utt 12.32); Jayaghosha, refused at his brother’s door, felt neither anger nor pleasure (Utt 25.9). In the inner sacrifice austerity is the fire, the soul its altar and karma the fuel (Utt 12.44); in the inner bath dharma is the lake and celibacy the holy bathing place (Utt 12.46).


A brahmin is made by deeds, and craving is what makes karma stick. A shaven head, the sound “Om”, the forest or bark clothes do not make a holy person; equanimity, celibacy, knowledge and austerity do (Utt 25.31–32), and one is a brahmin or a shudra by one’s actions (Utt 25.33). The true brahmin is untouched by pleasures, like a lotus in water (Utt 25.27). Two clay balls hit a wall: the wet one sticks, as those who crave pleasures get stuck, while the detached, like the dry ball, do not (Utt 25.42–43).


Connect
You met Utt 25.32–33 in Lesson 5, where people are judged by what they do; here are the full stories behind those verses. Lesson 7 already said outward signs do not save (Utt 5.21). Harikeshbal kept the five careful practices and the three restraints (Utt 12.1–3), which you can look up in Samiti and Gupti, and his inner fire is Tapas with restraint (samyama) as its prayer. His freedom from anger, even under blows, is the first antidote of Kashaya.
Reflect

When you meet someone new, what do you notice first: their family, job, looks, clothes, or what they do?
Is there a part of your own birth or background you are quietly proud of? What does it actually say about your conduct?
Have you ever been looked down on? Could you, like Jayaghosha, answer without anger and without wanting to win?

Practice this week
The Brahmins judged Harikeshbal by his caste, his looks and his rags. This week, each time you catch yourself sizing someone up by birth, family, job, looks or clothes, stop and name to yourself one thing you have actually seen that person do. Once during the week, show plain respect (a greeting by name, a thank-you) to someone whose work is usually overlooked.
Self-check
Question

Why, according to the commentary, was Harikeshbal born in a Chandala family?

In a past life, as the Brahmin monk Somadatta, he never repented his pride in caste and looks (Utt 12, commentary, pp.284–286).

Question

Who struck the young men at the sacrifice, and did the monk bear them any ill will?

The yaksha who served the monk struck them; the monk had no ill will in his mind before, now or in the future (Utt 12.32).

Question

In Harikeshbal’s inner sacrifice, what are the fire, the altar and the fuel?

Austerity is the fire, the soul is its altar, and karma is the fuel (Utt 12.44).

Question

What do the two balls of clay teach?

The wet ball sticks to the wall and the dry one does not: those who crave pleasures get stuck, and the detached do not (Utt 25.42–43).

10_course/lesson_11_family_and_past_live.title: Lesson 11 · Bonds of Family and Past Lives
10_course/lesson_11_family_and_past_live.content:
Lesson 11 · Bonds of Family and Past Lives
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will see how two chapters treat family love: as a real bond that can carry souls across many lives, but not a refuge at death, where only your own deeds and dharma go with you.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 13: Two Brothers, Two Paths: look for why two brothers, together for five lives, end up in opposite places.
Uttaradhyayan 14: King Ishukara: look for how two boys answer each of their father’s reasons for staying home.

Key ideas


One wish can split two souls who were always together. Chitta and Sambhuta were brothers as servants, deer, swans, outcaste boys and gods; in the sixth birth they are apart (Utt 13.6–7). The monk Chitta says it was the karma made out of desire, Sambhuta’s binding resolve (niyana) to become an emperor, that pulled them apart (Utt 13.8). The emperor Brahmadatta knows the dharma but cannot act on it, “like an elephant sunk in mud that sees the dry bank and cannot reach it” (Utt 13.30), and he goes to the lowest hell while Chitta reaches liberation (Utt 13.34–35).


Family cannot carry your karma for you. Chitta tells the king that no relative can share a person’s suffering:

ण तस्स दुक्खं विभयंति णाइओ, ण मित्तवग्गा ण सुया ण बंधवा ।
इक्को सयं पच्चणुहोइ दुक्खं, कत्तारमेव अणुजाइ कम्मं ॥२३॥

Relatives, friends, sons and kin cannot share his suffering. He bears it himself, alone, for karma follows only the one who did it. (Utt 13.23)
In Chapter 14 the sons say the same to their father: studying the Vedas does not protect, and “sons who are born do not protect either” (Utt 14.12).


A family can also wake up together. In Chapter 14 six friends who kept restraint (samyama) together in an earlier life are reborn as a king, a queen, a priest, his wife and their two sons (Utt 14.1–5). The sons go first; their reasons win over the father, then the mother, then the queen, who tells the king that “dharma alone is a refuge” at death (Utt 14.40), and all six reach the end of suffering (Utt 14.49–53). The sons also refuse to put dharma off: only someone who is a friend of death, or can run from it, can say “tomorrow” (Utt 14.27).


Connect
Lesson 7 taught that life cannot be mended and death can come at any time; here that truth is spoken inside a family. The rule that karma follows only the doer is the core of Karma, and the sons’ answer that the soul is formless and eternal, bound by its own faults (Utt 14.19), goes back to Lesson 2. Brahmadatta’s resolve is a form of craving, one of the passions in Kashaya.
Reflect

Who in your family do you feel you have “always” known? What do you most want to share with them that is not money or comfort?
Is there something good you know you should do, but keep putting off to “later”, like Brahmadatta stuck in the mud?
Have you ever made a strong wish, in a moment of hurt or pride, that later shaped your choices for years?

Practice this week
Monks in these chapters leave home; the householder’s version, as Chitta himself offers the king (Utt 13.31–33), is to stay in dharma, do noble deeds and have compassion for all beings. This week, pick one evening and do one small act of dharma with a family member: read one verse of this lesson to them, or go together to give something to someone in need. Do it today, not “next month” (Utt 14.27).
Self-check
Question

What, according to Chitta, separated the two brothers in their sixth life?

The karma made out of desire: Sambhuta’s binding resolve (niyana) that his austerities should make him an emperor (Utt 13.8; story on pages 309–311).

Question

What image does Brahmadatta use for knowing the dharma but not following it?

An elephant sunk in mud that sees the dry ground but cannot reach the bank (Utt 13.30).

Question

How do the sons answer their father’s claim that the soul perishes with the body?

The soul is formless, so the senses cannot grasp it; being formless it is eternal, and its own inner faults bind it to worldly life (Utt 14.18–19).

Question

Who must be the last to be won over in Chapter 14, and who wins him over?

King Ishukara, woken by Queen Kamalavati when he starts taking the priest’s abandoned wealth: “a man who eats what has been vomited is not praised” (Utt 14.37–40).

10_course/lesson_12_kings_and_princes_wh.title: Lesson 12 · Kings and Princes Who Woke
10_course/lesson_12_kings_and_princes_wh.content:
Lesson 12 · Kings and Princes Who Woke
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 45 minutes
Aim: You will understand, through three royal stories, what it means in the texts to be “protected”: not by power, money or family, but by your own soul set on the right path.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 18: King Sanjaya: look for what the silent monk asks the hunting king to give to others.
Uttaradhyayan 19: Mrigaputra: look for the prince’s answer when his parents say the monk’s life is too hard.
Uttaradhyayan 20: The Great Nirgrantha: look for the two kinds of “being without a protector”.

Key ideas


The safety you want, give to others. King Sanjaya, hunting deer, is terrified that he has angered a meditating monk. The monk tells him he has nothing to fear, and now he too must become a giver of fearlessness (abhaya) to other beings, for “why are you so attached to violence?” (Utt 18.11). Only our good and bad deeds go with us into the next life (Utt 18.14–17), and the king renounces (Utt 18.18–19).


Nothing is hard for one without craving. Prince Mrigaputra sees a monk from his window and remembers he was once a monk himself (Utt 19.4–9). When his parents list the hardships of monkhood, he answers:

सो बिंतऽम्मा पियरो, एवमेयं जहा फुडं ।
इह लोए णिप्पिवासस्स, णत्थि किंचि वि दुक्करं ॥४५॥

He said, “Mother and father, it is just as you say, the monk’s life is hard. But for one who has no thirst for the things of this world, nothing at all is hard.” (Utt 19.45)
He compares dharma to food for a long road: whoever goes on to the next life without it suffers on the way (Utt 19.19–20). He will live “like a deer”, alone, content with what he finds (Utt 19.76–84).


The soul is its own protector, friend and enemy. A young monk tells King Shrenik that he, the king, has no protector himself (Utt 20.12): when the monk was struck by burning pain, no doctor, wealth or loving family could take it away (Utt 20.18–30). The soul itself “makes and unmakes its sorrows and joys”, and is its own friend on the right path and its own enemy on the wrong one (Utt 20.37). But there is a second helplessness: the monk who takes the path and then grows slack is “an empty fist, a counterfeit coin” (Utt 20.38–50).


Connect
These stories join the earlier ones of King Nami (Lesson 9) and King Ishukara (Lesson 11): someone with everything sees one small thing and wakes up. Sanjaya’s lesson of giving fearlessness is the heart of Ahimsa; Mrigaputra’s five great vows, carefulnesses and guards (Utt 19.85–94) point ahead to Samiti and Gupti (Lesson 17); and the hardships his parents list are the Parishaha of Lesson 16. That the soul is its own maker of joy and sorrow is Karma seen from the inside.
Reflect

Who or what do you lean on as your “protector”: a job, savings, a parent, a partner? What would remain if that were gone tomorrow?
Is there a being, person or animal, who is afraid of you in some way? What would it take for you to be a giver of fearlessness to them?
Mrigaputra says nothing is hard for one without craving. Which thing feels “too hard” for you, and what craving sits behind that feeling?

Practice this week
A monk in these chapters gives up kingdom and home. A householder’s version of Sanjaya’s lesson: for one week, choose one small, daily way to give fearlessness. For example, catch and release insects instead of killing them, or speak softly to someone at home or work who is nervous around you. Each night, note one moment in which you made someone, or something, feel safe.
Self-check
Question

What does the monk Gardabhali ask King Sanjaya to become?

A giver of fearlessness (abhaya) to other beings, since the king himself has nothing to fear from the monk (Utt 18.11).

Question

How does Mrigaputra answer the question “Who will treat you when you fall ill as a monk?”

When a deer falls sick in the forest no one treats it; it rests and, when well, finds its own food and water. He will live the deer’s way (Utt 19.76–84).

Question

Why does the young monk say King Shrenik cannot be his protector?

Because the king is without a protector himself; no wealth, doctor or family could remove the monk’s own suffering, and the king’s power cannot remove his (Utt 20.12–30).

Question

What is the “second kind of helplessness” in Chapter 20?

A monk who takes the Nirgrantha path and then grows careless in his vows and conduct; he loses both this world and the next (Utt 20.38–50).

10_course/lesson_13_samudrapala_and_rath.content:
Lesson 13 · Samudrapala and Rathanemi
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will see two ways the path is kept: by being woken once and then staying steady through hardship (Samudrapala), and by being pulled back by a good friend’s firm words when you waver (Rathanemi and Rajemati).
Read

Uttaradhyayan 21: Samudrapala: look for what the merchant’s son sees from his window, and how he bears hardship afterwards.
Uttaradhyayan 22: Rathanemi: look for why Arishtanemi turns back from his wedding, and what Rajemati says in the cave.

Key ideas


Every bad deed has its own end. Samudrapala, a rich young man, sees a condemned man led to execution and says, “Ah! This is the bitter end of bad deeds” (Utt 21.9). He takes the five great vows (Utt 21.12) and then stays steady: like a royal elephant at the front of battle (Utt 21.17), “unshaken like Mount Meru in the wind” (Utt 21.19), neither puffed up by honour nor cast down by blame (Utt 21.20).


Compassion can turn a whole life. On the way to his own wedding, Prince Arishtanemi sees animals and birds penned up to feed his guests. He asks:

कस्स अट्ठा इमे पाणा, एए सव्वे सुहेसिणो ।
वाडेहिं पंजरेहिं च, सण्णिरुद्धा य अच्छहि ॥

For whose sake are all these creatures, who all want happiness, kept shut in pens and cages? (Utt 22.16)
Thinking that so many deaths “because of me” will not be for his good (Utt 22.19), he gives away his ornaments and renounces (Utt 22.20–27). His bride Rajemati, after her grief, renounces too (Utt 22.28–32).


A steady friend can bring back one who wavers. Alone in a cave, the monk Rathanemi is shaken by desire and asks Rajemati to enjoy pleasures with him “and afterwards” follow the Jina’s path (Utt 22.36–38). She answers that a proud snake would rather enter fire than take back its spat-out poison; he wants “to drink again what you have vomited out” (Utt 22.42–43). Hearing her, he is brought back to dharma “as an elephant is by the goad” and keeps his monkhood all his life (Utt 22.48–49).


Connect
Like Nami, Mrigaputra and the others (Lessons 9 and 12), Samudrapala wakes at one sight; the condemned man is Karma made visible. His steadiness through cold, heat and insects is Parishaha, taken up fully in Lesson 16. Arishtanemi’s question to the charioteer is Ahimsa in its plainest form, and Rajemati’s call to “master anger, pride, deceit and greed” (Utt 22.47) names the four passions of Kashaya from Lesson 4. Her “vomited” image echoes Queen Kamalavati in Lesson 11 (Utt 14.38).
Reflect

Have you ever seen something, in the news or on the street, that made you suddenly feel “my deeds will come back to me”? What did you do with that feeling?
Is there any celebration in your life (a wedding, a party, a festival meal) where living beings suffer for your sake without your seeing it?
Who in your life is a “Rajemati”: someone who would tell you plainly when you are slipping? Have you ever been that person for someone else?

Practice this week
Arishtanemi’s renunciation is a monk’s path. A householder’s version: plan your next meal for guests, or your next family celebration, so that no animal is killed for it, and, where you can, fewer small beings are harmed (less waste, no burning of insects, nothing bought “for the occasion” that you will throw away). Then, separately, ask one trusted friend or family member: “If you ever see me slipping from what I say I value, will you tell me?”
Self-check
Question

What sight wakes Samudrapala, and what does he say?

A condemned man being led to execution; he says, “Ah! This is the bitter end of bad deeds” (Utt 21.8–9).

Question

What image does the chapter use for Samudrapala’s steadiness in hardship?

A royal elephant at the head of a battle (Utt 21.17), and Mount Meru unshaken by the wind (Utt 21.19).

Question

Why does Arishtanemi turn back from his wedding?

The animals and birds in the pens were to be killed to feed his guests; out of compassion he thought that so many beings killed because of him would not be good for him in the next world (Utt 22.14–19).

Question

What finally brings Rathanemi back to restraint?

Rajemati’s well-spoken words, by which he was set firm in dharma as an elephant is turned by the goad (Utt 22.39–48).

10_course/lesson_14_keshi_and_gautama.title: Lesson 14 · Keshi and Gautama
10_course/lesson_14_keshi_and_gautama.content:
Lesson 14 · Keshi and Gautama
Unit 2: Waking up (Uttaradhyayan) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will understand how two great monks with different rules settled their differences with courtesy, and why the texts say the real path is inner: conquering the self, the mind and the passions.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 23: Keshi and Gautama: look for the two questions about outer rules, then the ten riddles whose answers are all inside us.

Key ideas


Differences in rules are settled by wisdom and courtesy. Parshva’s monks kept four great vows and could wear any cloth; Mahavira’s kept five and wore plain white cloth, and the disciples of both wondered why (Utt 23.10–13). Gautama, honouring the older line, goes to Keshi, and Keshi offers him a clean seat (Utt 23.14–20). Gautama’s answer: “it is wisdom that examines dharma” (Utt 23.25), and the rules were taught in two ways because disciples in different times were different (Utt 23.26). Outer marks only support restraint; the real means of liberation are knowledge, faith and conduct (Utt 23.29–34).


The real enemy is the unconquered self. Asked how he lives among thousands of enemies, Gautama answers:

एगप्पा अजिए सत्तू, कसाया इंदियाणि य ।
ते जिणित्तु जहाणायं, विहरामि अहं मुणी ॥

The one self, unconquered, is the enemy; so are the passions and the senses. Having conquered them in the right way, O sage, I live freely. (Utt 23.38)
The other riddles point the same way: the fire inside is the passions, put out by scripture, good conduct and austerity (Utt 23.50–54); the wild horse is the mind, trained by dharma (Utt 23.55–59).


Dharma is the island; the body is the boat. For beings swept along by the flood of old age and death, “dharma is the island, the firm ground, the goal and the highest refuge” (Utt 23.68). The body is the boat and the soul the sailor; a boat that leaks, letting in karma, sinks, while a sound one reaches the far shore (Utt 23.73–74). At the end Keshi joins Mahavira’s order and takes the five great vows (Utt 23.85–89).


Connect
Lesson 4 taught the four passions; here Gautama calls them, with the senses, the enemy to be conquered (Kashaya). “Knowledge, faith and conduct” as the true means is Ratnatraya, which Lesson 19 takes up fully from Chapter 28. The leaking boat is the inflow of karma from the nine realities (Nine Tattvas) of Lesson 2. And the courtesy between Keshi and Gautama is Vinaya between equals, the theme of Lesson 15.
Reflect

When you disagree with someone about “the right way” to practise (fasting, food rules, rituals), do you go to them with courtesy, as Gautama did, or wait for them to come to you?
Of Gautama’s riddles, which describes you best right now: a fire inside, a wild horse, a creeper of craving, or a snare of attachment?
Which of your habits are “outer marks” that support you, and which have you started to treat as the goal itself?

Practice this week
Monks in this chapter debate monks’ rules of vows and dress. A householder’s version: this week, when you notice a difference in practice with someone, another family, sect or friend, do not argue about the outer form. Ask them, with courtesy, what the practice means to them, and listen. Then, once a day, name to yourself one moment the “wild horse” of your mind ran off, and how you brought it back.
Self-check
Question

What two differences between the followers of Parshva and Mahavira prompted the meeting?

Four great vows versus five, and freedom to wear any cloth versus plain, limited white cloth (Utt 23.10–13).

Question

Why, according to Gautama, was dharma taught in two ways?

Because the first Tirthankara’s monks were straight but slow, the last one’s crooked and slow, and the middle ones’ straight and wise (Utt 23.26).

Question

In Gautama’s riddles, what is the wild horse and what holds it?

The mind, held by the reins of scripture and trained by dharma (Utt 23.55–59).

Question

In the boat image, what are the boat, the sailor and the ocean?

The body is the boat, the soul is the sailor, and worldly life is the ocean (Utt 23.73).

10_course/lesson_15_humility_and_learnin.title: Lesson 15 · Humility and Learning
10_course/lesson_15_humility_and_learnin.content:
Lesson 15 · Humility and Learning
Unit 3: The disciple’s life · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will understand why the Uttaradhyayan begins with humility (vinaya), how humility opens the door to learning, and what kind of student makes a teacher’s work light or heavy.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 1: Humility: look for how the humble disciple takes correction, and why it is better to tame yourself.
Uttaradhyayan 11: The Glory of the Learned: look for the five things that block learning.
Uttaradhyayan 27: The Unruly Bullocks: look for the excuses bad disciples make, and what Garga does at the end.

Key ideas


Tame yourself before others have to. The disciple’s first task is with his own self:

अप्पा चेव दमेयव्वो, अप्पा हु खलु दुद्दमो ।
अप्पा दंतो सुही होइ, अस्सिं लोए परत्थ य ॥१५॥

The self alone should be tamed, for the self is truly hard to tame. One who tames the self is happy in this world and in the next. (Utt 1.15)
It is better to do it oneself through restraint and austerity than to be tamed by others with chains and blows (Utt 1.16). A good horse turns at the mere sight of the whip (Utt 1.12).


How you hear correction decides what it does to you. The wise take even harsh instruction as being for their good; to fools, the same words become a cause of hatred (Utt 1.29). The good disciple feels treated like a son or brother, and if the teacher is angry he calms him with joined hands: “I will not do it again” (Utt 1.37–44).


Learning grows from humility and is blocked by five things. Pride, anger, carelessness, illness and laziness keep learning away (Utt 11.3); the proud, sense-greedy, chattering monk without humility is not learned (Utt 11.2). One who stays with the teacher and speaks pleasantly is worthy of teaching (Utt 11.14), and the learned monk shines “like milk in a conch” (Utt 11.15). The opposite is Chapter 27’s unruly bullocks: disciples who answer back and say “she won’t give, send another monk” (Utt 27.11–13), until the elder Garga leaves them and goes on alone, gentle and composed (Utt 27.16–17).


Connect
Unit 2 showed people waking up; Unit 3 asks how a woken person learns and lives. Humility is the concept Vinaya, and the pride that blocks learning is one of the four passions in Kashaya (Lesson 4). Gautama’s courtesy to Keshi in Lesson 14 was humility between two teachers. “Restraint and austerity” as the way to tame the self (Utt 1.16) links to Samyama and Tapas.
Reflect

Think of the last time someone corrected you, at home or at work. Did you hear it as “my gain” or as an attack?
Of the five blocks to learning (pride, anger, carelessness, illness, laziness), which one most often stops you from learning something new?
In some part of your life, are you the willing ox or the unruly bullock? Who is the “driver” who tires because of you?

Practice this week
These chapters are rules for a monk with his teacher. A householder’s version: choose one person you learn from (a parent, an elder, a senior at work, a teacher of the faith). This week, when they correct you, do not explain or defend for the first minute; say “thank you, I will look at that”, and act on it once. Also notice one excuse you make to avoid a task (“someone else can do it”), and do the task instead.
Self-check
Question

According to Utt 1.2, who is called humble (vinita)?

One who acts on the teacher’s commands and directions, stays near him, and understands his gestures and expressions (Utt 1.2).

Question

What are the five things that block learning?

Pride, anger, carelessness, illness and laziness (Utt 11.3).

Question

What does the image of milk in a conch mean?

Milk in a conch shines twice over; so in a learned monk dharma, good name and learning all shine (Utt 11.15).

Question

What does the elder Garga do with his bad disciples?

He gives them up, takes up austerity firmly and wanders the earth alone, gentle, deep and composed (Utt 27.16–17).

10_course/lesson_16_hardship_and_the_tru.title: Lesson 16 · Hardship and the True Monk
10_course/lesson_16_hardship_and_the_tru.content:
Lesson 16 · Hardship and the True Monk
Unit 3: The disciple’s life · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand the twenty-two hardships (parishaha) a monk learns to bear, and the marks that separate a true monk from one who is a monk “only in dress and name”.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 2: Enduring Hardships: look for how a monk thinks when he is abused, beaten or given nothing.
Uttaradhyayan 15: The True Monk: look for the refrain “he is a monk” and what each verse adds.
Uttaradhyayan 17: The Bad Monk: look for the excuses of the monk who took his vows “like a lion” and lives “like a jackal”.

Key ideas


Hardship is not an obstacle but a help. Mahavira named twenty-two hardships, from hunger, thirst, cold and insects to abuse, getting nothing, illness, honour, slow learning and doubt (Utt 2, prose passage and v.1–46). The introduction says they are not obstacles but help in destroying karma; they differ from austerity, which a monk chooses, because they arise on their own while he keeps his restraint (Utt 2.1). When given nothing, he thinks:

अज्जेवाहं ण लब्भामि, अवि लाभो सुए सिया ।
जो एवं पडिसंचिक्खे, अलाभो तं ण तज्जए ॥३१॥

“Today I have received nothing; perhaps tomorrow I will.” The hardship of getting nothing does not trouble the one who reflects like this. (Utt 2.31)


Insult is answered by not flaring up. If others abuse a monk, he does not flare up, for one who does “becomes like the ignorant” (Utt 2.24); if struck, he reflects that the soul cannot be destroyed (Utt 2.27). The true monk of Chapter 15 knows abuse and beating as the fruit of his own actions and stays “neither upset nor elated” (Utt 15.3); he wants no respect, worship or praise (Utt 15.5), and is not afraid of terrible sounds (Utt 15.14).


The robe does not make the monk; the life does. Chapter 17’s bad monk asks, “What will I do by studying scripture?” (Utt 17.2), sleeps after eating and drinking (Utt 17.3), is deceitful, proud and greedy (Utt 17.11), and keeps changing teachers (Utt 17.17). He is condemned “like poison”, while the monk who avoids these faults is “honoured like nectar” (Utt 17.20–21). Chapter 15’s introduction says the refrain “he is a monk” is not there to judge others but to set out the qualities a monk should live by (Utt 15, intro).


Connect
The hardships are the concept Parishaha; you have already met them in Samudrapala bearing cold, heat and mosquitoes (Lesson 13) and in Mrigaputra’s parents’ warnings (Lesson 12). Bearing them sheds old Karma, and the bad monk’s pride, deceit and greed are the four passions of Kashaya. The bad monk who “answers his guru back” is the opposite of the humble disciple of Lesson 15 (Vinaya).
Reflect

When someone speaks harshly to you, what happens in your body in the first second? What would it take to let the words pass like “village thorns” (Utt 2.24–27)?
When you do not get something you expected (a reply, a thank-you, a result), can you honestly say “perhaps tomorrow” and mean it?
Is there a practice you once took up “like a lion” and now keep “like a jackal”? What crept in: comfort, sleep, taste, or doing it your own way?

Practice this week
The twenty-two hardships are monks’ rules: no fire, no fan, no treatment when ill, no unboiled water. Do not copy those. A householder’s version: pick one small discomfort this week and bear it without complaint or quick fix, for example a hot afternoon without switching on the air-conditioner at once, or a delayed meal without irritation. And once, when someone is short with you, stay silent for a breath before answering, and answer without heat.
Self-check
Question

How does the introduction to Chapter 2 distinguish hardship (parishaha) from austerity?

Austerity is chosen by the monk; a hardship arises on its own while he keeps his restraint, and it helps in destroying karma (Utt 2, prose passage and v.1).

Question

What should a monk reflect when someone strikes him?

“The soul cannot be destroyed” (Utt 2.27).

Question

According to Chapter 15, how does the true monk view abuse and beating?

As the fruit of his own past actions; he bears every hardship evenly, neither upset nor elated (Utt 15.3).

Question

What excuse does the bad monk give for not studying scripture?

He has a safe place to stay, a cloth, food and water, and he knows what is happening now, so what will scripture do for him? (Utt 17.2)

10_course/lesson_17_guarding_the_mind.title: Lesson 17 · Guarding the Mind: Celibacy, the Eight Mothers, the Homeless Path
10_course/lesson_17_guarding_the_mind.content:
Lesson 17 · Guarding the Mind: Celibacy, the Eight Mothers, the Homeless Path
Unit 3: The disciple’s life · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand how a monk guards his practice from the outside in: ten supports for celibacy, the eight “mothers of the teaching” (five careful actions and three restraints), and the rules that keep home’s bonds from creeping back.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 16: The Supports of Celibacy: look for the ten supports and the reason given for every one.
Uttaradhyayan 24: Mothers of the Teaching: look for the five careful actions, the three restraints, and how they differ.
Uttaradhyayan 35: The Homeless Monk's Path: look for why a monk does not build, cook, light a fire, or buy and sell.

Key ideas


Celibacy is guarded by simple outer fences. The introduction calls celibacy (brahmacharya) the backbone of a monk’s life; rules alone do not end desire, but they are “watchful guards” (Utt 16, pp.368, 370). The ten supports cover where he lives, what he talks about, sees, hears and remembers, what and how much he eats, and whether he adorns himself (Utt 16, sutras 3–12; v.1–10). For each, the same reason is given: without it, doubt, longing and wavering may arise and the vow may break (Utt 16, sutras 3–12).


Eight “mothers” carry the whole teaching.

अट्ठ पवयणमायाओ, समिई गुत्ती तहेव य ।
पंचेव य समिईओ, तओ गुत्तीउ आहिया ॥

The eight mothers of the teaching are the careful actions and the restraints: five careful actions and three restraints, it is said. (Utt 24.1)
The five careful actions (samiti) are in walking, speaking, seeking, handling things and disposing of waste; the three restraints (gupti) are of mind, speech and body (Utt 24.2). Careful speech means giving up eight things, anger, pride, deceit, greed, laughter, fear, chatter and idle talk, and speaking blameless, measured words at the right time (Utt 24.9–10). Samiti is for doing right; gupti is for turning back from all harm (Utt 24.26).


Home’s bonds creep back unless they are cut. Even after leaving home, the pull of family, society and status returns (Utt 35, introduction). So a monk does not build a house, “for in house-building the killing of living beings is plainly seen” (Utt 35.8), does not cook or light a fire (Utt 35.10–12), treats earth and gold alike and does not buy or sell (Utt 35.13–15), and eats “not for taste but to sustain his life of restraint” (Utt 35.17).


Connect
The careful actions and restraints are the concept Samiti and Gupti; you met them in Mrigaputra’s monkhood (Lesson 12) and in Rathanemi, “guarded in mind, speech and body” (Lesson 13). The eight things to give up in speech include the four passions of Kashaya, and careful speech builds on Lesson 4. Not building or cooking, so as not to harm beings in water, earth and wood (Utt 35.10), is Ahimsa reaching to the smallest life, and all three chapters together are Samyama.
Reflect

What do you watch, read or scroll through that leaves your mind restless afterwards? What would a “secluded lodging” for your mind look like?
Of the eight things to give up in speech, which one most often colours your words: anger, pride, deceit, greed, laughter at others, fear, chatter or idle talk?
Where in your home or work do “bonds of status” (looking successful, being respected) quietly shape your choices?

Practice this week
Full celibacy, no cooking and no buying are monks’ rules. The householder’s version of celibacy in the sources is contentment with one’s own spouse (svadara-santosha), as Ananda vowed (Upasakdashang 1.19, in Conduct). This week, take up one “mother” in a householder’s form: careful walking. Each time you walk anywhere (to the car, the kitchen, the office), look at the ground a little ahead and give your full attention to walking for those few steps, without the phone (Utt 24.7–8). Note at night how many times you remembered.
Self-check
Question

What reason does Chapter 16 give for each of the ten supports of celibacy?

Without it, doubt, longing or wavering about celibacy may arise; the vow may break; he may lose his balance of mind, fall ill, or fall away from the dharma (Utt 16, sutras 3–12).

Question

Name the eight mothers of the teaching.

Care in walking, speaking, seeking, picking up and putting down, and disposal; restraint of mind, speech and body (Utt 24.2).

Question

How do samiti and gupti differ?

The careful actions are for carrying out right conduct; the restraints are for turning back completely from everything harmful (Utt 24.26).

Question

Why should a monk not build a house, according to Chapter 35?

Because in house-building the killing of living beings, moving and still, is plainly seen (Utt 35.8).

10_course/lesson_18_a_day_lived_well.title: Lesson 18 · A Day Lived Well
10_course/lesson_18_a_day_lived_well.content:
Lesson 18 · A Day Lived Well
Unit 3: The disciple’s life · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will see how a monk’s whole day and night is laid out as one careful routine, and how all of conduct comes down to a single rule: turn away from lack of restraint and turn toward restraint.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 26: Proper Conduct: look for the ten courtesies, the four watches of the day, and how the day ends.
Uttaradhyayan 31: Rules of Conduct: look for the one rule in v.2 and the “two sins” in v.3; skim the rest of the count from one to thirty-three.

Key ideas


A good day has a shape. The monk’s day has four watches: study, meditation, alms, study (Utt 26.12), and the night likewise has study, meditation, sleep, study (Utt 26.17–18). It begins with a question to the teacher, “should I serve or study?” (Utt 26.8–10), and it ends with confession (pratikraman): he reflects on his lapses in knowledge, faith and conduct and confesses them (Utt 26.37–43). Ten courtesies run through it, among them inviting others to share food, saying “micchami dukkadam” for one’s own fault, and rising for elders (Utt 26.2–7).


Small care protects all life. Inspecting his cloth and bowls is an act of compassion; done with full attention, it protects every kind of being:

पुढवी आउक्काए, तेऊ वाऊ वणस्सइ तसाणं ।
पडिलेहणा आउत्तो, छण्हं पि संरक्खओ होइ ॥

One who stays attentive while inspecting becomes a protector of all six kinds of beings: earth, water, fire, air, plant and moving beings. (Utt 26.31)
A monk who chats or tells stories while inspecting harms all six (Utt 26.29–30). Even eating and fasting are done for named reasons, six each (Utt 26.32–35).


All conduct is one turn. Chapter 31 counts from one to thirty-three, but it starts with the one rule: “turn away from lack of restraint, and toward restraint” (Utt 31.2). Next come the two sins, attachment and aversion, which “set sinful action going”; the commentary calls them seeds from which a whole banyan tree of sin grows (Utt 31.3). Every later number (the four passions, the five vows, the six kinds of beings, the ten virtues beginning with forgiveness) unfolds that one turn (Utt 31.6–10).


Connect
The ten courtesies are Vinaya made daily (Lesson 15), and inspection with attention is Samiti in action (Lesson 17). “Turn toward restraint” is Samyama in a single line, and the six kinds of beings protected by care are taught fully in Ahimsa and Lesson 25. Chapter 31’s mention of keeping to the three bright soul-colours (Utt 31.8) points ahead to Leshya in Lesson 22.
Reflect

Does your day have a shape you chose, or does it take whatever shape your phone and work give it?
When you have wronged someone, how long does it usually take you to say so? What stops you from saying it the same day?
Think of one strong like and one strong dislike you have. How have they “set going” choices you later regretted (Utt 31.3)?

Practice this week
The four watches, alms rounds and inspection of bowls are monks’ rules. A householder’s version, honestly smaller: each night this week, before sleep, take five quiet minutes for your own short “evening confession”. Ask: where today did I lack care in thought, word or deed? Name it plainly, and where someone was hurt, say “micchami dukkadam” (or simply “I’m sorry”) to them the next morning. Once in the week, invite someone to share your food before you eat, as the monk invites his fellows (Utt 26.2–7).
Self-check
Question

What are the four watches of a monk’s day?

First study, then meditation, then alms, then study again (Utt 26.12).

Question

Why is attentive inspection of cloth and bowls important?

One who stays attentive while inspecting protects all six kinds of beings; one who chats or studies while doing it harms them (Utt 26.29–31).

Question

What is the single rule with which Chapter 31 begins its count?

Turn away from lack of restraint, and turn toward restraint (Utt 31.2).

Question

What are the “two sins” of Chapter 31?

Attachment and aversion, which set all sinful action going (Utt 31.3).

10_course/lesson_19_the_path_to_liberati.title: Lesson 19 · The Path to Liberation
10_course/lesson_19_the_path_to_liberati.content:
Lesson 19 · The Path to Liberation
Unit 4: The path and reality · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will be able to name the four parts of the path to liberation (knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity), say what each one does, and explain why faith comes first.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 28: The Path to Liberation: look for the four parts in v.2, the nine truths in v.14, and what each part does in v.35.

Key ideas


The path has four parts, and each does its own work. “Knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity: this is the path, as proclaimed by the all-seeing Jinas” (Utt 28.2). Then:

णाणेण जाणइ भावे, दंसणेण य सद्दहे ।
चरित्तेण णिगिण्हाइ, तवेण परिसुज्झइ ॥

By knowledge one knows things as they are, and by faith one believes them. By conduct one holds karma back, and by austerity one is made pure. (Utt 28.35)
The commentary compares this to a patient, who must understand the illness, trust the doctor, take the medicine and keep the diet (Utt 28.35–36, commentary).


Knowledge knows a world of six substances; faith holds to nine truths. Knowledge is of five kinds, from sensory knowledge (mati) to omniscience (kevala) (Utt 28.4). What it knows is a universe of six substances: the media of motion and rest, space, time, matter and living beings (Utt 28.7–13). Right faith (samyaktva) is believing the nine truths as they are: soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, sin, inflow of karma, stopping it, shedding it and liberation (Utt 28.14–15). It can arise by ten roads, naturally or through teaching or study, and spreads “like a drop of oil on water” (Utt 28.16–27).


Faith comes first; conduct and austerity finish the work. Without faith there is no right knowledge, without knowledge no conduct, without conduct no freedom from karma, and without that no nirvana (Utt 28.30). Conduct is of five kinds, beginning with equanimity (samayika) (Utt 28.32–33). Austerity is twelve-fold: six outer (such as fasting and eating less) and six inner (such as atonement, humility, service, study and meditation) (Utt 28.34).


Connect
This chapter gathers what the course has taught so far. The six substances and nine truths are Six Substances and Nine Tattvas from Lesson 2; the five kinds of knowledge are Five Knowledges. Knowledge, faith and conduct together are the three jewels of Ratnatraya, which Gautama named as the real means of liberation in Lesson 14 (Utt 23.29–34). Austerity, the fourth part, is Tapas, and Lesson 21 gives its twelve kinds in detail; note that humility (Lesson 15) and study are themselves counted as inner austerity.
Reflect

Of the four parts, knowing, believing, restraining and purifying, which is strongest in your life now, and which is weakest?
Did your own faith come “naturally”, from family, or through teaching and study? Has it ever spread “like a drop of oil on water” from one idea to many?
Think of a time you knew something was right but did not act on it. Which link in the chain of Utt 28.30 was missing?

Practice this week
Monks practise all twelve kinds of austerity in full. A householder’s version, drawn from the list itself (Utt 28.34): choose one outer and one inner austerity for the week. For example, outer: eat a little less than you want at one meal a day (eating less), or give up one rich food; inner: fifteen minutes of study of these lessons each day, or one act of service for someone who needs it. Write down which two you chose, and check them off each evening.
Self-check
Question

What are the four parts of the path to liberation?

Knowledge, faith (darshana), conduct and austerity (Utt 28.2).

Question

What does each of the four parts do?

Knowledge knows things as they are, faith believes them, conduct holds karma back, and austerity purifies (Utt 28.35).

Question

What is right faith (samyaktva), according to Chapter 28?

Truly believing, from within or through teaching, in the nine real principles: soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, sin, inflow, stopping, shedding and liberation (Utt 28.14–15).

Question

Why does faith come first?

Without faith there is no right knowledge; without knowledge, no conduct; without conduct, no freedom from karma; and without that, no nirvana (Utt 28.30).
