10_course/lesson_20_right_effort.title: Lesson 20 · Right Effort: 73 Questions
10_course/lesson_20_right_effort.content:
Lesson 20 · Right Effort: 73 Questions
Unit 4: The path and reality · about 50 minutes
Aim: You will understand how one simple question, “Lord, what does the soul gain by this?”, turns 73 practices into a map of the path, and you will be able to pick one practice and say what it brings.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 29: Right Effort: read “How the chapter works” first, then the table of all 73 practices; look closely at s.3 (longing), s.19 (forgiveness) and s.61 (the threaded needle).

Key ideas


Right effort is effort turned inward. Effort turned outward, toward possessions and success, is not right effort; effort turned inward, toward purifying the soul, is (Utt 29 s.1, commentary). Each practice is asked the same question, “Lord, what does the soul gain through ___?” (Utt 29, “How the chapter works”), and the introduction says any one practice can be a starting point, since all of them lead to the soul’s purity. The first is longing for liberation (samvega), which brings the highest faith and destroys the passions that bind without end (Utt 29 s.3).


Everyday practices have real fruits. Equanimity (samayika) stops sinful activity (s.10); pratikramana mends the holes in one’s vows (s.13); kayotsarga leaves one light “like a porter who has put down his load” (s.14); self-study destroys the karma that covers knowledge (s.20). And asking forgiveness:

खमावणयाए णं भंते ! जीवे किं जणयइ ?
खमावणयाए णं पल्हायणभावं जणयइ । पल्हायण भावमुवगए य सव्वपाण-भूय-जीव-सत्तेसु मित्तीभावमुप्पाएइ । मित्तीभावमुवगए यावि जीवे भावविसोहिं काऊण णिब्भए भवइ ।

Lord, what does the soul gain by asking forgiveness? It gains gladness of heart. Glad at heart, it feels friendship for all living beings. In friendship, it purifies its feelings and becomes fearless. (Utt 29 s.19)


Conquering the passions and senses leads to the final stillness. Conquering anger brings forgiveness, pride brings softness, deceit brings straightforwardness, and greed brings contentment (s.69–72); restraining the five senses stops attachment and aversion toward their objects (s.64–68). A soul that holds the scripture is “not lost in the world”, like a needle with its thread (s.61). At the very end the omniscient one stops mind, speech, body and breath, and the soul rises in a single instant to the top of the universe (s.74–75).


Connect
Lesson 19 named the four parts of the path; this chapter shows them broken into 73 single steps. Asking forgiveness and friendship with all beings (s.19) is the heart of Lesson 5 (Forgiveness and Friendship). Conquering the four passions (s.69–72) is Kashaya turned to its cure, restraint and austerity (s.28–29) are Samyama and Tapas, and serving the guru, which brings humility (s.6), is Vinaya. Every fruit is described as karma bound, loosened or shed: Karma.
Reflect

Where in your life is most of your effort turned outward, toward possessions and success? What would turning even a part of it inward look like?
Is there someone you have not asked forgiveness of? What do you think you would gain, in the chapter’s words “gladness of heart”, if you did?
Which of the four passions would be the best one for you to start conquering, and what quality (forgiveness, softness, straightforwardness, contentment) would it bring?

Practice this week
Many of the 73 practices (giving up equipment, the lifelong fast, the rock-still state) belong to monks. Several belong to any follower: asking forgiveness (s.19), self-study (s.20), deep reflection (s.24), praise of the Tirthankaras (s.11). This week, pick one of these. Each day, do it once, and then ask yourself the chapter’s own question in your own words: “What did my soul gain by this today?” Write one line of answer.
Self-check
Question

What question is asked of every practice in Chapter 29?

“Lord, what does the soul gain through ___?” (Utt 29, “How the chapter works”).

Question

What does the soul gain from longing for liberation (samvega)?

The highest faith in dharma; it destroys the passions that bind without end and binds no new karma; some are freed in this life and the rest within three births (Utt 29 s.3).

Question

What does the image of the threaded needle mean?

A needle with its thread is not lost even when it falls; so a soul that holds the scripture is not lost in the world (Utt 29 s.61).

Question

What does conquering each of the four passions bring?

Conquering anger brings forgiveness, pride brings softness, deceit brings straightforwardness, and greed brings contentment (Utt 29 s.69–72).

10_course/lesson_21_austerity_and_neglig.title: Lesson 21 · Austerity and the Roots of Negligence
10_course/lesson_21_austerity_and_neglig.content:
Lesson 21 · Austerity and the Roots of Negligence
Unit 4: The path and reality · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will understand how austerity (tapa) dries up old karma once the inflow is stopped, and why the texts say suffering comes from our attachment and aversion, not from the things we see, hear, smell, taste and touch.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 30: The Path of Austerity: look for the lake that dries up, and the six outer and six inner austerities.
Uttaradhyayan 32: Sources of Negligence: look for the chain from owning to suffering, the five creatures that die by one sense, and the lotus leaf.

Key ideas


First close the channels, then dry the lake. A soul that gives up killing, lying, stealing, sex, possessions and eating at night, keeps the careful practices and guards, and masters the senses lets no new karma in (Utt 30.1–4). Then, as a lake whose streams are blocked dries in the sun, karma gathered over crores of births is burned away by austerity (Utt 30.5–6). Austerity without first stopping the inflow is like heating a lake that is still being filled.


Austerity is outer and inner, six of each. The outer six work through the body and others can see them: fasting, eating less, limits on begging alms, giving up rich food, bodily hardship and withdrawal (Utt 30.8). The inner six work on the heart: atonement, humility, service, study, meditation and letting go of the body (Utt 30.30). The commentary defines austerity as “restraining desire”, and true meditation means giving up distressed and cruel thinking (Utt 30.7, 30.35). Even “eating less” can be as small as one mouthful less (Utt 30.14–24).


The object is not at fault; the attachment is. Attachment and aversion (raga and dvesha) are the seeds of karma, and karma is the root of birth and death (Utt 32.7). The moth dies for light, the deer for music, the fish for the bait: in each case “the object is in no way at fault” (Utt 32.22–86). The chapter sums it up:

एविंदियत्था य मणस्स अत्था, दुक्खस्स हेउं मणुयस्स रागिणो ।
ते चेव थोवं पि कयाइ दुक्खं, ण वीयरागस्स करेंति किंचि ॥

So the objects of the senses and of the mind are a cause of suffering for a person with attachment. Those very objects never cause even the least suffering to one free of attachment. (Utt 32.100)


Connect
You first met the drying lake in Lesson 2 (from Utt 30.5–6), and Lesson 19 named austerity as the fourth part of the path; here it is laid out in full as Tapas. Humility, which Lesson 15 taught as the disciple’s first quality, turns up here as an inner austerity: see Vinaya. Stopping the inflow through the careful practices and guards is Samiti and Gupti, and the chain “attachment and aversion → karma → birth and death” is the heart of Karma.
Reflect

Think of one thing you keep reaching for (a food, a screen, a kind of praise). Is the trouble in the thing, or in your pull toward it?
Which of the six inner austerities (atonement, humility, service, study, meditation, letting go of the body) already has a small place in your week, and which has none?
When you have tried to change a habit, did you first stop feeding it, or only try to burn it off by effort?

Practice this week
Monks keep “eating less” (unodari) as a formal austerity in five ways (Utt 30.14–24). A householder’s version: at one meal each day, stop with one mouthful less than you want. When the urge for “just a bit more” comes, notice it, and remember that the food is not the problem; the pull is (Utt 32.100).
Self-check
Question

In the lake picture, what has to happen before the water can dry up?

The streams feeding the lake must be blocked; in the same way the inflow of sinful karma must be stopped before austerity can shed the old karma (Utt 30.5–6).

Question

Name the six inner austerities.

Atonement, humility, service, study, meditation and letting go of the body (Utt 30.30).

Question

Which creature dies through sight, and why?

The moth, which, greedy for light, rushes to its death in the flame (Utt 32.24).

Question

Where does the chain of suffering break from the bottom?

With owning nothing: for one who owns nothing there is no greed, then no craving, no delusion and no suffering (Utt 32.8).

10_course/lesson_22_karma_and_leshya.title: Lesson 22 · Karma and the Colours of the Soul
10_course/lesson_22_karma_and_leshya.content:
Lesson 22 · Karma and the Colours of the Soul
Unit 4: The path and reality · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will be able to name the eight kinds of karma, say what decides how long and how strongly karma acts, and recognise the six “colours” (leshya) of the soul in ordinary moods and actions.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 33: The Nature of Karma: look for the eight karmas with their pictures, and the four ways karma is bound.
Uttaradhyayan 34: The Colours of the Soul: look for the six colours and the marks of the person in each.

Key ideas


Eight kinds of karma keep the soul wandering. The soul is in itself pure consciousness, but it has been mixed with lifeless karma since beginningless time, as gold and earth lie mixed in a mine (Utt 33.1). The eight are knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, lifespan, body-making (nama), status-determining (gotra) and obstructing (antaraya) (Utt 33.2–3). The commentary gives each a picture, such as a cloud over the sun for knowledge-obscuring and liquor for deluding karma.


The passions decide how long and how strong. Karma is bound by nature, duration, intensity and quantity. Nature and quantity come from activity (yoga); duration and intensity come from the passions (kashaya) (Utt 33, introduction and v.2–3 commentary; 33.24). Deluding karma can last longest of all, up to seventy crore-crore sagaropamas (Utt 33.21). Knowing this, the wise person acts:

तम्हा एएसिं कम्माणं, अणुभागा वियाणिया ।
एएसिं संवरे चेव, खवणे य जए बुहो ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Therefore, knowing the strength of these karmas, the wise person should strive to stop them and to destroy them. Thus I say. (Utt 33.25)


The soul’s states have colours, dark and bright. Leshya means the states of the soul coloured by the passions, in six shades: black, blue, grey, fiery red, lotus yellow and white (Utt 34.3). Each has its marks: black is cruel, rash and harms the six kinds of beings; blue is envious and deceitful; grey is crooked and hides its faults; red is humble and steady; yellow has little anger, pride, deceit and greed; white is calm, careful and guarded (Utt 34.21–32). The dark three lead to a bad destiny and the bright three to a good one (Utt 34.56–57). The commentary adds that dark states come by long habit, while the bright are taken up by one’s own free effort (Utt 34.61).


Connect
Lesson 2 gave the eight karmas as a list; this lesson shows how they are bound, which is Karma in depth. The four passions of Lesson 4 now show their real cost: they set how long karma stays and how hard it strikes, see Kashaya. The marks of the white leshya repeat the “true meditation” of Lesson 21 (Utt 30.35, 34.31–32), and the six colours are gathered on Leshya. Stopping and destroying karma (Utt 33.25) are two of the Nine Tattvas: samvara and nirjara.
Reflect

Think of the last time you were angry. Was it mild and short, or strong and long? What made the difference?
Which of the six sets of marks (Utt 34.21–32) describes you on a bad day, and which on a good day?
The commentary says dark states come by habit and bright ones need effort. What is one bright habit you have had to build on purpose?

Practice this week
The monk is told to give up the dark leshyas and stand firm in the bright (Utt 34.61). A householder’s version: each evening, pick one moment from the day and ask which colour it had, using the marks in Utt 34.21–32. If it was dark, name the passion behind it (anger, pride, deceit or greed) and one thing you could do tomorrow to make the same moment milder, since the passions set karma’s strength (Utt 33.24).
Self-check
Question

Name the eight karmas.

Knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, lifespan, body-making, status-determining and obstructing (Utt 33.2–3).

Question

Of the four ways karma is bound, which two come from the passions?

Duration and intensity; nature and quantity come from activity (Utt 33, introduction and v.2–3 commentary).

Question

Which karma can last longest, and for how long?

Deluding karma, up to seventy crore-crore sagaropamas (Utt 33.21).

Question

Which three leshyas lead to a bad destiny?

Black, blue and grey, the leshyas of non-dharma (Utt 34.56).

10_course/lesson_23_living_and_non_livin.title: Lesson 23 · The Living and the Non-living
10_course/lesson_23_living_and_non_livin.content:
Lesson 23 · The Living and the Non-living
Unit 4: The path and reality · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will be able to sketch the Jain map of the world, from atoms to the liberated souls, and say why the Uttaradhyayan ends its teaching with this map: knowing what is alive is what makes restraint possible.
Read

Uttaradhyayan 36: The Living and the Non-living: look for the kinds of non-living things, the place where the liberated rest, the kinds of worldly beings, and the closing verses on restraint and a good death.

Key ideas


The world is living and non-living, with no beginning and no maker. Where living and non-living things exist is the world (loka); beyond it, where there is only space, is the non-world (aloka). Both have no beginning and no end, so there is no creator, keeper or destroyer (Utt 36.1–3). The non-living are the medium of motion, the medium of rest, space, time and matter; of these, matter (pudgala) alone has form, and atoms join into aggregates and break apart again (Utt 36.4–11).


Living beings run from one sense up to the liberated. Living beings are worldly or liberated. The liberated are stopped by the non-world and rest at the top of the world, formless, all knowledge and perception, in a happiness beyond comparison (Utt 36.49–68). Worldly beings include earth, water and plant beings that do not move, fire and air beings, beings with two, three and four senses, and five-sensed hell beings, animals, humans and gods (Utt 36.69–253). Some plants have one soul to a body, while root plants such as potato, radish, ginger, onion and garlic have many souls sharing one body (Utt 36.69–126).


Knowing leads to restraint, and to dying well. The map is not given for curiosity. Its closing verses say:

इय जीवमजीवे य, सोच्चा सद्दहिऊण य ।
सव्व णयाणमणुमए, रमेज्ज संजमे मुणी ॥

Having thus heard about the living and the non-living and believed it, the monk should delight in restraint, which is approved from every point of view. (Utt 36.255)
Those who die in right belief, free of wishes for reward (nidana) and in the white leshya find awakening easy to regain (Utt 36.264).


Connect
Lesson 2 gave the same opening verse (Utt 36.2) and the six substances; see Six Substances. The white leshya at death links back to Lesson 22 and Leshya. “First the map, then restraint” is the same order the Dashvaikalik will teach in Lesson 25 (“first knowledge, then compassion”), and it rests on the first two of the Nine Tattvas, soul and non-soul, leading to Samyama.
Reflect

The chapter says the world has no creator. Does that make you feel more alone, or more responsible, or both?
Before this lesson, which of these did you think of as alive: water, earth, fire, air, plants? What changes if they are?
How would you like your mind to be at the end of your life, using the chapter’s three marks (right belief, no wish for reward, the white leshya)?

Practice this week
The chapter gives no food rule for householders; it simply says root plants have many souls sharing one body (Utt 36.69–126). A householder’s experiment, labelled as such: choose one day this week and do without the root plants the chapter names (potato, radish, ginger, onion, garlic). As you eat, recall that what you spare is living.
Self-check
Question

What is the non-world (aloka)?

The region beyond the world where there is only space, a part of the non-living (Utt 36.2).

Question

Of the non-living substances, which alone has form?

Matter (pudgala): aggregate, part, point and atom (Utt 36.4–10).

Question

Where do the liberated souls rest, and what stops them?

At the top of the world; they are stopped by the non-world, beyond which they cannot go (Utt 36.57).

Question

Which three things at death make awakening easy to regain?

Devotion to right belief, freedom from wishes for reward, and being steeped in the white leshya (Utt 36.264).

10_course/lesson_24_dharma_and_the_bee.title: Lesson 24 · Dharma and the Bee
10_course/lesson_24_dharma_and_the_bee.content:
Lesson 24 · Dharma and the Bee
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand the Dashvaikalik’s opening definition of dharma, the bee as the picture of harmless living, and why giving up desire, not just going without, is the ground of a monk’s life.
Read

Dashvaikalik 1: The Monk and the Bee: look for the three parts of dharma and how the monk is like, and unlike, the bee.
Dashvaikalik 2: The Groundwork of Monkhood: look for who is “truly called a renouncer”, and how Rajemati brings Rathanemi back.
Dashvaikalik 3: Minor Rules of Conduct: look for the reason behind most of the small rules, and the closing picture of restraint and austerity.

Key ideas


Dharma is non-violence, restraint and austerity, and the monk lives like a bee. The book opens:

धम्मो मंगलमुक्किट्ठं, अहिंसा संजमो तवो ।
देवा वि तं णमंसंति, जस्स धम्मे सया मणो ॥

Dharma, which is non-violence, restraint and austerity, is the highest auspiciousness. Even the gods bow to the one whose mind is always in dharma. (Dash 1.1)
A bee drinks from many flowers without making them wither (Dash 1.2). So the monk takes a little from many houses, only what is gladly given and what the family cooked for itself, so that no one is harmed (Dash 1.3–4). Unlike the bee, he takes nothing that was not given (Dash 1.3, commentary).


Not having is not giving up. A man who goes without clothes, scents or comforts only because he cannot get them is not a renouncer; the true renouncer turns his back on pleasures that are in his own hands (Dash 2.2–3). When the mind strays, he plugs the thought at once with “She is not mine, nor am I hers” (Dash 2.4). When the monk Rathanemi’s mind turned to desire, Rajemati’s few hard words brought him back to dharma “as an elephant is brought back by the goad” (Dash 2.6–10), and the commentary calls one who slips, admits it and returns great (Dash 2.11).


The small rules guard against harm, and restraint plus austerity frees. Chapter 3 lists what a monk does not do: food made or bought for him, eating at night, bathing and adornment, comforts like umbrella and footwear, and raw living things (Dash 3.2–8). Behind most of these lies one reason: cooking and buying for a monk harm living beings, and accepting it makes him party to that harm (Dash 3.2–6). Through restraint and austerity the sages destroy past karma and are freed; the commentary’s picture is the pond whose inlets are closed and which the sun then dries (Dash 3.15).


Connect
Dash 1.1 is the same definition of dharma you met in Lesson 1; its three parts are Ahimsa, Samyama and Tapas. The bee’s way of living is gathered on Bhramar Vritti. Rathanemi’s story was told from the Uttaradhyayan side in Lesson 13, and the pond that dries in Dash 3.15 is the lake of Lesson 21 (Utt 30.5–6).
Reflect

Is there something you “don’t do” only because you can’t get it? How would it feel to give up something you could easily have?
When your mind strays to something it should not, how quickly do you notice, and what do you do?
Who in your life takes from you the way the bee takes from the flower, without wearing you out? Do you take from others that way?

Practice this week
The monk gives up all sense pleasures for life. A householder’s version: choose one pleasure you can easily have (a favourite snack, a certain show, scrolling at night) and give it up by your own choice for seven days, because a true renouncer turns from pleasures that are in his hands (Dash 2.3). When the wish for it rises, plug it at once, as the servant girl plugs the cracked pot with wet clay (Dash 2.4, commentary).
Self-check
Question

What three things make up dharma in Dash 1.1?

Non-violence (ahimsa), restraint (samyama) and austerity (tapa) (Dash 1.1).

Question

How is the monk different from the bee?

The bee takes nectar no one gave it; the monk takes only what the householder gives gladly, from food the family made for itself (Dash 1.3, commentary).

Question

Who is “truly called a renouncer”?

The one who turns his back on lovely, dear pleasures even when he has them and they are in his power (Dash 2.3).

Question

Why does the monk refuse food cooked or bought for him?

Cooking and buying for him harm living beings, and accepting it would make him a party to that harm (Dash 3.2–6).

10_course/lesson_25_six_kinds_of_living_.title: Lesson 25 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings
10_course/lesson_25_six_kinds_of_living_.content:
Lesson 25 · The Six Kinds of Living Beings
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will be able to name the six kinds of living beings, explain the monk’s six vows and the “nine ways” of giving up harm, and see why the Dashvaikalik’s answer to “how should I live?” is one word: with care.
Read

Dashvaikalik 4: The Six Kinds of Living Beings: look for the signs that earth, water and the rest are alive, the five great vows with the sixth, and the verses on careless and careful acts.

Key ideas


Six kinds of beings are alive, and all want happiness. Earth, water, fire, air and plants each contain many beings with their own existence, until changed by a “weapon” such as fire or trampling (Dash 4, s.4). The sixth kind is moving beings (trasa), known because they come forward, go back, curl up, cry out, take fright and run away; insects, animals, hell beings, humans and gods are all here, and all want happiness (Dash 4, s.5).


The monk gives up harm in nine ways, for life. He will not harm any of the six himself, have others harm them, or approve of harm, in mind, speech or body: three times three, nine ways (Dash 4, s.6). He takes the five great vows (no killing, no false speech, no taking what is not given, no sexual activity, no possessions) and a sixth, no eating at night, because tiny creatures cannot be seen in the dark (Dash 4, s.7–13). The vows are “great” because nothing is left out and they are for life (Dash 4, s.7–13, commentary).


Care, not stillness, keeps the soul clean. Walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, eating and speaking carelessly harm beings and bind bad karma with bitter fruit (Dash 4.1–6). These acts cannot be given up, but they can be done with care (yatana):

जयं चरे जयं चिट्ठे, जयमासे जयं सए ।
जयं भुंजंतो भासंतो पावकम्मं ण बंधइ ॥

Walk with care, stand with care, sit with care, sleep with care. Eating with care and speaking with care, one does not bind bad karma. (Dash 4.8)
Care needs knowledge first: “First knowledge, then compassion” (Dash 4.10), and knowing the living and non-living is the first step on a ladder that climbs to liberation (Dash 4.14–25).


Connect
Lessons 3 and 4 already used verses from this chapter: “do everything with care” (Dash 4.8), “first knowledge, then compassion” (Dash 4.10), and the monk’s first great vow set beside the householder’s small vow. That is Ahimsa made practical through Samyama. Lesson 23 gave the full map of beings; this chapter turns it into daily care, the root of Samiti and Gupti. The ladder’s middle steps (merit and sin, bondage and liberation) are among the Nine Tattvas.
Reflect

Of the six daily acts (walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, eating, speaking), which do you do most carelessly?
Before this, whose life did your kindness reach: only humans and animals, or wider? What would widen it?
The householder’s vow (Lesson 4) gives up doing and causing gross harm but leaves “approving” open. Where do you approve of harm without doing it yourself?

Practice this week
The monk’s rule is that if an insect or ant climbs onto his body, cloth or bowl, he looks, brushes it off gently and puts it down in a safe, quiet place (Dash 4, s.19). A householder’s version: this week, when an insect lands on you, your table or your sink, do not swat or wash it away; lift it gently on a piece of paper and put it outside.
Self-check
Question

Name the six kinds of living beings.

Earth, water, fire, air, plant and moving (trasa) beings (Dash 4, s.4–5).

Question

What are the “nine ways” of giving up harm?

Not doing it, not having it done and not approving it, each in mind, speech and body (Dash 4, s.6).

Question

Why is eating at night given up?

Because tiny creatures cannot be seen in the dark (Dash 4, s.7–13, commentary).

Question

What does the teacher answer when the disciple asks how to live without binding bad karma?

With care (yatana): walk, stand, sit, sleep, eat and speak with care (Dash 4.7–8).

10_course/lesson_26_alms_and_the_great_c.title: Lesson 26 · Alms and the Great Conduct
10_course/lesson_26_alms_and_the_great_c.content:
Lesson 26 · Alms and the Great Conduct
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will understand how a monk seeks, receives and eats food without harming anyone, what the eighteen points of “great conduct” are built on, and what the texts ask of the giver as well as the taker.
Read

Dashvaikalik 5: Seeking Alms: look for the three searches, the reasons a monk refuses food, and the rare giver and rare taker.
Dashvaikalik 6: The Great Conduct: look for why non-violence comes first, and what Mahavira called “possession”.

Key ideas


Food is sought so that no one is hurt or burdened. The search has three parts: finding faultless food, receiving it without fault, and eating it without attachment (Dash 5, introduction). The monk walks slowly, looking a yoke’s length ahead to avoid seeds and small creatures (Dash 5.1.3). He refuses food if giving it harms a living being, if it causes anyone pain or loss (a mother putting down her crying baby, food set aside for other beggars), or if it was made, bought or cooked extra for him (Dash 5.1.27–81).


Even-minded in plenty and in want. Whatever he receives, bitter or sweet, he eats “as if it were ghee and sugar” (Dash 5.1.97); if he gets nothing, he does not grieve but bears it as austerity (Dash 5.2.6); he is not angry when ignored nor proud when honoured (Dash 5.2.30). The first section ends with the giver and the taker side by side:

दुल्लहा उ मुहादाई, मुहाजीवी वि दुल्लहा ।
मुहादाई मुहाजीवी, दोवि गच्छंति सुग्गइं ॥ त्ति बेमि ॥

Rare is the one who gives expecting nothing, and rare too is the one who lives without giving anything in return. The selfless giver and the selfless taker both go to a good state. Thus I say. (Dash 5.1.100)


Great conduct rests on one fact: every being wants to live. Asked by kings how Jain monks live, the teacher gives eighteen points, and the first is non-violence, because “all beings wish to live, not to die” (Dash 6.9–11). Possession is not the cloth and bowl a monk keeps but attachment to them: “attachment (murchha) is possession” (Dash 6.21). No food is taken at night because tiny beings cannot be seen (Dash 6.23–26), and a monk refuses anything made or bought for him, since taking it approves the killing done for it (Dash 6.47–50).


Connect
Lesson 24’s bee is worked out here in full detail; see Bhramar Vritti. “All beings wish to live” and “attachment is possession” (Dash 6.11, 6.21) were in Lesson 3; they are the centre of Ahimsa. Bearing an empty bowl as austerity links to “limits in begging alms”, one of the outer austerities of Lesson 21 (Utt 30.8), and the whole chapter is Samyama applied to a single daily need.
Reflect

When you give something (money, time, help), how much of you is waiting for thanks or credit?
How do you react when the food in front of you is not what you wanted? What would “eating it as ghee and sugar” look like for you?
Think of one thing you own that you feel strongly is “mine”. Is the trouble the thing, or the grip?

Practice this week
The monk’s rules are about taking; the householder’s part in these chapters is giving. A householder’s version: once this week, give something (food, money, time or help) expecting nothing back: no thanks, no mention, no credit (Dash 5.1.100). If you have the chance to offer food to monks or nuns, offer what your family cooked for itself, not something made specially for them, since food made for the monk is what he must refuse (Dash 5.1.55–81).
Self-check
Question

Name the three parts of the search for food.

Finding faultless food, receiving it without the faults of receiving, and eating it without attachment (Dash 5, introduction).

Question

What does a monk do if he gets no alms?

He does not grieve; thinking “this is austerity”, he bears it (Dash 5.2.6).

Question

What did Mahavira call possession?

Not the monk’s few things, but attachment (murchha) (Dash 6.21).

Question

Why is non-violence the first of the eighteen points?

Because all living beings wish to live, not to die (Dash 6.9–11).

10_course/lesson_27_pure_speech_and_cond.title: Lesson 27 · Pure Speech and the Treasure of Conduct
10_course/lesson_27_pure_speech_and_cond.content:
Lesson 27 · Pure Speech and the Treasure of Conduct
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will be able to test your words the way the Dashvaikalik tests a monk’s, and use its plain remedies for anger, pride, deceit and greed in daily life.
Read

Dashvaikalik 7: Pure Speech: look for the four kinds of speech, and why some true words must not be spoken.
Dashvaikalik 8: The Treasure of Conduct: look for “see much, tell little” and the remedy for each of the four passions.

Key ideas


Of four kinds of speech, two are dropped and two are used with care. Speech is true, false, mixed or practical (neither true nor false, like an instruction). A wise monk never uses false or mixed speech, and uses true and practical speech only when it is blameless, not harsh, well thought out and free of doubt (Dash 7.1–3). He does not speak with certainty about what he does not know, saying “I will do it” or “this will happen”; the commentary suggests “I intend to come” instead (Dash 7.6–10).


A true word that wounds is still a fault. The chapter is plain:

तहेव फरुसा भासा, गुरुभूओवघाइणी ।
सच्चा वि सा ण वत्तव्वा, जओ पावस्स आगमो ॥

Likewise, harsh speech that badly hurts living beings should not be spoken even if it is true, because through it sinful karma flows in. (Dash 7.11)
So he does not call a one-eyed man “one-eyed” or a thief “thief” (Dash 7.12), and he avoids words that praise or prompt harm, such as calling a feast a good deed or saying fruit is “ripe, pick it” (Dash 7.26–46).


Conduct is a treasure to be used day by day. Taking vows is only entering school (Dash 8, introduction). The monk “hears much with his ears and sees much with his eyes” but does not tell all of it (Dash 8.20). Anger destroys love, pride humility, deceit friendship, and greed everything (Dash 8.38); kill anger with calm, pride with gentleness, deceit with straightforwardness and greed with contentment (Dash 8.39). And practise now, “as long as old age does not press on you” (Dash 8.36).


Connect
Lesson 4 met these same verses (Dash 7.3, 7.11–12, 8.37–39); here you see them in their full chapters. Lesson 22 showed that the passions set how long and how strongly karma binds, which is why Dash 8.40 says they “water the roots of rebirth”; see Kashaya. Careful speech is one of the careful practices and guards, Samiti and Gupti, and a wounding word is a form of harm, so it belongs under Ahimsa too.
Reflect

Think of a true thing you said recently that hurt someone. Did it need to be said, and in that way?
How often do you say “I will” about things you cannot be sure of?
Which of the four passions costs you the most: love, humility, friendship, or “everything”?

Practice this week
The monk weighs every word (Dash 7.55). A householder’s version: once a day, catch one sentence before you say it and run the four tests of Dash 7.3: is it blameless, is it not harsh, have I thought it through, is it free of doubt? If it fails one, change it or leave it unsaid.
Self-check
Question

Which two kinds of speech does a wise monk never use?

False speech and mixed speech (part true, part false) (Dash 7.1–3).

Question

Why should a monk not call a thief “thief”?

Because harsh words that badly hurt a being are not to be spoken even if true; through them sinful karma flows in (Dash 7.11–12).

Question

What is the remedy for greed?

Contentment (Dash 8.39).

Question

What does a monk not do with all he sees and hears in a householder’s home?

He does not tell all of it: a monk sees and hears much but does not tell everything (Dash 8.19–21).

10_course/lesson_28_humility_and_the_tru.title: Lesson 28 · Humility's Composure; the True Monk
10_course/lesson_28_humility_and_the_tru.content:
Lesson 28 · Humility’s Composure; the True Monk
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will understand why the Dashvaikalik calls humility (vinaya) the root of dharma, what four kinds of composure it leads to, and how a true monk is known by his virtues rather than his dress.
Read

Dashvaikalik 9: Composure Through Humility: look for the bamboo’s fruit, the tree of dharma, and the four kinds of composure (samadhi).
Dashvaikalik 10: The True Monk: look for the touchstone, the monk “like the earth”, and what he never says of others.

Key ideas


Humility is the root; disrespect burns the one who shows it. A monk who, from pride, anger, conceit or laziness, does not practise humility before his guru ruins himself, as the bamboo’s fruit kills the bamboo (Dash 9.1.1). The guru, like fire, does not mean to burn; the disciple burns himself (Dash 9.1.1–3, commentary). And as a tree grows from its root:

एवं धम्मस्स विणओ, मूलं परमो से मोक्खो ।
जेण कित्तिं सुयं सिग्घं, णीसेसं चाभिगच्छइ ॥

In the same way, humility is the root of dharma and liberation is its highest fruit. Through humility one gains fame, learning, praise, and everything worth gaining. (Dash 9.2.2)


Four kinds of composure, none for reward. One is worthy of honour by reading the guru’s wishes, bearing harsh words without hope of reward, and scorning no one, child or elder, monk or householder (Dash 9.3.1–12). “One is a monk through virtues and not a monk through faults” (Dash 9.3.11). Composure comes through humility, learning, austerity and conduct; austerity and conduct are done not for this world, the next or fame, but only to shed karma (Dash 9.4.1–7).


The true monk is known on the touchstone. Many live on alms; the true monk is known by his virtues, as real gold is known by the touchstone (Dash 10, introduction). He treats all six kinds of beings as equal to himself (Dash 10.5), bears insults and blows like the earth, wanting no reward and no revenge (Dash 10.13), does not say of another “this one is of bad conduct”, knowing each being’s merit and sin are its own (Dash 10.18), and is proud of nothing: not birth, looks, gain or learning (Dash 10.19).


Connect
Lesson 5 first gave the tree of humility (Dash 9.2.1–2), and Lesson 15 opened the disciple’s life with it; Lesson 21 then counted humility among the inner austerities (Utt 30.30). All three are Vinaya. Bearing blows “like the earth” is Parishaha, and austerity “only to shed karma” (Dash 9.4.4) is the right spirit of Tapas. Pride, the first enemy in Dash 9.1.1 and the last in Dash 10.19, is one of the four passions of Kashaya.
Reflect

Who taught you something important whom you once looked down on as too young, too slow or too unlearned?
When someone speaks harshly to you, does the word stay in you like a thorn? What would it take to pull it out?
When did you last call someone lax, careless or bad? Did knowing that “each being’s merit and sin are its own” change how that feels?

Practice this week
The true monk “does not say of another, ‘This one is of bad conduct’” (Dash 10.18). A householder’s version: for this week, when you are about to criticise someone who is not present, stop, and instead name to yourself one fault of your own that you still have not given up, knowing “the self by the self” (Dash 9.3.11).
Self-check
Question

What picture does the chapter use for a disciple who will not be humble?

The bamboo, killed by its own fruit: his lack of humility brings his own ruin (Dash 9.1.1).

Question

Name the four kinds of composure (samadhi).

Composure through humility, learning, austerity and conduct (Dash 9.4.1–7).

Question

Why is the true monk said to be “like the earth”?

Insulted, beaten or wounded, he bears it all and pushes back on nothing, wanting no reward and no revenge (Dash 10.13).

Question

Of what four things is the true monk not proud?

His birth, his looks, his gains and his learning (Dash 10.19).

10_course/lesson_29_staying_the_course.content:
Lesson 29 · Staying the Course
Unit 5: Careful living (Dashvaikalik) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will know what the Dashvaikalik offers when the wish to keep going fades, and you will be able to use its nightly self-examination to steady your own practice.
Read

Dashvaikalik 11 (Chulika 1): Delight in Restraint: look for the eighteen points, the pictures of the fallen monk’s regret, and “I will give up the body, but never the teaching”.
Dashvaikalik 12 (Chulika 2): The Solitary Way: look for going against the current, and the questions to ask yourself at night.

Key ideas


When restraint feels heavy, reflect before you leave. The first chulika is written for a monk who has come to dislike restraint and wants to go home but has not yet gone. Its eighteen points work like a bridle on a horse, a goad on an elephant and a sail on a ship (Dash 11, s.1). Among them: this suffering of mine will not last long; household pleasures are trivial and brief; going back is drinking what one has vomited; human life is as unsteady as a drop of water on a blade of kusha grass (Dash 11, s.2).


Delight decides whether the path is heaven or hell. The one who goes back later burns with regret, like a fish that has swallowed the hook (Dash 11.6). For those who delight in it, the monk’s life is like the world of the gods; for those who do not, like a great hell (Dash 11.10). Even suffering in hell runs out, so “what, then, is this mental pain of mine?” (Dash 11.15). The firm mind says, “I will give up the body, but never the teaching of dharma”, and stands like Mount Meru in the wind (Dash 11.17).


Go against the current, and look at yourself every night. Going with the current of the senses is samsara; going against it is the crossing out (Dash 12.2–3). The monk keeps few belongings, eats simply and studies (Dash 12.5–7), and every night asks:

जो पुव्वरत्तावररत्तकाले, संपेहए अप्पगमप्पएणं ।
किं मे कडं किं च मे किच्चसेसं, किं सक्कणिज्जं ण समायरामि ॥

In the first and last parts of the night he looks at himself by himself: “What have I done? What remains for me to do? What am I able to do that I am not doing?” (Dash 12.12)
Seeing himself going wrong, he pulls back at once, as a fine horse answers the bridle (Dash 12.14). Unguarded, the soul goes the way of birth and death; well guarded, it is freed from all suffering (Dash 12.16).


Connect
The “vomited” image of Lesson 24 (Rathanemi, Dash 2.6–7) returns here as one of the eighteen points, and the unsteady drop of water recalls the falling leaf of Lesson 6. The last of the eighteen points, that past karma is released only by living it out or burning it through austerity, is Lesson 21 again: see Tapas and Karma. Following the Jina’s word “guarded by the three restraints in body, speech and mind” (Dash 11.18) is Samiti and Gupti, and delight in restraint is the heart of Samyama.
Reflect

When you lost interest in something good you had started (a practice, a study, a vow), what did you tell yourself? Which of the eighteen points would have answered it?
What is “the current” in your own life, the thing that is easy and pleasant but keeps you going round?
Which of the three night questions is hardest for you to answer honestly?

Practice this week
Monks examine themselves in the first and last parts of every night (Dash 12.12). A householder’s version: each night this week, before sleep, take two minutes and ask the three questions: What have I done today? What is left to do? What can I do that I am not doing? Pick one answer and act on it the next day.
Self-check
Question

What three pictures does the first chulika use for its eighteen points?

A bridle on a horse, a goad on an elephant and a sail on a ship (Dash 11, s.1).

Question

How can the same monk’s life be like heaven or like hell?

For those who delight in it, it is like the world of the gods; for those who do not, it is like a great hell (Dash 11.10).

Question

What is going “with the current”, and what is going against it?

Going with the current is samsara; going against it is the crossing out of it (Dash 12.3).

Question

What happens to the soul that is well guarded?

It is freed from all suffering; unguarded, it goes the way of birth and death (Dash 12.16).

10_course/lesson_30_knowing_the_weapon.title: Lesson 30 · Knowing the Weapon: Harm to the Six Kinds of Life
10_course/lesson_30_knowing_the_weapon.content:
Lesson 30 · Knowing the Weapon: Harm to the Six Kinds of Life
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will understand why the Acharang begins with the soul and then walks through earth, water, fire, plants, moving creatures and air, and what it means to “know the weapon” and put it down.
Read

Acharang Book 1, Chapter 1: Knowing the Weapon: read the opening question about where we came from, then take the six kinds of life one section at a time and notice the image or argument each one is given. (References below read Ach book.chapter, then s.section.sutra, as the module numbers them.)

Key ideas


It starts with “that am I”. Many beings do not know where they came from, whether their soul is reborn, or what they will become after this body (Ach 1.1 s.1.1). By memory of past lives, a Tirthankara’s teaching or a learned teacher, a person comes to know “the one who wanders through all the directions is I”; such a person affirms the soul, the world, karma and action, and only he can practise non-violence well (Ach 1.1 s.1.2). Non-violence rests on knowing the soul.


A weapon is anything that destroys a being, inside or out. Knives and swords are outer weapons; attachment and aversion are inner ones, because they damage the soul’s own qualities. “Knowing” (parijna) has two sides: understanding and renouncing (introduction, p.63). We act in 27 ways, doing, having it done and approving, in past, present and future, by mind, speech and body, and we harm beings for this life, for praise, even for religion, and to ward off pain (Ach 1.1 s.1.3–6). Whoever knows the weapon knows the non-weapon, restraint (samyama) (Ach 1.1 s.4.1–5).


All six kinds of life feel pain as we do. Earth beings feel a blade like a man blind and dumb from birth who cannot cry out (Ach 1.1 s.2.1–6). Water is alive, and since its beings never gave their lives to anyone, a pond-owner’s permission does not make using it innocent (Ach 1.1 s.3.1–7). Fire is the sharpest weapon and burns the creatures in grass, wood and rubbish (Ach 1.1 s.4.1–5); a plant is born, grows, is conscious and withers when cut, like a human body (Ach 1.1 s.5.4); for moving creatures “pain is a great fear” (Ach 1.1 s.6.1). Air comes last because its beings cannot be seen, and the lesson is to measure every being by yourself:

पहू एजस्स दुगुंछणाए । आयंकदंसी अहियं ति णच्चा । जे अज्झत्थं जाणइ से बहिया जाणइ, जे बहिया जाणइ से अज्झत्थं जाणइ । एयं तुलमण्णेसिं । इह संतिगया दविया णावकंखंति जीविउं ।

One who sees the suffering harm brings, and knows it as harmful, is able to give up harming the air beings. Whoever knows what is within knows what is outside; whoever knows what is outside knows what is within. Weigh others against yourself in this way. Here, those whose passions are calmed and whose hearts are soft with compassion do not wish to live by harming.
Source: Acharang 1.1 s.7.1 (Shastra Parijna) · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Connect
Lesson 25 met the same six kinds of living beings in the Dashvaikalik (Lesson 25); here is the older, sharper version, with the reason for each one. The chapter ends with the same three-fold rule, neither harm, nor have harmed, nor approve (Ach 1.1 s.7.1–6), which is the heart of Ahimsa. The 27 ways of acting are 27 ways of binding Karma, and the “non-weapon” is Samyama. Compare Lesson 3, Non-violence and Awareness.
Reflect

Which of the six kinds of life do you find hardest to think of as alive: earth, water, fire, plants or air? Why?
What are your own “inner weapons”, the attachment or aversion that most often damages your peace?
When did you last harm something not by your own hand but by having it done, or by quietly approving?

Practice this week
The chapter’s rules are for homeless monks, who give up digging, using unboiled water, lighting fire and cutting plants altogether. A householder’s version: pick one of the six kinds of life each day and use it with care. For example, on water day, close the tap while soaping and do not waste a glass; on fire day, switch off a flame or heater as soon as you are done. Each evening, say once: “What I did before through carelessness, I will not do now” (Ach 1.1 s.4.1–5).
Self-check
Question

According to the chapter, what must a person know before he can practise non-violence well?

That the soul exists and is reborn: “the one who wanders through all the directions is I.” Such a person affirms the soul, the world, karma and action (Ach 1.1 s.1.2).

Question

What are the two sides of “knowing” (parijna)?

Understanding the weapon, and renouncing it (introduction, p.63).

Question

Why is a pond-owner’s permission not enough to make using water innocent?

Because the water beings themselves never gave their lives to anyone, so using them is also taking what is not given (Ach 1.1 s.3.1–7).

Question

In what ways does the chapter say a plant is like a human body?

Both are born, grow, are conscious, wither when cut and take food; the sutra goes on that both are impermanent and changing (Ach 1.1 s.5.4).

10_course/lesson_31_conquering_the_world.title: Lesson 31 · Conquering the World; Cold and Heat
10_course/lesson_31_conquering_the_world.content:
Lesson 31 · Conquering the World; Cold and Heat
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will see that the “world” the Acharang asks you to conquer is the sense of “mine” inside you, and how to meet pleasant and painful things with the same even, wakeful mind.
Read

Acharang Book 1, Chapter 2: Conquest of the World: look for the long list of “my mother, my father…” and for what the chapter says your own people can and cannot do for you.
Acharang Book 1, Chapter 3: Cold and Heat: notice what “cold” and “heat” stand for, and the short sayings about sleep, the sieve and being your own friend.

Key ideas


The world to conquer is inside. “World” here means attachment, aversion, anger, pride, deceit and greed; conquer that and the outer round of birth and death is conquered too (Ach 1.2, introduction). Sense objects are the root, and “mine” is the chain: the one who says “my mother, my father, my wife, my sons, my goods” burns day and night and harms beings again and again (Ach 1.2 s.1.1). Whoever gives up the sense of “mine” gives up what he called his; the sage with nothing he calls “mine” has seen the path (Ach 1.2 s.6.2).


Your own people cannot shelter you, so know your moment. As the senses weaken with age, family may turn away; “they cannot protect you or shelter you, and you cannot protect or shelter them” (Ach 1.2 s.1.2). While hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch are still whole, work properly for the good of the soul (Ach 1.2 s.1.5). No one is high and no one is low: the soul has been born in high and low families many times, so who would boast (Ach 1.2 s.3.1–7)? And all beings love life: “to all, life is dear” (Ach 1.2 s.3.4).


Cold and heat, and the friend within. “Cold” is what pleases, honour and pleasant sights; “heat” is what hurts, pain and illness; a seeker passes through both with equanimity (Ach 1.3, introduction). “The ignorant are asleep; sages are always awake” (Ach 1.3 s.1.1). The man of many minds tries to fill a sieve, and so he kills and seizes others (Ach 1.3 s.2.2). Anger, pride, deceit and greed are to be cast out like vomit (Ach 1.3 s.4.1–8). And the help you seek is already yours:

पुरिसा! तुममेव तुमं मित्तं, किं बहिया मित्तमिच्छसि ? जं जाणेज्जा उच्चालइयं तं जाणेज्जा दुरालइयं, जं जाणेज्जा दुरालइयं तं जाणेज्जा उच्चालइयं । पुरिसा ! अत्ताणमेव अभिणिगिज्झ, एवं दुक्खा पमोक्खसि ।

O man, you yourself are your friend; why do you want a friend outside? Know that the one who throws off karma is the one bound for liberation, and the one bound for liberation is the one who throws off karma. O man, restrain your own self; in this way you will be freed from suffering.
Source: Acharang 1.3 s.3.4 (Shitoshniya) · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Connect
“They cannot protect you” echoes Lesson 11, where family is a real bond but not a refuge at death (Lesson 11), and “know the moment” echoes the falling leaf of Lesson 6. The four passions to be vomited out are Kashaya; the “cold” and “hot” hardships are the twenty-two of Parishaha, which you met in Lesson 16. Restraining your own self is Samyama.
Reflect

Finish the sentence honestly: “my , my , my ___”. Which “mine” do you guard most anxiously?
Which troubles you more, “heat” (pain, criticism, illness) or “cold” (praise, comfort, pleasant things)? Where do you lose your evenness?
Where in your life are you trying to fill a sieve?

Practice this week
The chapter’s rules about taking nothing that is bought for you and owning nothing are monks’ rules. A householder’s version: each evening, notice one moment of “cold” (you were praised or enjoyed something) and one of “heat” (you were hurt or annoyed), and write one line about how you met each. Once this week, when you feel the urge to ask someone else to fix your mood, pause and remember “you yourself are your friend” (Ach 1.3 s.3.4).
Self-check
Question

What is the “world” that this chapter asks us to conquer?

The inner world of attachment, aversion, anger, pride, deceit and greed; conquering it conquers the outer round of birth and death (Ach 1.2, introduction).

Question

What does the chapter say our relatives can do for us in old age and illness?

They are not able to protect us or give us shelter, and we cannot protect or shelter them (Ach 1.2 s.1.2).

Question

In the title “Cold and Heat”, what do the two words stand for?

“Cold” is what pleases, such as honour and pleasant things; “heat” is what hurts, such as pain and illness (Ach 1.3, introduction).

Question

Who, according to the chapter, has fear from every side?

The careless person; the careful person has no fear from any side (Ach 1.3 s.4.3).

10_course/lesson_32_right_faith_and_esse.title: Lesson 32 · Right Faith and the Essence of the World
10_course/lesson_32_right_faith_and_esse.content:
Lesson 32 · Right Faith and the Essence of the World
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 30 minutes
Aim: You will be able to state the one dharma the Acharang says every Tirthankara teaches, explain why bondage and freedom depend on your inner state, and say what the book calls the essence of the world.
Read

Acharang Book 1, Chapter 4: Right Faith: look for the eternal dharma of all the Arihants, and the question the noble ones put to those who say violence is no fault.
Acharang Book 1, Chapter 5: Essence of the World: read the chain “dharma, knowledge, restraint, nirvana” in the introduction, then the sayings “fight with this very self” and “the one you think fit to kill is you”.

Key ideas


One dharma, for everyone: harm no living being. All the Arihants of past, present and future say that no living being is to be struck, ruled by force, enslaved, tormented or harmed; “this dharma is pure, eternal and everlasting” (Ach 1.4 s.1.1). It was taught to all, the listening and the absent, the violent and the non-violent. When some claim that killing is faultless, the noble ones ask each of them: “is suffering pleasant to you, or unpleasant?” Answered truly, suffering is unpleasant and fearful for every being (Ach 1.4 s.2.4–8). Holding to this with true understanding is right faith (samyaktva) (Ach 1.4, introduction).


Bondage and freedom lie within. What is a door of karmic inflow can become a door of shedding, and the reverse; the commentary gives Sthulibhadra, who stayed pure in a courtesan’s house, and Nagashri, who bound karma while giving alms with a spiteful mind (Ach 1.4 s.2.1). “Bondage and release come from within” (Ach 1.5 s.2.4). So the battle is inner: “fight with this very self; what good to you is fighting outside enemies?” (Ach 1.5 s.3.4). Life is short like a dewdrop on a blade of kusa grass (Ach 1.5 s.1.1–3), so give up anger and do not set the soul ablaze with passion (Ach 1.4 s.3.4–5).


The essence of the world, and the one you would harm. Dharma is the essence of the world, knowledge the essence of dharma, restraint the essence of knowledge, and nirvana the essence of restraint; pleasures, wealth and the body have no essence (Ach 1.5, introduction). “That alone is true and beyond doubt which the Jinas have taught” (Ach 1.5 s.5.2). And the reason not to harm becomes personal:

तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं हंतव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं अज्जावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परियावेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं परिघेयव्वं ति मण्णसि । तुमं सि णाम सच्चेव जं उद्दवेयव्वं ति मण्णसि ।

The one you think fit to kill is you yourself. The one you think fit to rule over is you. The one you think fit to torment is you. The one you think fit to seize and enslave is you. The one you think fit to trouble to death is you.
Source: Acharang 1.5 s.5.6 (Lokasara) · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Connect
The five verbs of the eternal dharma (strike, rule, enslave, torment, harm) come back word for word in “the one you think fit to kill is you”, tying Chapter 4 to Chapter 5; both deepen “weigh others against yourself” from Lesson 30 and the root of Ahimsa. Right faith is the first jewel of Ratnatraya, which you met in Lesson 19; doors of inflow and shedding are terms from Nine Tattvas. “Fight with this very self” is Nami’s greatest victory again (Lesson 9), and burning karma “as fire burns old dry wood” (Ach 1.4 s.3.3) points to Tapas.
Reflect

Think of a time someone was cruel to you. Now think of someone you were sharp with. Does “the one you think fit to torment is you” change how that second memory feels?
Where have you assumed a place or setting decides your goodness (“I can be calm only on retreat”, “I can’t be honest at work”)? What would Sthulibhadra say?
Of the four links in the chain (dharma, knowledge, restraint, nirvana), which is weakest in your life right now?

Practice this week
The chapter’s austerities and its rules for a young monk living near his guru are monks’ rules. A householder’s version: before any sharp word or act this week, ask yourself the noble ones’ question, “is suffering pleasant to you?” (Ach 1.4 s.2.8), and let the honest answer slow you down. Once a day, recall one thing the Jinas taught that you trust without doubt, and act on it once.
Self-check
Question

What do all the Arihants of past, present and future teach, according to Chapter 4?

That no living being is to be struck, ruled by force, enslaved, tormented or harmed; this dharma is pure, eternal and everlasting (Ach 1.4 s.1.1).

Question

What question do the noble ones put to those who say violence is no fault?

“Is suffering pleasant to you, or unpleasant?” Answered truly, it is unpleasant and fearful for every living being (Ach 1.4 s.2.8).

Question

What does the book name as the essence of the world, and the essence of restraint?

Dharma is the essence of the world, and nirvana is the essence of restraint (Ach 1.5, introduction).

Question

Where do bondage and release come from?

From within, from the soul’s own inner states (Ach 1.5 s.2.4).

10_course/lesson_33_shaking_off_and_libe.content:
Lesson 33 · Shaking Off, Liberation, and Mahavira’s Own Practice
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 35 minutes
Aim: You will understand how the last chapters of Acharang Book 1 describe a monk shaking off karma and growing lighter step by step, and how Mahavira himself lived every one of these teachings.
Read

Acharang Book 1, Chapter 6: Shaking Off: look for the tortoise under the weeds, the family’s tears, and “nothing is mine; I am alone”.
Acharang Book 1, Chapter 8: Liberation: read the refrain about lightness, and the verses on wanting neither life nor death. (Chapter 7, Great Comprehension, is lost; read its short page to learn why.)
Acharang Book 1, Chapter 9: Mahavira's Practice: read it as a biography, and match each hardship to a rule you met in the earlier chapters.

Key ideas


Shaking off karma, as dust is shaken off a cloth. “Dhuta” means shaking off: outwardly dust from clothes, inwardly the eight kinds of karma, through renunciation and restraint (Ach 1.6, introduction). Most people stay stuck like a tortoise in a lake covered with lotus leaves, or a tree that never leaves its place (Ach 1.6 s.1.3). The steadfast monk thinks “nothing is mine; I am alone” (Ach 1.6 s.2.2), and says “to live by the command is my dharma” (Ach 1.6 s.2.5). Out of compassion he teaches everyone peace, calm, straightforwardness, gentleness and non-violence, and becomes a refuge like an island that does not sink (Ach 1.6 s.5.2–4).


Liberation grows by degrees: fewer needs, more lightness. Vimoksha is release from the passions and from karma; it grows step by step and is complete in the perfected ones (Ach 1.8, introduction). Dharma is “neither in the village nor in the forest” but in the soul, and people have woken at every stage of life (Ach 1.8 s.1.5). Monks vow to keep three garments, two, one or none, and the refrain is “attaining lightness, he gains austerity” (Ach 1.8 s.4.2, s.6.2). At life’s end, when the body can no longer carry restraint, the monk gives it up calmly in one of three ways of dying in equanimity, wanting neither life nor death and seeing that “these hardships are in the body; they are not mine” (Ach 1.8 s.8.4, s.8.21). Chapter 7 between them is lost; the book says it dealt mostly with trials that stir up delusion and was dropped when the scriptures were written down (Ach 1.7, pp.329–330).


Mahavira lived it all first. The ninth chapter exists so that no one thinks the rules are imagined (Ach 1.9, introduction). The Lord gave up his one cloth after thirteen months (Ach 1.9 v.1.1–4), walked silent with his eyes on the path (Ach 1.9 v.1.21), knew all six kinds of beings to be living and harmed none (Ach 1.9 v.1.12–13), stayed in empty houses and cremation grounds for nearly thirteen years (Ach 1.9 v.2.4), and in the Ladha country was beaten and set upon by dogs, going through it “like an elephant at the front of a battle” (Ach 1.9 v.3.7–8). The chapter’s summit:

अकसायी विगयगेही य सद्द-रूवेसु अमुच्छिए झाइ ।
छउमत्थे विप्परक्कममाणे, ण पमायं सइं पि कुव्वित्था ॥

Free of passions, free of craving, not infatuated by sounds, forms and the like, he meditated. Striving hard while still not omniscient (chhadmastha), he did not fall into negligence (pramada) even once.
Source: Acharang 1.9 v.4.15 (Upadhana-shruta) · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Connect
Mahavira’s practice gathers up the whole of Book 1: the six kinds of beings of Lesson 30, bearing cold and heat from Lesson 31, and the one dharma of non-violence from Lesson 32. His enduring of insects, cold, blows and abuse is Parishaha lived out, and his fasts up to six months are Tapas. “Not negligent even once” answers the roots of negligence in Lesson 21; the slow, calm death of the wise recalls the two kinds of death in Lesson 7. Wanting neither life nor death is Samyama at its deepest.
Reflect

Where are you like the tortoise under the lotus leaves: you have glimpsed something higher, then gone back for your old ties?
What would “attaining lightness” mean in your own house or calendar: what one thing could you let go of, as the monk lets worn-out cloth go when summer comes?
When someone speaks to you harshly, what would it take to meet it as Mahavira did, without any thought of revenge?

Practice this week
Owning almost nothing, refusing food made for you and the three ways of dying in equanimity are monks’ vows, not householders’ rules. A householder’s version, drawn from the refrain of lightness: this week give away or let go of one thing you no longer use (a garment, a gadget, a subscription), and at the end of each day spend two minutes in silence repeating “nothing is mine; I am alone” (Ach 1.6 s.2.2), not to feel lonely, but to feel lighter.
Self-check
Question

What does “dhuta” mean, in its outer and inner senses?

Outwardly, shaking dust off clothes; inwardly, making the eight kinds of karma fall away through renunciation and restraint (Ach 1.6, introduction).

Question

Where, according to Chapter 8, is dharma to be found?

Neither in the village nor in the forest: it can be practised in either, but it is going beyond sin, as the all-knowing Lord taught it (Ach 1.8 s.1.5).

Question

Why does the book have no text for Chapter 7?

It is lost: it was judged unfit to write down, because it described what stirs up delusion and held special powers, and was dropped when the scriptures were put in writing (Ach 1.7, pp.329–330).

Question

Why was the chapter on Mahavira’s practice written, according to its introduction?

So that a practitioner is sure the earlier rules are not imagination but were lived by Mahavira himself (Ach 1.9, introduction).

10_course/lesson_34_the_careful_monk.title: Lesson 34 · The Careful Monk: Alms, Lodging, Walking, Speech
10_course/lesson_34_the_careful_monk.content:
Lesson 34 · The Careful Monk: Alms, Lodging, Walking, Speech
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 70 minutes
Aim: You will see how Book 2 of the Acharang turns the non-violence of Book 1 into everyday detail (how a monk seeks food, finds a place to stay, walks the road and speaks) and you will be able to apply its rules of speech to your own talk.
Read

Acharang 2.1: Seeking Alms: look for the two tests every piece of food must pass, the rule “doubt means no”, and the many “stations of deceit”.
Acharang 2.2: Seeking Lodging and Acharang 2.3: Careful Walking: notice that a place to stay and a road to walk are judged by the same care as food, and how calm the monk stays when he is thrown into a river or robbed.
Acharang 2.4: Kinds of Speech: look for the four kinds of speech, and why even true words can be sinful.

Key ideas


Food is taken only if it is lifeless, faultless and given without burden. Food must be free of life (prasuka) and free of the faults of seeking (eshaniya): anything touched by insects, seeds, green plants, raw water or living dust is refused, and so is food cooked, bought or carried in for the monk (Ach 2.1 s.1.1–11). If he is unsure whether food is acceptable, he does not take it (Ach 2.1 s.3.5). He must not make the householder’s work harder, stand where other beggars are crowded out, or flatter the giver; and eating the tasty parts while throwing away the plain, or hiding fine food under plain food in the bowl, is called “a station of deceit” (maya-sthana): “Good or poor, they should eat all of it” (Ach 2.1 s.4.2–6.7, s.9.5, s.10.2).


A place to stay and a road to walk are judged by the same care. A lodging full of eggs, insects or cobwebs is not used; a clear one is used only after inspecting and sweeping it, and never one built or repaired for monks (Ach 2.2 s.1.1–8). The monk asks the owner’s permission “for as long as you allow and in as much space as you give”, and lives in any lodging, even or uneven, dusty or full of mosquitoes, “without the slightest dejection” (Ach 2.2 s.3.3, s.3.30). In the rains he stays in one place, because the paths are full of new life; on the road he looks a yoke’s length ahead and steps around small creatures (Ach 2.3 s.1.1, s.1.6). Asked by travellers which way an animal went, he stays silent or says “I do not know”, since the questioner may be a hunter (Ach 2.3 s.3.7). Thrown from a boat or robbed of his bowl, he does not rise to hurt anyone and complains to no village or king (Ach 2.3 s.2.3, s.3.15).


Speech is weighed before it leaves the mouth. There are four kinds of speech: true, false, mixed, and ordinary everyday speech that is neither true nor false; a monk uses only well-weighed truth and ordinary speech, and only when they harm no one (Ach 2.4 s.1.3–6). Even a true word is not said if it is harsh, cutting or hurtful: he does not call anyone “leper” or “one-handed”, does not predict with certainty what will happen, does not wish for rain or for a king’s victory, and does not tell a woodcutter which tree is “fit for a door” (Ach 2.4 s.1.1, s.1.11–12, s.2.1, s.2.7–16). The whole chapter closes in one sutra:

से भिक्खू वा भिक्खुणी वा वंता कोहं च माणं च मायं च लोभं च अणुवीइ णिट्ठाभासी णिसम्मभासी अतुरियभासी विवेगभासी समियाए संजए भासं भासेज्जा ।

The monk or nun, having cast out anger, pride, deceit and greed, should speak as one restrained and careful in speech: after reflecting, with certainty, after hearing and understanding, without haste, and with discernment.
Source: Acharang 2.4 s.2.19 (Bhashajata) · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Connect
Book 1 of the Acharang (Lessons 30–33) taught that every one of the six kinds of life feels pain; Book 2 shows what that looks like at a householder’s door, in a borrowed room and on a muddy road. These four chapters are three of the five careful practices you met as the “eight mothers” in Lesson 17 (careful walking, careful speech, careful seeking): see Samiti and Gupti. The alms rules and the bee-like taking of Lessons 24 and 26 are the same teaching (Bhramar Vritti, Ahimsa), and the module notes that the speech chapter is very close to Dashvaikalik 7 from Lesson 27. Speech “moved by anger, pride, deceit or greed” is the four passions of Kashaya at work in the mouth.
Reflect

When you are unsure whether something is right (a deal, a remark, a purchase) do you go ahead or hold back? What would “doubt means no” change for you?
Do you ever “hide the fine food under the plain”, keeping the best of something for yourself while looking fair to others?
Which of your true remarks this month hurt someone more than they helped?

Practice this week
The speech rules are monks’ rules, but they need no robe. A householder’s version: for one week, before you say anything sharp, pause and check it against Ach 2.4 s.2.19: is it said from anger, pride, deceit or greed? Have I heard the other person fully? Am I hurrying? Also drop two habits the chapter names: calling people by a defect or insult (even in jest), and saying with certainty what will or will not happen (Ach 2.4 s.1.1, s.2.1). Each evening, note one sentence you changed or held back.
Self-check
Question

What two tests must every piece of food pass before a monk accepts it?

It must be free of life (prasuka) and free of the faults of seeking (eshaniya) (Ach 2.1 s.1.1–3).

Question

What does a monk do if he is unsure whether some food is acceptable?

He does not take it, even when it is offered (Ach 2.1 s.3.5).

Question

Travellers ask a monk whether he saw an animal pass. What does he do, and why?

He stays silent, or says “I do not know”, because the questioner may be a hunter and he would share in the killing (Ach 2.3 s.3.7).

Question

Of the four kinds of speech, which may a monk use?

Subtle, well-weighed true speech and ordinary everyday speech, and only when they are free of sin and harm no being (Ach 2.4 s.1.3–6).

10_course/lesson_35_few_possessions_and_.title: Lesson 35 · Few Possessions; the Five Great Vows and Their Bhavanas
10_course/lesson_35_few_possessions_and_.content:
Lesson 35 · Few Possessions; the Five Great Vows and Their Bhavanas
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 70 minutes
Aim: You will understand how little a monk keeps and how he holds it, how Mahavira’s own life leads into the five great vows with their twenty-five supporting reflections (bhavana), and what “release” means in the last chapter of the Acharang.
Read

Acharang 2.5–6: Clothes and Bowls and Acharang 2.7: Permission to Stay: look for how few things a monk keeps, how he receives them, and why he takes nothing, not even a fellow monk’s staff, without asking.
Acharang 2.15: Bhavana, the Five Vows: read Mahavira’s life as the book tells it, then take the five vows one at a time with their five bhavanas each.
Acharang 2.16: Vimukti: twelve short verses; notice the mountain, the silver and the snake’s old skin. If you have time, skim Acharang 2.8–14: The Seven Septets for the rules on sounds, sights and bodily service.

Key ideas


Keep little, and take nothing that is not given. Clothes are kept only for restraint and modesty; a young, healthy monk wears one kind of cloth and keeps one bowl of gourd, wood or clay, and costly cloth or metal bowls are refused because they invite attachment, theft and violence (Ach 2.5 s.1.1–6, Ach 2.6 s.1.1). He wears clothes as received, “not washing them, not dyeing them”, and if robbed he does not cling (Ach 2.5 s.2.1–7). Having renounced “all taking of what is not given”, he uses no place and no thing without the owner’s leave, sets clear limits of space and time when asking, and shares what he has begged with fellow monks (Ach 2.7 s.1.1–4). The seven septets carry this further: he does not go out of his way to hear music or see sights, and does not accept bodily service such as rubbing, oiling or adorning, because service done to him “binds karma” (Ach 2.11 s.1–19, Ach 2.12 s.1, Ach 2.13 s.1).


Mahavira’s life comes first, to strengthen faith. The chapter called Bhavana tells his story from his descent into the womb to omniscience: his three names (Vardhamana from his parents, Shramana, and Mahavira, given by the gods because he bore fearful hardships), thirty years at home, a year of giving, and going forth, when he pulled out his hair, bowed to the Siddhas and, saying “All sinful action is not to be done by me”, took up the conduct of equanimity (samayika) (Ach 2.15 s.11, s.14–37). He then resolved to bear for twelve years every hardship from gods, men or animals “rightly”, with forgiveness and calm, and in the thirteenth year gained omniscience (kevala) (Ach 2.15 s.38, s.41–43). The introduction calls bhavana a boat: a mind not filled with steady reflection falls away when hardship comes (Ach 2.15, pp. 362–363).


Each great vow has five supports. The five great vows are: no harm to any being, no falsehood, not taking what is not given, celibacy, and non-possession, each held up by five bhavanas, twenty-five in all: for example, care in walking and eating only food looked at in the light for the first, speaking only after thought and giving up anger, greed, fear and joking for the second (Ach 2.15 s.46–60). For non-possession, the support is not to cling to or recoil from anything the senses meet:

ण सक्का ण सोउं सद्दा, सोयविसयमागया ।
राग दोसा उ जे तत्थ, ते भिक्खू परिवज्जए ॥

Sounds that reach the ear cannot go unheard; but the liking and disliking that arise there, the monk gives up.
Source: Acharang 2.15 s.59 (Bhavana), the first bhavana of the fifth vow; the same is then said of sight, smell, taste and touch · checked against the scan, as given in the module
The last chapter, Vimukti, shows where the vows lead: the wise monk bears harsh words “as a mountain does not tremble in the wind”, his past karma is burnt off “as fire fanned by the wind cleans the dross from silver”, and he is freed from suffering “as a snake leaves its old skin” (Ach 2.16 v.3, v.8, v.9).


Connect
“Attachment is possession”, which you met in Lesson 3 and Lesson 26 (Dash 6.21), is what the clothes-and-bowls chapter puts into practice. The vow of non-violence here is the lifelong form, by mind, speech and body, in doing, causing and approving (Ach 2.15 s.46); in Lesson 38 you will see the householder’s smaller version of the same five. Mahavira taking samayika at his going forth (Ach 2.15 s.34) is the very pledge you will study in Lesson 36, and his twelve years of bearing hardship tie back to Lesson 33’s account of his practice and to Parishaha. See also Ahimsa, Samyama and Tapas.
Reflect

What do you own two or three of where one would do? Which of them do you keep mostly because it looks good?
Do you ever “borrow” something (a colleague’s pen, a shared space, someone’s time) without really asking?
A sound you dislike reaches your ear: traffic, a neighbour, a voice. What is the “liking and disliking” that follows it, and how long does it last?

Practice this week
The great vows are monks’ vows, taken for life. A householder’s version of the fifth bhavana of non-possession: once a day this week, when an unwelcome sound, smell or taste reaches you, notice the dislike as it arises and let it go, as Ach 2.15 s.59 teaches; the sound you cannot help, the reaction you can. And once this week, as Ach 2.7 asks of the monk, ask before you use anything that is not yours, even something small that you would normally just pick up.
Self-check
Question

What may a young, healthy monk keep in cloth and bowls?

One kind of cloth, not a second, and one bowl of gourd, wood or clay (Ach 2.5 s.1.1, Ach 2.6 s.1.1).

Question

What are Mahavira’s three names, and who gave the name “Mahavira”?

Vardhamana from his parents, Shramana, and Mahavira, which the gods gave him because he bore terrible hardships (Ach 2.15 s.11).

Question

What are the five great vows, and how many bhavanas are there in all?

No harm, no falsehood, not taking what is not given, celibacy and non-possession; each has five bhavanas, twenty-five in all (Ach 2.15 s.46–61).

Question

To what does Vimukti compare the monk freed from the bed of suffering?

To a snake leaving its old skin (Ach 2.16 v.9).
