10_course/lesson_36_samayik_praise_and_b.title: Lesson 36 · Samayik, Praise of the 24, and Bowing
10_course/lesson_36_samayik_praise_and_b.content:
Lesson 36 · Samayik, Praise of the 24, and Bowing
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 45 minutes
Aim: You will know what the six daily essentials (avashyak) are and why they come in their order, understand the words of the Namaskar Mantra, the Samayik pledge, the Logassa and the bow to the Guru, and be able to sit one samayik of your own.
Read

Avashyak 1: Samayik: read the introduction on the six Avashyaks first, then the Navkar and the pledge Karemi Bhante; notice how a householder’s samayik differs from a monk’s.
Avashyak 2: Praise of the 24: look for what the Logassa asks of the Tirthankaras, and what it does not ask.
Avashyak 3: Vandana: follow the bow to the Guru as a six-step conversation, and notice how it ends.

Key ideas


Six duties, every day and night, for everyone. The six are equanimity (samayik), praise of the 24 Tirthankaras, bowing to the Guru (vandana), turning back from faults (pratikraman), letting go of the body (kayotsarga) and renouncing (pratyakhyan), and they bind monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen alike (Av 1, pp. 67–68). Recited by rote with the mind elsewhere they are only the outer form; the real thing is done with full attention, seeking no fame or reward (Av 1, p. 69). The order follows the seeker’s growth: settle into equanimity, admire those who perfected it, bow to the Guru, repent, purify yourself in meditation, and only then renounce further (Av 1, pp. 69–71).


Samayik is equanimity, taken freely before a witness. The Navkar bows to virtues, not to persons: no one is named, and Arihants come before Siddhas because they teach the path (Av 1 L1.1, pp. 72–76). In the pledge Karemi Bhante, “I undertake” shows the choice is the disciple’s own, and Bhante is the Guru, or God when no Guru is present, or one’s own soul (Av 1 L2.1, pp. 81–84). A monk takes it for life; a householder takes it “for as long as the rule lasts”, fixed by tradition at 48 minutes, and vows in six ways, not nine, because his business and kitchen run on in his name and he cannot renounce approving of them (Av 1, pp. 84–85). The commentary sums it up: when the soul has turned from sinful activity, is guarded in mind, speech and body, and is careful toward the six kinds of beings, “that soul itself is Samayik” (Av 1, p. 83).


Praise the 24, and bow to the Guru with humility. The Logassa keeps the Tirthankaras before your eyes as a model, and its fruit is purer faith (Av 2, p. 86). It asks for nothing material:

कित्तिय-वंदिय-महिया, जे ए लोगस्स उत्तमा सिद्धा ।
आरुग्ग-बोहि लाभं, समाहि-वरमुत्तमं दिंतु ॥६॥

Praised, bowed to and honoured, they are the highest in the world, the perfected ones. May they grant health of the soul, the gain of right understanding, and the best, highest calm.
Source: Avashyak 2, Logassa v.6 · checked against the scan, as given in the module
The bow to the Guru begins with ichchhami, “I wish”, because practice done under pressure is forced labour; the disciple waits outside the Guru’s space until told “I permit”, asks after his day and his “journey of restraint”, and begs pardon for every kind of disrespect, in mind, speech or body (Av 3, pp. 96–101). At the end the Guru answers ahamapi khamayami, “I too ask forgiveness” (Av 3, pp. 104–105).


Connect
Lesson 35 ended with Mahavira taking the conduct of samayika at his going forth (Ach 2.15 s.34); here is the same pledge as a daily practice. The bow to the Guru is the humility of Lessons 15 and 28 put into words and gestures: humility brings service, service brings knowledge, knowledge brings restraint, and so on up to liberation (Av 3, p. 96); see Vinaya. “Right understanding” (bodhi) in the Logassa is called the seed of the three jewels (Av 2, pp. 94–95): see Ratnatraya. A soul “guarded in mind, speech and body” is the three restraints of Samiti and Gupti.
Reflect

Which of your daily religious habits (a mantra, a bow, a visit to the temple) do you do with the mind elsewhere?
In the Navkar you bow to qualities, not to people. Whose qualities would you bow to in your own life, and why?
When did you last ask a teacher or an elder how they were, and mean it?

Practice this week
Sit one samayik this week, as the module describes a householder’s samayik: a set time of 48 minutes, freely chosen, with your own soul as witness if no Guru is present (Av 1, pp. 81–85). Begin with the Navkar; take the pledge in the householder’s form your family or teacher uses (the module only says the householder says jav niyamam, “for as long as the rule lasts”, in place of the monk’s “for as long as I live”); then spend the time quietly, perhaps reading one of these modules or reciting the Logassa slowly with its meaning. Keep in mind the five faults the book names for samayik: misusing the mind (letting it wander), misusing speech, misusing the body (restlessness), forgetting you are in samayik, and doing it unsteadily (Av 7 s.10). When it ends, notice whether the 48 minutes changed anything.
Self-check
Question

Why does the Navkar bow to the Arihants before the Siddhas, though Siddhas are higher?

Because we know of the Siddhas only through the Arihants’ teaching, and the Arihant, still embodied, shows the path (Av 1, pp. 75–76).

Question

How long is a householder’s samayik, and why does he vow in six ways instead of nine?

48 minutes by tradition; he cannot renounce approving sinful activity, because his business and kitchen run on in his name (Av 1, pp. 84–85).

Question

What three things does the Logassa ask of the Tirthankaras?

Health of the soul, the gain of right understanding (bodhi), and the highest calm (samadhi) (Av 2 v.6).

Question

How does the Guru answer at the end of the bow?

Ahamapi khamayami, “I too ask forgiveness”, for any hurt he caused while guiding and correcting the disciple (Av 3, pp. 104–105).

10_course/lesson_37_pratikraman_kayotsar.title: Lesson 37 · Pratikraman, Kayotsarga, Pratyakhyan
10_course/lesson_37_pratikraman_kayotsar.content:
Lesson 37 · Pratikraman, Kayotsarga, Pratyakhyan
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 65 minutes
Aim: You will understand the last three daily essentials as one movement (look back at the day’s faults, heal them in stillness, then close the door on new ones) and be able to keep one small time-bound vow of your own.
Read

Avashyak 4: Pratikraman: the longest chapter; read “What the chapter teaches” closely, especially the four refuges, the walking sutra and the forgiveness sutra at the end.
Avashyak 5: Kayotsarga: look for why letting go of the body is called “wound-healing”, and the washing-cloth comparison.
Avashyak 6: Pratyakhyan: read the Navakarshi vow and its closing formula, and notice what the exceptions say about the purpose of a vow.

Key ideas


Pratikraman turns back from every lapse, and ends in friendship. It begins with the four refuges, the Arihants, Siddhas, Sadhus and the dharma taught by the omniscient, because no person or thing in the world can shelter the soul (Av 4 L2; pp. 109–113). The walking sutra names ten kinds of harm, from striking or covering a creature to moving it from its place, and answers each with michchhami dukkadam, “may that wrong of mine be undone”; a vow partly broken is cleansed by pratikraman, but one wholly broken needs the Guru’s penance (Av 4 L3–L4; pp. 113–123). Faults in sleep and dreams count too (Av 4 L5). It closes with these lines:

खामेमि सव्वे जीवा, सव्वे जीवा वि खमंतु मे ।
मित्तीमे सव्व भूएसू, वेरं मज्झं ण केणइ ॥१॥

I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none.
Source: Avashyak 4 L10.1 · checked against the scan, as given in the module


Kayotsarga heals what confession has not yet healed. Kaya is the body and utsarga letting go; since the body cannot be dropped while life lasts, what is dropped is the sense of “mine” toward it, with speech stilled into silence and the mind turned to good meditation (Av 5, p. 192). The Anuyogadvara Sutra calls it “wound-healing”: faults in one’s vows are wounds, kayotsarga their ointment (Av 5, pp. 192–193). The commentary’s picture: confession removes the dirt from a cloth, kayotsarga makes up what is lacking, and renunciation adds the shine (Av 5 l.3 s.1, pp. 194–196). Breathing, coughing, sneezing and small movements of the eyes are allowed in advance, because forcing them to stop would disturb the mind; and a standing body with a sleeping soul is only a show (Av 5 l.3 s.2, pp. 196–199).


Pratyakhyan closes the door on karma still to come. The 4th and 5th Avashyaks destroy karma already gathered; the 6th blocks what would come in future (Av 6, p. 201). The vows run from Navakarshi (no food or water from sunrise until one muhurta has passed and the Navkar has been said) through porisi, eating once (ekasana), bland food (ayambil) and the full fast from sunrise to sunrise (Av 6 l.1–7). The exceptions show the aim: “for the sake of complete equanimity” a sudden severe pain may be treated, because a vow that produces distress and anger has already lost its purpose; and a private resolve (abhigraha) is taken only after honestly weighing one’s own strength, not to copy others (Av 6 l.2, l.9; pp. 204–206, 212–214). When the vow ends it is closed properly, as “touched, kept, carried to the end”, and any failure is undone with michchhami dukkadam (Av 6, pp. 216–217).


Connect
Khamemi savve jiva is the forgiveness you practised in Lesson 5; here you see it as the last word of the whole daily review. Pratikraman’s monk takes “a little from many houses, like a bee” (Av 4 L6), the alms rule of Lessons 24, 26 and 34: see Bhramar Vritti. Its long list conquers anger with forgiveness, pride with gentleness, deceit with straightness and greed with contentment (Av 4 L8): see Kashaya. Kayotsarga is an inner austerity and the fasting vows outer ones, as in Lesson 21 and Tapas; by practising the three restraints, kayotsarga both stops new karma and sheds old (Av 5 l.3 s.3): see Samiti and Gupti and Karma.
Reflect

At the end of a day, do you look back over it, or only forward to tomorrow? What would you find if you did?
Is there one person or creature you have not yet forgiven, or not yet asked to forgive you?
When you have tried a fast or a vow before, did it bring calm or irritation? What does Av 6’s “complete equanimity” exception say about that?

Practice this week
Take the shortest vow the module teaches, Navakarshi, on two or three mornings this week (Av 6 l.1). On waking, resolve that you will take no food or water until one muhurta after sunrise has passed and you have said the Navkar; both conditions are needed. The module allows only two exceptions, complete forgetfulness and a sudden accident. When the time is up, say the Navkar, and before eating close the vow in your own words as the closing formula does: I took it, kept it, carried it to the end; whatever I did not fulfil, michchhami dukkadam (Av 6, pp. 216–217). Do not stretch it into something harder this week; the book warns against vows taken beyond one’s strength or to copy others.
Self-check
Question

What are the four refuges declared in pratikraman?

The Arihants, the Siddhas, the Sadhus, and the dharma taught by the omniscient (Av 4 L2.3).

Question

Which faults can pratikraman cleanse, and which need the Guru’s penance?

A vow partly broken or badly damaged is cleansed by pratikraman; a vow wholly broken (anachara) needs the Guru’s penance (Av 4 L3).

Question

In the washing-cloth comparison, what does each of the last three Avashyaks do?

Confession (pratikraman) removes the dirt, kayotsarga makes up what is lacking, and renunciation (pratyakhyan) adds the shine (Av 5 l.3 s.1).

Question

What two conditions end the Navakarshi vow?

One muhurta after sunrise must have passed, and the Navkar must have been said (Av 6 l.1).

10_course/lesson_38_householders_twelve_.title: Lesson 38 · The Householder's Twelve Vows
10_course/lesson_38_householders_twelve_.content:
Lesson 38 · The Householder’s Twelve Vows
Unit 6: The first Anga and the daily essentials (Acharang, Avashyak) · about 40 minutes
Aim: You will know the twelve vows of a lay follower (five small vows, three supporting vows, four training vows), see how each is sized to household life, and be able to choose one vow, or one part of one, to try for yourself.
Read

Avashyak 7: The Householder's Vows: read the first point (where this section comes from), then take the vows in order; for each, note what is given up and what its five faults are.

Key ideas


Right faith comes before any vow. This section is from Haribhadra’s commentary, which the book follows; the sutra itself does not set out the lay vows (Av 7, pp. 230–231). A shravaka is “one who listens” to dharma; some take vows, like Ananda, and some have only right faith, like King Shrenika (Av 7 s.1). First the lay follower turns back from wrong belief and takes up right faith, whose five faults are doubt, longing for another faith, doubting the fruit of dharma, praising other sects, and close association with them; but asking questions to strengthen faith, as Gautama did, is not doubt, and giving out of compassion is not forbidden (Av 7 s.1, pp. 231–234). Right faith is “the root” of the whole householder’s dharma (Av 7 s.14).


The five small vows are the monk’s five, sized for a household. A layman cannot give up the violence of cooking, farming or travel, so the first vow gives up intended violence:

थूलगपाणाइवायं समणोवासओ पच्चक्खाइ, से पाणाइवाए दुविहे पण्णत्ते, तं जहा- संकप्पओ अ आरंभओ अ । तत्थ समणोवासओ संकप्पओ जावज्जीवाए पच्चक्खाइ, नो आरंभओ ।

The lay follower gives up gross violence to living beings. That violence is of two kinds: intended and arising from work. Of these he gives up intended violence for life, not violence arising from work.
Source: Avashyak 7 s.2 (opening) · checked against the scan, as given in the module
Its faults are tying up, beating, cutting, overloading and withholding food, and today these include overworking servants and paying wages late (Av 7 s.2, pp. 234–239). The next vows give up five gross lies (about a bride or groom, cattle, land, a deposit held in trust, and false witness), stealing and its faults such as false weights and passing off bad goods as good, keep one to one’s own spouse, and set a limit on nine kinds of possessions; whatever comes beyond the limit is given away, because possession is really attachment (murchha) (Av 7 s.3–6). Throughout, a fault done by mistake is a lapse (atichara); done on purpose it breaks the vow (anachara) (Av 7, pp. 239–243).


Seven more vows guard the five, and the vows are taken as strength allows. Three supporting vows limit travel in each direction, limit daily things and avoid fifteen trades of great harm such as charcoal-making, forest-cutting and dealing in liquor, poison or weapons, and give up purposeless harm: brooding, careless habits, handing out weapons and urging others into sin (Av 7 s.7–9). Four training vows are practised again and again: samayik, shrinking the travel limit for a day, paushadh (a full day and night lived like a monk), and giving pure food to monks, honestly earned, with respect and joy (Av 7 s.10–13). The five small and three supporting vows are taken for life, the four training vows for a time; and the vows are “like gold ingots”: one may take one, two or three as one’s strength allows (Av 7 s.14). At life’s end, sallekhana lets go of food and body in equanimity; it comes from renunciation, not from anger, grief or despair, so it is as different from suicide as earth from sky (Av 7 s.15).


Connect
Lesson 4 first gave you the vows in outline; here are their exact words and faults. Set them beside the monk’s great vows of Lesson 35: same five, but where the monk gives up all harm for life by mind, speech and body (Ach 2.15 s.46), the householder gives up intended, purposeless harm to innocent moving beings; tradition puts a monk’s compassion at 20 parts and a layman’s at 1¼ (Av 7, pp. 234–239). The samayik of Lesson 36 is the ninth vow, and the giving of Lesson 26 is the twelfth. See Ahimsa, Samyama and, for faith as the root, Ratnatraya. This is the last lesson of the course: the path began in Lesson 1 with what Jainism is, and ends with the steps a householder can actually take.
Reflect

Which of the five faults of non-violence (tying up, beating, cutting, overloading, withholding food) still shows up in your life, with people who work for you, with animals, or with yourself?
If you set a limit on your possessions today, where would you draw it, and what would you do with what comes beyond it?
Which kinds of purposeless harm (brooding, careless habits, urging others into wrong) take up most of your day?

Practice this week
The book says a householder may take one, two or three vows as his strength allows (Av 7 s.14), and that the five small and three supporting vows, once taken, are for life. So this week is a trial, not the vow itself. Choose one vow, or one part of one, that fits your life: for example, a written limit on one kind of possession under the fifth vow (Av 7 s.6), dropping one form of purposeless harm under the eighth (Av 7 s.9), or one samayik under the ninth (Av 7 s.10). Write it down with its five faults, and each evening check the day against them. At the end of the week, decide honestly whether you are ready to keep it for life.
Self-check
Question

What must a lay follower do before taking any of the twelve vows?

Turn back from wrong belief and take up right faith (Av 7 s.1).

Question

Which kind of violence does the householder give up in the first small vow, and which can he not give up?

He gives up intended violence for life; he does not give up violence arising from work, such as cooking, farming or travel (Av 7 s.2).

Question

Which vows are taken for life, and which for a time?

The five small vows and the three supporting vows are for life; the four training vows are for a time (Av 7 s.14).

Question

Why is sallekhana not suicide?

Suicide comes from anger, grief or despair; sallekhana comes from renunciation, when the body can no longer serve spiritual practice, and is kept in equanimity (Av 7 s.15).

index.title: Jain Agamas: Learn from the Source
index.content:
Jain Agamas: Learn from the Source
A personal library for learning Jain dharma from the Agamas themselves: the Gujarati editions of jainaagam.org, read page by page and put into plain English. Every verse quoted in the course and modules was checked by hand against the printed page.
Where to start
🎓 The course
Start the course: lessons in order, from the basics to the great chapters of the Uttaradhyayan, the conduct of the Dashvaikalik, the Acharang and the daily essentials of the Avashyak. Each lesson has key ideas, questions to reflect on, a practice for the week and a short self-check.


The learning path: five short topics (Foundations, Reality, Way of Life, Conduct, Relationships) with the core verses.
Uttaradhyayan, chapter by chapter: Mahavira’s last teachings, 36 modules.
Dashvaikalik, chapter by chapter: the guide to careful living, 12 modules.
Acharang, chapter by chapter: the first Anga, on non-violence and the monk’s conduct, 18 modules.
Avashyak, the six daily essentials: samayik to pratyakhyan, plus the householder’s vows, 7 modules.
Key concepts: karma, the six substances, leshya, ahimsa, vinaya and more, each from the source.

What has been translated so far






























BookTranslated (whole pages, faithful English)ModulesUttaradhyayan Sutra1052 pages36 chapter modulesDashvaikalik Sutra613 pages12 chapter modulesAcharang Sutra954 pages18 chapter modulesAvashyak Sutra326 pages7 modules
The other 31 books of the 35 have been scanned and read by OCR (Gujarati text), but not yet translated.

Translations are machine translations of the Gujarati edition: faithful to the page, but verse spellings and verse numbers can carry small slips. The modules and course quote only verses checked against the scans.
